Trump publicly shared what he said was the Arkansas lawmaker’s cellphone number and urged voters to pressure the senator to support the measure.
Trump accused Cotton of blocking the Sunshine Protection Act, which would end the twice-yearly clock change for most Americans and keep daylight saving time in effect year-round.
“Everybody in Arkansas, Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important Bill,” Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social, telling residents to contact the senator and “GET IT DONE.” He argued that keeping daylight later in the afternoon would benefit workers, sports and other activities.

“Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first,” he wrote.
Trump responded, saying that if Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would support giving residents more afternoon daylight and eliminating the need to change clocks twice a year.
He also accused Cotton of allowing “ego” to stand in the way of the legislation and urged him to “TAKE THE WIN.” Trump later argued in another post that earlier winter darkness was depressing and could make people less safe while traveling home.
The Republican-controlled House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act 308-117 in July, sending it to the Senate, where it has faced opposition.
The proposal would make daylight saving time permanent while allowing states to opt instead for permanent standard time. Supporters favor later sunsets, while opponents warn that the change would mean darker winter mornings, particularly for children traveling to school.

What is celebrated on October 4 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
02:53:03 EEST
08:53:03 KST

What is celebrated on October 4 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On October 4, the world celebrates World Animal Day and begins UN World Space Week. Lesotho celebrates its independence, and the faithful honor the saints.
On October 4, the world observes World Animal Day and begins World Space Week under the auspices of the UN, while the African state of Lesotho celebrates Independence Day. According to the new-style church calendar, the Holy Martyr Quadratus, one of the Seventy Apostles, is commemorated, and the finding of the relics of Saint Demetrius of Rostov is remembered; according to the old style, the Holy Martyr Hierotheus, Bishop of Athens, is commemorated, UNN writes.
World Animal Day
Established in 1925 on the initiative of German writer and conservationist Heinrich Zimmermann and officially approved in 1931 at the International Congress of Supporters of the Nature Protection Movement in Florence. The date was chosen in honor of the feast day of Saint Francis of Assisi, the patron saint of animals in the Catholic tradition. The observance aims to mobilize society to preserve endangered species, ensure humane conditions for keeping domestic and wild animals, combat cruelty, and develop environmentally responsible coexistence between humans and the animal world.
World Space Week
An official annual global UN event established by the General Assembly in 1999 (Resolution 54/68), held from October 4 to 10. October 4 was chosen to commemorate the launch of the first artificial Earth satellite, "Sputnik 1," in 1957, which opened the space age for humanity. The event promotes space science and technology, highlights the contribution of the aerospace sector to improving living conditions on Earth and monitoring the climate, and encourages young people to pursue science and technology education.
Lesotho Independence Day
The main national holiday of the Kingdom of Lesotho, commemorating the proclamation of sovereignty and the end of the British protectorate of Basutoland on October 4, 1966. The country gained full political independence as a constitutional monarchy under King Moshoeshoe II, and the holiday is marked by ceremonial parades in the capital, Maseru, traditional dances, and cultural events.
The Day of Remembrance of the Holy Martyr Quadratus
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate the Holy Martyr Quadratus, one of the Seventy Apostles, who preached Christianity in Athens and Magnesia in the 2nd century and wrote one of the earliest apologies (defenses) of the Christian faith for Emperor Hadrian. On this day, they also remember the finding of the relics of Saint Demetrius, a prominent Ukrainian church figure, theologian, writer, and author of the extensive collection of saints’ lives, "Chet’i-Minei."
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate the Holy Martyr Hierotheus, Bishop of Athens—one of the members of the Athenian Areopagus, converted to Christianity by the Apostle Paul and ordained by him as Bishop of Athens in the 1st century. According to tradition, Saint Hierotheus was present at the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos, became renowned for his prayerful inspiration, and suffered martyrdom for his faith.

Great white sharks are increasingly swimming toward Canada&apos;s shores, and scientists have explained what is drawing them north
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Great white sharks are increasingly swimming toward Canada's shores, and scientists have explained what is drawing them north
Kyiv • UNN
Warming waters and the recovery of the seal population have increased the food supply for sharks off Canada's coast. Scientists are not recording a sharp increase in their numbers.
Great white sharks are appearing increasingly often off Canada's Atlantic coast, particularly near Nova Scotia. Researchers attribute this to the growing amount of available prey and changes in the marine ecosystem, BBC reports, writes UNN.
Details
One such "visitor" was a nearly 4.2-meter-long great white shark nicknamed Contender. Just a few months ago, it was off Florida, but as the waters warmed, it headed north to Canada.
Over the past several decades, the seal population off the coasts of the United States and Canada has recovered significantly—they are one of the great white shark's favorite prey. At the same time, as the waters warm, more and more fish species are moving north.
Sharks are finding more and more food
Over the past 30 years, surface waters near Nova Scotia have warmed by approximately 1.5°C, while temperatures near the seabed have risen by approximately 3°C. More fish attract seals, which in turn attract great white sharks.
There are many food options for them in Nova Scotia. It is a fairly healthy marine ecosystem with many large animals they can feed on—seals and tuna
He does not believe that the overall population of great white sharks has increased sharply. Instead, individual sharks have begun visiting Canadian waters more frequently, remembering food-rich areas and returning to them.
As the number of sightings grows, so does the likelihood of encounters with people. In September, a great white shark attacked a diver off the coast of Quebec, but his injuries were not life-threatening. Experts emphasize that the risk of an attack remains very low.

Trump taps Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as AI czar: WSJ reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
23:37:23 UTC
08:37:23 KST

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has been chosen as the Trump administration's new AI czar, leading its response to artificial intelligence amid growing concerns about the risks of this rapidly evolving technology, The Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday.
Clayton told the Journal he will lead a new White House task force, which will have 120 days to research and report on AI's risks and opportunities, and offer recommendations on the federal government's responsibilities regarding the new technology.
"The president asked that a group be put together that was going to ensure exactly what he said, which is that we stay the leaders in superintelligence, and that the interests of the American people are put first," Clayton said, the Journal reported.
The group will be called the "Super Intelligence Force," or SI — the term President Donald Trump prefers over AI — and Clayton will effectively become the new AI czar, the Journal said, citing a senior White House official.
The White House did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.
In September, Trump announced in a Truth Social post that he would create a new "AI Force" to help facilitate the industry and root out bad actors.
"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump said the post, which also announced plans to hire an AI czar.
"Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" the president added.
Clayton is a former chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission and U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. The Senate confirmed him in July as DNI, giving him authority over 18 U.S. intelligence agencies.
The announcement comes days after AI industry leaders met with Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson at the White House. The AI developers signed onto an agreement of voluntary safety standards that Trump said was "morally binding."
Despite dire warnings from within the industry and calls from AI leaders Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for federal guardrails on frontier AI models, Trump has so far opposed regulation.
In the same September post, Trump suggested AI fears were a hoax and blamed "Radical Left Dumocrats."
Venture capitalist David Sacks had previously served as AI and crypto czar under Trump, but in March said that his time as a special government employee had ended. Sacks is co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, a federal advisory committee made up of outside experts on technology, scientific research and innovation policy.

A 600-year-old hand cannon that could fire arrows and bullets has been found in South Korea
Kyiv • UNN
The bronze hand cannon was made in 1377 or 1437. The inscription indicates that it may have been produced by the state.
In South Korea, researchers identified a bronze weapon found on Mount Geumseong as a hwanja hwathon — a handheld gunpowder firearm that could have been used to fire arrows or bullets. It was made about 600 years ago, ZME Science reports, according to UNN.
Details
The weapon was discovered back in 2023 in the southwest of the country, but it became known about only now. It is approximately 23 cm long and weighs about 900 g.
An engraving bearing the weapon’s name, its weight, and details of the production supervisor and craftsman, as well as a partially erased date, has survived on the handle. By comparing the inscription with historical documents, researchers concluded that the gun may have been made in 1377 or 1437.
A rare weapon from a transitional era
It comes from a decisive transitional period between the late Goryeo Dynasty and the early Joseon Dynasty, when physical artifacts of firearms were extremely rare
Another symbol was found on the muzzle, which may have been an inventory or production number. According to researchers, this could indicate that the weapon was made as part of organized state production.
The discovery provides scientists with rare material evidence of how early gunpowder weapons developed on the Korean Peninsula.

Britain scraps heavily criticised plans to curb jury trials after backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
23:08:29 UTC
08:08:29 KST

Britain scraps heavily criticised plans to curb jury trials after backlash
- Britain has scrapped plans to limit jury trials for less serious crimes, responding to strong criticism from lawyers and politicians.
- The decision addresses concerns over defendants' rights but includes increasing magistrates' sentencing powers, which some fear could worsen court delays.
- The backlog of jury trials in England and Wales remains high, with nearly 81,000 cases pending, causing long waits for victims and defendants.
AI generated
LONDON - Britain will scrap plans to remove the historic right to trial by jury for defendants in less serious criminal cases, the government announced on Oct 4, in response to sustained criticism of the proposals by many lawyers and politicians.
The decision by Andy Burnham, who became prime minister in July, to drop his predecessor Keir Starmer's policy comes as hundreds of prisoners were released early to stop prisons becoming full, in just one element of a criminal justice crisis.
Plans to curb jury trials for cases where a jail sentence was likely to be less than three years would be abandoned, the Ministry of Justice said, which was broadly welcomed by the Criminal Bar Association and other groups.
But lawyers raised concerns over the MoJ's decision to increase sentencing powers for magistrates – who hear trials for more minor offences without a jury – and the removal of defendants' right to elect trial by jury.
"I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the Crown Court and have made the decision to change course," Justice Secretary Alex Norris said.
CBA chair Andrew Thomas thanked the government for "listening to the evidence and reaching the right verdict", though he said "a severe threat to our trial by jury remains".
The Bar Council's chair Kirsty Brimelow agreed, saying that giving magistrates greater powers when the backlog in magistrates' courts is increasing could be counterproductive.
Victims waiting for years for justice
The current backlog of cases awaiting trial by jury in Crown Courts in England and Wales was nearly 81,000 at the end of June, almost double the figure in 2020, and victims, defendants and witnesses often wait years for cases to come to trial.
Starmer's justice minister David Lammy in 2025 said reducing jury trials would speed up justice, but met a furious backlash from lawyers who said it curtailed the fundamental right of defendants to be tried by a jury of their peers.
Critics also argued that years of neglect and under-investment by successive governments, rather than jury trials, were the root cause of delays, while the head of England's judiciary raised "grave security concerns" for judges.
The MoJ said it would maintain plans that complex fraud trials could be heard by a judge alone, which has long been mooted to avoid jurors sitting on months-long cases, though a government-commissioned review in 2026 rejected the idea. REUTERS

Senate Act Would Boost Loan Forgiveness to $17.5k for EL Teachers

Unknown Publisher

23:03:31 UTC

U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) have introduced the Supporting Providers of English Language Learning (SPELL) Act to help address the national multilingual teacher shortage by increasing loan forgiveness from $5,000 to $17,500 for teachers of English learners (ELs). Representatives Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.-13) and Raúl M. Grijalva (D-Ariz.-07) introduced companion legislation in the House of Representatives.
Currently, if a highly-qualified teacher has been employed for five consecutive years in a low-income school, they are eligible for up to $5,000 of student loan forgiveness. Certain teachers who go into high demand subjects are eligible for an increased benefit of $17,500 of student loan forgiveness. Recognizing the growing EL teacher shortage, the SPELL Act adds EL teachers to this high demand category, making them eligible for additional debt relief.
Click here to find EL Teacher Education Programs that will Qualify for Loan Forgiveness
“Educating students learning English requires specialized instruction and unique teacher strategies,” said Senator Padilla. “Yet, we are facing a devastating shortage of teachers with the skills needed to support these students. By lessening the financial burden, we can help incentivize a greater number of passionate, and highly qualified teachers to enter and stay in the classroom.”
“Every student deserves a fair chance to succeed and thrive at school; teachers of English Learners are essential to making that possible,” said Senator Kim. “In the face of nationwide teacher shortages and attacks on critical education programs, this legislation would make it possible for more to answer the call to serve in our schools and to help generations of students along the way.”
“English Learners are among the fastest-growing groups of students in the country, especially in California, and it is crucial that they have qualified, passionate teachers in their classrooms,” said Senator Schiff. “The SPELL Act will encourage more prospective English teachers to pursue that path by ensuring the same loan forgiveness standards as math, science, and special education teachers. I am proud to join Senator Padilla in this effort, and I will continue to work with him to ensure that California’s students and teachers are in a position to succeed.”
The Department of Education has reported that 32 states have a shortage of teachers for EL students, making them unable to meet students’ needs and resulting in a discouraging academic achievement gap for this growing population. The cost of teacher preparation programs can be an obstacle for many to enter the profession, but data shows an association between teachers’ preparation level and their teaching effectiveness and retention. Research demonstrates that loan forgiveness programs are successful at encouraging teachers to take positions in fields and at locations where they are most needed, and forgiveness programs also help to support retention.
Specifically, the bill would provide up to $17,500 in loan forgiveness for teachers of ELs, bilingual students, and/or dual language immersion students. This matches the same level of enhanced forgiveness available to math, science, and special education teachers.
The SPELL Act is endorsed by organizations including TESOL, AFT, UnidosUS, and the California Community Colleges.
“At a time when the Trump administration seems intent on attacking English language learners, public school educators continue to fulfill their mission to serve each and every child who comes through their classroom door,” commented AFT President Randi Weingarten. “ELL teachers have dedicated their lives to helping kids, but student debt and the cost of living are dragging them down. The Supporting Providers of English Language Learning Act would allow ELL teachers to qualify for the highest level of Teacher Loan Forgiveness so they can pursue their careers free from the specter of permanent student debt.”
“To prepare students to succeed in school and beyond, they should have access early on to bilingual educators who understand their language, culture, and learning needs. Yet schools across the country continue to face shortages of bilingual and English learner teachers,” pointed out Carmen M. Feliciano, Vice President of Policy and Advocacy, UnidosUS. “The SPELL Act is a commonsense investment in strengthening that workforce by expanding student loan relief for educators who dedicate their careers to serving English learners and students in bilingual and dual-language programs. UnidosUS applauds Senator Padilla for championing this legislation and helping remove financial barriers to entering and remaining in the teaching profession. By investing in these educators, we are investing in the success of millions of English learners and in a stronger, more representative teacher workforce.”
Padilla also joined Senator Ben Ray Lujan (D-N.M) in reintroducing the Loan Forgiveness for Educators Act, legislation that would expand and modernize the federal loan forgiveness program for educators. This legislation would help address educator shortages and increase children’s access to a diverse and well-prepared educator workforce by strengthening the federal Teacher Loan Forgiveness (TLF) Program. In June, Padilla led Senate colleagues in condemning the Trump Administration’s attacks on English learners and the dissolution of the Department of Education’s Office of English Language Acquisition (OELA).

Ministers drop plans to cut jury trials in England and Wales after outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
23:01:11 UTC
08:01:11 KST

Ministers have scrapped plans that would have slashed the number of jury trials in England and Wales and replaced them with a judge sitting alone.
The proposals had sparked a fierce backlash from lawyers, who have welcomed the U-turn. But the victims’ commissioner expressed concern about the abandonment of measures drawn up by the then justice secretary, David Lammy, under Keir Starmer’s government, to tackle the record backlog in the courts.
There are almost 81,000 cases in the crown courts – with the number projected to hit 100,000 without the now-ditched changes – leaving victims and defendants waiting years for justice. The Ministry of Justice is selling the U-turn as a quicker way to address the problem, by saving the time it would take to set up a new judge-only crown court bench division.
The justice secretary, Alex Norris, said: “This government inherited criminal courts on the brink of collapse, with victims waiting years for their day in court. I remain committed to bringing down the backlog and delivering swifter justice for those who so desperately need it. But I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the crown court and have made the decision to change course.
“This allows us to start that work far earlier, ensuring that under this government we do not have victims waiting endlessly for justice.
“Justice delayed is justice denied, and I am committed to maximising efficiencies in our system alongside record investment.”
Lammy’s proposals came after a government-commissioned review by the former judge, Sir Brian Leveson, who recommended taking away the right to jury trial from thousands of defendants to prevent the criminal justice system from collapsing.
But critics, including Geoffrey Robertson, founding head of Doughty Street Chambers, where Starmer, Lammy and the attorney general, Richard Hermer KC, spent part of their professional careers, accused Labour of abandoning a centuries-old right and claiming that it would not reduce the backlog substantively. Some Labour MPs also opposed the move.
Legislation would have removed jury trials for defendants who were likely to receive a sentence of up to three years.
Ministers have not abandoned judge-only trials altogether, but they will only be for a small number of especially lengthy and technical fraud cases where the judge decides a jury trial is not appropriate.
The government will also retain Lammy’s plans to take away the right of a defendant charged with an “either way” offence to decide whether they will be tried by a jury in the crown court or magistrates. Instead those decisions will be in the hands of magistrates.
And the planned increase in magistrates’ sentencing powers – from the current 12 months maximum to 18 months, with an option to extend to two years – will still go ahead.
Kirsty Brimelow, chair of the Bar Council of England and Wales, welcomed the new government’s “swift action” but said: “We underline that it is a dangerous experiment to increase sentencing powers of magistrates and remove the right to elect from defendants at a time when prisons are at capacity and the backlog of cases is accelerating in the magistrates courts.
She added: “We know that women, black people, mixed race people and older people elect jury trials more often than other groups and this proposal risks deepening existing disparities and exacerbating distrust in the justice system from minoritised communities.”
The Law Society of England and Wales and the Criminal Bar Association also welcomed the change of heart while expressing concern about pushing more cases to magistrates. The former additionally called for more investment, including in legal aid.
The victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said: “Victims are entitled to ask whether what remains will be enough to meet the challenge [of delivering swifter justice]. “Indeed, they are being asked to place their faith in a plan that ministers themselves previously argued would not be.
“The lessons from the prisons crisis should be clear: postponing difficult decisions rarely solves problems. More often, it simply stores them up for the future.
“Victims need hope. Insurance companies want policyholders to pay 10% of health claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
22:51:58 UTC
07:51:58 KST

The proposal, being considered by the General Insurance Council, would pair the change with common hospital empanelment and a formal mechanism for settling disputes between insurers and hospitals.
MUMBAI: Non-life insurers are considering a 10% co-payment by policyholders on retail health policies from Jan 1, 2027, with the patient's contribution capped at Rs 5 lakh per claim. In return, customers would pay lower annual premiums.The proposal, being considered by the General Insurance Council, would pair the change with common hospital empanelment and a formal mechanism for settling disputes between insurers and hospitals. The arrangement would require even those with comprehensive health insurance to keep funds for medical emergencies, as they would have to pay 10% of admissible inpatient hospitalisation costs, including those arising from accidents, whether claims are settled through cashless procedure or reimbursement.
Outpatient claims would remain outside scheme
The proposal covers retail indemnity products, retail-under-group policies, indemnity components of combi products, internal migrations and portability business. Outpatient claims would remain outside the scheme.Co-payment cannot be waived, reduced or modified through riders or endorsements, and the customer’s 10% contribution cannot be recovered from another health insurance policy.“The choice between a cheaper policy with a deductible and a full-compensation policy should rest with the insured.
People buy insurance to be indemnified for their costs. It would be unfair to customers willing to pay a higher premium for a higher sum insured to still bear part of the cost, and this could discourage them from buying high-value policies,” said Shreeraj Deshpande, a health insurance expert who earlier headed operations at a general insurer. While the industry is seeking to address what it sees as cost distortions in healthcare, some fear a mandatory requirement could be anti-competitive. “If the industry collectively decides that no one will offer a full-compensation policy, it might catch the attention of the Competition Commission,” said an industry executive.The logic behind the measure is that hospitals may order additional diagnostic tests, recommend procedures and extend hospital stays when patients have comprehensive insurance cover. Higher-category rooms can also increase total bills because doctors’ fees and procedure charges are often linked to room tariffs.
With insurance covering the full bill, patients may have less incentive to question charges or choose lower-cost hospitals.“This behaviour (overbilling and provider-induced demand) stems from the perception that insurance-backed patients are less price-sensitive, leading to inflated healthcare costs,” a council note said.The proposal also calls for common hospital empanelment, outcome-based contracts and a payor-provider grievance forum. GI Council plans standard empanelment across more than 4,300 hospitals to set benchmark tariffs and curb arbitrary billing, while linking contracts to clinical and procedure-wise outcomes.

Red eyes, claws, and a mouth with three lips: Scientists discover two new species of sea spiders
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
01:14:20 EEST
07:14:20 KST

Red eyes, claws, and a mouth with three lips: Scientists discover two new species of sea spiders
Kyiv • UNN
Two new species of sea spiders have been discovered in the Salish Sea, one of which has red eyes, claws, and three lips. Researchers do not rule out further discoveries.
Scientists have discovered two new species of sea spiders that had not been described in this region for nearly 100 years. One of them has red eyes, claws for capturing prey, and a triangular mouth with three lips covered in sensory hairs, LRT reports, citing the University of British Columbia, writes UNN.
Details
The new species were found in the Salish Sea between Canada and the United States. The specimens were collected during dives to depths of up to 18 meters from September 2023 to August 2024.
One of the new species was named Callipallene pilosuspedes. In addition to its red eyes and unusual mouth, its legs are covered with long, curved spines. Scientists even observed the spider using specialized limbs to "wash its face."
They can have up to 12 legs and breathe through their skin
Sea spiders appeared about 500 million years ago and are relatives of scorpions and horseshoe crabs. Some species have up to 12 legs, while their size ranges from less than 1 cm to more than 70 cm.
Some small sea spiders live as parasites on larger animals and suck fluids from them. The spiders themselves breathe through their skin, while males carry the offspring, attaching the eggs to their bodies.
The second species discovered was named Tanystylum kiixin. Researchers repeatedly found tiny parasites on its body, prompting one of the scientists to describe the spider as a kind of "ecosystem within an ecosystem."
Both species have already been added to a global database. Researchers believe that other marine creatures still unknown to science may remain in the area.

According to maritime intelligence and research firm Kpler, at least 16.5 million barrels per day (mbd) of crude left the region between Sept 1 and 28, matching the prewar average. During the peak of the West Asia war in March, the average was 10.5 mbd.
While 83% of the region’s crude crossed Hormuz before the war, 40% was exported in Sept through pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the UAE without crossing the key chokepoint.Of the remaining 60% that physically crossed Hormuz, most was moved using shuttle tankers, Emmanuel Belostrino, head of global crude and geopolitical market data at Kpler, said in his analysis.Belostrino said more than 70% of the crude that crossed the Strait of Hormuz in Aug changed tankers offshore in the Gulf of Oman.
Crude via other routes made up the difference
Confirmed crude crossings were still more than a quarter below the pre-war level, but volumes moving through alternative routes had more than doubled and made up almost exactly the difference. Saudi pushed more crude through the east-west pipeline to Yanbu, with loadings rising from 0.8 mbd before the war to 4.3 mbd in June. UAE sent crude through the Abu Dhabi crude oil pipeline to Fujairah, where loadings rose from 1.1 mbd to 2.7 mbd.
325 million barrels released from oil reserves: IEA
The International Energy Agency said member countries had released 325 million barrels of oil and oil products from strategic reserves, out of 400 million barrels pledged in March.

US remains 'hell-bent' on preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, says Hegseth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
22:09:38 UTC
07:09:38 KST

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth warned Iran that US President Donald Trump remains determined to prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons, cautioning that Tehran must choose between relinquishing its nuclear ambitions and facing further American action.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Hegseth also declined to confirm whether the United States intends to deploy a third aircraft carrier to the region, saying his responsibility is to ensure that Trump retains the widest possible range of military options.
Asked directly whether three aircraft carriers would be deployed, Hegseth replied: “It’s a fair question, but I will never answer it.”
“I’d say maximizing the decision space for the commander in chief at any point is my job, while also recognizing the way we balance global demands as a force with global responsibilities,” he explained.
“So the president’s going to have options. Let’s put it that way, and I’ll leave it there.”
‘Iran will never, ever, ever have a nuclear weapon’
Hegseth delivered his strongest warning when asked to clarify the administration’s message to Tehran.
“Well, the message is very simple: Iran will never, ever, ever have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
“President Trump is hell-bent and determined to ensure that they do not. They will not. If they want to blink and think that he doesn’t mean it, it would be to their detriment.”
He added that Iran had reached a decision point.
“So now’s a moment where they can decide to give it up the way that they should, without any leverage that they have, or it may have to happen the hard way.”
Earlier in the exchange, Hegseth was asked whether he expected military operations to conclude before the end of the year. He declined to commit to a timetable, deferring the decision to Trump.
He nevertheless contrasted the administration’s approach with previous American military campaigns that, he said, had continued for years or decades without clearly defined objectives or an identifiable end state.
“As we’ve stated from the beginning, Iran will never have a nuclear bomb. Full stop. That is a vital national interest of the United States of America,” Hegseth said, citing Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury.
He stressed that Trump would not allow operations to continue unnecessarily, arguing that the administration understands its mission and has the capabilities required to accomplish it.
Hegseth acknowledges Iranian efforts to rebuild missile capabilities
Asked whether Washington had evidence that Iran was attempting to reconstitute its missile capabilities and launchers, Hegseth said the United States was monitoring developments in real time.
He acknowledged that Tehran would attempt to rebuild its military infrastructure but maintained that the damage inflicted during Operation Epic Fury had severely complicated those efforts.
“Think of it this way, their Raytheons, their Boeings, their Lockheeds, their Northrop Grummans are what was destroyed in Epic Fury,” he said, referring to the Iranian equivalents of major American defense manufacturers.
“So they’re going to attempt to reconstitute, and they’re a terror state. So they’re going to always attempt to reconstitute, but when you’ve been so destroyed and degraded the way that they have, it’s a very slow process, a very frustrating process, and we see that, and we understand that.”
Hegseth argued that the extent of the damage to Iran’s defense industrial base, economy, and ability to rebuild would continue to constrain Tehran’s military options.
‘They don’t control the Strait of Hormuz, we do’
The defense secretary also emphasized American control over the Strait of Hormuz, describing the US blockade as a central component of Washington’s pressure campaign against Iran.
“Iran wants to play games with things like the Strait of Hormuz. They don’t control it. We do,” Hegseth said.
“Our blockade has been ironclad, and we’re running almost at pre-war levels every single night through that,” he added, referring to maritime throughput.
Hegseth asserted that Iran’s naval and air capabilities had been so extensively degraded that it could no longer effectively challenge American dominance over the strategic waterway.
“It’s pretty tough for them to control the Strait of Hormuz when they don’t have a navy. They don’t have fast boats, and they’ve got no air force,” he said.
“And then we’ve done such incredible damage to their ability to see and sense the Strait of Hormuz. We control it. We dominate it in both an asymmetric and a conventional sense.”
He added that Washington was capable of maintaining the blockade for as long as necessary and adapting its implementation according to operational requirements.
“The longer we hold the blockade, and we can hold it as long as we need to. Trust me, we can adapt that as necessary,” he said, arguing that the pressure would further restrict Tehran’s remaining options.
Asked whether the conflict could ultimately have a military solution, Hegseth said it could be resolved in multiple ways and maintained that Trump had repeatedly offered Iran an opportunity to reach an agreement through negotiations.
“The president has given Iran every opportunity to do it at the table,” he said.
However, he reiterated that the combination of American military strikes and the continuing blockade had left Washington in a strong position.
“Iran ought to make the right choice. If they don’t, the president’s going to have all the options he needs on the table,” Hegseth concluded.

Indians live longer than Pakistanis, lag Bangladeshis, says WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
22:02:50 UTC
07:02:50 KST

The logic behind the measure is that hospitals may order additional diagnostic tests, recommend procedures and extend hospital stays when patients have comprehensive insurance cover.
NEW DELHI: Indians can expect to live longer than their counterparts in Pakistan, but have shorter lives than people in Bangladesh, the US and Canada, according to the latest World Health Organization estimates.India's life expectancy at birth was 71 years in 2023, compared with 68.2 years in Pakistan, 72.7 years in Bangladesh, 78.5 years in the US and 81.4 years in Canada. But living longer does not necessarily mean living more years in good health. India's healthy life expectancy was 60.6 years in 2023, compared with 60.5 in 2019. It had fallen to 58.4 years in 2021 before recovering to 60.2 years in 2022. The figures are part of WHO's Global Health Estimates, released Friday, covering life expectancy, healthy life expectancy, causes of death and disease burden from 2000 to 2023. WHO said global life expectancy recovered close to pre-pandemic levels, while healthy life expectancy has recovered more slowly.
In 2 years from 2021, India regained 2.9 years of expected lifespan: WHO
For India, the difference is particularly visible over the pandemic years. Life expectancy fell from 70.5 years in 2019 to 68.1 years in 2021 before rising to 70.5 years in 2022 and 71 years in 2023. In just two years, India regained 2.9 years of expected lifespan.Healthy life expectancy, however, recovered by only 2.2 years, from 58.4 years in 2021 to 60.6 years in 2023, leaving it just 0.1 year above the 2019 level.
The gap is also visible among older Indians. At age 60, a person could expect another 18.8 years of life in 2023, compared with 18.4 years in 2019. But 13.7 of those years were expected to be lived in full health, up from 13.4 years in 2019.India’s disease profile has changed sharply. Communicable diseases, such as tuberculosis and diarrhoeal infections, can spread from person to person, while non-communicable diseases (NCDs), such as heart disease, stroke and diabetes, are generally long-term conditions.In 2000, communicable diseases accounted for nearly 62% of the combined death rate from the country’s 10 leading causes, while NCDs accounted for 34%. By 2023, the pattern had reversed, with NCDs accounting for nearly 75% and communicable diseases 16% of the combined death rate from the top 10 causes. The rest was from injuries.
The shift is evident in the leading causes. In 2000, tuberculosis and diarrhoeal diseases topped the list, with 92.4 and 87.8 deaths per 100,000 population. By 2023, ischaemic heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, stroke and diabetes were among the leading causes, with rates of 138.5, 83.19, 74.8 and 49.01, respectively. Yet infectious diseases remain a significant burden, with diarrhoeal diseases, tuberculosis and lower respiratory infections still among India’s top 10 causes of death in 2023.Globally, the shift towards chronic diseases is also pronounced. NCDs accounted for 74% of deaths in 2023, up from 58% in 2000, while eight of the world’s 10 leading causes of death were NCDs. Global life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2023, almost back to the 73.4 years recorded in 2019, while healthy life expectancy stood at 62.8 years, still 0.4 years below its 2019 level.

She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Americans often fail to notice when Democrats and Republicans are moving in the same direction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
22:00:25 UTC
07:00:25 KST

Informing people about how the political attitudes of opposing parties are moving in the same direction over time might help reduce partisan hostility. New research published in Political Psychology suggests that people frequently fail to notice how much support for certain social issues has grown within both parties. When people read about these shared trajectories of opinion change without being reminded of the current gap between parties, they tend to expect more future common ground and report slightly warmer feelings toward their political opponents.
To understand how political divides operate, psychologists often look at descriptive social norms, which are individuals’ perceptions of what other people believe or do. In politics, perceptions of these norms are frequently distorted. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2021 indicated that both Democrats and Republicans overestimate how much the opposing party dislikes them. When people assume their political opponents hold extreme or hostile views, it often drives further polarization.
Researchers often try to correct these false assumptions by presenting static norms, which describe the current level of support for a specific issue within a group. However, static norms only capture a single moment in time. Dynamic norms, on the other hand, describe how a group’s beliefs or behaviors are changing over time. A 2017 study found that showing people a trend is growing in popularity can persuade them to adopt new behaviors, even if current support is relatively low.
Applying this idea to politics requires overcoming another layer of misperception. A 2022 study indicated that Americans often misjudge how public opinion has shifted over decades, usually overestimating how much attitudes have changed, especially in a liberal direction. The authors of the new study set out to test whether correcting misperceptions about these trends could soften partisan hostility. How such a message is framed may matter: a 2021 paper argued that describing partisan divisions can make division seem like the norm and inadvertently deepen polarization.
The research was led by Trystan Loustau, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Psychology and Neuroscience at Boston College. “A lot of research shows that Democrats and Republicans have distorted perceptions of one another, and that these misperceptions can make political divisions seem larger than they really are,” Loustau told PsyPost. “But most of that work focuses on a snapshot of the present: what Democrats or Republicans believe right now. We were interested in whether people also misperceive change: even when members of both parties are moving in the same direction on an issue, do people recognize that convergence?”
“That seemed especially important because the direction people think society is moving may shape how they imagine its future,” Loustau explained. “If you believe the two parties are becoming increasingly divided, you might respond very differently to political opponents than if you believe there are areas where they are gradually finding more common ground.”
In the first study, 368 Democrats and Republicans estimated current support and changes in support for 12 social issues on which support had actually risen in both parties. The researchers found that participants systematically underestimated attitude change. Only about half of the estimates accurately recognized that support for these issues was increasing. They also underestimated current levels of support by about 12 points for Democrats and 20 points for Republicans.
Misperceptions were especially pronounced when evaluating Republicans. Only about 25 percent of Democrats’ estimates and 44 percent of Republicans’ estimates regarding Republican attitude changes were accurate, compared to 77 percent and 66 percent accuracy for Democratic attitude changes. This finding is in tension with the 2022 study: here, participants often missed real increases in support for progressive positions, especially among Republicans. The authors suggest people may expect Democrats, but not Republicans, to move left.
In addition, the researchers found a correlation between recognizing these trends and intergroup attitudes. For every additional 10 percent of estimates that correctly identified change in the opposing party, participants felt about 3 points warmer toward that party on a 0-to-100 scale. This association held after accounting for accuracy about current support, which itself was unrelated to warmth.
“Political disagreement is real, but our perceptions of it are not always accurate,” Loustau pointed out. “We may be particularly bad at noticing when attitudes are changing.”
To see if correcting these misperceptions could help, the researchers randomly assigned 1,187 partisans to a dynamic norm condition, a static norm condition, or a control condition featuring apolitical topics. The dynamic norm message provided both the past and current levels of partisan support alongside the percentage-point increases over time. The static norm message only provided current support levels.
The results indicated that the dynamic norm group expected more future common ground between parties than the control group. Combining the current support levels with the trend data did not produce broader positive changes in attitudes toward the outparty, meaning the opposing party, such as warmth or expectations of belonging. The authors suggest that presenting the current levels of support alongside the trend may have inadvertently reminded participants of the existing gaps between the parties.
For the third study, the team refined the intervention using a new sample of 1,154 participants. This time, the dynamic norm condition isolated the trend information by completely removing references to current levels of partisan support. The message focused solely on how support had grown within each party over time. Participants were randomly assigned to read the refined message, the original combined message from the second study, the static message, or the control material.
The refined message increased expected common ground and expected future feelings of belonging with the outparty. People who read it reported outparty warmth of about 32.5 on a 100-point scale, compared to 25.9 in the control group, and also rated members of the other party more positively. The researchers noted that a recent review of 77 depolarization interventions found an average gain of about 5.4 points in outparty warmth, making the refined message’s 6.6-point difference comparable to that average.
The refined message was the only one to outperform the control condition on all four of these measures. On warmth and positive evaluations, however, it did not statistically outperform the original combined message or the static message, and the static message also raised warmth relative to control. No version of the message changed how much people saw the other party as overlapping with themselves.
“What surprised me most was how much the way we presented the same information mattered,” Loustau said. “It was a useful reminder that more information is not necessarily better: emphasizing how far apart the parties remain may overshadow evidence that they are moving in the same direction.”
He added, “The broader takeaway is that focusing exclusively on today’s partisan divisions can obscure meaningful ways in which public opinion is changing.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that showing partisans how much their core personal values overlap increased perceived similarity, strengthened beliefs that compromise is possible, and made people more hopeful. That study focused on present-day overlap in values, whereas the new study focused on how opinions on specific issues have shifted over time.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The sample was an online group of participants rather than a nationally representative one, and outcomes were measured right after reading the messages, with no follow-up.
The study also relied on real statistics for issues that were primarily progressive in nature, so it is not known whether these effects would hold for conservative policies or in different political contexts. Using real polling data also meant the researchers could not test larger shifts in opinion, and many of the real changes they presented were modest.
“The effects on attitudes toward the opposing party were small, and I think it is important to be clear about that,” Loustau noted. “A brief informational message is not going to eliminate partisan polarization. At the same time, polarization is a large, persistent social problem, so even small changes produced by a relatively minimal intervention can be informative, particularly because the intervention consisted simply of changing which accurate information about public opinion people saw.”
“I would view the findings less as evidence for a single solution to polarization and more as evidence that people’s expectations about where political groups are headed can influence how they think about those groups in the present,” he observed.
It is also possible that emphasizing negative trajectories could have the opposite effect. Messages highlighting increasing disagreement or polarization might inadvertently increase hostility. Future research could explore whether this kind of dynamic messaging works for other intergroup conflicts, such as those involving race or religion, and whether the observed changes in attitude persist over longer periods of time.
“Long term, I’m interested in what happens when we encourage people to think about political differences in a more future-oriented way,” Loustau said. “Rather than focusing only on how different we are right now, I want to understand what changes when people recognize both their own and others’ capacity to change. That shared capacity may itself be a form of common ground, opening space to imagine not just what society currently looks like, but what we want our relationships and world to look like in the future.”
The study, “Partisans misperceive and are influenced by dynamic norms,” was authored by Trystan Loustau, Ashley Fabrizio, Liane Young, Jordan Wylie, and Stylianos Syropoulos.

Kyiv • UNN
A Gulfstream G100 disappeared after the pilot issued an emergency transmission during a flight from Bermuda to Boston. A search is underway near Nantucket.
A Gulfstream G100 medical aircraft carrying 6 people disappeared over the Atlantic Ocean. Before communications were lost, the pilot declared an emergency, the Associated Press reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
The aircraft, with the call sign "Heartbeat 104," was flying from Bermuda to Boston. There were 4 crew members and 2 passengers on board. At least 4 of them are Canadian citizens.
The last communications with air traffic controllers indicated problems during the flight. One of the controllers asked the pilot to confirm whether he had really reported that he was "flying blind." Shortly after the emergency was declared, contact with the aircraft was lost.
The aircraft is being searched for by air and sea
Controllers tried to determine the Gulfstream's location using other aircraft in the area, but they were unable to establish contact with its crew again.
The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration notified the Coast Guard about the aircraft's disappearance early in the morning on October 3.
The search-and-rescue operation is under way in the waters near Nantucket Island in Massachusetts. U.S. Coast Guard aircraft and maritime crews have been involved.
The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board is also collecting information about the incident. There is currently no information about the fate of the 6 people on board.

Roundup: Growing presence of Chinese brands in Greek market highlighted at AUTO ATHINA 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:56:12 CST
06:56:12 KST

ATHENS, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- The growing presence of Chinese car brands has been showcased at AUTO ATHINA 2026, an international auto show that began Saturday in the Greek capital of Athens.
The auto show, which runs from Oct. 3 to 11 at the Metropolitan Expo in Athens, features 52 brands, the largest number in the show's history. More than a dozen Chinese brands are among the exhibitors.
Chinese cars are drawing attention in Greece for their competitive prices and technological features, according to dealers and visitors to the auto show.
Thomas Kouris, a visitor to the BYD booth, said the cars' high quality, competitive prices and electric vehicle(EV) subsidies had prompted him to take a closer look at Chinese brands.
For Nikos Ioannou, a visitor to the Chery booth, the driving experience was important. He said Chinese cars offered reliable performance, good driving dynamics and competitive prices.
"They are very good cars. They turn well, brake well, ride well, have a lot of technology, and offer incredible prices," he said.
The growing presence of Chinese automakers, which have begun entering the Greek market in recent years, is also reflected in statistics.
Chinese brands accounted for nearly 10 percent of new passenger car registrations in Greece in the first eight months of 2026, according to data from the Association of Motor Vehicle Importers-Representatives (AMVIR).
BYD has registered more than 6,000 electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles in Greece since entering the market in March 2024, with registrations up by 47 pct in the first eight months of 2026 from the same period last year, Yiannis Kakouris, public relations manager for BYD at Greek dealer Sfakianakis Group, told Xinhua.
At Chery's booth, George Spanos, CEO of Greek dealer Spanos SA, said Chery had achieved strong retail sales in September, with the Tiggo 4 hybrid among its leading models.
The growth comes amid a broader shift in consumer demand toward EV, according to an analysis by AMVIR based on new-car registration data from the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT).
Hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) remained dominant, accounting for 57.7 percent of new-car registrations in the January-August period, compared with 49.2 percent a year earlier.
Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) accounted for 6.7 percent of new-car registrations, up 1.4 percentage points from the same period last year, while plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) accounted for 6.3 percent. Gasoline-powered cars accounted for 24 percent, down 8.4 percentage points year-on-year.
That market mix has also created opportunities for Chinese manufacturers, many of which have entered Greece with hybrid models alongside fully electric vehicles.
"The trend is toward new-technology vehicles that definitely have a battery and an electric motor. However, hybrids are still more popular," Spanos said.
"Chinese cars are now embraced by Greek consumers," he added. ■

ESSEN, Germany, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Chinese and German students took the stage together on Saturday in the western German city of Essen for a youth exchange concert aimed at fostering cultural understanding and friendship through music.
Students from Germany's Burg Chinese Chorus and Yunnan University Secondary School performed a selection of Chinese songs at the concert, drawing warm applause from an audience of around 200.
The Burg Chinese Chorus is a non-profit organization that runs a "Learn Chinese by Singing" program for young people in Germany. Combining language learning with music and exchange activities, the group works to promote people-to-people ties between the two countries.
Olaf Millmann, chairman of the Burg Chinese Chorus association, said in his speech that learning through singing offers young Germans an accessible way to take their first steps in Chinese.
"A song can spark curiosity and make people want to understand more," Millmann said. "That curiosity can then create the motivation to continue learning the language and to get to know the people who speak it."
For 18-year-old chorus member Nikolaos Topoulos, that interest in Chinese has grown steadily since he began studying the language about two years ago. He told Xinhua that joining the chorus had helped him improve his vocabulary and spoken Chinese a lot. "I really like Chinese and want to keep learning it."
In July, he traveled to China with the chorus, visiting Beijing, Kunming and other cities. He said he was impressed by China's vastness, vitality and the warmth of its people. "Wherever we went, people were very friendly and welcoming," he said, adding that he plans to apply to China's Sichuan University after graduating from high school.
Zhang Yungang, leader of the chorus, told Xinhua that the "Learn Chinese by Singing" program has been running for more than a decade, introducing many young Germans to the Chinese language. Some have later studied in China or pursued careers related to China-Germany business and cultural exchanges.
"When they sing together, their hearts come together," Zhang said, adding that more than a decade of experience has strengthened his belief in music as a way to sustain youth exchanges between the two countries. ■

The books, including the English edition of the first volume of "China's Governance Under Xi Jinping's Leadership," have undergone a selection and curation process by the national library in accordance with its collection development principles, the library said in a press release, adding that the curation process took into account users' needs, accessibility, relevance, subject diversity, and suitability as sources of reference.
Wang Siping, cultural counselor of the Chinese Embassy in Indonesia, said at the event that the donated books cover a wide range of fields, including Chinese culture, history, literature, science and technology, and language learning, representing a carefully selected cultural gift from China's publishing sector.

For his part, Director of the National Library of Indonesia E. Aminudin Aziz emphasized that the collection should not be seen merely as an addition to the library's holdings, but also as an effort to broaden the public's access to knowledge.
The library will work closely with the donors to complete the handover and process the collection, so the public can access the books early on, Aziz said.
The director said he also sees this event as an opportunity to explore further cooperation, such as exchanges of publications, discussions with authors and publishers, and sharing professional experience in collection development and library services. ■

SANAA, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Saturday it launched ballistic missiles and drones at an Aramco facility in the Saudi capital Riyadh, in retaliation for what it described as intensified Saudi air and missile strikes on Yemen.
In a statement broadcast by the Houthi-run al-Masirah TV, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea claimed the attack achieved its objective, with "direct hits" setting fire to the targeted sites.
He said the attack was in response to what the Houthis described as Saudi airstrikes on the Yemeni capital Sanaa and other Houthi-controlled areas earlier in the day.
In a separate statement on Saturday, Sarea said 60 air and missile strikes had hit Yemen over the previous 24 hours, bringing the total number of such attacks since the latest escalation began to 1,410.
Sarea said on social media platform X that the 60 strikes hit areas in Sanaa, Saada, Taiz, Hajjah and Marib provinces, claiming that civilian sites were among the targets.
The statement came after a series of powerful explosions shook Sanaa on Saturday afternoon. Residents told Xinhua that more than seven blasts were heard within a short period, with the sound of warplanes overhead and smoke rising from the mountainous areas of Al-Nahdayn and Jabal Attan, key Houthi-held military sites.
Meanwhile, Houthi and government forces kept trading attacks on Saturday to seek control of key mountainous positions in southwestern Taiz province, a Yemeni government military official told Xinhua.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said several people on both sides had been killed or wounded amid exchanges of drone attacks and heavy airstrikes, without providing a precise toll.
Against that backdrop, government forces, largely backed by Saudi Arabia, announced a new wave of military operations against Houthi positions across war-ravaged Yemen.
Majid al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for the government forces, said in a statement on X on Saturday that the military had carried out 257 strikes against Houthi positions, troop movements and military assets, using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and multiple-launch rocket systems.
He claimed that at least 700 Houthi fighters were killed or wounded and 170 military vehicles and other pieces of equipment were destroyed.
Tensions between Houthis and Saudi Arabia intensified after the group announced a ban on Saudi-linked vessels entering Houthi-controlled Red Sea ports on July 20, followed by an escalation in cross-border missile and drone attacks and airstrikes.
The confrontation widened further in September amid the fighting between Houthis and the Yemeni government forces, largely backed by Saudi Arabia. The Houthis captured the Red Sea port city of Mocha on Sept. 10 and the strategically located Mayyun Island a day later.
Yemen's conflict began in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

Greece, Bulgaria sign protocol for return of cultural artefacts
China

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev (1st L) and other officials welcome the remains identified as those of Tsar Samuel, who ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, at the airport in Sofia, Bulgaria, Oct. 3, 2026. Greece and Bulgaria signed a protocol Saturday on the reciprocal handover of cultural artefacts, under which 48 Greek artefacts will return from Bulgaria, while Greece will hand over to Bulgaria the remains identified as those of medieval Bulgarian ruler Tsar Samuel, Greek national broadcaster ERT reported. After the handover ceremony in Greece, the remains identified as those of Tsar Samuel, who ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, arrived in Bulgarian capital of Sofia on Saturday. (Photo by Bulgarian Government Information Service/Xinhua)
ATHENS, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Greece and Bulgaria signed a protocol Saturday on the reciprocal handover of cultural artefacts, under which 48 Greek artefacts will return from Bulgaria, while Greece will hand over to Bulgaria the remains identified as those of medieval Bulgarian ruler Tsar Samuel, Greek national broadcaster ERT reported.
The protocol was signed by the two countries' culture ministers at the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki, northern Greece, in the presence of Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev.
The 48 artefacts are being displayed at the museum until Nov. 5, 2026, after which they will be returned to their institutions of origin: the Monastery of Panagia Eikosifoinissa, the Monastery of Timios Prodromos in Serres, and the Holy Metropolis of Serres and Nigrita.
After the handover ceremony in Greece, the remains identified as those of Tsar Samuel, who ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, arrived in Bulgarian capital of Sofia on Saturday.
The remains were discovered in 1965 during archaeological excavations at the Basilica of St. Achillius in Prespa in northern Greece and have since been kept at the Museum of Byzantine Culture. The Prespa area was a center of Tsar Samuel's rule in the late 10th century, and the basilica is believed to have been built by him as a major religious center.
The two countries also agreed to continue talks on identifying other historical objects of mutual interest that could be included in a future agreement. ■

Explainer: Why G7 agrees to release fuel reserves, how helpful will it be?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
05:55:19 CST
06:55:19 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Group of Seven (G7) leaders agreed Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an action coordinated through the International Energy Agency (IEA), as surging fuel prices, disrupted refined-product supplies and threatened U.S. export restrictions added pressure on global energy markets.
Under the agreement, the 100 million barrels will be released over four months, starting immediately, with a substantial amount of diesel to be frontloaded within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners.
The G7 did not specify how much of the total would be diesel or crude oil, or how many individual countries would contribute. It said further diesel releases could be considered if necessary.
IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said Friday that around 325 million barrels have so far been released under the collective action announced in March, representing more than 80 percent of the 400 million barrels originally pledged, the largest move of its kind in the agency's history.
The group also agreed to coordinate refinery maintenance to avoid simultaneous shutdowns, temporarily raise refinery utilization where possible and encourage countries with significant refining capacity to increase production, particularly of diesel.
Pressure has been acute in global fuel markets, particularly diesel, as two major sources of diesel and gasoil supply have been hit at the same time.
Net diesel and gasoil exports from Gulf countries averaged just slightly more than a quarter of pre-U.S.-Iran war levels, as flows through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely constrained, according to the IEA.
Birol also said that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have added to the pressure on diesel supplies, pushing up prices.
Europe has felt the strain acutely. The European Commission said Friday that diesel prices had doubled since the end of February when the U.S.-Iran war started, contributing to what it described as an "affordability crisis."
EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen said Tuesday that the bloc had paid more than 100 billion euros (about 113.3 billion U.S. dollars) extra for fossil fuel imports since the start of the U.S.-Iran conflict, without receiving additional energy.
The decision also followed mounting transatlantic friction over how to respond.
The Trump administration had pressed European governments to draw down more emergency diesel stocks and warned that restrictions on U.S. diesel exports could follow if Europe did not act.
The threat carried weight for Europe. The European Commission said last week that the United States accounted for around half of EU diesel imports in August, making the bloc highly exposed to any disruption in U.S. supplies.
Hours before the G7 agreement, the Commission publicly rejected the prospect of a U.S. diesel export ban, saying such a move would benefit neither side and undermine trust in the United States as a reliable partner.
The eventual G7 agreement combined coordinated reserve releases with a commitment to refrain from restricting energy exports among members, a move later welcomed by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Analysts say the release could provide meaningful short-term relief, particularly if large diesel volumes reach the market quickly.
Alan Gelder, senior vice president for refining, chemicals and oil markets at Wood Mackenzie, estimated that a major diesel stock release could lower wholesale prices by 20 to 30 U.S. dollars per barrel.
But the effect may prove temporary. Gelder said further stock releases essentially buy time while global diesel supply remains below demand and inventories continue to be drawn down, adding that the EU continues to be vulnerable to the export policies of others such as the United States.
Ultimately, the longer-term stability of prices will depend on the restoration of refined-product flows from the Middle East. But with the U.S.-Iran conflict proving difficult to resolve, a swift return to more stable flows may remain out of reach. ■

Details

The structure of Russian divisions is changing due to losses
Since the beginning of the full-scale war, the number of divisions in the Russian army has increased significantly. Whereas there were 12 in 2022, by the beginning of February 2025 there were already 23.
At the same time, the structure of the motor rifle divisions themselves has also changed. Before the invasion, their "core" usually consisted of one tank regiment and two motor rifle regiments. In the new divisions formed in 2024–2025, the structure already provided for three motor rifle regiments and only one tank battalion.
Defense Express links this change primarily to the heavy losses of the Russian army in heavy equipment and manpower during the war against Ukraine.

Support for Merz’s party hits record low as AfD surges – poll
Nationwide support for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU/CSU alliance has collapsed to a historic low following a series of defeats in regional elections, a new poll suggests.
The bloc’s popular backing stood at just 18%, its worst in German postwar history, according to a survey conducted by the INSA polling institution on behalf of Bild.
The poll put the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) at 30%, the highest since the party was established in 2013. It remains the most popular party in Germany by a wide margin, the poll suggests. The CDU/CSU’s junior coalition partners, the Social Democrats and the Greens are polling at 14% each, with the Left Party at 10%.
The survey was conducted September 28 to October 2 among 1,202 eligible voters; the results were published on Saturday.
Support for the CDU/CSU has fallen sharply since Merz took office as chancellor in May 2025. INSA put the bloc at around 30% shortly before he assumed the post, compared with 18% now.
Merz has been described as Germany’s least popular head of government in around 30 years. He came to power following snap elections in February 2025, promising to revive Germany’s struggling economy, but has since poured more money into the military while blaming economic problems on Germans themselves.
He has told citizens to work more and argued that the “welfare state as we have it today can no longer be financed.” In May, his government announced plans for social spending cuts and unveiled an unpopular pension reform.
The survey also came after the CDU suffered defeats to the AfD in the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, results Merz described as a “disaster.”
The right-wing party won 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt and 38.3% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The CDU finished a distant second in Saxony-Anhalt with 17.5% and failed to clear the electoral threshold in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where it received just 4.9%.
Despite the defeats, Merz said he will not change course and will keep focusing on the military buildup and antagonizing Russia. “I will not deviate by a single millimeter from my fundamental conviction that, especially now, we must defend our freedom against Russia,” he stated in early September.

Does a new plague epidemic threaten the world because of the case in Russia, and how dangerous is the disease today?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-04
00:38:06 EEST
06:38:06 KST

Does a new plague epidemic threaten the world because of the case in Russia, and how dangerous is the disease today?
Kyiv • UNN
A suspected case of pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast claimed the life of a laboratory technician, and around 200 contacts were isolated. The WHO considers a global epidemic unlikely.
Reports of a suspected case of pneumonic plague in Russia's Irkutsk Region, where a 28-year-old employee of a plague-control institute died and about 200 of her contacts were isolated, have raised concerns about the possible spread of the dangerous infection. However, modern plague, despite its high risk, no longer poses the same global threat as it did during historic pandemics, since it can be effectively treated with antibiotics, the WHO reports, UNN writes.
Details
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. The disease has not disappeared: natural foci exist in various parts of the world, while the largest number of cases in recent years have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar.
The pneumonic form of plague is considered the most dangerous. Unlike the much more common bubonic form, it can be transmitted directly from person to person through respiratory particles. Without treatment, pneumonic plague is almost always fatal, and the patient's condition can deteriorate extremely quickly.
Could plague cause an epidemic like the one in the Middle Ages again?
Theoretically, yes. The WHO emphasizes that pneumonic plague, due to its ability to spread between people, can cause serious outbreaks. However, the situation is fundamentally different from the time of the "Black Death," which claimed tens of millions of lives in the 14th century.
Today, plague is treated with antibiotics. The most important thing is to establish the diagnosis and begin therapy as early as possible. According to the WHO, when detected and treated promptly, the chances of recovery from pneumonic plague are high. At the same time, without treatment, it can lead to death within just 18–24 hours after symptoms appear.
People who have had close contact with a patient suffering from pneumonic plague are given a preventive course of antibiotics. The patient is isolated, while medical workers use personal protective equipment. The CDC notes that transmission usually requires close contact with an infected person and their respiratory droplets.
Therefore, based on the information currently available, there are no grounds to speak of a threat of a global epidemic because of the events in the Irkutsk Region. It is much more important to determine whether there have been any new infections among the contacts and how quickly they were isolated and preventive treatment was initiated.
What happened in Russia
According to Russian media, 28-year-old Darya Shipilova worked as a laboratory technician at the Irkutsk plague-control institute. On September 25, she allegedly broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen, after which she became ill. The woman was hospitalized, and she died during the night of October 2.
A drug that may prevent Ebola infection is being tested in Congo03.10.26, 20:08 • 4986 views
After that, about 200 people who may have had contact with her were identified. According to media reports, 189 people were hospitalized for observation, while the Shelekhov District Hospital was placed under quarantine. Anti-epidemic measures were launched in the region.
At the same time, much uncertainty remains surrounding the situation. As of the time the first reports appeared, Russian federal authorities had not released complete information about the circumstances of the infection or the results of examinations of the contacts. Therefore, it is still too early to conclude that there has been a full-scale plague outbreak based solely on reports of a laboratory technician's death and the quarantine.
The scale of isolating contacts in such a situation does not itself mean that all of them are infected. In the case of pneumonic plague, the rapid identification of contacts, their medical observation, preventive antibiotics, and the isolation of possible patients are standard measures intended to prevent an epidemic from developing.
