Former IDF negotiator says Israel could have ended Gaza war, freed hostages a year earlier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:36:07 UTC
06:36:07 KST

Maj.-Gen. (res.) Nitzan Alon, who headed the IDF's hostage and missing persons directorate during the war, said Friday that Israel could have ended the war in Gaza and returned the hostages significantly earlier, possibly as much as a year before the intense fighting ultimately ended, Walla reported on Saturday.
Alon said different decisions could have saved thousands of lives on both sides and that some of the hostages who were killed or murdered in captivity might have returned alive to their families.
He made the remarks during a Washington Institute for Near East Policy panel titled "Three Years After October 7: A Bridge or a Chasm Between the Peoples?"
During the discussion, moderated by David Makovsky and featuring Israeli, Palestinian, and American experts, Alon was asked about the decisions that prolonged the war and whether an opportunity to return the hostages earlier had been missed.
'We missed the opportunity. The war was too long'
"I think we could have reached this point much earlier, perhaps a year earlier, without significantly harming the other strategic objectives of the war," Alon said.
"We could have achieved the same strategic accomplishments in terms of damaging Hamas's military strength, and in terms of many other security issues, much earlier. Perhaps we would have brought back alive some of the hostages who were killed or murdered during captivity," he said. "We missed that opportunity. The war was too long."
Alon stressed that he was not attempting to analyze Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's personal motivations.
"I'm not a psychologist who can know exactly what is going on in the prime minister's mind," he said, adding that political leaders are influenced by strategic and ideological considerations, political constraints, and personal matters, and that it was impossible to determine which factor had been decisive.
Still, he said, "I'm fairly certain that we could and should have shortened the war, brought back all the hostages, perhaps a year earlier, moved forward, and maybe saved thousands of lives on both sides. It is likely that some of the hostages who were killed or murdered in Gaza could also have returned alive to their families."
Alon was later asked about the tension between the war's two objectives, destroying Hamas and returning the hostages. He acknowledged that there had been significant tension between them, but argued that, in retrospect, the strategic achievements obtained after two years of intense fighting were not materially different from those that could have been achieved earlier.
He said the agreement reached in October 2025 was slightly better than an arrangement that could have been reached several months earlier, but not from a strategic standpoint. He noted that even after the war, Hamas remained in power and continued to control Gaza's population, although it no longer controlled more than half of the territory of the Gaza Strip.
'Not leadership based on slogans such as total victory'
In another part of the discussion, Alon addressed the October 7 failure and the leadership's conduct during the war.
"On October 7, there was of course a severe intelligence and military failure, alongside a mistaken and catastrophic conception by the political leadership," he said.
Alon said that while the government struggled to manage the war, Israeli society demonstrated initiative, solidarity, and mutual responsibility. He said meeting members of the public and thousands of Israelis who worked on behalf of the hostages and their families gave him personal strength during the difficult period in which he headed the directorate.
He contrasted what he viewed as the positive qualities of Israeli society with sharp criticism of the country's leadership.
"Israel needs leadership that takes responsibility as it is and offers hope. Not leadership that relies on slogans such as 'total victory,' but leadership that presents realistic and balanced plans for dealing with our security, economic, and social challenges."
Alon added that despite manifestations of extremism in Israeli society, the war had also revealed extraordinary civilian strengths.
"We definitely need different leadership, which will take these wonderful people forward with a realistic approach," he said.
Changing security doctrine: Buffer zones and military freedom of action
Alon also addressed the profound change that October 7 brought to Israeli attitudes toward the Palestinians and the prospects for a diplomatic agreement.
He said many Israelis had developed a deep loss of trust in the Palestinian side, in the two-state solution, and in the very possibility of reaching an agreement. The fact that the Hamas attack was carried out inside the June 4, 1967, lines, rather than only in connection with the dispute over territories captured that year, deepened the sense that the conflict extended beyond the question of borders.
He added that the brutality of the massacre, its documentation on social media, and the kidnapping of women, children, and elderly people deepened the trauma and made it more difficult for many Israelis to distinguish between Hamas and the broader Palestinian population, or to feel empathy for suffering on the other side.
Security thinking had changed as well, Alon said. The current approach relies on establishing buffer zones not only in Gaza but also in Lebanon and Syria, while demanding full military freedom of action, including extensive destruction of neighborhoods and villages within those buffer zones.
Nevertheless, Alon expressed hope that after Israel's elections, scheduled for October 27, a deeper understanding would emerge regarding the limitations of military force.
"I believe that over time there will be a deeper understanding of the limitations of the use of force, alongside recognition that diplomatic measures and nonmilitary solutions are necessary to deal with our national security problems," he said.
In closing, Alon pointed to diplomatic possibilities involving Lebanon and Syria as an opportunity for regional change. Progress in those arenas, he said, could be the first step toward creating renewed optimism regarding the broader Israeli-Arab conflict.

Pardes Hanna-Karkur offers new food scene
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:35:27 UTC
06:35:27 KST

I’ve lived in Israel for almost 40 years, and as far as I can remember, I’ve never been to Pardes Hanna-Karkur. I knew it had a reputation as a kind of hippie mecca but had no idea it was also a food destination.
With just 50,000 people and no hotels (although one is in the planning stage), it is surprising how extensive the food scene is.
“Pardes Hanna is a colorful community, and that is an advantage for us,” Eyal Kogan, the deputy mayor of Pardes Hanna-Karkur, told The Jerusalem Post. “We already have at least 30 restaurants, and it’s going to get bigger and bigger.”
The city offers a range of restaurants, from casual to chef-driven. Some are kosher with a kashrut certificate, others are kosher without a certificate, and a few are non-kosher. All of the restaurants I visited were kosher with a teudah.
We started our morning at Bagels, a food truck behind the Sonol gas station, owned by 26-year-old Eitan Vallach. He originally opened the bagel truck in Kibbutz Hagoshrim in the summer of 2025. After the war with Lebanon expanded, he moved south and ended up here.
Eitan's food truck imports its bagels from New York
What’s unique about his food truck is that Eitan imports the bagels from New York. They come 80% baked, and he finishes them here. As a former New Yorker, I can attest that the bagels were excellent. They also have great tuna salad and several other dishes. Definitely worth a stop.
We stepped into the Being Wellness Center, which is basically like a WeWork but with a sauna, ice bath, and smoothie bar. Wonder if you can do a Zoom from an ice bath?
Our next stop was Café Hatzvi, where everyone who wasn’t at the Being Wellness Center seemed to be, all of them pecking away at laptops. There is a large outdoor area, and the menu is vegetarian/vegan.
We tried two vegan smoothies: a viral blue one made with spirulina and a banana-cocoa-mango mix that I preferred over the blue one, even though the color was prettier.
Lentil hummus vs chickpea hummus
One of the more interesting dishes was lentil hummus, which tasted very different from chickpea hummus. We didn’t want to eat too much because we still had two more stops ahead of us.
Next was Hersheleh’s bistro, a chef-run restaurant run by three siblings and often visited by Israeli celebrities like Eden Hason and Hanan Ben Ari. The food is unique and creative, including raw fish dishes like tuna tartare, bruschetta, and fatayer, a Palestinian dish made from pockets of dough stuffed with spinach and cheese. Really outstanding food and presentation.
Our last stop was Pasta Loco, run by a husband-and-wife team, and tucked into a small strip mall. A laundry line runs through the center of the small restaurant, where Chef Gilad Vazana and his wife Adi make customers feel like family. Gilad and Adi have spent a lot of time in Italy, and it shows.
I love surprises and was happy to taste the Pasta Loco Surprise, which basically means whatever Gilad feels like serving you. In this case, it was inky black tortellini (the secret is zinc mixed into the dough) with black garlic served on a cream garlic confit with butter and pecorino. Just wow!
There was also one of the best pizzas I’ve had in Israel.
“We have a community, not customers,” Gilad told me. “I go to their bar mitzvahs and weddings. I want people to feel like I’m hosting them in my home.”

- The backlash comes as Hilton trails Democratic front-runner Xavier Becerra, while some conservatives who called the ad “grotesque” say they still support him.
A provocative, sexually suggestive ad by GOP gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton is drawing heat from his fellow Republicans while drawing millions of viewers online.
Two young women sit on a bed, with an LGBTQ+ flag in the background, with one urging the other to try a new experience.
“I can’t believe I’m doing this,” one woman says, and the other replies. “Don’t be nervous. It’s not that bad ... Just try it. Look, give me your hand. Close your eyes, and I’ll do all the work.”
She leads the hesitant woman’s hand to mark her ballot for Hilton rather than Democrat Xavier Becerra, the front-runner in the race, and says, “Now lick it,” referring to the mail ballot envelope.
Fellow Republicans as well as several Democrats denounced Hilton over the messaging.
Two members of Hilton’s GOP “Golden Ticket” on the Nov. 3 ballot lashed out about the ad’s content.
“I emphatically denounce the use of young women as a political tool,” Michael Gates, the Republican candidate for attorney general who has frequently appeared alongside Hilton at campaign events, wrote on X. “California families deserve better, and as AG, I will fight every day to protect our girls, young women, and parental rights.”
Sonja Shaw, who is running to be the next state superintendent of schools, castigated Hilton, the state Republican party and its chairwoman for promoting the ad, which had been viewed by nearly 5 million people as of Saturday afternoon.
“Shame on you ... for reposting and cheering this creepy, weird, disturbing garbage,” Shaw wrote on X. “This is a clear example of exactly why good people are walking away from the Republican Party. As a mother and someone who has fought to protect the innocence of children, this crosses a line. We have lost our way. Embarrassing.”
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Long Beach), an openly gay member of Congress, and state Democratic Party chairman Rusty Hicks also condemned the ad.
“This is a bizarre and desperate ad from a person who has attacked the LGBTQ+ community and stands with Donald Trump,” Garcia said. “Hilton is losing and more interested in AI slop than actually talking about issues Californians care about.”
Hilton acknowledged the ad has provoked strong reactions, but it underscored the foundation of his campaign — that many Californians may be put off by his party affiliation but want change given the state’s myriad problems, such as growing unaffordability, that have taken place under a Democratic lock of every statewide office and the state Legislature.
“We’re just saying, you know, just try it,” he said in an interview. “It’s a provocative and humorous way of making a point, right? Which often the best communication does.”
He also said the ad does not conflict with his beliefs about restrictions on gender-affirming care and on youth sports because those would only apply to people who are not adults.
A spokesman for Becerra, who led Hilton 58% to 33% in a recent UC Berkeley/Los Angeles Times poll, was gleeful about the rift the ad was creating among Republicans.
“MAGA is melting down over Steve Hilton’s creepy ad because they’re finally seeing him for the sellout he really is, willing to abandon his own twisted values to get ahead,” said Jonathan Underland.
As Californians prepare to elect a new governor in November, the top concern they want the new leader to prioritize is reducing the state’s entrenched high cost of living, according to a new poll.
However, some conservatives who were dismayed by the message stood by Hilton’s side.
Pastor Jack Hibbs of Calvary Chapel Chino Hills, a Christian nationalist, called the ad “grotesque” and said it promoted lesbianism among young women, on a Facebook Live post Saturday. However, he said he still supports Hilton over Becerra. He did not respond to requests for comment.
Hilton is scheduled to speak on Monday to a chapter of the Log Cabin Republicans, an LGBTQ group, at a brewery in Palm Desert. The organization did not respond to requests for comment.
Former California GOP chairwoman Jessica Millan Patterson said that while the ad wasn’t for her, she understood the campaign’s desire to expand its reach to different voters.
“Does the ad speak to me? No. He’s not going after my vote. He already has my vote. He’s trying to think of new and creative ways to make people who wouldn’t normally feel like voting for a Republican feel safe to do so,” she said. “He’s going out of his comfort zone and going for people that wouldn’t normally feel comfortable voting for him.”
Californian Fred Karger, who made history in 2012 as the first openly gay person to run for president, had mixed views about the ad, calling it shrewd yet hypocritical. And he questioned its effectiveness.
“The audience that he’s targeting there — the hipster, young hipster, lesbian audience — probably has a 1% chance of voting for him,” Karger said. “So it’s kind of a long shot. But it is a clever ad.”

Baby bonuses fail to address the fear of falling behind
In highly competitive societies like Hong Kong and Singapore, subsidies and parental leave can’t overcome the cultural pressure keeping young couples from starting families
When one of my seniors from medical school was pregnant during her surgical residency, she planned the exact date of her C-section so she could complete her training on time. When I asked why she didn’t consider taking maternity leave to recuperate afterwards, she said she couldn’t bring herself to lag behind her peers. “I didn’t want motherhood to slow me down,” she said.
In medicine, it is common for women to delay childbearing until after their early career years, often into their mid-thirties or later. When I speak to friends in professional careers such as law, accounting and consulting, they echo a similar sentiment.

Comando may be tiny, but Mexico’s national guard is giving him a very big role.
Outfitted with miniature goggles, a fitted tactical vest, a helmet and even a petite head-mounted camera, the 7lb (15lb) chihuahua has become the most unusual – and smallest – canine member of the force.
Officers said the 13-month-old pup is being trained not just as a crowd-pleasing mascot but for search-and-rescue work as well.
Diminutive Comando, who stands 21cm (8in) tall, looks nothing like the powerful dogs usually associated with military or police units.
During a training session in Mexico City last week, the little dog scampered up stairs and over obstacles while a much larger, fully trained canine named Roko looked on.
Lt Debora Hernandez said Comando challenges two stereotypes: that only big dogs can serve in the national guard, and that a military-style force cannot build a warmer connection with the public. His presence, she said, reminds people that “beneath the uniform, we are human beings”.
The force adopted Comando about six months ago in the northern state of Chihuahua, which inspired the breed’s name, after his elderly owners became unable to care for him. Comando now appears at civic ceremonies, school events and community outreach programs.
Comando is an outlier in a national guard canine force of about 350 dogs, most of them traditional working breeds such as German shepherds and labrador retrievers.
Chihuahuas, known for their large, upright ears, big personalities and expressive eyes, may be alert and energetic, but they are rarely seen as candidates for serious operational work.
Comando has already appeared in Mexico’s Independence Day parade and has inspired his own animated likeness and a growing crop of memes on social media.

Ukraine’s bomber drones, ones that dropped ground robots in its recent Donetsk counteroffensive, are getting 2.4-kilogram jammer to shield them from FPVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:26:50 UTC
06:26:50 KST

A Ukrainian firm is testing a jammer light enough to ride on a heavy bomber drone and shield it from the enemy FPVs that hunt it. Aura-Ukraine has begun final tests of the system, called Aura 3K mini, the Dignitas Fund, a charity developing it with the manufacturer, Oboronka reports.
The bombers it is built to protect have become some of Ukraine's most valued drones. In the Donetsk operation last month, heavy bombers dropped kamikaze ground robots more than 10 kilometers behind Russian lines. The same weapon has been fitted with guided bombs that strike at long range with high precision.
At the same time, heavy bombers are large, making them prime targets for Russia. Keeping them in the air, and out of enemy hands, is the point of the new shield.
Two jammers cover 360 degrees
Aura 3K mini wraps the drone in a spherical, 360-degree cover using two broadband jammers, the fund says. Two emitters, not one, close the blind angles a single jammer would leave.
They work across the 2.1 to 2.8 GHz band, enough to disrupt FPV drones without cutting the bomber's own Starlink link. The whole device weighs about 2.4 kilograms.
"Radiation-pattern tests start on the front line in the coming days," the fund's press service says, and if they succeed, the system is set for serial production.
The fund moves to automate it
The next step is to make the jammer smarter, the fund says. It wants an auto-on function that fires only when a threat is detected, so the bomber does not give away its position with constant emission.
The team also plans to adapt Aura 3K mini to Vampire-type bombers, the heavy night drones that Russian troops nickname "Baba Yaga". That would widen the shield's reach across more of Ukraine's bomber fleet.
Russia hunts the Baba Yaga
The nickname points to a fairytale Slavic witch who flies by night. The real thing has been hard for Russia to counter: in 2024, a Ukrainian night bomber was often impossible to jam and, by one account, could be destroyed only with a flamethrower. By 2025, Russia was offering its soldiers 10 days' leave for capturing a Baba Yaga it could not build itself.

Rev Mariann Edgar Budde, the Episcopal bishop of Washington DC who gained national attention when she called on Donald Trump to “have mercy” on the country’s immigrants and LGBTQ+ community after his second inauguration, is resigning.
Budde shared in her resignation letter that she will be leaving her post on 3 June 2028 after the consecration and ordination of the new diocesan bishop.
“I write today because I have discerned, in consultation with diocesan leadership and the Presiding Bishop’s office, that it is time to begin preparing for the election of your next bishop. I have not come to this decision lightly or alone, and it will not be easy to say goodbye to the diocese I love,” her letter said.
Next week, the standing committee will outline the steps required, which include the appointment of two committees to undertake this work, the letter added.
Budde, 66, is the first woman to serve as the spiritual leader of the Episcopal diocese of Washington. She has been leading the diocese since her election to the role in 2011. Before that, she served as the rector of St John’s Episcopal church in Minneapolis for 18 years.
She made headlines for urging Trump during her sermon to show mercy to “gay, lesbian and transgender children” from all political backgrounds, some of whom, she said, “fear for their lives”.
Trump demanded an apology in a post shared on social media.
“She brought her church into the World of politics in a very ungracious way. She was nasty in tone, and not compelling or smart,” the president said.
“Apart from her inappropriate statements, the service was a very boring and uninspiring one. She is not very good at her job! She and her church owe the public an apology!”
It was not the first time Budde had called out and clashed with Trump.
During Trump’s first term, she published an opinion piece in the New York Times, expressing outrage over Trump’s appearance in front of St John’s Episcopal holding up a Bible for a photo after federal officers had used force to clear a crowd of peaceful protesters demonstrating against the police killing of George Floyd the previous week.
Budde wrote that Trump had “used sacred symbols to cloak himself in the mantle of spiritual authority, while espousing positions antithetical to the Bible that he held in his hands”.
Looking towards the future of the Episcopal diocese of Washington, Budde wrote, she is committed to ensuring a strong and healthy transition for her successor.
“Alongside the diocesan staff and leadership bodies, I will do everything in my power to ensure that the diocese is as strong and healthy as possible for this leadership transition. I am praying for all involved, and especially for the one God is preparing to serve as the tenth bishop of the Diocese of Washington,” Budde concluded.

‘Which homeland?’ American Jews do not have to choose between Israel and US - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:17:59 UTC
06:17:59 KST

As America celebrated its Bicentennial on July 4, 1976, my father called me over to the television. I was outside enjoying the local fireworks, so I was surprised that he would interrupt the fun on such a special night.
Putting his arm around me, he pointed at the screen. “Look.”
I expected to see fireworks over Boston Harbor. Instead, the news was focused on a word I could not pronounce, let alone understand: Entebbe.
My father explained that an airplane carrying many Israelis and Jews had been hijacked, that the hostages were being held in Uganda, and that Israel had undertaken a courageous mission to rescue them. We watched prime minister Yitzhak Rabin welcome the hostages home as blue and white flags waved in the background.
With tears pooling in his eyes, my father said, “This is why we have a homeland.”
As an eight-year-old, I did not fully understand what had happened, but my father’s impassioned message etched itself into my soul and helped shape my Jewish identity.
Over the past 50 years, I have returned to that moment many times. Only recently did I recognize the question I never thought to ask him that night:
Which homeland?
I know that my father meant Israel. But 50 years later, I hear his words differently.
Israel and America occupy distinct but deeply connected places in the modern Jewish story. Israel is the ancestral homeland of the Jewish people, representing Jewish sovereignty, peoplehood, and return. Its strength made the improbable rescue at Entebbe possible.
America, meanwhile, became a civic home for generations of Jews, offering something historically extraordinary: a haven from persecution and the possibility of becoming full participants in society while remaining distinctly Jewish.
These are not equivalent forms of belonging in the public square, but neither must they be competing ones. A strong Israel and a confident American Jewish community are not rival projects. Like Babylon and Jerusalem centuries ago, each is essential to the future of the Jewish people, and each places responsibilities upon those who call it home.
That unresolved question, what it means to belong deeply to the Jewish people while participating fully in American life, inspired Rabbi Menachem Creditor, scholar-in-residence at UJA-Federation of New York, and me to co-edit American Torah at 250. This collection of original sermons and Torah reflections for the weekly portions of 5787 marks the 250th anniversary of the United States.
The volume invites Jewish communities to encounter the American story through Torah, and Torah through the experience of American democracy. The overarching theme examines what America has made possible for Jews and other minorities while asking what its unfinished experiment in self-government requires of us.
That question has become more urgent since October 7. The massacre, the suffering of the hostages, the ensuing war, and the alarming normalization of antisemitism have shaken the sense of security long enjoyed by many American Jews.
The blurring of anti-Zionism and antisemitism has demonstrated how readily attacks on Israel’s legitimacy become attacks on Jewish history, American Jewish identity, and our belonging in the public square and the halls of government.
American Jewry has created an extraordinary network of synagogues, schools, scholarship, philanthropy, advocacy, and public leadership with global significance. It is a vital center of Jewish religious, intellectual, educational, and communal life. Its strength matters to Israel, just as Israel’s strength matters to Jews throughout the world.
The contributors to American Torah at 250 represent different movements, communities, and political perspectives. They do not speak with one voice, nor should they. Jewish tradition has never demanded uniformity of thought. Our sacred literature preserves disagreement because the search for wisdom is strengthened by multiple voices wrestling seriously with enduring questions.
Throughout the collection, rabbis, educators, and thought leaders examine freedom and responsibility, covenant and the Constitution, justice and religious liberty, pluralism and public trust, memory and hope. They ask how Jews can participate fully in American civic life without surrendering our particular commitments, including our bond with Israel and the Jewish people.
These are not questions separate from Torah. They are Torah questions.
Torah asks what it means to build a society worthy of our highest values. Jewish tradition teaches that disagreement need not destroy community, that power carries obligations, that the rule of law is the bedrock of a just society, and that human beings are responsible for one another.
American Jewish experience
For Israeli readers, America’s 250th anniversary may seem like a distant national commemoration. Yet America’s democratic ideals, global influence, and relationship with Israel have profoundly shaped modern Jewish history.
Understanding America’s promises, tensions, and unfinished work is essential to understanding the largest Jewish community outside Israel and the relationship between the two great centers of contemporary Jewish life.
Fifty years after that July 4 night, I can still see my father pointing toward the television and hear his voice: “This is why we have a homeland.”
Today, I understand that I inherited more than one story of home from my parents. Each has shaped me and carries obligations. And each has sustained the Jewish people in different ways.
As we prepare to read the Torah again, American Torah at 250 invites us to examine the rights, responsibilities, and reasons for hope embedded in the American Jewish experience.
Perhaps the question before us as Jews is not simply where we belong. It is what our belonging asks of us. As Pirkei Avot reminds us, “Turn it over and turn it over; it’s all in there.”
The writer is a civic educator and the executive director of Civic Spirit, a nonpartisan organization that provides training in civic education to Jewish, Catholic, and Christian day schools to prepare students to be informed and engaged members of American democracy. He is the 2026 recipient of The Covenant Foundation Award for Excellence in Jewish Education.

Green members give their take on the Zionism is Racism motion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:16:50 UTC
06:16:50 KST

Breadcrumb
‘It has to pass’: Green Party members give their take on the Zionism is Racism motion
Members of the Green Party voiced strong opinions on the upcoming Zionism is racism motion at the annual conference in Brighton, with some saying they would struggle to remain members if it did not pass.
The motion, set to be voted on Sunday, calls for the party to define Zionism as a racist, settler‑colonial ideology and declare itself against it.
While the motion drew a record number of co-proposers and was endorsed by the likes of Greta Thunberg, concerns have been raised about key demands.
"If you want a homeland, then therefore you're taking somebody's land for it based on identity; that is racism, so yes, Zionism is racism. Of course, I want the motion to go through," Green Party member Alex Blower told The New Arab.
"If we're going to fight against settlements, and we're going to fight against genocide and apartheid, the same way as this country did back in the 80s against South Africa, which we recognise as a racist ideology, we have to recognise this as the racist ideology it is," Blower continued.
"Look at what [Zionism is] doing, look at what it's done, there is no manifestation of this ideology that does not involve the suffering, the subjugation, of other people seen as lesser than those who want the land."
Zoë Garbett, the newly elected mayor of Hackney in London, explained that she wanted to separate the concept from the question of whether Zionism is racism from the motion.
"I think it's been quite clear that we can say…that the acts that we see taking place in Palestine are clearly racist and clearly taken from a political ideology that is racist, and I think that's clear," Zoë Garbett told The New Arab.
While she agrees with the concept of Zionism being racism, the mayor wanted to leave the motion to the conference floor.
Many expressed optimism that the motion would pass.
"I think it's an important one we need to be having as a conversation in this country," member Humza Egal told The New Arab.
"Sometimes things go your way, sometimes they don't go your way. But I think from the overwhelming support for the motion, and how it's been put together, I think it will pass."
Green Party member Keith Garrett agreed with the sentiment, saying the motion was the main reason he went to Brighton. “[The motion] should totally pass. I mean it has to pass for the Green Party to have a position on this," he said.
When asked how he would feel if the motion failed, Garrett said he believes he would struggle to remain a member of the Green Party.
"I think it's that serious. We need to take a stand on what's happening across the world," Garrett explained. "I think a lot of it is essentially just giving determination to the Palestinian people."
"So, we have essentially forced a solution that wasn't theirs onto them. So now we need to help them and the people who are still in Israel work out a solution together."
Meanwhile, Garbett said she recognised the connection many may have to the issue, referring to the Green Party's strong stance towards Palestine, adding that "it would be a shame" if the motion causes divisions within the party.
However, for others, whether the motion fails or passes will not be the "be all or end all".
"We are already an anti-Zionist party… there's not really any disagreement about the need for Palestinian liberation within the party," member Eugene McCarthy told The New Arab.
"Ethnonationalism is racism, and Zionism is ethnonationalism. I don't think you need a motion to say that."

====================================================================================================

Northern Czechia travel guide: Rock cities, forest trails, and Saxon Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:01:54 UTC
06:01:54 KST

Prague may be the main draw for first-time visitors to Czechia, but just beyond the capital lies a very different side of the country. Northern Czechia combines dramatic sandstone landscapes, forest trails, picturesque towns, family attractions, and thermal wellness, while across the border, Saxon Switzerland adds some of the region’s most spectacular viewpoints.
We spent our first two days exploring Prague before heading north, blending active outdoor adventures with time to slow down and unwind.
48 hours in Prague with the Prague visitor pass
Countless articles have been written about Prague, one of Europe’s most beautiful cities. Although you could easily spend an entire trip exploring the capital, it remains an essential stop for anyone visiting Czechia for the first time. With 48 hours to spare, we opted for the Prague Visitor Pass.
Available for various durations, the pass includes public transit, a ride on historic Tram 42, and admission to museums, towers, guided tours, and river cruises. Additionally, pass holders can access reserved admission to high-demand attractions, where regular tickets can sell out weeks in advance, such as the Clementinum.
Armed with our 48-hour passes, we set out to explore the city. We rode the historic tram, stopped at some of Prague’s key sights, and joined introductory tours of the Old Town and Jewish Quarter. One of the more unusual experiences was a medieval Prague tour, which took us beneath the present-day streets.
Parts of Prague were rebuilt at a higher level after repeated floods, leaving former ground-floor rooms beneath the modern city. Walking through these underground spaces offered a fascinating glimpse into everyday life in medieval Prague.
The Clementinum was another highlight, with its beautifully preserved Baroque Library Hall and Astronomical Tower. We timed our visit for sunset, when the city below began to light up, and the view from the tower was particularly striking.
Another standout experience was the guided tour of New City Hall, which includes a ride on Prague’s famous paternoster elevators. These doorless, continuously moving lifts have no buttons or stops between floors; passengers simply step in and out while the elevator keeps moving. The unusual system makes the ride itself one of the tour’s highlights.
Leaving Prague
While a car is unnecessary in Prague, where parking is both scarce and expensive, having your own wheels becomes essential once you leave the capital. We booked our car through Europcar Israel, which offers a broad selection of vehicles and locations, including major airports.
Driving in Czechia was relatively straightforward, although the narrow roads and frequent villages required close attention. This was where our high-end Czech-made Škoda Kodiaq proved its worth, particularly with features like adaptive cruise control, which adjusts to changing speed limits based on traffic signs, and Lane Assist.
Booking on the Israeli Europcar site also offers Israeli residents promotions and the option of “darkonit larechev,” an excess waiver that reimburses the deductible in the event of an accident or theft at a lower cost. A nice little bonus awaited us when we returned the car we had rented in Israel at the Europcar branch at Ben-Gurion Airport: a free library where travelers can pick up a book for their flight.
Czechia’s rock cities: From Prachov to Adršpach
Bohemian Paradise (Ceský ráj) is one of northern Czechia’s most striking landscapes, known for its dramatic sandstone formations, forests, castles, and natural viewpoints.
Among the area’s most popular routes are the Prachov Rocks (Prachovské skály). We chose a challenging 3.5-kilometer circular trail that took about two and a half hours, including an ascent of roughly 250 meters. The route winds through towering sandstone formations, narrow gorges, and panoramic viewpoints. On clear days, rock climbers can also be seen scaling the cliffs.
Not far away, Hrubá Skála Castle makes a great stop for lunch with a view and a quick tour. For an easier walk, the route to Mariánská vyhlídka offers a relatively flat 3 km. trail takes about an hour and a half, with views toward the castle and surrounding rock formations.
Another of the region’s best-known attractions is Adršpach Rock City, where scenes from The Chronicles of Narnia were filmed.
The reserve offers several routes. We followed the 3.5 km. green-marked trail, which passes a lake, the Gothic Gate, dramatic rock formations, a waterfall, a viewpoint, and narrow gorges. The walk takes around three hours at a relaxed pace, with plenty of opportunities to stop for photographs, and includes numerous stairs.
The towering sandstone formations have names like The Lovers, The Tooth, The Indian, and The Elephants. With its narrow passages, unusual rock shapes, and forested valleys, the landscape has an unmistakably otherworldly feel.
Reservations are recommended, particularly during busy periods, as visitor numbers are controlled and the reserve is extremely popular.
Treetop walk Krkonoše
The region also offers a wide range of accommodations and attractions, from family-friendly resorts to alpine coasters, rope parks, ziplines, museums and water parks. One of our highlights was the Treetop Walk Krkonoše.
The attraction offers a different perspective on the forests of Krkonoše National Park, taking visitors from the forest floor into the treetops along an elevated wooden walkway. The route winds through the forest before reaching a 43-meter observation tower offering views across the surrounding mountains and forests.
A newer family feature is the Bear Trail, an interactive path where visitors can learn about brown bears and observe two resident bears, Michal and Alica, from above in a large, forested enclosure designed with their needs in mind.
Despite arriving in rainy weather, we enjoyed wandering among the treetops, testing our courage on the high-altitude suspended net platforms and watching the surrounding landscape disappear into the mist. The informative displays along the way added another dimension to the experience, making it enjoyable for everyone in our group.
Saxon Switzerland
We concluded our journey in Saxon Switzerland, a dramatic region straddling the border between Germany and Czechia. The area is home to two famous landmarks: the Bastei Bridge on the German side and Pravcická brána on the Czech side, which served as yet another filming location for The Chronicles of Narnia.
Originally built of wood in the early 19th century for pioneering travelers, the Bastei Bridge was rebuilt in sandstone in 1851. It offers a fascinating glimpse into the early days of European romantic tourism. Walking across the historic structure, surrounded by towering sandstone formations, is an impressive experience in itself.
Nearby viewing platforms offer spectacular panoramas of the Elbe Valley, stretching across the landscape below. Because of its breathtaking scenery and easy access, the site is a major tourist magnet that gets extremely crowded, especially on clear days.
In the picturesque town of Bad Schandau, we took the historic elevator up to a panoramic viewpoint and enjoyed a leisurely walk back down. For those seeking an extra surge of adrenaline, the Czech side also features an exciting via ferrata route.
Hotel Elbresidenz and Toskana Therme, Bad Schandau
After several days of hiking, we were more than ready for a hotel where wellness was part of the experience rather than an afterthought. We stayed at the elegant Hotel Elbresidenz in Bad Schandau, located in the heart of Saxon Switzerland.
The hotel sits beside the Elbe River, with gardens overlooking the water and surrounding cliffs. Its architecture combines preserved 19th-century structures with newer additions built following extensive restoration after severe flooding in the region over the past two decades. The property has its own wellness facilities, while hotel guests also receive unlimited access to the adjacent Toskana Therme.
Each morning began with a generous breakfast buffet, and we headed out on the trails. After several hours of walking, one of the most enjoyable parts of the day was returning to the hotel and heading straight to the wellness complex. Wearing our hotel robes, we simply walked next door to the Toskana Therme.
The complex features moderately heated indoor and outdoor pools overlooking the Elbe, a lazy river, a children’s pool with a small slide, a variety of saunas, and even an ice fountain. We also treated ourselves to a massage with sea salt scrub and velvety lotion from the extensive body treatment menu, which was particularly welcome after long days on the trails.
The centerpiece of the facility is the Liquid Sound® experience: a softly lit circular pool filled with warm saltwater, with music playing simultaneously above and under the water. Visual projections move across the domed ceiling as you float, creating an immersive and unusually peaceful experience.
After hours spent hiking, floating in the warm saltwater to the sound of music and watching the projections move across the dome was a memorable way to end the journey.

Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of air strikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kiev and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.
Ukraine's intelligence services has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a "new doctrine" of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of this winter, Zelenskyy claimed on Saturday.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals," Zelenskyy told Reuters in an interview.
"To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation."
Driving the shift in policy, Zelenskyy said, was Putin's desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key frontline region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment.
Russia urges foreigners to leave Kiev
But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kiev, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Zelenskyy said a successful Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named "Vivaldi", had recaptured around 140 sq km of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region and was still ongoing.
Russia has said it must control Donbass in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, US President Donald Trump's administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict – Europe's bloodiest since World War Two.
The US leader last month urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelenskyy, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks, or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure.
For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro river connecting east and west Kiev.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine would react to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not target civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
"We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners etc: what gives money to them for this war," Zelenskyy said in English.
"But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."

Tories plan to expand free childcare to high earners to end ‘cliff edge’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:00:09 UTC
06:00:09 KST

The Conservatives have unveiled a proposed £700m childcare giveaway for high earners ahead of their annual conference, saying they would end the “cliff edge” where free entitlement ends at salaries above £100,000.
The plan, set out the day before the event begins in Birmingham, follows the earlier proposal by Kemi Badenoch’s party to abolish most stamp duty, another change to taxation that would disproportionately benefit wealthier people.
Under the current system, put in place under Rishi Sunak’s government, families with young children in England are eligible for 30 hours a week of free childcare, but this cuts off if one parent earns more than £100,000, irrespective of another parent’s salary.
Under the Conservative plans, this limit would be abolished, with all parents working 16 or more hours a week able to claim the childcare.
The party says it would cost aabout £700m a year, which it says would be paid for by cutting jobs at organisations such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency.
In comments released to promote the idea, Badenoch said the current system was “absurd” and a disincentive to work more.
She said: “Conservatives believe that you shouldn’t be punished for working more, but this childcare cliff edge does exactly that.
“I’m a mum-of-three and I’ve had to make the same choices many families have had to make on work and childcare. Those choices are difficult already, government should not be making them harder.
“No one should be turning down a promotion or a pay rise because they literally cannot afford to earn more.
“It is often women who end up carrying more of the childcare responsibility so a system that makes it harder for them to progress in their careers is not helping families, it is not helping women and it is definitely not helping the economy.”
A Labour spokesperson said: “It tells you everything you need to know about the Tories that the first of their own tax policies they want to unpick is one helping higher earners. They clearly don’t want to admit that they set the thresholds in the first place.”
The idea of abolishing stamp duty on people’s primary residences in England and Northern Ireland was unveiled by Badenoch at last year’s conference, costing an estimated £9bn a year.
While some economists have argued that stamp duty can have a drag on the housing market and even the economy, as it disincentivises moving, scrapping it rather than reforming the tax would disproportionately benefit better-off people and those in London and south-east England.
The other main policy set out ahead of the conference was a plan to build 50,000 new prison spaces in England and Wales, a 50% expansion in capacity.
This would be paid for in part by slashing overseas aid to £1bn a year, a 90% cut on current plans. Under Keir Starmer, Labour said they would reduce aid from 0.5% of GDP to 0.3% by 2027, but even that lower proportion would still amount to £9bn a year.
When Reform UK announced plans to cut aid to £1bn a year, aid groups warned that this would not cover existing contributions to global bodies such as the UN and World Bank, shredding Britain’s international influence.

Filmed El Al jet days after Oct. 7: What we know about flydubai suspect and his troubling online trail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
20:58:55 UTC
05:58:55 KST

The investigation is still in its early stages, but troubling details are already emerging about the background of Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, accused of trying to crash a flydubai passenger jet bound for Israel — information that raises questions about whether warning signs should have been detected by Israeli transportation and security authorities.
Despite those apparent red flags, al-Hammami was cleared to fly to Israel. The alleged attack was thwarted only after Indian captain Smit Machchhar, despite being badly wounded, managed to open the cockpit door, allowing Israeli passengers and others aboard to rush in and subdue the co-pilot.
An Israeli security official told CNN that authorities are examining whether al-Hammami intended to carry out a terrorist attack modeled on the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks in the United States.
Here is what is known so far about the Omani pilot — and about social media posts CNN reported appeared on accounts bearing his name after the attempted attack.
From Oman Air to flydubai
Al-Hammami, an Omani citizen, was born in the United Arab Emirates to an Omani father and Syrian mother and spent part of his life in the UAE.
According to a LinkedIn profile bearing his name that was deleted after the incident, he worked for Oman Air, the country’s national carrier, for seven years, until February 2025.
In 2024, while still working as a co-pilot for Oman Air, “extremist material” was reportedly found in his possession. He was subsequently removed from flying duties but continued working for the airline in an administrative position.
CBS reported a somewhat different account, saying he worked for Oman Air for only a “short time” and was suspended from flying after accessing “extremist websites.” According to that report, he subsequently left the airline.
Another report said the suspension followed suspicions that al-Hammami had undergone jihadist radicalization, apparently while spending time in Syria.
According to the LinkedIn profile, al-Hammami joined Moroccan carrier Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and left six months later, in January 2026. The airline, however, said al-Hammami underwent three months of training but was not ultimately hired.
The profile also said al-Hammami studied at Buckinghamshire New University in England. A university official confirmed that a person by that name completed a three-year distance-learning program, graduating in 2023 with a degree in aviation management.
His subsequent employment with flydubai, which began this year, was not listed on the LinkedIn profile.
A diplomat from a Gulf country told The Associated Press that al-Hammami underwent standard security screening before he was hired. The checks, however, appeared to focus primarily on whether he had a criminal record rather than examining his background more deeply for potential signs of radicalization.
Posts appear hours after the attack
CNN reported that only two posts appeared on the LinkedIn profile bearing al-Hammami’s name — and both were published Wednesday, about nine hours after the attack.
It remains unclear who published the posts, CNN said, though the network raised the possibility that they had been scheduled in advance.
The first post contained a series of videos filmed from the cockpits of Boeing 737 MAX aircraft — the same aircraft family as the flydubai jet involved in Wednesday’s incident.
One of the videos was filmed at Dubai International Airport, according to CNN, and showed the person behind the camera zooming in on an El Al aircraft.
The cockpit display visible in the video showed the flight number of an Oman Air flight from Dubai to Muscat on Oct. 11, 2023, four days after the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attack on southern Israel.
The post included additional footage showing El Al aircraft and one plane belonging to Arkia, another Israeli carrier. It ended with an image of Ayman al-Zawahiri, the former leader of al-Qaida who succeeded Osama bin Laden and was killed in a U.S. drone strike in Kabul in 2022.
The alleged ‘prostitute test’
The second post on the deleted LinkedIn account contained an artificial intelligence-generated image depicting three cities sacred in Islam — Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem — connected by a continuous glowing path.
A song could be heard in the background containing declarations against “humiliation,” with the speaker saying he did not fear death and would defend his honor.
CNN also reported that an account on X, formerly Twitter, belonging to a person with al-Hammami’s name contained extreme religious views. The account has since been deleted.
According to CNN, the account contained about 3,000 posts. Some dealt with his mother’s attempts to arrange a marriage for him and his requirement that a prospective wife wear a niqab, the Islamic face covering that leaves only a narrow opening around the eyes.
“They all refused,” read a February 2022 post cited by CNN. “Then my mother told them, ‘My son is a pilot,’ and suddenly they all agreed.”
In another post, he expressed opposition to men and women working together.
“How many respectable and religious young women have been ruined in mixed workplaces between men and women and manipulated?” read a January 2022 post.
Another post described what he called tests he subjected women to while getting to know them.
“I don’t know how you have the patience to talk to one girl for four years,” the post said. “Most of the girls I talk to last two or three days, and I give them 100 tests, including the prostitute test. Thank God, none has lasted more than a week with me.”
The accounts and posts are now part of a growing body of information being examined as investigators seek to determine al-Hammami’s motives, whether he acted alone and how a pilot who had reportedly raised extremism concerns at a previous airline was later hired by flydubai and cleared to operate a flight carrying passengers to Israel.

Latvia partial election results put PM's pro-Ukraine party ahead but coalition partners stumble
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' pro-Ukraine and pro-Europe party was seen winning a parliamentary election on Saturday by an unexpectedly wide margin, partial results showed, even as projected results for other coalition parties suggested the centrist PM would have to form a new ruling coalition.

Partial results from Latvia's parliamentary election released on Sunday favoured Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centre-right party, suggesting the country will maintain its pro-European and pro-Ukrainian course.
But populist parties also had a good night after an election campaign dominated by fears over neighbouring Russia and the cost of living at home.
Kulbergs' centre-right United List party was in the lead with 35.8 percent, according to results published by the election commission, with over half of the vote counted.
"It's not the end still, but it's higher than expected," Kulbergs told journalists.
"That means people truly want change," he added, which he said meant "economic growth" and "a future for (Latvia's) children".
Kulbergs only assumed the post of prime minister in May.
But his coalition, which pre-election polling had suggested would weaken, will probably not survive in its current form.
One coalition partner, the Union of Greens and Farmers, was teetering around the five-percent threshold needed to enter parliament, with partial results released around 04:30am (0130 GMT) showing it finished with 5.1 percent of the vote.
Read moreRussian secret services target Latvia as Ukraine's drone offensive worries the Kremlin
Projected results from other coalition parties suggest Kulbergs will have to form a new ruling coalition.
Exit polls – which had put Kulbergs' party in the lead – are usually reliable, but voter reluctance to admit support for more radical parties may mean the populist parties perform better than anticipated.
"I do believe that the biggest increase (of the) actual results, compared to the exit polls, will be to the ... Russian-speaking electorate's supported parties, which are the Sovereign Power and Latvia First," Roberts Kits, an analyst at the Latvian think tank LaSER, told AFP.
Sigita Struberga, secretary general of Latvian transatlantic association LATO, said it was too early to accurately predict the shape of any future coalition.
"We really need to wait for (the) real percentage, which might be slightly different from what we see at this point," she told AFP.
Populist gains
Security questions were the main topic during the campaign in Latvia, an EU and NATO member state sitting on the eastern flank of both blocs.
But populist parties gained ground by focusing on domestic issues such as the cost of living.

Sovereign Power, criticised as pro-Russian by its detractors, finished in third place with 11 percent of the vote, according to partial results.
It has opposed military aid to Ukraine and further increases to defence spending, highlighting instead domestic economic problems.
Despite its gains, the party is unlikely to enter government because most major parties have ruled out working with it.
Another populist force, Latvia First, finished in second place (13.4 percent) according to partial results. Led by businessman Ainars Slesers, it could prove a more viable coalition partner.
The Progressives, a pro-European social democratic party advocating stronger social protections and continued support for Ukraine, finished fifth at 6.6 percent, partial results indicated.
Geopolitics and economics
Security remains central to political debate four years after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Latvia, a member of NATO and the European Union since 2004, views Russia as its principal security threat and has significantly increased defence spending in response.
It has sharply increased its defence spending since Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, now allocating nearly five percent of its GDP to defence.
Most parties expected to enter parliament back both high military spending and maintaining aid to Kyiv.
But rising living costs, low wages, strains on the healthcare system and long-term population decline all featured prominently in campaign debates.

Voting patterns among Latvia's large Russian-speaking minority are also changing.
Once concentrated behind the Harmony party, which lost parliamentary representation in 2022, many voters are increasingly making choices based on economic and social issues rather than identity politics alone.
"Because we are the external border of Europe, we must have a strong economy, a strong Latgale, a strong border region," Kulbergs said.
"That is the main task."
The preliminary, official results are expected on Sunday, at which point attention will quickly shift to the coalition talks, which could prove lengthy and complex.

A Nobel laureate’s deal: free Russia’s prisoners, fund the missiles hitting Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
20:57:42 UTC
05:57:42 KST

Dmitry Muratov, the Nobel Peace Prize laureate and co-founder of Russia's shuttered Novaya Gazeta, has lent his name to an idea that sounds like pure humanitarianism. Russia frees some of the people it jails for opposing the war; in return, the United States eases its sanctions on the Russian economy.
The scheme did not even start in an American office. According to The Atlantic, which reported the plan on 29 September, it was Muratov himself who urged Donald Trump's envoy, John Coale, to try it. Coale had used the same model on Belarus, where some 500 prisoners were released, sanctions softened, and trade talks reopened.
Now, with Trump's approval, he wants to run it on the Kremlin.
“A direct investment in ammunition flying across the border”: Belarusian defectors warn US sanctions relief is funding Russia’s war
The prisoners should go free. There is nothing to argue about there. No one jailed for anti-war words, for journalism, or for political dissent belongs in a cell. But here is the small detail: the price for their freedom is easing the pressure on a state that is waging war, not on the United States, which is being asked to ease the sanctions, but on Ukraine.
And here is where the real humanitarian arithmetic begins. We do not yet know which sanctions would be lifted. Whichever they are, the logic is the same: Moscow lets some of its political prisoners go, and Washington gives the Russian economy some breathing room in return. People walk out of Russian prisons, and the Kremlin gets more oxygen.
More money for the Russian state in wartime is not merely a figure in a bank report. It is more resources for the army, for missiles, for drones, for the war's continuation. And Ukrainians are the ones who feel it.
I can picture the Kremlin ghoul rubbing his hands at an idea like this. Now he can be not just president, but the director of a prisoner market: release a hundred today, jail three hundred tomorrow, so there is something to trade next time. New dissidents, journalists, activists, and merely inconvenient citizens he can pack away far faster than the West can lift a sanction.
A tidy little business model: Russia produces the prisoners, the West buys them back with its policy, and Ukraine settles the account.
Because if easing sanctions widens Russia's room to finance the war, then Ukrainians effectively get a very strange bill for someone else's humanism: a Russian political prisoner walks out of prison, and a Ukrainian gets a fresh portion of missiles and drones on their head.
By the way, about those Ukrainian civilians. By the estimates of international and Ukrainian rights groups, Russia is holding, or has held, some 16,000 of them illegally. The real figure may be higher, since not every case can be documented.
This is exactly where Muratov, as a Nobel peace laureate, might find his powers of persuasion useful. Why not put in a word for the Ukrainians in Russian prisons? The same people seized in occupied territory during "filtration," taken from their homes, buried under fabricated cases, held for years without a proper trial.
And among them are children.
And here onto the stage steps Russia's Baba Yaga of "child protection": Maria Lvova-Belova, the so-called presidential commissioner for children's rights. She herself told Putin, in public, about a boy from Mariupol she had taken into her care after he was removed from the occupied city. Ukraine and international organizations view such cases as part of a wider system of unlawful transfers of Ukrainian children to Russia. The International Criminal Court has issued a warrant for her arrest on exactly those charges: the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.
That is what Russian care for children looks like: take a Ukrainian child from Mariupol, carry him off to Russia, and set about turning him into a Russian. If this is how Russia's children's commissioner works in public, it is frightening to imagine what happens where there are no cameras and no international warrants.
Nobody is offering to lift a single sanction for them.
And Muratov's pacifist initiatives are not new, either. After the full-scale invasion, he was among the authors and promoters of the ceasefire appeals. One public statement, signed by 51 Nobel laureates, called for an end to the fighting, which Muratov later described as a plea for a "genuine ceasefire" before talks.
On paper it all looks wonderful: stop shooting, stop killing one another, make peace. But there is one small problem. Russia did not wander into this war alongside Ukraine. Russia launched the full-scale invasion itself.
And in these appeals, Muratov did not demand that the Kremlin withdraw its troops from Ukraine. He did not demand the de-occupation of Ukrainian territory. He did not put the question of responsibility for the aggression and the war crimes to Russia. The formula was far more convenient: just stop shooting.
But "stop killing each other" is a beautiful phrase for people who would rather not notice who attacked whom.
It turns aggressor and victim into two symmetrical sides, as though Ukraine and Russia had simply quarreled and now both must show wisdom and stop firing. There is just one nuance: if, after such a "peace," the Russian army remains on occupied Ukrainian territory, that is not an end to the aggression. It is a pause with a Russian flag on Ukrainian soil.
Now add the prisoner proposal on top. Russia does not withdraw its troops. Ukraine does not get its occupied territory back. The Kremlin answers for nothing. But a few Russian political prisoners are released, and for that, Russia's sanctions are eased too. And Ukraine, meanwhile, is simply supposed to stand to one side and rejoice that humanism has triumphed.
Except there is a difference of principle. A Russian political prisoner can walk out of a Russian prison. A Ukrainian civilian can stay in one. And a Ukrainian soldier can be killed by a weapon Russia bought thanks to that same sanctions relief.
And then a very simple question arises for the great humanist and Nobel laureate: why should the freedom of Russia's political prisoners be bought at the expense of the freedom, the safety, and the lives of Ukrainians?

ISW called Putin's claims about the capture of 1,300 sq km of Ukraine "hallucinations," as Russia lost territory
Kyiv • UNN
According to ISW, in September Russia did not capture 1,301 sq km, but lost up to 175.18 sq km of territory. The Kremlin's statements were called part of cognitive warfare.
Vladimir Putin’s claims about the alleged large-scale advance of the Russian army in Ukraine in September differ so markedly from the actual situation at the front that they “resemble hallucinations.” In fact, over the month, Russia did not seize any new territories; on the contrary, it lost some areas it had previously controlled, according to a report by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), UNN writes.
Details
On October 1, Putin stated that Russian troops had allegedly captured 1,301 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory during September. According to him, this was 2.5 times more than in previous months.
However, ISW calculations show the opposite picture. In September, Russian forces recorded a net territorial loss of 80.81 square kilometers. If areas that Russian military personnel entered but failed to establish control over are included, the figure reaches 175.18 square kilometers.
ISW explained where Putin may be getting such figures
Analysts believe that the Kremlin is attempting to create an exaggerated impression of the Russian army’s successes and convince Ukraine and the West that further Russian advances are supposedly inevitable. ISW views such statements as part of Russia’s cognitive warfare.
At the same time, the analysts do not claim that Putin is knowingly citing false figures. According to one version, the Russian military command itself may be passing him vastly exaggerated data about the situation at the front. ISW has previously drawn attention to the practice of so-called “beautiful reports,” in which Russian commanders inflate the scale of advances and conceal failures.
The situation at the front
This also contradicts recent assessments of the situation at the front. At the end of September, even a Russian military blogger linked to the Kremlin described the front line as “static,” which, according to ISW’s assessment, effectively indicates almost zero net advances by Russian forces over the past several months.
Putin also continues to claim that it is possible to seize the entire Donetsk region and uses such statements to justify demands concerning Ukrainian territories. At the same time, ISW has repeatedly recorded that the Russian command significantly exaggerates its successes on the battlefield.

3D printed concrete sculptures blend classical fragments with sci-fi forms at frieze sculpture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
20:35:51 UTC
05:35:51 KST

3D printed concrete sculptures blend classical fragments with sci-fi forms at frieze sculpture
three sculptures by matyáš chochola combine digital modeling, robotic fabrication, and handwork.
Matyáš Chochola’s artworks on show at Frieze Sculpture 2026
Czech artist Matyáš Chochola presents three 3D printed concrete sculptures at Frieze Sculpture 2026 in London: BRUTALIST, METEOR, and MACE II. On view in The Regent’s Park until November 1, 2026, the works combine digital modeling, robotic fabrication, and handwork, bringing together architectural fragments, classical references, science fiction, and irregular forms.
The sculptures are part of Virtues and Vices of Our Time: 300 Years Later, a contemporary reinterpretation of the Baroque Virtues and Vices by Matthias Bernard Braun. Created around 300 years after Braun’s original 24 sandstone figures, Chochola’s twelve-work series reinterprets their allegories through references to Antiquity, Cubism, Brutalism, mythology, science fiction, and contemporary popular culture.
all images by Reece Straw
From Carved Stone to 3D Printed Concrete
Developed with Czech company Voxell, the series uses 3D concrete printing as a framework for combining robotic fabrication with manual intervention. The sculptures stand approximately three to four meters tall and weigh around one ton each.
The printing process uses different orientations, non-planar paths, large overhangs supported by lightweight clay aggregate, and programmed irregularities. After printing, the concrete is ground, carved, and polished, while glass, bronze, brass, and pigments are added by hand. The resulting works by artist Matyáš Chochola combine digital fabrication with physical and material interventions.
BRUTALIST, METEOR, and MACE II at Regent’s Park
At Frieze Sculpture, BRUTALIST, METEOR, and MACE II form what Chochola describes as a ‘solemn triad.’ BRUTALIST combines a deconstructed classical column with Brutalism, the Memphis Group, twentieth-century architecture, and cinematic visions of the future.
METEOR connects classical architecture with cosmic and geological references. Inspired by Tomanowos, a meteorite discovered in Oregon and known by that name to the Chinook people, it incorporates hand-embedded glass shards into its concrete surface.
MACE II, a development of MACE I, draws on Brutalist architecture, fantasy, and 1980s science fiction. Its angular structure references both a monumental weapon and a futuristic technological relic. Printed in anthracite-tinted concrete, it is finished with metallic copper powder.
Historical references meet a new public setting
Braun’s original sculptures were created for Kuks Hospital in eastern Bohemia, where they formed part of an architectural ensemble representing the Baroque Christian moral order. Today, the sandstone figures are protected inside the complex’s lapidarium, while concrete casts occupy their former outdoor positions.
Chochola’s sculptures continue this shift between original, reproduction, and reinterpretation. Installed among the trees and paths of The Regent’s Park, they bring together different materials, historical references, and visual languages within a contemporary public setting. Curated by Fatoş Üstek, Frieze Sculpture 2026 explores a ‘vibrant hybrid ecology,’ placing sculpture in relation to its surrounding landscape and audience.
project info:
name: Virtues and Vices of Our Time at Frieze Sculpture 2026
artist: Matyáš Chochola | @matyaschochola
presented by: The Chemistry Gallery | @thechemistrygallery
producer: Voxell
architectural supervision: Jiří Vítek
data processing: Tomáš Cenek [Voxell]

photographer: Reece Straw | @reecestraw
