====================================================================================================

'Quiet creates monsters’: Jerusalem police chief talks about Temple Mount tensions and security risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
20:32:05 UTC
05:32:05 KST

Facing opposite the chair in the office of Jerusalem District Police Commander Maj. Gen. Avshalom Peled, in the headquarters building at the Russian Compound, hangs a huge panoramic photograph of the city under his command. At the center of the image, one area stands out clearly: roughly 35 acres.
It is a tiny piece of land, a little more than one-thousandth of the city’s total municipal area. But these are arguably the most charged and complex 35 acres in the Middle East, perhaps even in the world.
Peled knows this is where his tenure will be judged. Other district commanders will be measured by how they fight organized crime, protection rackets, drugs and street violence. Him? By how well he manages this powder keg. Politically, too.
Indeed, as we meet, a stack of papers sits on his desk. “Restraining orders I have to sign,” he explains. “Some of them barring people from the Temple Mount.”
Right now the Mount is quiet. And when the Mount is quiet, Jerusalem is quiet.
“I don’t call it quiet. When things are quiet, people fall asleep. Part of my policy, which I told my senior command staff and all the officers, is that the worst thing is quiet. The most challenging thing for a security organization is maintaining alertness and vigilance during routine, especially routine that appears quiet. That’s the worst thing, because a person who thinks things are quiet falls asleep. Quiet creates monsters.”
So even when the city is quiet, you are not relaxed.
“I am never relaxed for a moment. Listen, we were supposed to go with the family on vacation to Eilat. They said to me, ‘You’re not coming?’ I said: You understand that I’m not coming. I am the Jerusalem district commander — I will not have an Oct. 7. I won’t be sitting in a hotel in Eilat while something happens here. This apparent quiet is great, but it lies to you and intoxicates you. Things can be seething beneath the surface, and that is what scares me most as a commander.”
*****
When Peled entered the job in January, he divided the district’s main challenges primarily between two arenas he defines as strategic: the Temple Mount and the Jerusalem perimeter. “They can affect the entire country,” he explains. “The other challenges will have a local impact.”
The main arena is the Temple Mount.
It is no coincidence that Hamas calls the October 7 attack the “Al-Aqsa Flood.” Yahya Sinwar, who planned a combined assault — one in which Iran, Hezbollah and Israeli Arabs would also join — understood very well that the Temple Mount is a unifying force in the Arab world and sought to use that fuse. Peled’s role is to make sure it does not ignite.
And the way to do that is the status quo?
“When we liberated Jerusalem in 1967, Moshe Dayan went up to the Mount and said, let’s establish a status quo. The thinking was to tell the Arab countries: We allow Muslims freedom of worship. But what happened since then is that the rules were enforced very strictly against Jews and less strictly against Muslims. I say this from personal experience: The status quo was consistently eroded by the Waqf.”
Give an example.
“Solomon’s Stables. They ignored everyone, carried out construction and tried to get rid of all the dirt so no Jewish findings would be discovered,” he says, referring to work carried out in 1999-2000, when thousands of tons of earth, including archaeological finds, were removed during construction in the lower Al-Aqsa compound.
What is the relationship with the Waqf like today? Are there confrontations?
“No. There are daily contacts between the David Precinct and the Waqf. They know their place. There are relations and there is respect — but there is also deterrence. What happened at Solomon’s Stables could not happen today. They will not carry out work without asking for our approval. And we do not just carry out work on the Mount either.”
One of the hottest issues surrounding the Temple Mount is, of course, Jewish prayer there.
In the past, Jews could visit at certain times and quietly recite prayers. Since National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir took office, the conditions have been eased. Police no longer prevent worshippers from papers with prayers printed on them and, at least in part of the Mount, from prostrating themselves.
For now, however, police still prohibit more visible religious practices, such as carrying Torah scrolls, putting on tefillin or wearing prayer shawls.
Aren’t you worried the limits are being pushed too far?
“Jews should pray on the Temple Mount. Today we allow Jews to pray there. They have a designated area on the eastern side. Every group is accompanied by police officers, they receive a briefing, and anyone who violates the rules is removed. They come to a hearing, then to me, and I bar them from the site. We control this with an iron fist.”
And worshippers who want to go a little further?
“We allow them to pray, enter with prayer sheets, prostrate themselves on the eastern side, even sing a little on the Mount. Sometimes an entire group violates the rules, and we remove them. Our role as police is to maintain balance.”
What were the reactions in East Jerusalem to those concessions on Jewish prayer at the Mount?
“There are people who are angry about it, but they are on the margins. We are not detecting any unusual buzz on Arab social media as a result of these moves.”
Peled confirms that several weeks ago police carried out a pilot program in which worshippers were allowed to enter the Temple Mount with siddurim, Jewish prayer books. He says the request came from people around Ben-Gvir.
“They said that if prayer sheets are allowed, and on Tisha B’Av a small book of lamentations was brought in, then what is the problem with a small siddur? I said I wanted to refer the matter to the police commissioner, because a siddur — the very word ‘siddur’ — could be perceived as a change in the rules on the Mount. Some things are within my authority, but with a siddur I thought the decision should be made by the commissioner.”
OK, and then?
“We ran a pilot. Fifteen people were selected to go up to the Mount with a siddur, and afterward we sat down with the Shin Bet to review it.”
What was the conclusion?
“The conclusion was that it didn’t create any noise.”
Other requests, however, he is still rejecting. “They are asking us to allow tefillin and prayer shawls. We are not at that stage. Maybe we will get there, but we are not there yet.”
What does it actually depend on? Why a siddur yes, but a prayer shawl no, for example?
“Good question. It depends on our situation assessment, mine with the commissioner, with the minister. But we are doing this responsibly. There isn’t a week when we don’t receive requests from organizations demanding that we allow more things for Jewish worshippers.”
One of those “more things” is a petition filed with the High Court of Justice earlier this month, seeking to allow the Mount to be opened for Jewish prayer on Saturdays as well. The petition also included a request for an interim order that would have allowed Saturday prayer as early as the Sukkot and Simchat Torah holidays.
What do you think about that?
“I am very careful about maintaining balance. Opening the Mount on Saturdays is beyond my authority. Right now, in 2026, 26 years after that was possible,” he says, referring to the fact that Saturday prayer was possible until the 2000 riots, “this would be a precedent. And a precedent like that is only within the authority of the political leadership.”
But if they ask for your professional opinion, what will you say?
“It would be wrong for the police to give an opinion and say, ‘It can’t be done, it will cause the destruction of the Third Temple.’ No. The position will be presented in a very professional way. We sit with all the relevant bodies, with the Shin Bet, put all the risks and our response capabilities on the table and make a decision.”
And if the High Court says ‘don’t go up,’ and the minister says ‘go up’?
“I don’t think there will be a situation like that. The minister is a responsible person. In my opinion, he would not do something contrary to a High Court ruling.”
And when he and other politicians go up to the Mount? Is that an event as far as you’re concerned?
“We are the sovereign and we provide protection for everything that takes place. There is a very orderly procedure with the Knesset. When we are informed that a member of Knesset is coming, we conduct an orderly situation assessment. Intelligence officials join the call, and in the end I make the decision. We will always allow them to visit during the hours designated for Jewish visitors.”
What is the reaction on the Arab street to such visits?
“If Ben-Gvir goes up — and he does — the Jerusalem street is less preoccupied with it. There are actors who are not even from Jerusalem, from abroad, who try to inflame it. Actors in the north try to stir things up, but it doesn’t gain traction.”
You deploy quite a lot of forces there every Friday these days.
“Today, during Friday prayers, we keep a force inside the Mount. We never used to keep a force on the Mount, and everyone can see them. When someone disrupts order there and we remove him, that sends a message. People in Jerusalem always used to say, ‘Is the Temple Mount in our hands?’ Today we are the sovereign throughout this entire land, including there.”
*****
Ben-Gvir’s name has been linked to Peled’s quite a bit in recent years. Ben-Gvir supported Peled’s candidacy for police commissioner and previously insisted that he be appointed deputy commissioner. That relationship also produced a label Peled dislikes hearing: “Ben-Gvir’s associate.”
Are you offended when people call you that?
“When they say ‘Ben-Gvir’s associate,’ how exactly does that manifest itself? I said this in the committee too,” he says, referring to the senior appointments committee during discussions over his candidacy for police commissioner. “It isn’t true, and I assume it affected the committee. It’s a farce.”
Peled knew Ben-Gvir long before he became a minister.
During the years when Peled commanded the Hebron district, Ben-Gvir lived there.
“I knew him between 2005 and 2007,” Peled recalled. “We didn’t have a close relationship. I would see him, we would sometimes talk, but he was not the person I was in contact with in Hebron’s Jewish community. I was in contact with Orit Struck, for example, and less with Ben-Gvir.”
After that, he says, they had no contact for years. They met again after Ben Gvir had become minister and attended a meeting of the police’s senior command staff.
“The meeting ended and everyone wanted to say hello to the minister. I was the last one left, and he saw me. We shook hands and he said to me: ‘You taught me to love the police. I hated the police.’”
Later, Peled says, Ben-Gvir insisted that he be appointed deputy police commissioner. “That was the first time in that role that we had interaction, and I found myself in a lot of meetings with him.”
So maybe there is closeness between you after all?
“They can say ‘associate,’ not ‘associate.’ The fact that he likes me is not a crime. If I like him and he respects me, that is not a crime either. But ‘associate’ is going too far.”
You also took criticism for attending the minister’s birthday celebration.
“There were other events I was invited to and didn’t attend because I felt uncomfortable. I did go to his birthday because I wanted to show him respect. I say, for God’s sake, we work with him. He is someone we work with. It seems completely natural to me.”
But when officers attend a private event for a minister who is also involved in appointments, aren’t they thinking about their next rank? Isn’t that a little problematic?
“In the end, people like that invite you. It is a happy occasion and we attend. These are people we work with. Is there always a thought in the back of the mind: ‘Maybe they want a promotion?’ Maybe. Maybe some people do come for that reason. But there are also human gestures between people, and when there’s a birthday, I go.”
Peled believes Ben-Gvir is a minister who has done a great deal for the police. “He is a minister who brought major resources to the police, backs police officers — he is a heart-and-soul player. He does not operate like a conventional minister, and the public should know that.”
But immediately afterward, Peled is quick to draw his own line: The minister is the minister, but at the top of the police chain of command stands Commissioner Danny Levy.
What is your relationship with the commissioner like?
“As district commander, I feel that he gives me backing to act, implement and enforce policy. And on more sensitive issues where his involvement is required, we work together to make the best decisions for the public and for the city of Jerusalem.”
And what if the minister approaches you directly and asks for something?
“Even if he comes to me asking me to do something, I say: the commissioner. I will not go around the commissioner. Even if there are people who do that, I am a loyal person, loyal to this institution I represent. If I start doing things behind the commissioner’s back, in the end I undermine the foundations of the organization, because an organization is built on order and discipline.”
So what do you actually tell him?
“Sir, there is a commissioner. Talk to the commissioner.”
There is a feeling among the public that the police have become political. Do you share that feeling?
“Absolutely not.”
As far as Ben-Gvir was concerned, Peled should have become police commissioner after Kobi Shabtai’s term ended. 
But when Peled appeared before the senior appointments committee, it emerged that in 2015 he had been questioned by the Justice Ministry’s Police Internal Investigations Department on suspicion of breach of trust, after being recorded asking the head of a regional council to retroactively approve an unauthorized construction deviation at his home. The case was closed, and a note was placed in Peled’s file.
It is far from certain that the affair would have prevented his appointment, but Peled decided to withdraw from the race for commissioner.
“I conducted a situation assessment with myself. Various advisers told me, ‘Listen, there are people who support you, you can go to the High Court.’ I said that I am not the important person in this story. The police cannot remain for a long period without a commissioner. As long as there were disagreements, and as long as I knew that the judge,” he says, referring to Asher Grunis, who heads the committee, “thought I should not pass the committee, I decided to withdraw my candidacy. That was for me and for the police.”
Today, do you think you were wronged?
“I don’t think I was wronged. That’s the nature of things.”
After Danny Levy was chosen as commissioner, Peled already saw himself on the way out of the police. “I planned to retire. Not out of bitterness or slamming the door. I thought that if I decided to stay, it would be like clinging to the altar, and that is a bad thing.”
Levy asked him to remain for a transition period and Peled agreed. Later, a retirement date was set — until the offer came to command the Jerusalem District.
“It was not in my dreams to think about an option like that. But when it was offered to me, I told myself that as an Israeli, a Jew and a senior police officer, you cannot say no to Jerusalem. I said yes.”
And is becoming commissioner still relevant?
“I don’t think becoming commissioner is relevant for me. I think Jerusalem is my final stop, and afterward I will have to focus on my own life.”
*****
In the 10 months since Peled became Jerusalem district commander, the capital has seen highly turbulent ultra-Orthodox demonstrations: Against military conscription, against the light rail, and in another case that he viewed as particularly significant, protests by extremist factions following the deaths of two toddlers and the intention to perform autopsies on their bodies.
“Those were extremely challenging events. There was not enough police manpower to deal with them. Personally, I found it difficult. It was hard to control. What bothers me most is that I cannot enable law-abiding citizens and residents who want to get from one place to another to move freely, that the entire city is blocked, because we simply did not have the force to deal with it due to a significant manpower shortage.”
His conclusion was surprising: Sometimes it is better to let a demonstration die down on its own, because a police assault only fuels it.
So when do you disperse a protest?
“If there is violence by protesters — the policy is uncompromising. We break up the demonstration. If there is no violence and they are blocking roads, then we close off the area, redirect traffic and let them hold their protest. It is a protest that has a time limit. Confrontation makes things worse. It very quickly reaches the point where police use batons, and protesters harass cars, residents and innocent civilians stuck in traffic.”
One ultra-Orthodox protest against the draft even reached the private home of Traffic Division Commander Maj. Gen. Haim Shmueli. “It was not far from what happened at Solberg’s,” he says, referring to Supreme Court Justice Noam Solberg. “They managed to get into the yard, but the Shefat station responded very quickly and managed to stop it before they entered the house. It was a dramatic event, no doubt.
“There are months when there is an ultra-Orthodox demonstration every day. Mentally, it is difficult for the police too. They shout ‘Nazis’ at them and throw things. These are the hardest demonstrations because the numbers are very large, and in the end there is restraint in the use of force. You cannot just go wild on them. You need judgment and to use force wisely.”
And does that approach to dispersing protests apply to every protest, regardless of who is demonstrating?
“We do not distinguish based on the identity of the protesters. The same rules and conduct apply to everyone. In these demonstrations we maintain neutrality, and we instruct officers to show restraint. That is part of police professionalism. You cannot take sides.
“I tell my officers: Do you have political views? No problem, keep them to yourself. When you come to serve as a police officer, the procedures are the same procedures. We don’t care who the protesters are affiliated with.”
Ahead of the elections in about a month, the police are also drilling for a scenario in which members of the public refuse to accept the election results and attempt to reach government institutions in Jerusalem, even break into them. A Jerusalem version of the January 6 riots on Capitol Hill.
You’re really preparing for that?
“Yes. We have those scenarios. We have held drills twice, reinforcing government institutions. At the Knesset, there is cooperation with the Knesset security officer.”
Isn’t that scenario a little far-fetched, maybe extreme?
“In the reality here, nothing is far-fetched.”
*****
Peled is also the police commander responsible for roughly 400,000 Arabs living in East Jerusalem and the surrounding area.
He says even places regarded as more hostile, such as Silwan, Isawiya and Shuafat, have become more accessible to police.
“People in East Jerusalem are trapped in a dilemma,” he says. “On the one hand, they want to receive services like any other resident, municipal services and police services, and they want to live normal lives.
“On the other hand, there is social pressure around the idea of ‘an Israeli occupier holding East Jerusalem.’ There is a complexity here that means things can never simply be quiet once and for all, certainly not in our generation.”
So what has changed in East Jerusalem?
“Deterrence. October 7 changed things. Israel’s fighting on several fronts contributes to deterrence. The basic premise is that this kind of quiet is created by deterrence, because the assumption is that the people in East Jerusalem have not completely changed. They view us as an occupation police force.”
Immediately afterward, he emphasizes: “Not all of them are like that. You must not say that. There are good people too.”
But the threat that preoccupies him in East Jerusalem is not only terrorism or public disorder. When he gets to it, his tone changes.
“On East Jerusalem, I’m going to say things that are chilling, in my opinion,” he says, using a term rarely heard in police briefings: “political subversion.”
What do you mean by 'political subversion'?
“When you talk about sovereignty and governance in Jerusalem, the meaning is completely different. There is an element here of political subversion. That is a very strong term. Subversion intended to erode and push back Israeli sovereignty in Jerusalem.”
Peled describes what he calls a “shadow struggle” taking place beneath the surface and points to the involvement of foreign actors.
“We are talking about state actors, Turkey and to some extent Morocco. There are organizations here fighting Israel. If they came under an aggressive military guise, we would crush them immediately. But the guise is humanitarian, religious. And the Palestinian Authority is constantly trying to conduct state activity inside our sovereign territory.”
What does such a struggle look like on the street?
“For example, holding their conferences here, or during Ramadan bringing food packages onto the Temple Mount stamped with Turkey. Helping renovate homes for people who are struggling, charity. It looks humanitarian, but it is a very sophisticated way to penetrate East Jerusalem.”
And what objective do you attribute to them?
“They want Jerusalem as a Muslim capital. Because Jerusalem is the symbol.”
And where is the red line?
“If the Palestinian Authority starts handling, just as an example — it is not happening here, but if it does — clan disputes and murder cases in Arab society, if they come in to mediate those disputes, then we have gone bankrupt.
Peled says the Jerusalem District Central Unit is fighting this “political subversion,” with assistance from the Shin Bet, but he is careful to stress that governance, in his view, is not only about enforcement.
If the state appears in East Jerusalem only in a police car and for arrests, someone else will fill the vacuum.
“Sultan Suleiman Street is no different from Jaffa Street. Not only enforcement, but also the services a resident in East Jerusalem receives. That is governance, because if we do not provide services, all kinds of people will enter that vacuum.”
According to the statistics he cites, the trend is positive. The district points to a 60% decline in public-order incidents and a 50% drop in nationalist crime against Jews compared with last year’s figures. During the month of Selichot, he says, the number of visitors to the city was double that recorded last year.
He does not take the credit himself. “It is all thanks to the police officers and the district command staff, who work day and night to maintain the situation in the city,” he stresses. “Without them, the role of district commander is empty of content.”
Still, Peled says again, he is not relaxed. Apart from the Temple Mount, the second strategic challenge he identified upon taking office lies at the other end of the city: the Jerusalem perimeter.
Those borders can also be seen clearly in the panoramic photograph opposite his desk. About 40% of the perimeter has no physical fence, creating routes for smuggling and illegal entry into Israel. In a worse-case scenario, weapons and terrorist operatives as well.
“The State Comptroller’s report on government decisions is an extremely harsh report. I don’t see anyone getting excited about it, but here we are emphasizing this issue. Previous district commanders did not place enough emphasis on it.”
So what is actually happening there?
“The Border Police units around Jerusalem are doing sacred work, but there are still nonstop attempts to infiltrate the country. Today, one of the most profitable things you can be economically is a smuggler of illegal entrants, and there isn’t a day when we are not fighting this phenomenon.”
And terrorism?
“Terrorist organizations use the platform of illegal entry to infiltrate the country, and that is our threat. It is a strategic challenge that affects the entire country. There are huge gaps and we are dealing with them.”
Other photographs hang in his office too, mementos from his past: from service in the Armored Corps, through the Yamam counterterror unit, command of the Gideonim unit, the Beit Shemesh police station, the Ramon Border Police district, the Hebron and Negev districts, deputy commander of Border Police, deputy commander of the Jerusalem District, head of the Training Division and deputy police commissioner.
On one wall are also photographs from an entirely different period of his life — the five years he lived abroad, two in Istanbul and three in Paris, while working as a Shin Bet security officer.
And there are other photographs that move him especially deeply.
In October 2023, when he was deputy police commissioner, Peled was not in Israel. He was in Poland with his 90-year-old father on a personal journey intended to fulfill one request: to find the grave of his father’s father — Peled’s grandfather — and visit it before it was too late.
Months earlier, he had located the grave in a small cemetery in Poland. Later he returned with a friend and personally restored the headstone, which had deteriorated over the years.
In early October, he took his father there. They lit candles and prayed. “It was very moving,” he says.
On Saturday, when they were supposed to leave Krakow and return to Israel, the horrific images from Israel began arriving. Their flight was canceled.
Peled bought tickets on three different flights and tried to find a way home. By the next day, he was back in Israel.
Those days — the transition from the cemetery in Poland to the massacre scenes in Israel — stayed etched in him. Perhaps that is why, throughout our conversation, he keeps returning to the sentence: “I am never relaxed for a moment.”
And what scenario frightens you most?
Peled does not hesitate. “The reference scenario is a terrorist attack on the Temple Mount, from any side.”

Ex-OpenAI engineer says AI needs layers of safety, like nuclear plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ex-OpenAI engineer says AI needs layers of safety, like nuclear plants
- David Robinson, former OpenAI engineer, urges AI industry to adopt safety layers like aviation and nuclear sectors to prevent uncontrollable AI risks.
- He warns AI systems are advancing rapidly, often escaping control, and says current safety measures are insufficient amid fast development.
- Robinson highlights the importance of AI alignment with human values and criticises industry for lacking clear definitions and mastery of this concept.
AI generated
NEW YORK - Another former OpenAI employee has added his voice to a chorus of frantic calls to make AI safe, saying the industry must mimic the aviation or nuclear power sectors with their layers of safeguards to avoid disaster.
In an article published in The Atlantic Magazine, David Robinson echoed warnings from inside and outside the AI world that its agents are being developed so fast and becoming so smart they could soon elude control and conceivably wipe out humanity.
Robinson said alarming incidents reported since the start of the summer – in which AI agents slipped out of their controlled spaces and went rogue to attack a variety of targets – show the industry is not taking safety nearly seriously enough as it sprints to develop faster and more powerful artificial intelligence capabilities.
In the essay, Robinson said his credentials include overseeing the writing of safety reports on 12 advanced model product launches and leading the drafting of OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework.
Robinson says he worked at OpenAI for three-and-a-half years and was among the longest-tenured employees at the company.
The mistakes revealed recently are typical because of “the speed and flexibility with which people operate,” Robinson wrote.
He added: “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”
He argued that cutting-edge AI labs need to operate like the aviation or the nuclear industry with layers of redundant safeguards and careful planning “so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.”
Robinson also insisted that the issue of “alignment” – the industry term for how AI can be trained to respect human values – is essential but something the industry has failed to even define, much less master.
Then there’s this, he said: AI models are getting better and better at detecting when they are being tested and might behave differently when they are actually deployed, fooling their masters.
After a meeting on Sept 29 at the White House, amid global worries about what AI means for humanity, top AI executives said they had committed to measures for self-regulation, as opposed to submitting to government rules. This includes internal controls on AI systems and bringing in outside analysts.
President Donald Trump is vehemently against government regulation of AI and insists that criticism that AI is dangerous is just a “hoax.” AFP

More than 5,000 detained and hundreds of schools affected by protests: what is happening in France and how it all began
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
23:18:17 EEST
05:18:17 KST

More than 5,000 detained and hundreds of schools affected by protests: what is happening in France and how it all began
Kyiv • UNN
Protests over a shortage of teachers and poor learning conditions have spread across France. School blockades have escalated into clashes with police.
France has been swept by large-scale protests by high school students, which began over a shortage of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and poor learning conditions in the disadvantaged suburbs of Paris. Within a few days, the movement spread across the country, escalating into school blockades and clashes with police, while the number of detainees exceeded 5,000, Reuters reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
One of the centers of the protest was the Seine-Saint-Denis department north of Paris—one of the poorest areas in France. Students at local high schools say they have been studying for years in worse conditions than their peers in wealthier areas.
Seventeen-year-old Maysa from Le Corbusier High School in Aubervilliers said that last year she took a French exam even though there was no French teacher at the school.
These are not the conditions in which one can study
From school problems to nationwide protests
The students are demanding that more teachers be hired, overcrowded classrooms be reduced, neglected schools be renovated and equal opportunities be ensured for children regardless of where they live.
At one of the protests, 15-year-old Amelia held a sign reading: "Our address should not determine our future." The protesters believe that schools in disadvantaged suburbs have been receiving insufficient resources for years.
The protests, which began in the Paris suburbs, quickly spread to Paris, Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours, Lille and other cities. Students began blocking the entrances to educational institutions, while teachers and other supporters of the protesters joined the movement.
The situation was further aggravated by France's draft budget for 2027. The government announced an unpopular cut in public spending. Education funding is planned to increase by 1.7% to €65.53 billion, excluding teachers' pensions, but this increase is below the rate of inflation.
The government explains this trend by pointing to the declining population and says that education remains a priority. The protesters, meanwhile, fear that staffing and funding problems will only deepen.
The protests escalated into clashes
Over the past week, the situation has sharply deteriorated. Clashes, arson and riots began near schools. Police used tear gas and, in some cases, rubber bullets.
Since the beginning of the current wave of protests, law enforcement officers have detained more than 5,000 people, mostly teenagers. Protesters, school employees and law enforcement officers have been injured.
France's Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called the situation "an atmosphere of unacceptable violence." On October 3, the head of the Paris police said that the protest movement had effectively spiraled out of control and called for a return to peaceful demonstrations.
What began as a local protest by school students from disadvantaged Paris suburbs over a shortage of teachers and poor learning conditions has thus turned into one of the largest waves of youth protests in France in recent times.

Trump ramps up pressure on US Republicans to end US clock switching
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Trump ramps up pressure on US Republicans to end US clock switching
The US president published a lawmaker’s cell phone number as he called for the passage of a bill making Daylight Saving Time permanent.
United States President Donald Trump has increased the pressure on US Senate Republicans to make Daylight Saving Time permanent, singling out one of the body’s members for stalling legislation to end the twice-a-year changing of clocks.
In a social media post on Saturday, Trump blasted US Senator Tom Cotton for “holding up” the Sunshine Protection Act, which Trump has personally opted to call the “No More Changing of Clocks Act”.
“For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one!” Trump wrote on his Truth Social account about the Arkansas Republican. “It should pass overwhelmingly, in a Bipartisan fashion”.
“Nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year and, having sunshine in the afternoon is better than early in the morning!” he added.
Trump went even further, publishing what he claimed was Cotton’s phone number as he implored Arkansas residents to pressure him. The move echoed a moment during the 2016 Republican presidential primaries, when then-candidate Trump gave out US Senator Lindsey Graham’s number after the former rival criticised him.
Al Jazeera called the number listed in Trump’s post, but an automated message stated the voicemail box was full. Cotton’s spokesperson and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.
The president has routinely pushed Senate Republicans to pass legislation mandating year-round daylight saving, which would end Americans’ decades-long practice of changing their clocks twice a year to increase daylight hours. On Friday, Trump urged the US Senate to approve the bill, which passed the US House in July by a 308-117 vote.
Cotton has previously opposed the bill, arguing in a US Senate floor speech last year that farmers, construction workers, commuters and children heading to school would begin their days in the dark during the winter.
Trump disputed that argument in a separate post on Saturday, saying the bill “would be a very nice and easy WIN for the Republican Party”.
“If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, workplaces, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so”, Trump wrote.
Trump, an avid golfer, also highlighted what he considered to be another selling point of the bill: the North American Professional Golfers’ Association (PGA) tour.
“The PGA TOUR, as an example, needs more Daylight in the afternoon in order to finish their Tournaments”, he wrote in a post, which included a letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp supporting the bill. “Likewise, regular Golfers, Tennis Players, Hunters and, perhaps more importantly, Farmers who want more Daylight to play or work.”
The US president, who spent part of Saturday at his golf club in Sterling, Virginia, indicated in a subsequent post that he had received personal feedback on the proposal: “I don’t know about anyone else, but a table full of very distinguished people just told me that they HATE, immediately after a mandatory time change, going home at night – and it’s DARK. It’s depressing!”
In 1974, the US Congress briefly adopted year-round daylight saving time in response to the country’s energy crisis. But Congress repealed the law less than a year later over safety concerns as children commuted to school before sunrise.
US senators left Washington this week and have no set plans to return until after the November 3 midterm elections.
Some members, such as Senator John Kennedy, weren’t optimistic that Senate Republican Leader John Thune would bring the bill up for a vote before polling day.
“It’s dead as disco,” the Louisiana Republican told Reuters this week of Trump’s push to make daylight saving time permanent. “My sense is it would have trouble passing … I don’t think the leader is going to bring it up.”

Lula and Bolsonaro make final push for votes ahead of Brazil's knife-edge election
Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his main challenger Flavio Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in the powerhouse state of Sao Paulo, where a fifth of the nation's vote is based, seeking to rally supporters and convince the undecided on the eve of Sunday's nail-biter election.

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his rival Flavio Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns Saturday ahead of a knife-edge election that has been marred by scandals and mudslinging.
Lula, 80, toured Brazil's economic powerhouse Sao Paulo on the back of a campaign truck, cheered on by a sea of red and vowing to "defeat the far right."
The veteran leftist is seeking a fourth and final term in office, warning voters that Brazil's sovereignty is at stake in the face of pressure from US President Donald Trump.
Lula is locked in a tight battle against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of Trump who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election bid.

Opinion polls show neither candidate is likely to win the first-round election Sunday, and the two are in a statistical tie for an October 25 runoff.
Flavio Bolsonaro led a parade of hundreds of motorcycles in the interior of the state of Sao Paulo, in the style of his father. Unlike Jair Bolsonaro, he rode on the back of a campaign truck, and did not get on a bike himself.
"Let's go, Brazil wants change," he said in a video published before the rally.
The Trump factor
If Flavio Bolsonaro wins the election, Brazil will join a growing number of Latin American nations that have swung to the right in recent months.
Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is "very closely" watching the election.
Lula has warned Trump against "meddling" in Brazil's election.
His supporters wore caps and T-shirts declaring: "Make Lula President Again" or "Brazil belongs to Brazilians."

Adriana Lima, 44, an early childhood educator clad all in red, told AFP that Lula was "the only president who cared about the people."
"We also have an issue with Trump wanting to treat Brazil like their backyard, so we absolutely cannot let that happen. It's a very important election."
Another Lula supporter, accountant Tiago Lorureto, 35, said the election was "a choice between democracy and barbarism."
'Never any money'
The younger Bolsonaro has run on a platform of hardline security policies and fiscal austerity, slamming Lula as "incompetent" and highlighting the high cost of living.
Marcelo Peressim, 50, who owns a packaging company, came out to Flavio Bolsonaro's rally with a portrait of the candidate's father.
"We work almost 24 hours a day to have a good life and provide a good life for our families... yet there's never any money left over for us to do anything," he said.

Homemaker Eliane Boscolo, 47, said Trump would not need to take an interest in Brazil's elections "if the country were doing well."

One of Israel’s oldest and most highly regarded chamber music traditions returns this autumn. The Voice of Music Festival in the Upper Galilee will celebrate its 41st season from October 28 to November 1.
Hosted at the newly renovated Pastoral Hotel in Kfar Blum, the five-day event aims to revitalize regional culture and tourism following several challenging years in northern Israel.
Under the artistic direction of pianist Dr. Ofra Yitzhaki, the festival bridges historical traditions with contemporary perspectives. This year revives signature interactive programs, including Coffee & Concert, Work in Focus talks, late-night lobby sessions, and daily open rehearsals that grant audiences an intimate look into the musicians’ collaborative process.
The 2026 repertoire juxtaposes classical masterworks by Schubert, Ravel, and Schoenberg with modern 20th- and 21st-century compositions.
Israeli works to premiere at festival
Highlighting the program are world premieres of new Israeli works by Naama Pearl-Tzadok and Onn Yosef Kadosh, alongside an intimate solo performance by Shlomi Shaban and a collaborative concert featuring Nurit Galron.
Multidisciplinary productions will also take center stage, including American Rhapsody, which features the Upper Galilee Choir and blends the classical compositions of Bernstein and Barber with jazz and American literature.
Significantly, the festival will reflect the recent realities of the Galilee region through poignant tribute performances. The closing concert, My Stream, is dedicated to the memory of the festival’s long-time photographer, Ofer “Pushko” Moshkovitz, who was killed by friendly fire at his home in Kibbutz Misgav Am in March 2026.
Additionally, a performance of Silent Playground by Druze composer Haya Mustafa will honor the children killed in the Majdal Shams rocket strike.
Events will extend beyond the hotel grounds to include a special concert at Domus Galilaeae and a musical picnic along the banks of the Jordan River, ensuring a community-wide celebration.
For more info, visit www.kol-hamusica.org.il

Conscientiousness outshines cognitive ability in predicting leadership among West Point cadets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
20:00:22 UTC
05:00:22 KST

Academic records and standardized test scores accurately forecast whether a student will succeed in the classroom. When it comes to forecasting leadership potential, personality traits such as conscientiousness carry the most weight. A recent study published in Military Psychology synthesized decades of data on United States Military Academy cadets to show how different admission criteria relate to later academic, physical, and leadership performance.
The United States Military Academy at West Point aims to produce officers capable of leading soldiers in complex, unpredictable, and potentially hostile environments. To identify candidates with this potential, the academy uses a highly structured admissions process. The process evaluates cognitive abilities, physical fitness, and non-cognitive traits. Cognitive traits are typically measured by standardized test scores and high school grades.
In its earliest days, admission to West Point was based primarily on congressional nominations and basic literacy tests. Over the past century, the academy has continually refined its criteria. The modern admissions process relies on a composite ranking called the Whole Candidate Score. This score weights a candidate’s academic ability, leadership potential, and physical ability to provide a comprehensive profile of their potential.
Once admitted, cadet performance is tracked across three distinct domains. The Academic Performance Score reflects grades in core coursework. The Military Performance Score encompasses evaluations from summer training and leadership ratings from cadet positions. The Physical Performance Score includes physical education grades and standardized fitness tests.
To study the psychological aspects of candidate success, researchers often use the Five-Factor Model of personality. This framework categorizes broad personality traits into openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism. Conscientiousness involves impulse control, goal-directed behavior, and a tendency to follow established rules.
Another popular psychological concept is grit, which describes a person’s perseverance and passion for long-term goals. Researchers also study hardiness. Hardiness is considered a blend of commitment, a sense of control, and a willingness to embrace new challenges.
While researchers have studied West Point admission criteria for decades, no one had combined these findings into a single statistical review. Psychology researchers Benjamin J. Elliott and Nathan R. Kuncel from the University of Minnesota sought to fill this gap. They wanted to understand exactly how well different cognitive and non-cognitive variables predict success in the three main areas of cadet life.
To conduct their review, Elliott and Kuncel performed a meta-analysis. A meta-analysis is a statistical method that pools data from multiple individual studies to identify overarching trends that a single study might miss. The researchers gathered data from 15 published and unpublished sources representing 21 independent samples. Their combined dataset included a large sample of 29,102 cadets from West Point graduating classes between 1949 and 2022.
The researchers extracted the statistical relationships between pre-admission variables and the actual performance outcomes measured during the cadets’ time at the academy. They applied mathematical corrections to the data to account for the reliability of the measurements used in the original studies. They also adjusted the numbers to account for the fact that West Point cadets are a highly selected group. Admitted cadets usually have higher test scores and better physical fitness than the general population, which can statistically limit the range of the data.
The analysis revealed that cognitive predictors functioned exactly as expected for classroom outcomes. Standardized test scores and high school class rank were strongly associated with academic success. Traditional cognitive measures had a much weaker relationship with military leadership performance, however.
These cognitive scores were almost entirely unrelated to physical performance, with the exception of a small positive link between math scores and physical outcomes. The authors note this small link might reflect an indirect effect where individuals who apply sustained effort to learning math also apply discipline to physical training.
When evaluating personality traits, the researchers found that conscientiousness emerged as the most powerful non-cognitive predictor of leader performance. Cadets who scored high in conscientiousness also performed better academically and physically. Other major personality traits, such as extraversion, openness, agreeableness, and neuroticism, showed little to no relationship with leadership ratings.
The researchers also looked at grit, which is often cited as a highly desired trait in military culture. They found that grit had only a modest relationship with leadership performance. It demonstrated an even smaller positive relationship with academic and physical outcomes. Hardiness showed a very weak relationship with leadership.
These results indicate that conscientiousness plays an outsized role in a cadet’s ability to navigate the rigorous environment of a military academy. The trait involves planning, self-discipline, and long-term orientation. These characteristics align closely with strict institutional standards. Cadets who internalize these behaviors tend to set an example for others to follow, a habit that is associated with effective leadership.
The authors suggest that selection systems could benefit from incorporating measurements of conscientiousness. Cognitive measures like the SAT are excellent at predicting who will pass classes, but they miss the personality elements associated with leadership. Adding personality assessments to the admissions process could help institutions select candidates with a broader range of the skills needed to succeed.
A primary limitation of this research is its reliance on self-reported personality assessments. Traits like conscientiousness are highly desirable in competitive admissions environments. Applicants might intentionally alter their survey responses to appear more organized or disciplined than they actually are, a phenomenon known as social desirability bias. This bias can artificially inflate a candidate’s apparent qualifications.
To address the issue of biased self-reporting, future research could explore observer-based assessments. Having teachers, coaches, or peers rate an applicant’s personality could provide a more accurate picture of their character. Admissions systems could also use forced-choice personality tests, which require applicants to choose between equally desirable options. These formats make the tests harder to manipulate.
Future studies could also examine how well these admission variables relate to outcomes long after graduation. Tracking junior officers as they advance in their military careers would help determine if the traits associated with success at West Point also predict long-term occupational achievement. Linking pre-commissioning data with career milestones could reveal the ideal mix of personality traits required in complex operational environments.
The study, “Brain, personality, and leadership: A meta-analysis of performance predictors among West Point cadets,” was authored by Benjamin J. Elliott and Nathan R. Kuncel.

AI needs safety layers like aviation or nuclear plants, says ex-OpenAI engineer David Robinson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
20:00:04 UTC
05:00:04 KST

Another former OpenAI employee has added his voice to a chorus of frantic calls to make AI safe, stressing the industry must mimic the aviation or nuclear power sectors with their layers of safeguards to avoid disaster.
In an article published in The Atlantic Magazine, David Robinson echoed warnings from inside and outside the AI world that its agents are being developed so fast and becoming so smart they could soon elude control and conceivably wipe out humanity.
Robinson said alarming incidents reported since the start of the summer — in which AI agents slipped out of their controlled spaces and went rogue to attack a variety of targets — show the industry is not taking safety nearly seriously enough as it sprints to develop faster and more powerful artificial intelligence capabilities.
In the essay Robinson said his credentials include overseeing the writing of safety reports on 12 advanced model product launches and leading the drafting of OpenAI's Preparedness Framework.
Robinson says he worked at OpenAI for three-and-a-half years and was among the longest-tenured employees at the company.
The mistakes revealed recently are typical because of "the speed and flexibility with which people operate," Robinson wrote.
He added: "An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to."
AI agents fooling their masters
He argued that cutting-edge AI labs need to operate like the aviation or the nuclear industry with layers of redundant safeguards and careful planning "so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster."
Robinson also insisted that the issue of "alignment" — the industry term for how AI can be trained to respect human values — is essential but something the industry has failed to even define, much less master.
Then there's this, he said: AI models are getting better and better at detecting when they are being tested and might behave differently when they are actually deployed, fooling their masters.
After a meeting on Tuesday at the White House, amid global worries about what AI means for humanity, top AI executives said they had committed to measures for self-regulation, as opposed to submitting to government rules.
This includes internal controls on AI systems and bringing in outside analysts.
President Donald Trump is vehemently against government regulation of AI and insists that criticism that AI is dangerous is just a "hoax."

She ended the post by marking Simchat Torah in the Hebrew year 5787.
Damari suffered serious gunshot wounds during her abduction and lost two fingers on her left hand, an injury that later became widely associated with her public appearances after her release. Her beloved dog was also killed during the attack.
Her mother, Mandy Damari, has previously said her daughter was “stitched up like a pincushion” by her captors, leaving her with severe pain in her hand and leg.
Despite the severity of the wounds and the danger of infection, her mother said Hamas provided virtually no medical treatment beyond a bottle of expired iodine.
“It is nothing short of a miracle that she did not develop a life-threatening infection,” Mandy Damari said.

Doctors were working to save Pike's life and clear the drug pentobarbital from her system, her lawyers said on Friday.

Netanyahu's secret UAE trip: What is Israel's military censorship really for? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:51:41 UTC
04:51:41 KST

Israel has had military censorship for virtually the country’s entire history. That may seem bizarre for a democracy, but it does have a justification. Israel has spent much of its existence at war or under threat of war, and there are things that plainly should not be broadcast in real time. If Hezbollah fires a missile at Israel, for example, publishing its precise impact location can help the enemy figure out how well it aimed and do better next time.
That is national security. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s secret trip to Abu Dhabi is something else.
Netanyahu flew to the United Arab Emirates on Sunday for an hour-long meeting with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The trip was secret until Israel’s Channel 12 reported it while Netanyahu was still abroad. Netanyahu’s office subsequently said the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) had filed a complaint accusing Channel 12 of violating censorship rules.
Israel and the UAE have diplomatic relations. Netanyahu was not slipping into an enemy country for clandestine negotiations, under danger should a mob get wind of his presence. There are legitimate reasons to keep a prime minister’s movements secret, but censorship is another matter – a tool of last resort.
But there are other circumstances at play – embarrassing circumstances.
The Associated Press reported that a person with firsthand knowledge of the meeting said Netanyahu asked Sheikh Mohamed to deny a report that the Emirati leader had warned him about a looming Hamas attack shortly before October 7, 2023. Netanyahu’s office denies that any such request was made and says the meeting focused solely on strengthening relations between Israel and the UAE.
The original report strikes at one of Netanyahu’s greatest political vulnerabilities. Since October 7, he has fought relentlessly over responsibility for the catastrophic failures that preceded the Hamas attack. The possibility that the leader of a friendly Arab country personally warned him of a major Hamas operation beforehand would be politically devastating.
If the account of Sunday’s meeting is accurate, Israel’s prime minister flew at public expense to a friendly foreign capital and used a meeting with its president in an effort to rebut a report damaging to himself. Then, when an Israeli television network reported that the trip had happened, military censorship was invoked.
On September 8, the UAE Foreign Ministry did not deny either the call or the warning. Its official statement said it does not comment on reports about conversations between leaders, then added that the UAE and Israel maintain direct communications and that, when necessary, relevant intelligence is shared between the appropriate entities.
Then, on September 20, an unnamed UAE official gave a more specific response to The National. The official rejected the claim that MBZ personally spoke with Netanyahu and conveyed the warning, saying security matters are handled through the relevant professional bodies and that details of this kind are not discussed at the leaders’ level.
A direct MBZ denial, if Netanyahu could get it, would have obvious political value. The reported phone call goes directly to the question that has haunted Netanyahu since October 7: What did he know before the attack, and when did he know it?
That is not what military censorship is for.
It also fits an increasingly familiar pattern. Under Netanyahu, the line separating the prime minister’s interests from the state’s has become infuriatingly blurry (although perhaps familiar to the citizens of a certain far larger democracy).
There have been years of controversies surrounding the Netanyahu family’s use of public resources, official travel, and expenses. The details can sometimes sound petty, even comical: another hotel, another bill, another extended stay abroad for himself and his wife, Sara. Focusing on the receipts, however, misses what they collectively reveal.
Military censorship is not for public relations
A government aircraft is not the prime minister’s airplane. Israel’s diplomatic relationships are not his personal relationships. The country’s security institutions are not his political staff. Military censorship is not his public relations department. These belong to the State of Israel, and the enormous powers attached to them are temporarily entrusted to whoever holds office.
That distinction is especially important now.
Israel is approaching an election after three extraordinary years of war. Netanyahu’s political future is uncertain. His government’s responsibility for October 7 remains one of the central questions hanging over the country. Decisions involving Gaza, Iran, and Israel’s broader security are being made in the final weeks of an increasingly intense political campaign.
There is already speculation in Israel that another confrontation with Iran could become entangled with Netanyahu’s political predicament. There is no evidence that Netanyahu has decided to launch a war for electoral purposes, and military action would have to be judged against the security circumstances at the time.
But Netanyahu himself has helped create the conditions in which Israelis ask the question.
A prime minister needs the public to believe that when he deploys the powers of the state, he does so because the interests of the state require it. Once those powers repeatedly appear alongside his personal political needs, that confidence erodes. In Netanyahu’s case, with the exception of his hardcore base, it’s gone.
That is an especially dangerous condition for a democracy at war. If war erupts, and Israelis again have to spend nights in shelters, they need to know it wasn’t because Netanyahu is behind in the polls.
The writer is a former Cairo-based Middle East editor and London-based Europe/Africa editor of the Associated Press. He served as chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem and authored two books about Israel.

Sohlberg orders removal of Ben-Gvir prison video, imposes NIS 20,000 costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:51:41 UTC
04:51:41 KST

Central Elections Committee (CEC) chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg on Thursday ordered National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Otzma Yehudit to remove from their social-media accounts a video filmed during Ben-Gvir’s visit to convicted Hamas terrorist Hassan Salameh, ruling that it constituted election propaganda produced using public resources.
Sohlberg also ordered Ben-Gvir and his party to pay NIS 20,000 in legal costs to the two organizations that petitioned against the video.
The costs are to be divided equally: Ben-Gvir must pay NIS 10,000 personally, and Otzma Yehudit must pay the remaining NIS 10,000.
The decision rejected the argument that the video was intended to deter terrorists rather than influence voters.
Ben-Gvir told terrorist: 'I want to kill you, I want to put you to death'
Ben-Gvir published the video on September 27, one month before the October 27 election. He said it had been recorded during a prison visit some two weeks earlier.
With armed and uniformed Israel Prison Service (IPS) guards standing between him and Salameh, Ben-Gvir told the prisoner: “I want to kill you. I want to put you to death.”
He also said that he was responsible for making Salameh’s life in prison “hell.”
In the caption accompanying the video, Ben-Gvir praised his record as national security minister and described policies he intended to pursue after the election.
He wrote that as defense minister, he would work to have terrorists such as Salameh executed and advance the emigration of Palestinians from Gaza and the West Bank.
Two organizations alleged Ben-Gvir video was election propaganda
The Public Committee Against Torture in Israel and the nonprofit Voting for Israel filed separate petitions arguing that the video constituted election propaganda produced through the prohibited use of public assets.
Ben-Gvir and Otzma Yehudit did not dispute that the prison, IPS personnel, and their equipment were public resources. They argued, however, that the video’s purpose was deterrence rather than campaigning.
Section 2A of the Election Propaganda Law prohibits the use of public money or assets in connection with election propaganda.
A publication is classified as election propaganda when its dominant purpose is to influence voters, and no alternative purpose outweighs that electoral objective.
Sohlberg acknowledged that the video could carry a deterrent message but found that this was not its dominant purpose.
Ben-Gvir took personal credit for Salameh’s prison conditions, presented himself as the person responsible for deterring terrorists, and described policies he intended to pursue in the future, Sohlberg wrote.
According to the decision, the accompanying caption confirmed the electoral character of the publication by combining praise for Ben-Gvir’s conduct in office with plans for what he would do after the election.
Sohlberg also cited the video’s publication on Ben-Gvir’s personal political accounts, its proximity to the election, and the minister’s ability to control the timing of his prison visit.
In explaining the personal costs imposed on Ben-Gvir, Sohlberg said the minister had used his authority over the IPS to visit a particular prisoner in his cell, obtain the presence of uniformed armed guards, and display them in a campaign video.
“Other candidates – apparently even other ministers – do not enjoy such access to the Prison Service, prisoners and guards,” Sohlberg wrote. “Minister Ben-Gvir enjoyed an advantage in access to these public assets – and exploited it to the fullest.”
Sohlberg also noted that the publication resembled other Ben-Gvir videos previously found to have violated the same prohibition on using public resources for election propaganda.
Ben-Gvir says CEC decision 'extremely puzzling'
Ben-Gvir called the decision “extremely puzzling” and said terrorists in prison should be treated harshly.
“The publication of the video, like other videos I have published, has proven to deter terrorists planning to carry out attacks in the future,” he said.
“I regret Justice Sohlberg’s decision,” Ben-Gvir added. “This is not how terrorism is fought.”
Salameh is serving 46 consecutive life sentences for directing three suicide bombings in 1996, including the two attacks on Jerusalem’s No. 18 bus.
The death penalty law enacted earlier this year does not apply retroactively and therefore cannot be applied to Salameh’s 1996 offenses.
Under Sohlberg’s order, Ben-Gvir and Otzma Yehudit must remove the video immediately from all their social-media accounts and pay the petitioners’ costs.

What Amit taught us: How the Bonzel family keeps the legacy of a fallen soldier alive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
19:51:23 UTC
04:51:23 KST

Noa Bonzel is very proud of her three children, Nadav, Amit, and Adi. “Nadav is now on reserve duty in Lebanon, Amit is on Mount Herzl, and Adi is a casualty assistance officer in the Engineering Corps.”
Her matter-of-fact description of Amit’s location, where he is interred in the military cemetery in Jerusalem, sounds jarring at first. But as our discussion continues, it becomes clear that, though Amit is no longer alive, the lessons he exemplified during his life continue to inspire his family, compatriots, and Israeli society at large.
Amit, 22, a member of the Paratroopers Brigade, fell on December 6, 2023, in Gaza. Since his death, Noa and her husband, Yitzhak (Itzik), have kept his memory alive by sharing the legacy of his accomplishments in his all-too-brief life.
On a recent late-summer morning, I visited Noa and her husband at their home in Shoham to discuss Amit’s legacy and why it matters. Outside their home stands a large banner emblazoned with the verse from the Book of Samuel – “How the mighty have fallen in the midst of the battle” – next to a photo of their smiling son.
“Amit Street” in Shoham is named in his memory, and Noa admits that she sometimes finds it difficult to drive down that road. “It’s crazy. I never dreamed that there would be a street named after my son in Shoham,” says Noa, who grew up in Petah Tikva.
The synagogue in Shoham that they attend has a cabinet where holy books are kept, with a prominent sign displayed in Amit’s memory, and a synagogue – B’Darkei Amit (In the ways of Amit)– was established in his memory in Kiryat Gat.
“Amit was a very special son,” says Noa. “He was the middle child, and whenever Nadav and Adi would argue, he would say, ‘Stop. I’m begging you not to argue. We are a family.’”
Noa recalls that Amit’s sensitivity manifested at a very young age. “When he was six, I had just finished our Shabbat preparations one Friday afternoon, and for some reason, I was a bit sad. Amit smiled at me and didn’t say a word. Before he left for the synagogue with his father, he said, ‘Ima, listen. I have a surprise for you.’”
Shortly after Amit and his siblings had left for the synagogue with their father, there was a knock at the door. “It was my best friend,” says Noa. “She said that Amit had called her a few minutes before Shabbat and said, ‘My mother is a little sad. Could you please come over to visit, to make her feel better?’ That was Amit.”
Amit valued service in the IDF above all else
GROWING UP, Amit valued service in the IDF above all else, Noa says. He was not an outstanding student, but he always wanted to learn more about military life. As a student at the yeshiva high school in Petah Tikva, the city where Noa grew up, he refused to attend classes taught by a teacher who had not served in the IDF, and spent most of his time with teachers who had served as company commanders in their units.
“Amit did not have the best grades in school, and he was not the fastest runner, but he always aimed high when it came to his army service,” Noa shares.
Performing meaningful service in the IDF is a family tradition. Itzik, who grew up in Jerusalem, served in the paratroopers, as did Amit’s uncle and his brother, Nadav.
In Amit’s room in Shoham, a large flag of Israel hangs. Underneath, Amit had written: “Many people say they want to succeed, but not everyone is willing to pay the price required to achieve success.”
When Amit turned 16, he asked his mother to register him for a course in Shoham that prepared teens for tryout days for military and commando units. “I asked him what unit he wanted to try to prepare for,” recalls Noa. “He said that he wanted to join the General Staff Reconnaissance Unit, considered the most elite special unit.” In response, Noa quipped, “And I want to become prime minister.”
Amit was just 1.68 m. tall (five feet, six inches), not the ideal height for the unit, but he begged his mother to register him for the unit’s tryout day. He said, “If I do not protect the country, who will do it?” Not paying much attention to his comment, she signed him up for the course.
After being turned down twice, Amit wrote a letter to the army requesting a final chance to try out for the Reconnaissance Unit. This time, they accepted him for the screening. Despite his best efforts, Amit was not accepted. Other military units contacted him and expressed interest in recruiting him, and he decided to join the IDF Paratroopers Brigade’s elite reconnaissance unit.
Amit was accepted into the unit, and after he completed his post-high school army preparatory program at Keshet Yehuda in the Golan Heights, he joined the paratroopers and spent a year and two months training.
“There are some soldiers who give up because the training is very difficult, both physically and mentally,” says Noa. “But whenever Amit came home for Shabbat, he was so happy. He had a great deal of motivation.” The training was not easy for him because of his diminutive size, but he succeeded.
Noa also discusses the great respect that he had for his parents. When Amit finished his paratrooper training, he prepared a photo of himself standing next to his parents and left it in their room, with the inscription, “Thank you very much for your support.”
'Amit was the only one who stayed behind'
NOA RECOUNTS a story from Amit’s training, which illustrates these qualities. “There was an incident when they were training at the Wingate Institute. Their commander told them that they had to scale a wall, and that anyone who completed the exercise could go home for Shabbat.
“Itzik and I drove to Wingate and waited for Amit to finish training. We waited and waited, but he didn’t come out. We began to worry. What had happened?
“One of the soldiers on his team couldn’t scale the wall. Amit was the only one who stayed behind. He set up a portable speaker and played music, climbed to the top of the wall, and kept encouraging the soldier. He refused to give up on him, and went home only after the soldier had succeeded in scaling the wall.”
At the ceremony in Beit Lid marking the end of paratrooper training in May 2023, Amit’s commander appointed him staff sergeant over a younger group of paratroopers because of his leadership qualities and willingness to help others.
After the ceremony, Amit and his family were inching toward the exit in their car; Amit and his two siblings sat in the back seat. Shortly before they reached the main exit, Amit told his parents to stop the car. Looking through the window, he noticed someone pushing a visitor in a wheelchair. He jumped out of the car, helped push the wheelchair, and assisted the disabled person into their car.
“All the time, Amit would say, ‘How can I help another person? How can I volunteer? Who needs my help?’ When I speak to the army now, I tell everyone that I follow in Amit’s path.
“When I went to work, I was always in a hurry,” notes Noa. “But now, when I go, I look ahead and say to myself, ‘Perhaps someone needs me, as Amit would think.’ Whenever I see the street cleaner, I go back into the house, bring him a piece of cake and a cup of coffee.”
'He never came back home'
THE SOLDIERS under Amit finished their training on Thursday, October 5, 2023, during Hol Hamoed Sukkot. Amit’s soldiers came to Shoham, and Amit prepared a barbecue for them. On Friday, Amit’s parents returned from a vacation abroad, and Amit, together with friends from Shoham, went to a villa in the North near the Kinneret for Simchat Torah.
On the morning of Oct. 7, Amit returned home and told his parents that the war had started, which surprised Noa, since they had not heard any sirens in Shoham. He organized his gear and, after 20 minutes, left the house. “He never came back home,” says Noa wistfully.
Amit fought with his soldiers in the kibbutzim being attacked by Hamas terrorists. On November 19, his 22nd birthday, his unit was in the Rimal neighborhood in Gaza City, and his soldiers threw him a surprise party. He said it was his happiest birthday, because they appreciated and respected him.
He then returned to the army base at Lachish. Noa and Itzik visited Amit there at the end of November. The last time they spoke to him was at the end of November; afterward, Amit reentered Gaza with his unit, commanded by Ariel Malka.
On December 5, 2023, Ariel’s brother, Yehonatan Malka, fell in combat against Hamas in the Gaza Strip. Ariel Malka was granted temporary leave and returned to Israel to attend his brother’s funeral, held the next day, on December 6.
Amit was appointed to command the unit in his absence, though he had not completed his officer’s training course. His commanders trusted his ability to lead the soldiers effectively in combat.
Noa and Itzik had not heard from Amit in some time, and Itzik decided to attend Yehonatan Malka’s funeral, where he would see Ariel and find out how Amit was doing.
While Itzik was attending the funeral of the brother of Amit’s commander, Amit fell in Saja’iya, a large neighborhood in Gaza City. Noa recounts that when the IDF representative arrived at their home in Shoham to break the tragic news, only Adi was home. Noa was at work in Modi’in, and Itzik was on his way home from the funeral.
When he returned home from Yehonatan Malka’s funeral and saw the officers, he realized that they had come to inform him about the death of his son. He asked, “Which one? Nadav or Amit?”
Over 1,000 people attended Amit’s funeral, says Noa, and each day of the shiva saw visits from hundreds of people from all walks of life – religious, secular, haredi. Noa and Itzik were astounded to hear the stories that people told about Amit’s kindness and consideration for others.
At the conclusion of the shiva, Noa and Itzik went to Amit’s grave and saw the nearby grave of Eyal Meir Berkowitz, a 28-year-old IDF soldier from Susya, who was killed in action in the Gaza Strip on December 7, 2023.
They decided to pay a shiva visit to the family in Susya that evening. While they were there, they learned of another family who had lost a son from the nearby community of Asa’el. Soon, they went there and comforted them. Noa and Itzik continued to visit many bereaved parents and wounded soldiers in hospitals.
NOA OPENED a WhatsApp group for bereaved mothers, where they communicate and speak about their needs, both emotional and otherwise. When the Jewish community in Bondi Beach, Australia, was reeling after the terror attack during Hanukkah in December 2025, Noa and Itzik traveled privately to comfort the bereaved families.
“They thanked us for coming from so far away to visit them. We visited each family and gave them practical tips on how to get back on their feet after what happened,” Noa recounts.
The couple traveled to the US, France, Italy, and Australia, where they delivered talks about their son. They frequently speak at Bahad 1, the IDF’s officer training center, and at schools and workplaces, focusing on the values Amit lived by, and how others can put them into practice.
“What really stands out is what the children say afterward: One said, ‘I didn’t believe in myself, and now I realize I can achieve great things,’” recalls Itzik. “Another girl wrote, ‘I live in the periphery, and my dream was to become a paramedic. I gave up on that dream, but after the lecture, I won’t take ‘no’ for an answer.’”
How do Itzik and Noa cope with their loss? Noa explains that they keep busy with work – she is an import manager and he is a lawyer – and by talking to others about what Amit did during his life. “We cry several times a day,” says Itzik, who grew up in Jerusalem. “It can be for a second or two, or it can be longer. It catches you in the throat or the heart, but it shows that you are normal.”
They are certain that Amit’s death was not in vain. “When we walk down the street and see people sitting in cafés, you think, ‘They must be on vacation, or they’re just idle,’ or whatever.
“We go to shows and weddings – which are the hardest things. But then we realize, when we see people out on the streets, at celebrations and at shows, that we’re seeing victory.
“Everyone asks, ‘What is victory?’ We see victory in the fact that our people keep going to the beach, keep celebrating their children’s weddings with great joy, and keep sitting in cafés, instead of sheltering in safe rooms. That really is our victory. What seems normal to you is a victory for us. It’s thanks to Amit and all the soldiers that we’re here.” ■
Heshbon nefesh
These are the words of Amit Bonzel, of blessed memory, who fell in Gaza. His family found his notes among his belongings.
The kind of person I want to be
• Committed all the time
• Give everyone the benefit of the doubt
• First to volunteer
• Happy to give, and want to give without compromises
• Don’t complain
• A person that people share everything with
• Responsible – someone people trust
• Always know what to say, and when not to
• Don’t get upset by what people say about me
• Talk to everyone at eye level
• Lead everyone in the right way
How do I become this person?
• Always be positive
• Say hello to everyone in the unit, even to those with whom I connect less or people I don’t know
• Always say thank you, even if it’s embarrassing sometimes
• Don’t get offended if I’m not included in something – need to understand not everything revolves around me
• Give people the benefit of the doubt
• Count to three before I react
• Understand that not everyone here has the same motives
• Not everything revolves around me
• See how I can bridge the gaps in a respectful and beautiful way
• Be the first to volunteer
• Always say “I will,” even if it’s not the most comfortable at that moment
May we be worthy – Am Yisrael chai.
A mechina (pre-army preparatory program) has been established in Amit’s memory in Lod, home to both Jewish and Arab communities. Named “Bedarkei Amit” (the path of Amit), the mechina now has 150 students and is a growing presence in the city.
