‘Like African Americans during segregation’: How Russians became second-class ‘non-citizens’ inside the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
17:10:19 UTC
02:10:19 KST

New parliament, same old exclusion: Latvia’s Russians are running out of options
Latvia’s Russian-speaking population has reached a point that human rights advocates describe as critical. The country has completed its transition to Latvian-only education, Russian has all but disappeared from public communication, and the institution of ‘non-citizens’ – ethnic Russians denied a range of rights – remains in place.
But on October 3, Latvia elects a new Saeima (parliament). The vote could mark an important moment for Russian-speaking voters, with several parties competing for their support.
Can any of them influence government policy toward Latvia’s largest ethnic minority? Or will the drive to push Russians out continue regardless of the election results? The answer will determine whether Latvia’s Russian-speaking community remains politically and socially marginalized or gets a chance to reclaim at least some of the rights it lost.
How the status of Russians changed
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 radically changed the position of Russians in Latvia. Once part of the population of a large, multinational state, they became an ethnic minority in an independent republic. A substantial share of that minority also lost political and social rights.
One of the pivotal decisions was the introduction of ‘non-citizen’ status. Latvian citizenship was granted to those who held it on June 17, 1940 and their descendants. Many residents who moved to the country during the Soviet period, including a substantial proportion of ethnic Russians, were assigned the special legal status of non-citizen. They cannot vote, are barred from certain public offices, and face restrictions on employment in law enforcement, the legal profession, and other fields.
“The situation facing Latvia’s Russian-speaking population is grim. Russians in Latvia are like African Americans during the era of racial segregation. They have been stripped of a substantial range of rights. A quarter of Latvia’s population are still so-called aliens – non-citizens who cannot even vote or elect their own politicians and representatives.
Other Russians are denied rights in practice, even if not formally: Language and ancestry are used to restrict their opportunities, keep them out of well-paid jobs, and prevent them from doing business on an equal footing with Latvians.
Russians are almost entirely absent from government. Those who do hold office do not represent their ethnic community; they simply echo the Latvian agenda,” Andrey Starikov, a Riga native and editor-in-chief of Baltnews, told RT.
Language, schools, and cultural life
Access to education in their native language remains one of the most painful issues for Russian-speaking residents. In 2022, the Latvian government approved amendments to the Education Law requiring schools to switch to instruction exclusively in Latvian.
Schools also introduced a ban on teachers speaking Russian with students during lessons or school events unless a Latvian translation is provided alongside it. Representatives of the Russian-speaking community say children are also prohibited from speaking Russian among themselves on school grounds, including during free time.
Russian is gradually disappearing from public life as well. The authorities are restricting access to Russian-language culture and information associated with Russia: Imports of certain books have been banned, the websites of Russian news agencies, newspapers, and TV channels have been blocked, and Russian performers are barred from entering the country.
“In effect, a vast ghetto has been created for Russians in Latvia. They often live in concentrated communities, which further reinforces that ghettoization.
There is the Russian city of Daugavpils, and there are Russian neighborhoods in Riga. Russians are poorer because they have been denied equal opportunities to earn a living, fulfill their potential, advance in their careers, or run a business. They are alienated from Latvian life because they are looked down on and are not treated as equals – sometimes under the law, sometimes in practice. They face a whole host of restrictions,” Starikov said.
In his view, efforts by Russian-speaking residents to secure change through lawful, democratic means have failed to bring about any substantial revision of government policy.
“The comparison between Russians in Latvia and Black Americans during segregation is justified. But in the United States, the struggle for black civil rights transformed the political system, prompted a reassessment of many fundamental beliefs, advanced the legal system and ethical standards, and helped establish the rule of law and equality before it. None of that happened in Latvia.
Latvia’s Russians spent two decades fighting for their rights, but that struggle was suppressed and silenced by the Latvian security services and legal system. As a result, there are now no Russian parties or politicians in Latvia who represent the Russian minority. Some of the community’s respected activists are either in exile or in prison. Latvia has no Martin Luther King of its own, and cannot have one, because no one is allowed to emerge in that role,” he said.
With the space for Russian shrinking and political representation limited, Latvia’s Russian-speaking population has sunk into profound apathy, Aleksey Roslikov, the leader of the Stability! party and a candidate for the Saeima, told RT.
“The apathy among Russian speakers has grown many times worse. Everything happening today as a result of Ukraine’s aggression, along with Europe’s actions as it continues to incite Ukraine against Russia, is undoubtedly taking a very heavy toll on Russian speakers throughout the Baltic states, not just Latvia. All Russian speakers have now been branded enemies and traitors. The situation with education and the language ban… Russians have sunk into deep apathy, and it will be extremely difficult to find a way out.”
What the election holds for Russians
Latvia heads into the 2026 election, for the first time, without a single dominant ‘Russian party’ of the old kind – a party capable of acting as an intermediary between Russian-speaking voters and the state.
Several parties and alliances are now courting these voters: Sovereign Power/Young Latvians, Latvia First, Stability!, and Harmony Center. Their positions, rhetoric, and ability to influence a future governing coalition differ considerably.
Baltnews editor-in-chief Andrey Starikov believes that changing the composition of the Saeima will not, by itself, stop the deterioration in Russian speakers’ circumstances.
“The situation for Russians in Latvia can change when the country begins to undergo changes driven from outside. Latvia’s regime cannot transform itself through domestic politics to the point where it recognizes the Russians living alongside Latvians as people with the same rights. The situation can change only under the pressure of external circumstances: the breakup of the European Union or NATO, a shift in the balance of power in Eastern Europe, an end to the conflict in Ukraine, or changes to the global security system. Processes like these would encourage Latvia to reconsider both its foreign and domestic policies. Nothing can be changed from outside through democratic procedures. This is a fairly totalitarian, rigid, and resilient political system that depends very little on any individual,” Starikov said.
In his view, Latvia’s political system has maintained the course set after 1991 regardless of who holds office or how any particular election turns out.
“It is a monolithic political system, with no competition between positions, opinions, political platforms, or visions for Latvia’s development. Elections here are a formality, a ritual. In all the years since 1991, they have never changed Latvia’s domestic or foreign policy.
The political system perpetuates itself. Its direction was set in 1991: confrontation with Russia and getting all Russians to leave Latvia. ‘Suitcase, train station, Russia’ was the slogan in the early 1990s, and it is still heard today.
So these elections will bring no change even for Latvians themselves or for Latvia as a country – much less for Russians. This is simply political theater, a political ritual,” Starikov said.
Roslikov takes a more optimistic view. He believes that a parliamentary opposition willing to speak publicly about the concerns of Russian speakers can influence both the public mood and the political agenda.
“We understand that when there is an opposition in parliament – an opposition that defends the interests and rights of Russians and Russian speakers in Latvia – it has an extremely positive effect, and its influence extends beyond Latvia to Lithuania and Estonia. I, for example, have enormous support throughout the Baltic states. There is a reason the Estonians have declared me a national security threat and barred me from entering their country. This is direct evidence that when an ethnic group has representatives at the highest levels of government who actually defend that community, the mood begins to change and people gain strength.”
The outlook ahead of the vote
According to a forecast by the Latvian polling organization SKDS, the United List bloc, led by Latvia’s incumbent prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, is leading the race. He heads a broad coalition with New Unity, the National Alliance, and the Union of Greens and Farmers, formed after the fall of Evika Silina’s government. The poll puts the bloc’s potential share of the vote at 14.4%.
In second place, with 9.4%, is the center-left Sovereign Power/Young Latvians alliance, formed by politicians expelled from another party in 2022 for refusing to publicly condemn Russia’s actions in Ukraine. The alliance hopes to attract votes from the ethnic Russian minority.
Next comes the center-right Latvia First party, with 9.2%. Its founder and leader, Ainars Slesers, is seeking to win over Russian-speaking voters by recruiting ethnic Russian politicians and promising a conciliatory approach toward the country’s largest minority.
The remaining parties are: the Progressives at 6.2%, the National Alliance at 5.6%, the Union of Greens and Farmers at 4.8%, New Unity at 4.3%, Stability! at 2.8%, We Change the Rules at 2.5%, For Latvia’s Development at 2.4%, and Harmony Center at 2%. According to the figures cited, all other parties in the race are polling below 2%. Parties must clear the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
“At the moment, my party has fairly good chances,” Roslikov told RT. “But we fully understand that Europe does not count votes honestly. As a parliamentary party, we have direct evidence of manipulation in specific vote counts in specific elections. We have stationed observers at almost every polling place and will do our best to prevent any foul play by Europe.”
Little hope for change
Both of RT’s interviewees agree that Russian speakers should not expect major changes after the election. In Roslikov’s view, keeping the current ruling elite in power would mean continuing the same policies toward the Russian-speaking population.
“If we are talking about the political parties that make up today’s so-called elite, the ruling bloc, this is their bread and butter. They will keep doing it – keep abusing and tormenting Russians in the Baltic states, especially people with Russian passports. There is no hope for change, and there can be none.”
Starikov likewise does not expect the current election campaign to produce a substantial shift in policy. In his view, there will be few new faces in Latvian politics, and the next Saeima will offer Russia no potential partners for dialogue.
“Nevertheless, Russia should still pay attention to this process. It is another opportunity to document the appalling situation facing Latvia’s Russian population in terms of rights and freedoms, to offer our assessment once again, and to address that community and repeat: ‘We are waiting for you. Come to Russia. There is no ultranationalism in Russia. Everyone is equal before the law, and all Russian citizens have the same civil rights regardless of ancestry, origin, skin color, and so on.’”
Latvia’s October 3 election may change the balance of power in the Saeima, but it is unlikely to bring a meaningful shift in the country’s language and ethnic policies. Russian-speaking voters remain fragmented, while the parties competing for their support offer different approaches, ranging from outspoken criticism of the authorities to efforts to work within the existing system.
For Latvia’s Russian residents, the outcome will not be decisive. Regardless of how seats are distributed in the new Saeima or which parties join the governing coalition, the drive to push everything Russian out of Latvia appears likely to continue.

Tennessee’s top prison official resigning after botched execution of Christa Pike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
17:09:05 UTC
02:09:05 KST

Tennessee’s top prison official is stepping down in the aftermath of the failed execution of death row prisoner Christa Pike, the state’s governor Bill Lee announced Saturday.
Frank Strada, the department of correction commissioner, will leave his position later in October as the state launches an independent investigation into what went wrong during Wednesday’s botched execution of Pike, according to Lee.
Strada for his part said his resignation would allow that review to move forward in the best interests of Tennessee.
“Serving as commissioner of the Tennessee department of correction has been a great honor, and I continue to believe the department carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol,” Strada said in his resignation statement.
“Even so, stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward,” he said. “I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred.”
Strada handed in his resignation amid intensifying scrutiny of Tennessee’s closely guarded execution procedures after Pike was injected with lethal drugs on Wednesday but survived. She became the first death row prisoner in the US to undergo such an execution attempt and live.
Pike’s attorney Randy Spivey, who witnessed the procedure from inside the death chamber, described what happened as “cruel and torturous”. He said he personally counted seven needles inserted into Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”.
Attorneys have alleged that Pike’s failed lethal injection was the fifth “botched” execution carried out under Strada’s leadership in two states since 2022, as the Guardian reported on Saturday, hours before his resignation was announced.
Pike remained unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital as of Friday, according to a court filing submitted by her attorneys. Her lawyers said hospital personnel were trying to save her life and, as of late Thursday, were working to clear the two doses of the execution drug from her system.
Wednesday’s extraordinary breakdown inside Tennessee’s execution chamber has triggered demands for an explanation from people on both sides of the death penalty debate. Besides ordering the independent review into case, Lee has paused the scheduling of executions in Tennessee.
Pike’s attorneys said they believe complications involving intravenous lines caused pentobarbital to enter her body rather than her bloodstream.
“Frank Strada’s resignation does not change the fact that Tennessee is shrouding its executions in secrecy,” Kit Thomas, a death row attorney in the federal public defender’s office in Nashville, said in a statement. “When Governor Lee hired Strada to fix execution problems in Tennessee his problematic history of executions in Arizona was well known. Strada then oversaw the implementation of a new protocol that ignored the recommendations of the independent investigation and weakened protections leading to a string of problems in Tennessee, including this week’s horrific botched execution attempt and another one in May. Until there is transparency and accountability, botched executions will keep happening.”
Laura Porter, the executive director of the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty, said in a statement: “Hopefully this is the beginning of accountability and an end to secrecy that enables these debacles.”
“Attorneys and community leaders across Tennessee have been trying for some time to get the Governor and the administration to take seriously the huge problems with the competency of the state’s execution process,” Porter’s statement continued. “They were ignored.”
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of teenage classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, killed Slemmer at a job training camp in Knoxville.
A pentagram had been carved into Slemmer’s chest.
After the murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”
Had her execution that day succeeded, Pike on Wednesday would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

A drug that may prevent Ebola infection is being tested in Congo

Unknown Publisher

A drug that may prevent Ebola infection is being tested in Congo
Kyiv • UNN
More than 250 people in Congo are testing obeldesivir after exposure to the Ebola virus. The study is planned to expand to nearly 1,000 participants.
In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, more than 250 people have joined a trial of the experimental drug obeldesivir, which may prevent Ebola from developing after contact with an infected person. Associated Press reports this, writes UNN.
Details
It is noted that the study is being conducted against the backdrop of the deadliest outbreak of the disease in the country's history.
The drug in question is Gilead's antiviral obeldesivir. It is being tested as post-exposure prophylaxis—the drug is given to people after likely contact with the virus but before symptoms appear, in an attempt to prevent the disease from developing.
The trial began in July in Ituri Province, the epicenter of the current Ebola outbreak. Participants include healthcare workers and relatives of infected people who may have been exposed to the virus. Overall, the researchers plan to enroll nearly 1,000 people.
Adults and children aged 12 and older who have been in contact with a confirmed case during the previous five days but have no symptoms are eligible for the study. Half of the participants receive the drug, while the other half receive a placebo. Their condition is monitored daily for 21 days, followed by an additional interview after 42 days.
If a participant develops Ebola symptoms, they immediately receive supportive treatment. The researchers hope that, if obeldesivir's effectiveness is confirmed, it will help break chains of virus transmission.
The current outbreak was caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain, for which there are currently no approved specific medicines or vaccines. At the same time, authorities in the Congo are vaccinating healthcare workers with Ervebo, which was used during previous outbreaks of other Ebola strains, although its effectiveness specifically against Bundibugyo is still being studied.

Turkey football ref chief jailed pending trial for graft
The Turkish Football Federation (TFF) said Saturday it was working to shake up its refereeing oversight body after its top official was jailed pending trial on graft charges.
Ferhat Gundogdu, who heads the Central Referees Committee (MHK), and six other referee officials appeared in court Friday on suspicion of manipulating the referee administration process.
The judge placed Gundogdu and four others in pre-trial detention, while granting the two other officials conditional release.
"In light of these developments, work is ongoing to form a new Central Referees Committee," the TFF said in a statement on its website, its first comment on the arrests, which happened on Tuesday.
Referees for Turkish cup matches next week would be chosen by four MHK members not caught up in the scandal, it added.
The seven accused face charges that include "official document forgery", "breach of trust" and "illegal acquisition of personal data".
The scandal came exactly a year after the TFF suspended 149 referees on charges of illegal betting.
On Thursday night, police from the illegal betting and sports crime unit also detained Yasin Kol, a referee from Turkey's top-flight Super Lig, as well as an assistant referee, media reports said.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek has said prosecutors are examining claims about "interference in the processes of referee classification, assignments, scoring and appointments, as well as the exams on rules".
During Tuesday's raids, police searched the VAR room at TFF's headquarters in Istanbul, with observers saying the investigation was likely linked to last year's betting scandal and would have implications for the federation.
"It does seem to be a continuation of 2025, and it looks like it will continue further," sports journalist Ayhan Sensoy told AFP.
Sensoy, who wrote a 2024 book The Gambling Pit", said it was unlikely federation bosses "have any chance of staying in office".
Top TFF officials are due to fly home on Saturday after attending Friday night's Belgium-Turkey UEFA Nations League clash in Liege, which Turkey lost 3-0.

Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC

Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC
Local architecture studio INC has designed each guest room at this hotel overlooking New York's Rockefeller Plaza to emulate "a stateroom on an ocean liner".
The 529-key Kimpton Era is housed within a purpose-built, 33-storey tower on West 48th Street, just south of the art deco Rockefeller Center complex.
For the interiors, INC pulled in references from New York City itself, blending Uptown elegance and Downtown grit, as well as the compact grandeur of the luxury liners that once docked along the Hudson.
"Every detail of the Kimpton Era is engineered elegance with a room that feels more like a stateroom on an ocean liner – compact, crafted, and refined to the luxury of just enough," said INC partner Adam Rolston.
Materials throughout were chosen to reflect the city's dichotomy, pairing marbles, brass, leather and glazed ceramics with more industrial concrete and blackened steel.
In a triple-height atrium wrapped in fluted concrete, a blackened steel-and-glass stair coils around a mobile of organic forms that descends from the ceiling.
Cerused wood, terrazzo borders and diffused lighting define the elevator lobbies, while the tiered black-marble reception counter provides a weighted presence.
"Inspired by the city itself, the Kimpton Era captures New York's layered character — elegant yet gritty, refined yet raw – woven into a vertical voyage of venues and comfort in a purpose-built skyscraper at the heart of Rockefeller Center," said INC's Hillary Kroll.
The hotel's five dining venues include a Latin American eatery with terracotta walls and ceramic pendants that spans from the ground floor to the cellar.
A second-floor brasserie features banquette seating, panelled walls, a scarlet ceramic bar and mosaic floors, while the third-floor lobby cafe offers coffee in the mornings and cocktails at night.
On the roof, a bar references the dining rooms of Chinatown via a tomato-red counter framed by tiled portals, temple-like joinery and hand-painted lotus motifs.
The Kimpton Era's guest rooms are designed like compact ship cabins, with each "berth" featuring full white-oak walls that integrate a bed, desk and storage into a single furniture element.
Neutral colour palettes are offset by jewel-toned fabrics and brass accents, while wet-room-style bathrooms are defined by frosted, blackened metal-framed sliding glass doors that conserve space.
"[The Kimpton Era] is a self-contained voyage where guest rooms are like staterooms and lounges, and dining rooms unfold like the salons of a great ocean liner in a new expression of New York luxury," said INC's Louisa Revitte.
INC's previous hotel projects have included the 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge with Marvel Architects, and the event spaces at the TWA Hotel inside Eero Saarinen's JFK Airport terminal.
The studio – which celebrates its 20th anniversary this year – has also completed "gritty yet inviting" interiors for a restaurant in BIG's The Spiral skyscraper, and filled its own concrete-forward offices with eclectic furniture and plants.
The photography is by Read McKendree.

Kyiv to start building pontoon bridges over Dnipro – Kalashnyk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:57:00 UTC
01:57:00 KST

Kyiv to start building pontoon bridges over Dnipro – Kalashnyk
Infrastructure and Transport Minister Mykola Kalashnyk said this in an interview with Suspilne, Ukrinform reports.
According to the minister, the ministry's top priority is to strengthen existing bridge infrastructure and protect it from attacks in order to increase the resilience of the structures.
Kalashnyk added that authorities are currently considering a rapid option for connecting Kyiv's left and right banks if bridges are damaged: building embankment dams with pontoon crossings to maintain traffic across the Dnipro.
"Urgent solutions are a dam and a pontoon crossing, which can be built quickly. This work has already begun. A coordination meeting was held with the president. We received all the assignments, taking into account the critical situation. It was decided that the ministry, the Restoration Agency and the military, together with the city authorities, would take up this work," Kalashnyk said.
According to him, construction of such crossings could take up to three months, while the structures should provide at least half the capacity of the existing bridges.
"Preparatory work is currently underway, and construction will begin shortly. All infrastructure will be involved to ensure maximum throughput. On average, about 600,000 vehicles cross the bridges between Kyiv's left and right banks every day. And the task is to preserve this capacity. Therefore, locations have been identified where construction will begin," Kalashnyk said.
According to the minister, the locations where construction will begin have already been identified. Such work is planned not only in Kyiv but also in other regions of Ukraine and not only on the Dnipro.
In addition, the ministry is considering other options, including the construction of rapidly deployable concrete structures and, in the longer term, a tunnel under the Dnipro. However, such projects could cost tens of billions of hryvnias, so their implementation would be possible only with the support of partners.
"We can now start looking for investment, donors and international partners and implement what is needed to ensure a connection between the left and right banks. There are estimates – tens of billions of hryvnias, and sometimes, for huge infrastructure projects, hundreds of billions. So we do not currently have the financial capacity to afford this. But the task is to find such resources," Kalashnyk said.
At the same time, the main priority remains preserving the bridges and preventing their destruction. To this end, "the maximum possible amount of equipment has been deployed," the minister added.
"Obviously, every bridge has a certain safety margin. And our first task is to ensure protection from the air, which we are working on together with the military. So the first stage is to prevent hits. The second is to ensure protection. The third is rapid restoration. And the fourth is to make decisions on alternative backup crossings, that is, the construction of new facilities as alternative bridge infrastructure," Kalashnyk said.
As reported, Russian forces attacked Kyiv's Northern Bridge early on October 3. The attack damaged the roadway and the trolleybus overhead contact network.
On October 2, the Southern Bridge in Kyiv was completely closed to traffic following several enemy attacks.

Ukraine’s top general wants to end Soviet rules in army. But president’s wartime headquarters may still hold reforms, commander says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:51:52 UTC
01:51:52 KST

Ukraine's top general is held responsible for the entire army but cannot freely choose the people who run it, says drone company commander Yurii Butusov, according to Radio NV. Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi still lacks full power to form his own command team, with key appointments controlled by the president's wartime lead, which unbalances the force, he believes.
Drapatyi was named a commander-in-chief in July. Since then, he has moved fast where he can: cutting more than 30 obsolete, Soviet-era General Staff orders, pressing to give combat-tested sergeants real authority, and opening a review of the officer corps to weed out those without combat experience.
For the reform of the force, Butusov argues, he has to be able to build his own team, and that is just what he is not being allowed to do. Key appointments, from the Air Force to the Air Assault Forces, stay under the direct control of the Supreme Commander's headquarters.
The headquarters keeps control
"One person should be responsible for managing the General Staff. It is Mykhailo Drapatyi, if he is given the chance to really be the sole commander-in-chief," Butusov says.
Any leader, he continues, has the right to build a structure to his own standards. But when people are slotted into the chain of command without the commander's knowledge, it breeds dysfunction.
"If there are political appointments to the General Staff without his knowledge, to the commanders of the branches without his knowledge, there will be problems, opposition, internal conflicts," he says, the kind that have dogged the army for years.
One deputy stays 'acting'
The limits show in Drapatyi's own inner circle, Butusov says. One of his first moves was to name Serhii Sobko deputy chief of the General Staff, yet Sobko remains only "acting", the prefix never lifted.
Only the president, as supreme commander, can finalize such appointments, he notes, and the delay points to "artificial restraints." Drapatyi has been allowed to shape the Ground Forces, by his account, while other structures remain under the headquarters' control.
Blame outruns the power
The result, in Butusov's words, is a commander-in-chief who carries the responsibility without the authority: the public and leadership hold him answerable for an army he cannot fully command.

MEA rejects Pak's claims on Ferozepur border incident
NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Saturday summoned the Chargé d'Affaires of the Pakistan high commission to lodge a strong protest over what it described as the continued facilitation of illegal cross-border infiltration from Pakistan.It also rejected as “baseless and motivated” Pakistan’s allegations over an October 2 incident in the Ferozepur sector of Punjab along the International Border.MEA said that Pakistan was informed that three individuals had entered Indian territory and continued moving towards the border fence despite repeated warnings from the BSF to return. The force subsequently engaged them after they were assessed to pose an imminent security threat."The Pakistani side was informed that three individuals infiltrated into Indian territory and despite multiple warnings by BSF to return to Pakistan, continued to move towards the border fence. The BSF was compelled to engage them for posing an imminent security threat," MEA said in a statement.MEA said the incident was part of a repeated pattern of cross-border movement by armed narcotics syndicates operating from Pakistan.
Islamabad was urged to investigate such infiltration and drug-smuggling activities, including the alleged involvement of Pakistani border forces, and take appropriate corrective measures."This incident highlights a clear pattern of repeated cross-border movement by armed narcotics syndicates operating from Pakistan. Government of Pakistan was urged to investigate these cross-border infiltration, drug smuggling activities and the complicity of Pakistan Border Guarding forces therein, and to take appropriate remedial measures," it said.
"Pakistan was further urged to ensure respect for the sanctity of the International Border, strictly observe relevant bilateral arrangements, mandate its forces to exercise effective control to prevent unauthorized movement from its side, and take definitive measures to prevent the recurrence of such incidents," it added.

Aramco facility in Riyadh comes under attack
TEHRAN – A large plume of smoke and fire was seen rising in the vicinity of an Aramco facility in Riyadh on Saturday, a witness told Reuters.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities about the fire. Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The fire comes amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Ansarallah, who have stepped up attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for Saturday's fire.
On September 24, Ansarallah said they had attacked Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu with missiles and drones. Saudi Arabia said at the time that it had intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Ansarallah – officially called Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF - towards Taif and the Yanbu area, but did not report damage to Aramco facilities.
Also, on September 13, a drone attack hit Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, disrupting oil flows to Yanbu.
On July 20, Ansarallah announced a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, saying the move was in response to Saudi naval and air siege on areas it controls in Yemen.
Saudi strikes on Yemen have reached 1,350
Meanwhile, regional and Western officials told Reuters that Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive against YAF, with options being considered including a coastal push to secure the Red Sea shipping route or an assault on multiple fronts.
The operation, expected to be launched in the coming weeks, will be led by the Riyadh backed-forces on the ground and air strikes by Saudi Arabia, according to six people with knowledge of the preparations.
Over the past 24 hours, Saudi warplanes carried out 94 airstrikes and missile attacks targeting civilian sites in the provinces of Sana’a, Saada, Taiz, Hajjah, Amran and Ibb, killing and wounding civilians, YAF spokesman Yahya Saree declared in a statement on Saturday October 3.
The attacks were carried out by F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets that took off from the Khamis Mushait and Taif air bases, while the missile attacks were launched from Najran and Jizan, Saree stated.
The brigadier general added the total number of Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks since the escalation began has reached 1,350.
In a post on X, the Al-Masirah TV also said Saudi aircraft fired missiles at a telecommunications network in Saqain district in Saada as well as Amran in the same province.
Meanwhile, the independent Al-Masdar Online website reported hearing the sounds of eight explosions resulting from airstrikes on sites inside Sanaa, accompanied by the sound of aircraft flying overhead.
No details were provided about injuries or damage.

Is the UAE trying to save Netanyahu?
TEHRAN – Israeli media sought to explain Netanyahu’s surprise visit to Abu Dhabi as an effort to ease the tension between him and Mohammed bin Zayed.

According to Israeli Channel 14, which is close to Netanyahu, representatives from several Arab countries, Saudi Arabia, Morocco, Libya, Jordan and the UAE, took part in the meeting hosted by Abu Dhabi on September 27. The channel reported that Israeli and U.S. representatives also attended the talks.
The Israeli channel reported that the meeting covered developments in Yemen, Iran, Lebanon, and the region as a whole.
Just hours after Netanyahu left Abu Dhabi, he held talks with Mohammed bin Zayed. The Emirati capital then witnessed extensive and important discussions between bin Zayed and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan. Fidan later met with UAE Vice President Mansour bin Zayed and National Security Adviser Tahnoun bin Zayed.
This underscores the importance of the talks. They took place almost immediately after Netanyahu’s visit to Abu Dhabi. This is particularly significant because Turkey is part of the “Mecca alliance” that Saudi Arabia wants to target Yemen.
Fidan’s visit drew further attention after Mansour bin Zayed made a surprise visit to Riyadh. There, he met Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his brother, Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman.
During the meeting, they discussed whether the UAE could join the Mecca alliance after repairing its relations with Riyadh. Ben Gvir says entire West Bank belongs to Israel

Ben Gvir says entire West Bank belongs to Israel
Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir claimed that the entire occupied West Bank “belongs to Israel” and has vowed to dismantle the Palestinian Authority and pursue the displacement of Palestinians if he becomes defense minister, Israeli media have reported.
Speaking to Israel’s Channel 14, Ben Gvir said that, if appointed defense minister, he would work to dismantle the Palestinian Authority and push for Palestinians to leave the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
The minister claimed that 60 percent of Palestinians want to “emigrate”.
“I will dedicate time to this, and I will manage the process continuously. Every week, I will hold a discussion involving all relevant parties,” he said, Middle East Eye reported. “There is no difference between Areas A, B and C. The entire land is ours."
Under the territorial framework established in the Oslo agreement between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization in 1995, Areas A and B were placed under varying degrees of Palestinian jurisdiction, while Israel retained control over Area C.
The United Nations regards the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, as occupied Palestinian territory, stating that Israeli settlements in territory occupied since 1967 have “no legal validity”.
The minister, who has repeatedly made genocidal statements against Palestinians, also called for fewer restrictions on Israeli soldiers’ use of force in the occupied territories.
Asked how Israel could provide additional forces for operations in the West Bank and Gaza, he replied: “It is very simple: The more you allow soldiers to shoot and use force, the less manpower you need.”
“I will remove the restrictions on our soldiers. Today, the police rules of engagement are much more lenient than those of the army,” he added.
The developments followed a visit by Netanyahu to tunnels beneath Al-Aqsa. The Israeli prime minister said during the visit: “It is moving to touch the rock of our existence. We are here very close to the Holy of Holies. We are here, and we will always remain here.”
The status quo governing Al-Aqsa recognizes the courtyard as an Islamic holy site administered by the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, although Israel controls security and access.
Ben Gvir also visited the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron on September 29 alongside hundreds of Israeli settlers during Sukkot.
“When I arrive at the Ibrahimi Mosque, I draw energy that makes me want to sing and rejoice,” he told Channel 14 during the visit.
Israeli authorities had closed the mosque to Muslim worshippers during the Jewish holiday. The Palestinian Ministry of Endowments and Religious Affairs condemned the closure, calling it an assault on the mosque and on Muslim freedom of worship.
The Ibrahimi Mosque has been divided between Muslim and Jewish worshippers since 1994, when an Israeli settler killed 29 Palestinian worshippers inside the mosque.
Ben Gvir also criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, saying the premier had “not want[ed] it enough” when it came to advancing a policy of Palestinian displacement.
The remarks come weeks before Israel’s October 27 Knesset election, with Ben Gvir seeking to strengthen his position on the Israeli far right.
Growing provocations
Ben Gvir’s comments follow a series of Israeli incursions into Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem and Hebron during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot.
On September 29, some 966 Israeli settlers entered the Al-Aqsa Mosque courtyard in occupied East Jerusalem. Videos circulated by Israeli far-right groups showed participants conducting religious rituals, praying, singing, and dancing inside the courtyard.
Ben Gvir was among those who entered Al-Aqsa during the earlier incursions.

6 awards for Iran from World Film Festival in Cannes
TEHRAN – The World Film Festival in Cannes – Remember the Future has announced the winners of its September online edition, with two Iranian films winning six awards.
Iranian short film “Artificial Human,” written, directed, and produced by Pouya Golpour, won five awards and “Staccato” by Ghazaleh Mazinani received one award, Mehr reported.
“Artificial Human” received the Best Asian Film and Best Director in a Short Film awards for Golpour, Best Actress in a Short Film award for Sharareh Sadri, Best Actor in an Indie Film award for Mahdi Afshari, and Best Young Actor in a Short Film award for Aylin Homaun. “Staccato” won the Best Experimental Film award.
A science-fiction film, “Artificial Human” depicts a post-apocalyptic world devastated by nuclear bombardments, where an inventor and his family survive and struggle to rebuild their lives with the help of his invention.
World Film Festival in Cannes – Remember the Future organizes a monthly and annual competition of all genres for international filmmakers, a qualifier on IMDb and dedicated to feature films, short films, independent films, documentaries, experimental films, animated films, music videos, screenwriters, songwriters, singers and bands, commercials, Web/TV series and much more.

Melbourne exhibition highlights victims of Minab school attack, Gaza war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:45:39 UTC
01:45:39 KST

Melbourne exhibition highlights victims of Minab school attack, Gaza war
TEHRAN- The Sydney-based Benevolent Iranian Women Association (BIWA), invited by the Campaign for International Cooperation and Disarmament (CICD) and the Unitarian Peace Memorial Church Melbourne, held the “Bombs for Peace” art exhibition at the Melbourne church last week.
The church’s Sunday prayer service opened with a memorial for the child victims of the Minab school attack and a condemnation of what organizers described as atrocities committed by the United States and Israel in West Asia.
Australian anti-war activist John Shipton, the keynote speaker, reviewed what he described as a longstanding pattern of US and Israeli military and political interventions, referring to events ranging from the 1948 Nakba and the 1953 overthrow of Iran’s democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mosaddegh, to recent conflicts in West Asia.
Shipton also drew parallels between these historical events and the Minab school tragedy, in which more than 168 students, teachers and staff were killed, according to the organizers.
For her part, BIWA President Masoomeh Alaibakhsh spoke about the beginning of the new academic year in Iran and the reopening of schools. She presented figures on student and teacher casualties in recent conflicts, along with information on damage to schools and educational centers.
Alaibakhsh expressed hope that such tragedies would not be repeated and stressed the need for those responsible for attacks on civilians and educational institutions to be held accountable under international law.
The event continued with a tour of the exhibition and a screening of “Minab: An Independent Inquiry,” a documentary directed by Maryam Sadr. The film examines the circumstances surrounding the Minab school attack and presents documents and other evidence concerning Shajareh Tayyebeh School, which had functioned solely as an educational institution for more than a decade.
The screening was followed by a live discussion with Sadr, who spoke about her firsthand experience visiting the Minab school site and interviewing families of the students who were killed in the attack.
The documentary created a somber atmosphere among the audience, while visitors from different nationalities and backgrounds expressed solidarity with families affected by recent conflicts, particularly children. Many also voiced hopes for lasting peace and security around the world.
The exhibition featured two main sections focusing on Iran and Palestine.
The Iran section displayed works by Iranian-Australian artists, drawings by Iranian children who had experienced war, and artworks created by students of the Minab school who were killed in the attack. Portraits of the child victims and their school assignments, including classroom drawings and free-form illustrations reflecting their interests and aspirations, attracted considerable attention.
The Palestine section was presented by the Iranians Friends of Palestine NSW (IFOPNSW) and featured artworks depicting the suffering in Gaza and Palestine. The section included works by Palestinian artists living in Gaza, as well as Australian and Palestinian artists based in Australia.
The organizers said they hoped similar events held in communities and cities across Australia would help raise awareness of the impact of recent conflicts in West Asia and preserve the memory of children who were killed or affected by the wars.

Documentary “A Fox Under a Pink Moon” wins at Matera International Film Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:45:08 UTC
01:45:08 KST

Documentary “A Fox Under a Pink Moon” wins at Matera International Film Festival
TEHRAN – The documentary “A Fox Under a Pink Moon” co-directed by Mehrdad Oskouei and Soraya Akhlaghi won an award at the Matera International Film Festival (MATIFF), which was held from September 26 to October 4 in Matera, Italy.
MATIFF 2026 celebrated the talent and vision of Oskouei and Akhlaghi, who has also performed in the film, with the prestigious Bini-Pasolini Foundation Award , ISNA reported.
In its citation, the Alfredo Bini Foundation recognized their “authorial courage” and a production method that transforms the smartphone from a simple technical device to an instrument of expression, testimony, and resistance. This work embodies MATIFF's mission: independent cinema capable of building bridges between worlds and cultures.
A joint production of Iran, France, the UK, Denmark, and the US, the 76-minute film had its world premiere at the 38th International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA) in the Netherlands in November 2025 and won its first international award.
Since then, the documentary has participated in over 70 international film festivals and won some 38 awards.
The movie shows 16-year-old Soraya, who is already creating stunning drawings and sculptures that are as beautiful as they are dark. This strong-willed Afghan sculptor and illustrator has been trying for five years to leave Iran and join her mother in Austria.
Mehrdad Oskouei directed the film entirely remotely, with Soraya filming all the footage herself over five years using her phone.
This material is interspersed with shots of her drawings and surreal animations. Making art is no idle pastime for Soraya: she puts all her worries, joys, and fears into her drawings and the sculptures she makes from soaked egg cartons or clay that she finds along her routes. Many of her drawings feature recurring figures: a loyal fox who is her traveling companion, a pink moon that always watches over her, and a clown who never laughs—a character Soraya identifies with.
According to Oskouei, a renowned Iranian documentary filmmaker, in the past 19 years, working with the Center for Rehabilitation, he has made four films about young delinquents and murderers. “In my first film, ‘It’s Always Late for Freedom,’ I felt that my characters wanted a larger part in forming the narration of the film, and this thought stayed with me until my last film, ‘Sunless Shadows,’ where I succeeded in obtaining this result in parts of the film,” he said.
“Later, when I looked through the footage in the editing room, I was amazed by the atmosphere I felt through this material. When I decided to make this happen in my newest film, I did away with my entire filming crew on set,” he added.
“After Soraya’s first trip to Turkey, when the filming continued upon her return to Tehran, she increased her knowledge of filmmaking by enrolling in classes on how to use a cell phone for making films. I spoke to her each night about the scenes she had taken and planned to take, and in this way, we coordinated a joint directorship,” Oskouei noted.
According to Akhlaghi, when she first turned the camera towards herself, she was not ready. “Life in those days was full of fear, suppressed anger, and a search for a way to continue living and surviving. The very moment I filmed my first images, it was as if a piece of reality awoke within me, a reality I had tried to hide for years,” she said.
“From 2018 until today, this film was not just a filmmaking project for me; it was a journey not only of watching myself but of knowing and building myself. At first, the camera was like a cold witness to me, but gradually it became a friend. A friend I truly needed to confide in,” she added.
“When I first met Mehrdad Oskouei (who has become ‘Uncle Mehrdad’ to me), something broke inside me. He said honestly, ‘Who you are right now is not your real self.’ Then he gave me paper and colored pencils and asked me to draw. So, I drew clowns; only clowns. Clowns that never laughed. Those clowns were my inner pains. They were my unseen wounds,” she stated.
“From that point, I began to draw my pains, one by one. It was as if Uncle Mehrdad knew that by drawing those pictures, I would gradually become calm and free. Today, I want to say that working with Mehrdad Oskouei, the professional documentary film director, was like a school of life for me. I learned from him that what an artist sees is not just about beauty, but beyond that, it is about truth,” she emphasized.
“Making a film alongside Uncle Mehrdad brought back trust for me; trust in others, and more importantly, trust in myself. He wasn’t just a filmmaker. Throughout this journey, he was like a friend, a therapist, and a trustworthy person by my side at a time when I trusted no one. For him, the film wasn’t important; saving my life was important. And I felt this with my entire being,” Akhlaghi asserted.
“Today, looking back on this seven-year journey, I understand he didn’t just teach me how to film myself; he taught me how to survive and how to live. And that is the miracle of cinema and documentary film. And now, after all these years, I stand here. Not as the teenage girl who narrowly escaped death many times, but as a woman who found belief in herself and rebuilt herself from scratch,” she said.

Iran has ‘legitimate right’ to civilian nuclear program – China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:45:02 UTC
01:45:02 KST

Iran has ‘legitimate right’ to civilian nuclear program – China
Iran has the right to pursue a peaceful nuclear program as a party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), Beijing has said.
China’s deputy permanent representative to the UN, Sun Lei, made the statement to the General Assembly on Thursday.
“As a non-nuclear-weapon State party to the Treaty on the NPT, Iran should honor its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons, and its legitimate right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy should be respected,” Sun said in a plenary meeting on the use of the veto.
The debate followed a vote in September in which China and Russia blocked a resolution submitted by the US to extend the mandate of a UN sanctions watchdog panel on Iran sanctions.
The monitoring body was reinstated as part of the ‘snapback’ mechanism invoked in August by the UK, France, and Germany (the E3), aimed at reimposing sanctions. China and Russia consider the snapback legally invalid and maintain that the sanctions were not restored.
According to Sun, China used its veto to “uphold a correct understanding of right and wrong,” support a political settlement of the Iranian nuclear issue, address non-proliferation concerns, and promote long-term peace and stability in the Middle East.
The stalemate over Iran’s nuclear program stems from Washington’s unilateral withdrawal from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), and subsequent failures by the E3 to exhaust diplomatic options under the plan before invoking the snapback, the diplomat said.
Under the 2015 agreement, Iran agreed to curtail its enrichment activities in exchange for sanctions relief. President Donald Trump pulled the US out of the agreement in 2018 during his first term and reimposed sanctions on Iran.
In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran in what Trump described as an effort to prevent the country from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
Russia condemned the attack and maintains that Iran’s nuclear program is peaceful.
President Vladimir Putin, speaking at the annual Valdai forum on Thursday, said a Russian proposal to transfer Iran’s enriched uranium to Russia remains on the table. The US initially agreed to this but later toughened its position and refused, he said.
“If all the participants in this process ultimately conclude that this would help defuse tensions in any way, we are ready to engage in that work,” Putin stated.

Donya-e-Eqtesad: Washington’s response on Tehran’s table
Donya-e-Eqtesad analyzed Tehran’s seven-day proposal and the current US approach. The US response to Iran’s seven-day proposal was reviewed in Tehran on Wednesday, marking a new phase in negotiations that are now focused less on the substance of an agreement and more on the sequencing of commitments, mutual guarantees, and the degree of flexibility shown by each side. These issues could determine the future trajectory of diplomacy. Receiving Washington’s response should not by itself be interpreted as a sign that an agreement is imminent. Even if a new understanding is reached, it would not necessarily resolve the fundamental disputes between Iran and the United States. Therefore, the newspaper considers the most likely short-term scenario to be continued intensive diplomacy and phased agreements aimed at crisis management. Such arrangements may temporarily reduce tensions, but a durable solution would require more substantial changes in the positions of both sides.
Jam-e-Jam: Netanyahu plans to drag Trump into a new crisis with Iran
Jam-e-Jam evaluated what it described as an alleged plot involving the hijacking of an Israeli-bound aircraft. The newspaper claimed that the objective of such an operation would be to force Trump into a new confrontation and potentially another war with Iran. Netanyahu is deeply concerned about his political future and fears that, if elections for the Knesset were held under current conditions, his coalition would fail to secure a majority and form a government. Netanyahu hopes to use his influence over the White House and Trump to draw the United States into another large-scale conflict, thereby using American military power, economic resources, and international standing to improve his domestic political position. Iran is closely monitoring American and Zionist activities and is prepared to respond decisively to any hostile action by Israel or the United States.
Ham-Mihan: Why did Trump reject Iran’s proposal?
Ham-Mihan examined the reasons behind Trump’s rejection of Tehran’s seven-day proposal. The newspaper wrote that Trump initially rejected the offer, arguing that Iran was seeking a quick agreement to end Washington’s economic pressure campaign while under significant strain. From Trump’s perspective, accepting the proposal could have created the impression that, after incurring military and political costs and enforcing economic pressure, the United States had been compelled to offer economic concessions in order to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Instead, Trump reportedly seeks an agreement that can be presented not as a new version of the JCPOA, but as a stricter arrangement in which Iran first accepts verifiable nuclear restrictions and only afterward receives sanctions relief. Some experts on Iran- US relations believe that if Washington continues to demand nuclear concessions before taking any economic steps, the seven-day initiative may represent not the beginning of an agreement but the final diplomatic effort before a new phase of escalation.
Iran: Iran’s multi-layered nuclear file
The Iran newspaper assessed the 70th General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). According to the paper, the conference represented a confrontation between two different logics: the logic of institutions and the logic of politics. Under the institutional logic, formal mechanisms still allow participation, voting, dialogue, and multilateral cooperation. Under the political logic, however, power dynamics, national interests, and the security environment surrounding major issues strongly influence outcomes. The newspaper added that a third layer, the media dimension, shapes how public opinion interprets events. It argued that the significance of Vienna lies precisely in the interaction of these three layers: Iran’s nuclear file is no longer merely a technical issue but a complex, multidimensional matter that interconnects law, diplomacy, security, safety, and media. The recent Vienna meeting, therefore, should be viewed not simply as an annual conference but as a condensed reflection of the current state of nuclear diplomacy, where maintaining a place within international mechanisms, managing political disagreements, preserving technical channels, and presenting accurate, well-documented narratives have all become equally important.

Valtersson exposes NATO military exhaustion, Russian air superiority, US strategic defeat  in Iran

Valtersson exposes NATO military exhaustion, Russian air superiority, US strategic defeat in Iran
TEHRAN — In the latest joint X Space broadcast co-hosted by the Tehran Times and Sputnik, military analyst Mikael Valtersson—a former officer of the Swedish Armed Forces specializing in air defense, former defense politician, and chief of staff with the Sweden Democrats—provided an incisive assessment of shifting global strategic realities.
Valtersson detailed Russia's undeniable air superiority in Ukraine, the severe depletion of European military stockpiles, and the profound economic and strategic defeat suffered by the United States in its military confrontation with Iran. Highlighting the collapse of Western security narratives, Valtersson underscored how Washington's reckless interventions have eroded American soft power, exposed NATO's structural vulnerabilities, and accelerated the long-term contraction of the U.S. military footprint across the Middle East.
Sputnik Question: Following the quiet abandonment of Ukraine's publicized 40-day drone campaign, how have the air war dynamics shifted between Russia and Ukraine—particularly given reports that Russian reconnaissance and jet-powered drones are flying virtually unopposed over Kyiv to film strike impacts in high quality, while sustained strikes target Odesa's port infrastructure?
The Ukrainian 40-day drone campaign was a classic PR stunt designed for Western public consumption. Once it failed to paralyze Russia's economy or force political concessions, Kyiv simply ceased mentioning it altogether. Western media coverage remains egregiously biased, seizing on isolated incidents to accuse Russia of targeting civilians while ignoring major Russian operational successes. In reality, civilian casualty rates in Ukraine remain remarkably low compared to military losses—a standard of restraint that should be commended in modern warfare.
Russian air superiority across the theater is absolute and manifest. Ukraine possesses a critical deficit of high-end air defense assets, such as Patriot missile batteries, which are rationed sparingly to protect select high-value sites in Kyiv. Furthermore, Ukraine lacks the medium-level air defense systems necessary to counter Russia's newer jet-powered drones, leading to at least a tripling of successful drone penetrations. The sight of Russian reconnaissance drones loitering over Kyiv to capture high-resolution strike footage highlights this total air defense breakdown.
Beyond the capital, key maritime hubs like Odesa demonstrate the extent of Ukrainian vulnerability. Russia's daily, sustained strike campaign against Ukrainian shipping and harbor infrastructure in Odesa has proceeded virtually unopposed for three months, devastating Ukraine's grain export capacity and striking a fatal blow to its national economy.
Tehran Times Question: U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that the war in Iran could be concluded within two weeks. Given Iran's capture of a second U.S. unmanned submarine in the Strait of Hormuz and the heavy expenditure of U.S. air defense interceptors during Iranian strikes on Jordan's Muwaffaq Salti air base, what is the reality of Washington's military posture and strategic standing?
The claim that the war with Iran will end in two weeks is completely detached from military reality. Such a timeframe would require the United States to offer Iran an extraordinarily favorable deal, as Tehran holds the superior strategic position and will not accept a bad peace arrangement.
Trump faces mounting domestic political pressure over soaring fuel prices and impending midterm election losses, leaving Washington with minimal leverage. Trump's bombastic statements—claiming Iran is "totally destroyed" and declaring the "greatest victory in world history"—indicate that he is either becoming demented or simply lying, as his assertions directly contradict operational facts on the ground.
Tactically and technologically, a strategic deadlock has set in that favors Tehran. Iran's capture of a second U.S. unmanned submarine in the Strait of Hormuz represents a major intelligence harvest, providing Iranian engineers direct access to advanced American technology. Operationally, the limits of American air defense were laid bare during the Iranian attack on Jordan's Muwaffaq Salti air base. U.S. forces expended an immense volume of interceptors—firing approximately 70 Patriot missiles and over 12 THAAD interceptors—yet Iranian missiles still penetrated the defense grid, destroying or damaging around 10 aircraft. Washington cannot sustain this rate of interceptor expenditure without compromising its global force posture. Ultimately, this war represents a catastrophic strategic defeat for U.S. influence, missile reserves, and global soft power, while significantly elevating the strategic standing of both Iran and China.
Sputnik Question: What realistic military options remain for European nations seeking to sustain Ukraine, given the severe exhaustion of Western weapon stockpiles, unsustainable Ukrainian casualty figures, a dark winter outlook, and rising political volatility within Europe?
European nations have virtually no viable military options left to alter the war's trajectory. European defense inventories are thoroughly drained, and because the United States must prioritize replenishing its own critically depleted stockpiles, Europe cannot expect American rearmament assistance for years. At best, European aid can temporarily delay a complete Ukrainian military collapse, but it cannot support effective offensive operations.
The human toll on Ukraine is mathematically unsustainable. Citing data acknowledged by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk from Ukrainian military sources, Ukraine is losing roughly 28,000 soldiers per month to deaths and severe injuries—totaling approximately 325,000 casualties per year. In the territory currently controlled by Kyiv, the population is probably below 20 million, with two million men actively dodging military service. Ukraine is exhausting its human reserves far faster than it can draft replacement personnel, pointing toward a dark and difficult winter as Russian forces methodically strike critical logistics and energy infrastructure. While reckless political rhetoric from European elites carries risks of unintended escalation reminiscent of 1914, shifting domestic political dynamics—such as the growth of AfD and BSW in Germany and the National Rally in France—will likely force a significant reduction in European military backing for Kyiv in the years ahead.
Tehran Times Question: How are Washington's claims of maintaining complete control over the Strait of Hormuz received by the European public, and how is energy inflation shaping European attitudes toward U.S. foreign policy?
Mikael Valtersson Answer: Official assertions by the U.S. administration that it controls the Strait of Hormuz and that commercial shipping has returned to normal are treated as a complete joke by the European public. If an election for U.S. president were held in Europe today, Donald Trump would receive perhaps 5 to 10 percent of the vote, reflecting deep public cynicism toward official Washington narratives. Unlike the heavily slanted coverage of Ukraine, European media reporting on the Middle East has been noticeably more neutral, allowing citizens to see through American propaganda.
Furthermore, Western public perception of Iran has shifted noticeably. Prior to the war, European discourse focused almost exclusively on human rights allegations; today, public debate centers on Iranian resilience and the realization that Washington's military aggression was a grave error. The public increasingly views the conflict as a blunder driven not by American or European security interests, but by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's desperate attempt to avoid domestic prosecution and prison. Economically, European citizens are suffering under severe energy inflation. Having cut off cheap Russian energy due to sanctions, Europe exposed itself to global market shocks resulting from Middle Eastern volatility. While European governments temporarily buffered price spikes through domestic tax cuts on fuel, long-term economic damage remains inevitable, fueling public resentment against both Washington and European political elites.
Sputnik Question: How valid are Western accusations regarding Russian hybrid threats, and under international law, what legal rights does Russia possess to target European supply lines directly sustaining Ukraine's war effort?
Accusations regarding hybrid warfare merely highlight Europe's profound internal security vulnerabilities. European governments lack the security infrastructure and manpower needed to guard their vast industrial and economic assets, leaving localized vulnerabilities exposed to disruption.
 
Under established international law, European states have long since crossed the threshold into active co-belligerency. European governments do not merely offer passive sympathy; they provide direct budgetary support, heavy combat systems, operational training, intelligence, and equipment repair services. European direct budget support is the absolute operational backbone of the Ukrainian state; if Western economic budget support were withdrawn, the Ukrainian economy would collapse within three to six months, completely destroying its capability to maintain a defense. Drawing a historical parallel to U.S. material support for the British Empire prior to World War II and Germany's subsequent declaration of war, Russia possesses full legal justification under international law to target European logistical vectors and military infrastructure sustaining the enemy war effort.
Tehran Times Question: What does the permanent withdrawal of U.S. military forces from Iraq signal regarding the durability and strategic utility of American military bases across the Middle East?
The permanent withdrawal of U.S. forces from Iraq signals a structural decline in the American regional presence. Far from acting as strategic assets or instruments of deterrence, U.S. facilities across the Middle East have transformed into acute strategic liabilities and prime targets for regional defense forces.
For regional host nations, housing American facilities has backfired spectacularly. Rather than securing U.S. protection, regional host states have found their local infrastructure exposed to collateral damage and military strikes during broader regional escalations. Crucially, regional leaders feel deep resentment toward Washington's unilateral behavior; Gulf state politicians have openly complained that they were not even consulted or informed prior to U.S. strikes, learning through media reports that American forces had launched attacks from or near their sovereign territory without their knowledge. As regional allies realize that hosting American bases yields zero security benefits while incurring enormous security costs, they will increasingly demand the removal of U.S. troops, permanently diminishing Washington's military footprint in the region.

Russia rebukes US, defends Iran’s ‘inalienable’ nuclear rights
TEHRAN – Russia has strongly rebuked the United States over its calls for Tehran to abandon its peaceful nuclear program, reaffirming that the Islamic Republic possesses an inalienable right to pursue peaceful nuclear energy under international law.
In a post on X on Friday, Mikhail Ulyanov, Russia’s permanent representative to Vienna-based international organizations, slammed Washington for relying on “wrong assumptions” regarding non-proliferation norms and the mandate of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
“Iran is not obliged to abandon its nuclear program. It is Iran’s inalienable right,” Ulyanov emphasized. “Unfortunately, the position of the Republican administration is based on wrong assumptions of non-proliferation norms and the IAEA activities.”
The Russian diplomat made the remarks in response to US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz, who claimed Tehran had “broken the rules” by enriching uranium to 60 percent.
Iran has maintained a firm, principled stance regarding its peaceful atomic activities, particularly in the aftermath of the unprovoked US-Israeli military aggressions in June 2025 and February 2026. In both instances, the aggressors struck civilian and nuclear infrastructure in flagrant violation of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) and the UN Charter.
Following the initial aggression, which occurred amid indirect diplomatic engagements, the Iranian Parliament unanimously passed legislation in June 2025 suspending all cooperation with the IAEA. The decisive move came after the agency adopted a politically motivated resolution that set the stage for foreign strikes, followed by the UN nuclear watchdog’s refusal to condemn the illegal attacks on Iranian facilities.
Under the law, IAEA inspectors will not be permitted to resume monitoring unless verifiable security guarantees are established, subject to the approval of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC). Senior Iranian officials, including Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, have repeatedly stressed that neither Tehran’s legitimate nuclear rights nor its conventional deterrent capabilities are up for negotiation.
China also rallied behind Tehran. Addressing a recent UN General Assembly session, China’s deputy permanent representative to the UN, Sun Lei, reiterated that “Iran’s legitimate right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy should be respected.”
Sun held Washington responsible for the current crisis, pointing to its unilateral withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear deal (JCPOA), brutal “maximum pressure” campaigns, and military escalations during ongoing diplomacy.
