Helicopters, influencers and nail art: The money trail of 2026 assembly elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:39:46 UTC
01:39:46 KST

The filings offer a fascinating account of the financial machinery behind modern election campaigns.
From paying social-media influencers to allocating money for 'nail art', the BJP's expenditure statements reveal the range of campaign activities funded during its bid to win the West Bengal assembly election. A closer look at political parties' filings with the Election Commission of India (ECI) makes for interesting reading, revealing how spending priorities varied according to the political stakes in different states. However, the TVK example is only a humbling reminder that in democracy, greater outreach may lead to greater eyeballs, but it is no guarantee for success.The BJP declared Rs 529.39 crore expense for this year's assembly elections in West Bengal, Assam, Keralam, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. Congress declared Rs 248.55 crore as spending, less than half that amount.A TOI analysis of the expenditure filings shows that Rs 178.78 crore of the Rs 280.84-crore difference, nearly two-thirds, came from advertisements and travel by star campaigners, the top leaders a party sends around a state to address rallies. Money given directly to candidates accounted for only Rs 16.27 crore of the gap. At least on paper, the BJP's extensive advertising campaigns and deployment of senior leaders, many of them massive crowd pullers, distinguished its expenditure pattern from that of Congress.
The BJP won 207 seats in West Bengal in the results declared on May 4 and later won the Falta repoll to take its tally to 208. It formed its first government in the state, ending the Trinamool Congress's 15-year rule. TMC chief Mamata Banerjee lost her own seat, Bhabanipur, to the BJP's Suvendu Adhikari. The BJP-led NDA won Assam for a third consecutive term, while the NDA led by the All India NR Congress retained Puducherry.In Keralam, the Congress-led UDF returned to power after 10 years. Congress won 63 of the 140 seats, the CPI(M)-led LDF 35 and the BJP three. In Tamil Nadu, film star Vijay's TVK, contesting its first assembly election on the whistle symbol, won 108 of the 234 seats, ahead of the DMK with 59 and the AIADMK with 47. Subsequently, Vijay became chief minister.
The campaign war chests
The BJP, Congress and CPI(M) filed accounts covering all five elections, with the CPI(M) declaring only Rs 39.04 crore as expenditure. The DMK declared Rs 197.85 crore spending for Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, while the AIADMK reported Rs 112.40 crore expenses in a statement covering Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Keralam.TVK reported Rs 19.81 crore for Tamil Nadu, according to TOI report. TMC's full 2026 expenditure statement is not available on the ECI website.Political parties have no overall election expenditure ceiling, but individual candidates face spending limits. The accounts can also include expenditure authorised but not yet paid. The BJP's Bengal return, for instance, recorded Rs 89.32 crore in outstanding general-campaign expenditure at the end of the election period.
More than half the BJP's money, Rs 286.99 crore or 54.2 per cent, went to Bengal, followed by Rs 96.27 crore in Assam. Together, the two states accounted for Rs 383.26 crore, or 72.4 per cent of the party's total. The BJP also declared Rs 82.67 crore in Keralam, Rs 51.56 crore in Tamil Nadu and Rs 11.90 crore in Puducherry.
A statewise representation of poll expenditure by the BJP and Congress.
The spending pattern broadly reflected the different political stakes.The figure broadly aligns with what was at stake too. BJP was desperate to get power in Bengal after catapulting to second position in 2021 and sensing anti-incumbency was heavily weighing down on Mamata Banerjee. In Assam, it was looking to consolidate a strong position. The party had much less at stake in Tamil Nadu where it is still an emerging force. In Keralam, a much smaller state than Tamil Nadu, more amount was pumped in sensing an opportunity to break the binary nature of the state politics.For Congress, the situation was totally different. Its biggest chance for coming to power was in Keralam and it’s no surprise that the party spent the most in Keralam, Rs 105.34 crore or 42.4 per cent of its total, followed by Assam at Rs 67.62 crore, or 27.2 per cent. It declared Rs 42.08 crore in Bengal, Rs 22.25 crore in Tamil Nadu and Rs 11.25 crore in Puducherry.Bengal accounts for most of the gap between the two parties, perhaps unsurprisingly, although both parties were contesting almost the same number of seats in the state. The BJP declared Rs 244.91 crore more than Congress there, about 87 per cent of the total difference. Keralam was the only state where Congress declared more, by Rs 22.67 crore.
Ads, aircraft and the spending gap
Party filings divide spending into different categories, and three of them help explain the BJP–Congress difference to an extent.The BJP declared Rs 187.54 crore on general-party media advertisements, which promote the party as a whole rather than individual candidates. Congress declared Rs 92.52 crore, a difference of Rs 95.02 crore.
The funding gap between BJP and Congress, and where the money was spent.
Star-campaigner travel covers trips by a party's senior leaders, and the BJP's schedules list aircraft and helicopter travel for several of them. The BJP declared Rs 106.25 crore under this head against Congress's Rs 22.49 crore, about 4.7 times as much and Rs 83.76 crore more.Direct grants, the money a party transfers to candidates, were much closer. The BJP declared Rs 111.79 crore and Congress Rs 95.52 crore, a difference of Rs 16.27 crore, with the BJP's grants about 17 per cent higher. Congress spent slightly more on grants than on general-party media advertisements.In Bengal, the BJP recorded grants of Rs 20 lakh each to its 294 candidates, totalling Rs 58.80 crore. In the same state, it declared Rs 88.48 crore on general-party media advertisements and Rs 52.18 crore on star-campaigner travel.Grants, however, are only part of the support candidates receive, since parties also pay centrally for publicity, rallies and other campaign activities.The difference extended beyond advertisements and star campaigners' travel. The BJP declared ₹52.34 crore on publicity materials, including posters, banners and flags, against Congress's ₹11.48 crore. Under other general-party expenses, the BJP recorded ₹48.83 crore against Congress's ₹6.78 crore, another ₹42.05-crore gap. Congress, however, declared more expenditure on general-party meetings and rallies, ₹7.99 crore against the BJP's ₹4.06 crore.
From nail art to AI calls
The filings name the people and firms that were paid, though they do not always specify what services were delivered.In Bengal, the BJP's accounts include payments recorded against social-media influencers and content creators. TOI earlier reported that influencer Sayak Chakraborty acknowledged receiving Rs 2.5 lakh for two videos, The Bengal accounts also contain entries for nail art. Four entries of Rs 1 lakh each, marked "Nail Art", appear under public meetings and rallies. Another Rs 9.65 lakh is recorded against Visionary Edge for a "Nail Art Prog" under media advertisements.Sayak was not the only influencer or content creator named in the accounts. Others have also acknowledged receiving payments. Yet the separate virtual-campaign schedules recorded no expenditure.Across the five elections, the BJP's accounts list Rs 41.83 crore against Google India and Rs 15.65 crore against Facebook India Online Services, a total of Rs 57.48 crore, of which Rs 31.39 crore was attributed to Bengal. This amount is already included in the BJP's advertising expenditure. Advertising purchased through agencies for social media may also appear under other names.The filings also point to the use of artificial intelligence in election outreach. Congress's headquarters recorded Rs 3.72 crore against Neomarq Flare Solution LLP in Assam for a service described as "AI 2 Way Voice Calling".In Tamil Nadu, the DMK's Rs 197.85 crore included Rs 70.63 crore on general-party media advertisements and Rs 45.75 crore in grants to candidates. Five entries marked "Social media" added up to Rs 16.87 crore, naming Vipras Ads, Ravi Publicity Services, Glovy Trading and Populus Empowerment Network.Populus appeared four times in the accounts, for manpower and consultancy, campaign production, digital advertising (Rs 6.37 crore) and social media. Together, these entries totalled Rs 74.94 crore, about 37.9 per cent of the DMK's expenditure.The AIADMK recorded Rs 103.99 crore of its Rs 112.40 crore, or 92.5 per cent, in a single entry for Pramanya Strategy Consulting, described as "Social Media Promotion, TV, Website". Because the filing does not break down this amount, it cannot be compared directly with the DMK's specifically labelled social-media entries.The CPI(M)'s Keralam unit accounted for Rs 28.60 crore of the party's Rs 39.04 crore, and its Bengal unit Rs 8.23 crore. In Keralam, the party recorded Rs 19.53 crore on general-party media advertisements, of which Rs 18.77 crore, about 96 per cent, appeared in four entries naming Maitri Advertising for print, television and electronic media.These entries identify the companies named in the expenditure schedules, not necessarily the ultimate media outlets or platforms.
When spending and seats diverged
The BJP won Bengal, the state where it declared its largest expenditure, while the Congress-led UDF won Keralam, where Congress spent the most.Tamil Nadu, however, presented a striking contrast.TVK reported expenditure of Rs 19.81 crore, including about Rs 6.3 crore on media advertisements, Rs 3.5 crore on Vijay's air travel and Rs 2.1 crore on public meetings and roadshows, according to TOI's September 26 report.The DMK declared Rs 197.85 crore across Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, while the AIADMK reported Rs 112.40 crore in a statement covering three jurisdictions. Although the reporting coverage differed, TVK's declared expenditure was substantially smaller than that of either established Dravidian party.
Yet TVK won 108 assembly seats, compared with the DMK's 59 and the AIADMK's 47.Vijay entered politics with a considerable advantage in public recognition, having spent decades as one of Tamil cinema's biggest stars. His existing fan base and celebrity appeal may have given TVK organic visibility, yet the difference in spendings can’t be ignored.The filings offer a fascinating account of the financial machinery behind modern election campaigns, from helicopters and digital advertisements to influencers, consultants and AI-powered calls. They also expose the limits of pumping funds to win elections. Hence Tamil Nadu perhaps had the most important lesson for mainstream political parties.

Resilience comes from redundancy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:37 UTC
01:38:37 KST

The First Island Chain is one of the most powerful geopolitical features in the Indo-Pacific region. It is also an incomplete one. Drawn as a strategic line stretching from Japan through Taiwan toward the Philippines, it highlights military geography while largely overlooking the islands, ports and communities that connect across these waters.
The journey from Japan’s Kagoshima Prefecture down the Nansei Islands (commonly known in English as the Ryukyu Islands) offered a different perspective, travelling via Amami-Oshima and Okinawa, on to Ishigaki Island of the Yaeyama Islands at the southernmost tip of the Ryukyu archipelago, and then to Taiwan. Traveling through these islands and ports, I saw a maritime geography in which places that appear close on a map can remain disconnected in practice.
The strategic question should not be only how to defend the First Island Chain, but how to reconnect the maritime space within it.
This is not an entirely new idea. The Ryukyu Kingdom was once a major hub of maritime exchange linking Japan, China, Korea and Southeast Asia. Naha, the capital of Okinawa, was a node in a wider network extending across the East and Southeast Asian seas. Routes also connected the Ryukyu Islands with Amami-Oshima and Kagoshima and onward into the Japanese archipelago.
These sea-route networks served the political and commercial interests of their time and should not be romanticized. Yet they reveal an enduring geographical fact: The sea can connect islands as much as it separates them.
That connectivity was reshaped, for very different purposes, under the Japanese colonial rule of Taiwan. In the late 19th century, Japan developed shipping and communications links between Taiwan and the Japanese archipelago through the Ryukyu Islands. A shipping route connected Kobe with Keelung via Kagoshima and Okinawa. Even more strikingly, a submarine telegraph cable linked southern Kagoshima with Amami, Okinawa and the Yaeyama Islands before reaching Keelung.
This was an imperial network, built for administrative and strategic purposes, but its geography is revealing. The islands between Japan and Taiwan were not peripheral spaces. They functioned as nodes in a wider system of maritime transport and communications.
What if that geographical logic were applied to the 21st century?
I propose a modern Ryukyu Kaido (sea route) — a resilient maritime network beginning with stronger connections between Taiwan and Japan’s southwestern Islands, and eventually extending toward the Philippines and Southeast Asia.
It should not mean building one grand ferry route between Taiwan and Japan. A Ryukyu Kaido in the 21st century should be a network, not a line. Ferries, Roll-on/Roll-out (RoRo) vessels, cargo shipping, ports, tourism, logistics and air links should complement one another.
The immediate priority is the Taiwan-Ryukyu connection: Taiwan with the Yaeyama and Miyako Islands, Okinawa and, further north, Amami and Kagoshima. Where direct connections are commercially difficult, complementary routes and alternative modes can provide the missing links.
Three priorities should follow. First, Japan and Taiwan should explore practical pilot connections for passengers and freight, including ferries and RoRo services, while coordinating customs, immigration and quarantine procedures at participating ports. Second, ports and telecommunications networks should be designed with greater redundancy, including alternative shipping routes and submarine-cable links. Third, local and national authorities should establish mechanisms for disaster response and information sharing across the islands.
Connectivity should be treated not simply as an economic benefit, but as a form of resilience. Typhoons, earthquakes and port closures can isolate islands as effectively as other crises. If one route fails, a resilient network should allow people, goods and essential services to move through another.
Nor is connectivity only about ships. The Ryukyu Kaido could link physical infrastructure, digital infrastructure and people. Ports and shipping would form one layer; undersea cables, satellite communications and other telecommunications another. Disaster-response arrangements, information sharing, tourism and people-to-people exchanges would add further layers.
Taiwan already understands the importance of such redundancy. Its Ministry of Digital Affairs has been developing additional submarine-cable routes, backup communications, microwave links and satellite systems to reduce the impact of cable disruptions.
The lesson is simple: resilience comes from redundancy.
The same principle should apply to the maritime geography around Taiwan and the Ryukyu Islands. Security should not mean making islands self-contained. It should mean ensuring that no single disrupted route can isolate an island from the wider region.
This is where the Ryukyu Kaido challenges the conventional geopolitical map. The conventional map sees islands as positions to be defended. The alternative map sees them as nodes to be connected.
The resilient network could eventually extend southward toward the Philippines and, over time, into wider Southeast Asian maritime networks. However, the immediate task is more modest: strengthen the Taiwan-Ryukyu core and demonstrate that connectivity can reinforce resilience.
The goal is not to recreate the maritime worlds of the Ryukyu Kingdom or the imperial era, but to recover a geographical insight that both histories make visible: islands need not be isolated spaces. Japan and Taiwan can begin by treating maritime transport, ports, telecommunications, tourism and disaster preparedness not as separate policy silos, but as mutually reinforcing parts of a resilient network. The First Island Chain need not remain merely a strategic line on a map. It can become a network of maritime connections — a Ryukyu Kaido for the 21st century, with the sea itself serving not as the space between Taiwan and Japan’s islands, but as the road that connects them.
Yasuyuki Ishida is a Japanese academic specializing in Japan-India relations, maritime security and the Indo-Pacific region, with a research focus on maritime connectivity and resilience.

2026-10-03

Argentine President Javier Milei’s government on Friday said the country would offer citizenship to foreigners who invest at least US$350,000 in the country.
Latin America’s third-largest economy lagged far behind Brazil and Mexico in the foreign direct investment stakes last year, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).
Milei, a free-market radical, has slashed public spending, deregulated the economy and dismantled trade barriers in a bid to make Argentina more competitive and boost the Treasury’s dwindling dollar reserves.
Photo: AFP
However, investors are still waiting for Argentina’s roller-coaster economy to “prove that what it’s doing will actually be sustainable over time,” economist Marcelo Elizondo said.
The Citizenship by Investment Program announced by the government to coincide with Argentina Week in Paris proposes two “simple and transparent mechanisms” for obtaining an Argentine passport.
Investors can either make a “direct, non-refundable contribution of US$350,000 to the National Treasury” or “subscribe to an US$800,000 government bond created specifically” for the purpose.
The spouses and children of applicants can also secure citizenship, in exchange for a contribution of US$100,000 to the Treasury, or US$25,000 if they are younger than 18.
“The resources obtained will be used to continue strengthening the fiscal and financial position of the Argentine Republic,” the government said.
The Argentine Ministry of Economy said the investments would be subject to a “rigorous evaluation process ... guaranteeing the traceability of funds, the prevention of money laundering, and national security.”
However, some analysts expressed doubts over what kind of investor the scheme would attract.
“It could lead to us bringing in drug traffickers, people of dubious origin who are not allowed in other countries,” economist Pablo Tigani said.

MOA defends slow approval of Huwei plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:33 UTC
01:38:33 KST

The Ministry of Agriculture (MOA) on Friday defended its handling of a farmland conversion proposal by the Huwei Industrial Park development project, saying it had reviewed the plan in accordance with the law, and asked the Yunlin County Government to provide additional documents.
The ministry made the remarks after the county government criticized it for repeatedly questioning the project.
The county government proposed the project in 2024, aiming to construct an industrial park in the county’s Huwei Township (虎尾).
Photo: Taipei Times
The project site is located 300m south of the Central Taiwan Science Park’s Huwei Science Park near the Taiwan High Speed Rail’s (HSR) Yunlin Station, covering 29.75 hectares.
The county government on Thursday issued a press release, saying it had sent the project to central authorities for review seven times from March 2024 to last month.
The proposal was “repeatedly met with skepticism from the agriculture ministry,” which has yet to approve its proposed conversion of agricultural land, it said.
The county government also questioned the ministry’s demand made last month for prior approval from the Executive Yuan to recognize the project as a major investment or major infrastructure project.
Without the Executive Yuan’s approval, the ministry would deny the project’s necessity of development — a stricter standard compared with other proposed industrial park construction plans, the county government said.
The Southern Taiwan Science Park’s Chiayi Science Park, the Baipu Industrial Park in Kaohsiung and the Pingtung Science Park — which are all under construction — also applied to the central agricultural authority for farmland conversion, it said.
Their farmland conversion proposals were not met with the same skepticism and were approved by the ministry, citing that they aligned with the Executive Yuan’s policy, or that their development necessity had been recognized by the Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) or local governments, the county government said.
The MOA on Friday rebutted claims that it “deliberately made things difficult” for the project, adding that it reviews the land use change proposal based on the principle of safeguarding agricultural production environment and agricultural workers’ welfare.
The project not only covers about 29 hectares for the industrial park, but is also planning to expand the into a 250-hectare science park in the future, the MOA said.
The county government in 2021 said that it expected the proposed Huwei Industrial Park to be an extension of the Central Taiwan Science Park’s Huwei Science Park for building a regional industrial chain.
Industrial parks and science parks have different development approaches and land use planning, while the development of local industrial chains must be considered as well, the MOA said.
The MOA also cited the National Science and Technology Council as saying that the Central Taiwan Science Park’s Huwei Science Park currently does not to be expanded.
The Huwei Industrial Park project proposed by the county government includes farmland designated as part of the local specific agricultural zone.
The farmland provides a good agricultural production environment in the vicinity of Maguang Organic Group Cultivation Area (馬光有機集團栽培區), the MOA said.
It is also within the monitored areas of land subsidence along the Taiwan HSR line, it said.
The MOA has asked the county government multiple times to submit supplementary documents addressing concerns over the project’s farmland conversion proposal, it said.
Key issues include unclear industrial positioning, water conflicts between the industry and agriculture, insufficient groundwater monitoring, low water reuse rates, local residential and transportation safety, as well as existing backlash from local farmers and residents, the MOA said.
The county government has yet to submit documents to fully account for the issues, it said, adding that on Sept. 17 it asked the MOEA to assist the county government with document preparation.
The MOA said it reviewed farmland conversion proposals in accordance with Article 10 of the Agricultural Development Act (農業發展條例) and relevant regulations.
The MOA did not review the Huwei Industrial Park project’s farmland conversion proposal differently from others previously submitted, it said, adding that it would handle the project with the nation’s industrial development, agricultural sustainability and farmers’ benefits in mind.

Italian translator Silvia Pozzi has won a Pisa Book Translation Award for her translation of Ghost Town (鬼地方), a novel by Taiwanese author Kevin Chen (陳思宏).
The Italian edition, titled Citta fantasma, was recognized at a ceremony held Friday at the Palazzo della Sapienza in Rome as part of the Pisa Book Festival, an annual literary event that brings together authors, publishers and readers.
The novel is set in Yongjing, a town in Changhua County, and follows a man who returns home after serving a prison sentence in Germany for killing his boyfriend. Through his return and interactions with his family, the novel explores family trauma, hometown ties and the impact of Taiwan’s past.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Culture
In a news release, Minister of Culture Li Yuan (李遠) said Chen’s distinctive writing style gives local history a magical, dark and melancholic character, making his work appealing to international publishers.
Pozzi is a professor of Chinese and Southeast Asian languages and literature at the University of Milano-Bicocca. Besides Ghost Town, she has translated Chiu Miao-chin’s (邱妙津) Last Words from Montmartre (蒙馬特遺書) and Wu Ming-yi’s (吳明益) The Man with the Compound Eyes (複眼人) into Italian. She has also been commissioned by an Italian publisher to translate Yang Shuang-tzu’s Taiwan Travelogue (台灣漫遊錄), which won the International Booker Prize earlier this year.

Reigning champion Marquez maintained his lead and coasted to victory, moving him to 306 points — seven behind Martin’s 313 ahead of today’s race.
Photo: EPA
“The target was front row in the qualifying. Starting on first or second was the best place to do a great sprint race,” seven-time world champion Marquez said. “We did a small modification for the sprint race, and I felt much better on the bike.”
Aprilia’s Martin finished second, but was demoted to third behind LCR Honda’s Diogo Moreira.
The Spaniard had found it hard going toward the end of the sprint as he was put under pressure by Tech3’s Enea Bastianini, with the thrilling duel leading both riders to stray outside the track.
“I tried in the last lap to do everything I could to keep Enea behind. I achieved that,” Martin said.
“I don’t know exactly where I touched [the outside], because I was really focused on not doing it. So, big mistake.”
Brazilian Moreira earned his first sprint podium. It was the first sprint podium for satellite team LCR since 2023.
“Today was the day. We saw the crash and I said, ‘OK, today I will try to push to see’. At the end, lap by lap, I was feeling more comfortable with the bike,” Moreira said.
KTM’s Pedro Acosta, fresh off the first MotoGP victory of his career, started in the front row but quickly found himself in the gravel after being involved in a three-rider crash along with Alex Marquez and Fabio Di Giannantonio.
Japan’s Ai Ogura (Trackhouse) finished fifth, ahead of Martin’s Aprilia teammate Marco Bezzecchi, whose outside bid for the championship was dealt another blow.

Russia’s budget for defense to increase, social welfare to fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:28 UTC
01:38:28 KST

Russia plans to sharply increase defense spending, cut funding for education and raise taxes next year as costs mount in its war with Ukraine, draft budget documents showed.
The plans have been submitted to Russia’s lower house of parliament for approval.
The government plans to spend a record 17.1 trillion rubles (US$204 billion) on defense next year, about 26 percent higher than last year’s forecast, the draft budget showed.
Photo: AFP
Defense spending would account for more than one-third of all outlays and would be higher than spending earmarked for healthcare, education and social welfare combined, the documents showed.
While the documents forecast defense spending to decrease in 2028 and 2029, Russia has repeatedly overshot long-term defense spending forecasts since launching its Ukraine offensive.
Actual spending on defence is classified and could rise even further, Center for European Policy Analysis senior fellow Alexander Kolyandr said.
“The published totals are merely an opening bid in the negotiation between the finance ministry and the security establishment,” he said.
Unveiling the draft budget last week, Russian Minister of Finance Anton Siluanov described funding for social welfare and defense spending as a “priority,” but the documents show big cuts in non-military sectors, including social policy.
Planned outgoings on healthcare and education are set to drop by more than 5 percent each compared with the original plans, while funding on social programs are set to plunge by more than 6 percent.
Among the planned cuts are the federal government’s anti-cancer program, which is set to lose about 97 percent of its budgeted funding, the documents showed.
“The government is cutting back on civil servant pay and reducing their numbers, while slashing infrastructure projects, including construction and roadwork,” columnist Boris Grozovsky said.
To cover the shortfall, the government has proposed tax hikes, among them higher rates on bank deposits and property sales.
Russia has clocked a deficit each year since launching its Ukraine offensive.
Total shortfalls are estimated to be about 5.4 trillion rubles next year, more than 70 percent higher than the 3.2 trillion ruble deficit forecast last year.
State debt is set to rise above 20 percent of GDP next year, which is low for international standards, but above the level the finance ministry had previously described as “safe.”
Total government borrowing next year is estimated to be about 43 percent more than had been planned last year.
“There’s not enough money,” Grozovsky said. “The government is sending a signal to everyone: Don’t count on budget funds: they’ll go to those who absolutely must be given them.”

S Korean golfer wins gold and more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:27 UTC
01:38:27 KST

Tom Kim shot a sparkling final-round six-under 64 on yesterday to win golf gold at the Asian Games — and avoid a long spell in the Republic of Korea Armed Forces
He let out a roar of “Come on!” as he tapped in for par at the last in Nagoya and celebrated a three-stroke victory after a superb round containing five birdies and an eagle.
He was visibly relieved at getting over the line and was mobbed by his teammates as they draped him in the South Korean flag and doused him in water to celebrate.
Photo: AP
Kim knew there was more at stake than just a gold medal. Able-bodied South Korean males are usually required to perform between 18 months and two years of military service before the age of 28.
The Republic of Korea government exempts winners of Asian Games gold medals and Olympic medallists from a full period of service, requiring just four weeks of abbreviated basic training instead.
It enables the 24-year-old South Korean Kim to keep his blossoming career on track, having already claimed an Asian Tour order of merit crown and four PGA Tour titles.
He won this year’s prestigious Scottish Open and was downcast in Paris two years ago after letting the chance of winning an Olympic medal slip away on the final day, finishing eighth.
Three players were tied for second on 15-under, meaning that Kazuki Higa of Japan, Ding Wenyi of China and Sadom Kaewkanjana of Thailand would need a playoff to decide the rest of the podium. Earlier, Pranavi Urs held her nerve to shoot a 1m putt for par on the final green to become the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games golf gold.
Urs was doused in water in celebration by her fellow Indians Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar after completing a final round of level-par 70, which proved to be enough.
She finished on 15-under par, one stroke ahead of her playing partners Yin Ruoning — the former world number one from China who made a final-round charge with a three-under 67 — and Singapore’s Shannon Tan who carded a 68.
“That’s always the goal to always be the first one to do anything,” Urs said. “The first will always be the first, and I’ve always had that motto growing up and I’m just glad I could do it.”
Yin claimed the silver medal after Tan had a bogey five at the first playoff hole and had to settle for bronze.
Yin, known on the LPGA Tour as “Ronnie,” did win a gold in the team event with her China teammates Liu Yan and Zhang Weiwei after they finished top of the leaderboard with an aggregate of 20-under par.
India took silver with Taiwan, whose trio included former world No. 1 Yani Tseng, taking bronze.
It was the second Asian Games bronze for five-time major champion Tseng, now 37 years old.
She won her first, also in the team event, in Doha 20 years ago.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:25 UTC
01:38:25 KST

A Taichung-based doctor said there has been a spike in wart removals after the Mid-Autumn Festival weekend last month, urging safe sex over the upcoming three-day Double Ten National Day holiday.
Huang Pin-jui (黃品叡), head of urology at the Dajia branch of Lee’s General Hospital, said on Friday that the hospital saw human papillomavirus (HPV) cases after the long weekend.
Huang stressed that reducing the risk of genital wart re-infection depends on follow-up care, vaccination and practicing safe sex.
Photo: Chang Hsuan-tse, Taipei Times
Using protection remains essential to sexual health even for those who have been fully vaccinated against the HPV, because receiving three shots does not confer complete immunity to every strain of the virus, he said.
This is especially true if one has multiple sexual partners or recently entered into a sexual relationship with someone new, he added.
HPV infections also have a high recurrence rate, meaning those who have received surgical treatment should return for follow-up consultations as instructed by their doctors and stay vigilant about sexual health, he said.

Fresh housing protests to hit Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:21 UTC
01:38:21 KST

Fresh protests over housing were due to take place yesterday in Madrid and other Spanish cities, a day after parliament rejected two government measures to improve protection for tenants.
The government introduced the measures after nationwide protests following the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a Madrid apartment she had occupied for about seven decades.
The defeat was another political setback for Socialist Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and has renewed questions over whether his minority government can survive until the general election next year.
Photo: AFP
Catalan separatist party Junts — whose support was essential to approve the two decrees — voted against them, saying they lacked rigor.
After the vote, main opposition conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo urged Sanchez to “call elections as soon as possible.”
After eight years in power, Sanchez had the backing of “neither the streets nor parliament,” he added.
Recent opinion polls have generally placed the Popular Party ahead of the Socialists.
The Tenants’ Union, which has been coordinating the protests, called for demonstrations in more than 50 cities.
“There is an irreparable disconnect between what the people want and what the parties vote for,” it said in a statement.
In Madrid, activists and protesters have been camping for about a week in Puerta del Sol, one of the capital’s main tourist squares.
Demonstrators were due to set off from several locations around the city at noon before converging on Plaza de Cibeles in central Madrid.
The package of measures defeated on Friday included the automatic renewal of rental contracts when they expire, as well as measures aimed at restricting the eviction of vulnerable tenants.
They also targeted so-called vulture funds — investment firms that buy properties at low prices in pursuit of higher returns.
Housing has for years been a top concern for Spaniards as supply falls short of demand, with rents and house prices soaring as elsewhere in the EU.
Average rents in Spain have almost doubled over the past decade, while asking prices for homes have risen by about 90 percent, according to real-estate Web site Idealista.
Abascal’s eviction catalyzed long-running anger about runaway housing costs.
She was forced to leave the Madrid flat where she had lived after it was acquired by an investment company that sought to increase her rent by 275 percent, according to housing campaigners.
The backlash led the property’s new owners to reach a deal allowing her to return to the flat at a low rent.

Improve digital safety mechanisms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:19 UTC
01:38:19 KST

Recently, reports of Line account hacking have surged. On Sept. 9, Line announced that customer service reports related to such incidents in August had nearly doubled, increasing by 97 percent from July. Among these scams, requests to “vote for my child” and “help my pet get more votes” have become common ploys designed to exploit the trust of friends and acquaintances.
Victims lose access to their accounts, but the public response to these scams often questions whether they clicked suspicious links or gave out verification codes. If anti-fraud efforts only focus on victim blaming, platforms and telecommunications operators easily escape accountability.
In April, the Ministry of Digital Affairs revealed that the default password mechanisms for the voicemail accounts of former Taiwan Star Telecom Corp users could have potentially been exploited to obtain Line voice verification codes. This suggests that account hijackings might not necessarily stem from users giving out their information, but could also result from vulnerabilities in telecommunications services and platform verification systems. It is unacceptable for service providers to leave such significant security loopholes and expect consumers to patch them.
Line already offers a re-login feature that allows eligible users to recover their accounts and log out of all other devices. However, when the recovery process fails and the case is referred to customer service, Line still lists measures such as deleting the account and transferring paid items as the solution. If self-help is not an option, should there not be sufficient alternative verification methods and manual review processes for account recovery?
An account carries years of connections with family, friends and colleagues. Being able to recover only purchased sticker packages and having to rebuild contact lists from scratch is like having your home burglarized and being left with nothing but your house number, leaving you to rebuild your life on your own. Restricting account misuse and preventing impersonation is necessary, but that does not mean that victims of hacking receive adequate assistance.
Although the Ministry of Digital Affairs has urged service providers to address vulnerabilities and conduct security audits, repairing a system does not mean recovering users’ accounts, and a customer service reply does not mean the problem has been resolved.
The government should ask: How many people have successfully recovered their accounts? How long does it take? How many users were forced to create new accounts? If authorities only confirm that the vulnerability has been patched without getting answers to these questions, the losses suffered by victims might never appear in the final report.
The government should establish minimum service standards for account recovery, requiring clear reporting channels, tiered risk-based handling, manual review, reasonable response times and explanations for rejected recovery requests. Platforms need not guarantee that all data can be restored, but they should ensure that users with legitimate claims have a viable avenue for appeal. Verification procedures must also balance personal data protection with fraud prevention so as not to allow the recovery process itself to become another vulnerability.
The Ministry of Digital Affairs should continuously monitor Line and other platforms, requiring them to regularly disclose their account recovery outcomes, set deadlines for fixing procedural deficiencies and follow up on their progress.
Authorities should act as supervisors of digital security, not merely recipients of reports. Improving defenses requires verifying their actual ability to prevent account misuse and provide support to victims. People’s relationships and property should not be left to fill systemic gaps.

To keep AI robots from killing humans, look at driverless trucks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:19 UTC
01:38:19 KST

The most bothersome aspect of the warning that artificial intelligence (AI) could wipe out humanity is that there are few details about how a rogue computer model could actually accomplish it.
The top scenarios, and it is by no means an exhaustive list, involve nuclear missiles, biological weapons and killer robots.
We have long been familiar with the first one. A maverick AI takes over the nuclear-launch codes and sends the world down the path to doomsday. (See the 1983 movie War Games.) The second involves AI tricking a human into releasing a deadly virus, which is a new twist on the old concerns of lab leaks by mistake (Outbreak in 1995), terrorist plots (12 Monkeys in 1995) or profit-making schemes (Mission: Impossible II).
While all of those are scary, there are a lot of obstacles before reaching Armageddon, including security agencies keeping close watch for illicit or dangerous biological research. The cybersecurity industry is more than capable of staving off an AI hacker, especially by adopting bespoke AI defenses and tapping into quantum computing for stronger cryptography.
Which brings us to killer AI robots.
This is where the thinking gets a bit speculative, because mobile robots that can perform multiple tasks do not exist now. Pilot programs are experimenting with humanoid robots that perform simple jobs in warehouses and factories, but their capabilities are limited. All the humanoid robots dancing or running marathons on TikTok are preprogrammed or are being controlled remotely by a human operator and are not acting independently. These robots are coming, just not yet.
Still, the idea of squads of killer machines eliminating civilization lives in popular imagination. Luckily, there is already a real-world example of how AI can be released into the world without murderous conspiracy.
The autonomous-vehicle industry is proving that AI can be tightly controlled and work safely around humans. Waymo LLC, Tesla Inc, Aurora Innovation Inc, Kodiak AI Inc and other self-driving companies are paving the way for how AI can be applied to mobile robots that can perform multiple tasks.
It turns out that driving is a good place to start deploying physical AI around humans, because there are already lots of established rules and protocols.
The computer that runs the AI that interprets inputs from vision sensors is on board the vehicle and does not require an Internet signal to operate. Different layers of AI are assigned tasks, such as foundational models that recognize real-world objects, large language models that understand commands, and action models that perform maneuvers depending on sensor data and rules of the road. The coding trail is transparent, so programmers can see how and why the system reached a decision. There is no “black box” AI in which it is impossible to know how the computer reached a conclusion.
As a last layer of defense, the onboard computer has a simpler model that provides a “sanity check” to prevent unsafe or unexpected maneuvers, said Don Burnette, chief executive officer of Kodiak, which has deployed driverless trucks in the Permian Basin oil patch and is poised to put them on interstate highways by the end of this year. In the unlikely event that the driverless system does not understand a scenario, the truck would slow down, move to a safe area and request help.
“We know systematically exactly how it works, and we’ve tested all the failure cases so that nothing can go wrong,” Burnette said in an interview. “If anything is out of the ordinary, it just refuses to execute.”
Autonomous vehicles have a focused job, just as the multitask robots would. The decisionmaking model should be on board the robot, which restricts its computing capabilities because of power and space, and limited to the tasks it needs to perform. The system does not need to know Shakespeare sonnets or the physics of orbital bodies or have the wherewithal to plan a revolt against humanity.
Mobile robots should be regulated by the standards now being worked on by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) instead of government regulations, which cannot keep up with the technology. Companies work to obtain these certifications to show they meet industry standards to help win customers and contracts. The ANSI and ISO standards are reviewed and changed much more often than government regulations to keep up with innovation.
One standard should be that these powerful AI models need to be contained and focused on the specific assigned tasks. If a tool is dangerous, it should be treated that way, just as biology laboratories are careful to avoid the release of viruses. Models that can deviate from their instructions should not power the mobile robots that would operate around humans.
A so-called kill switch is complicated, or perhaps impossible, for an AI model that is integrated into the cloud and feeds off multiple interconnected data centers. On physical AI, a kill switch or emergency-stop button makes a lot of sense and should be visible and accessible in case something goes wrong.
Robots are tools to assist humans and do not need to be that smart. They should not accidentally hurt humans and certainly should never have the opportunity to hurt them intentionally. Autonomous vehicles are the blueprint for making sure robots do only what they are told.

Taiwan in Time: Lord Su’s grand inspection returns after 57 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:17 UTC
01:38:17 KST

OCT. 5 to OCT. 11
Many worshippers of Taoist deity Lord Su (蘇府王爺) had never witnessed his “north-south grand inspection tour” of central Taiwan. The historic procession last took place in 1969, and before that, in 1893.
Lukang’s Fengtian Temple (奉天宮) in Changhua County last Sunday completed Lord Su’s sixth grand inspection tour ever, taking its three main statues to settlements from Miaoli to Yunlin over 10 days. According to news reports, this year’s event also included a boat patrol that set out from Taichung, bringing luck and safety to fishers and offshore wind farm workers.
Photo courtesy of Fengtian Temple
Why did it take 57 years for the event to happen again? Temple officials say the procession is held only when a spirit medium receives instructions from Lord Su.
Folklorist Lee Hsiu-e (李秀娥) writes in a study of Fengtian Temple’s grand inspection had typically coincided with misfortune, including floods, earthquakes, disease and local unrest. Earlier processions lasted more than 60 days and mobilized hundreds of people, reflecting the wealth and connections of Lukang’s merchants and the influence of its religious institutions. Lukang was once considered the second-most prosperous town in Taiwan.
Lee found that most of the communities visited had a local shrine for Lord Su. The arrival of the three main statues was seen as a blessing, with residents inviting the procession into their villages and extending its route over time. Lee’s study records local memories of “miracles” attributed to Lord Su during the journeys, including one account in which he was said to have changed the course of a river and stopped its frequent flooding.
TEMPLE ORIGIN
Fengtian Temple’s worship of Lord Su has an origin story typical of many temples across Taiwan. Around 1684, legend has it that three pieces of wood were picked up by a fisherman off the waters of today’s Dongshi Borough (東石). After witnessing the wood glowing, locals received divine instructions to carve each of them into a statue of Lord Su.
This event became one of three main sources of Lord Su worship in central Taiwan. At the time of Lee’s 1996 study, only eight temples in Lukang had Lord Su as their principal deity, with at least five tracing their origins to these three statues. Lee also found that more than 700 temples across Taiwan venerated Lord Su statues that branched off from these three.
The statues were worshipped in the Beitou (北頭) area north of Lukang, with the main statue rotating annually among different incense masters. Each year, the caretaker would build a new structure to house the deity, which they were allowed to use privately after their year of service. The three statues had different birthdays, but all were celebrated on the 12th day of the fourth lunar month.
While permanent temples were eventually established for the second and third statues, the main statue continued to be housed in a different home each year until the 1960s, when Taiwan’s growing population left too little vacant land for new shrines.
Locals in 1962 began building Fengtian Temple on land purchased from the National Taxation Bureau, Lee writes. Completed in 1968, it became the permanent home of all three statues.
EARLY INSPECTIONS
While the temple hosted a number of regular and occasional rituals, the north-south grand inspection was the largest. The “inspection” was modeled on Qing-era naval patrols, with Lord Su accompanied by his own Five Camps soldiers (五營) and divine generals.
Old temple texts describe the tour as a way of patrolling the area on behalf of Heaven, driving out pestilence and protecting the people. It was also intended to bring prosperity and good harvests.
The first procession took place in 1831, when Lord Su reportedly noted the spread of disease. It set out in October, traveling in a loop through Changhua and Nantou over more than 50 days.
Lee examined local annals and found that a drought had struck that summer. In the autumn, floods brought seawater into farmland, ruining crops and causing houses to collapse. Later that winter, an earthquake struck.
The second inspection took place in 1877. By then, Lukang’s port had been suffering from sediment buildup, forcing larger ships to transfer their cargo to smaller boats. Fewer ships were visiting, contributing to the town’s economic decline. This time, the procession visited Taichung and communities around Baguashan (八卦山).
Earthquakes affected the area for two years in a row before the 1882 inspection, which lasted more than 60 days.
UPRISINGS AND TYPHOONS
Times were rough leading up to the fourth inspection. The Jhuoshuei River (濁水溪) repeatedly flooded, while civil unrest also shook the region. A dispute over unfair government land surveys in 1888 escalated into the Shih Chiu-tuan Incident (施九緞事件), in which hundreds of angry locals besieged the walled county seat of Changhua City.
The uprising was eventually quelled with the help of local militia led by the Wufeng Lin Family (霧峰林家). It’s said that Lukang narrowly avoided a government attack for allegedly aiding the rebels.
In 1889, the Jhuoshuei River flooded again, exacerbating the sedimentation in Lukang’s port. Locals had to pool their resources to clear it so bamboo rafts could reach the shore.
A grand inspection was set for 1891, but according to a manuscript preserved by the temple, the organizer failed to obtain a formal letter from Lukang’s Quan Guild (泉郊), which was needed to arrange the procession with villages along the route. Without it, many communities showed little interest, and the event was canceled and rescheduled for 1893. The episode shows how closely the procession was tied to Lukang’s commercial networks.
The Japanese took over Taiwan in 1895, and no further grand inspections were held for seven decades.
A year after the completion of Fengtian Temple, temple leaders were planning to revive the procession when Typhoon Elsie struck the area in September 1969, causing much damage to coastal communities. Around 360 people participated in the event in October, which due to improved transportation only took 21 days.
Taiwan in Time, a column about Taiwan’s history that is published every Sunday, spotlights important or interesting events around the nation that either have anniversaries this week or are tied to current events.
In 1951, the Central Propaganda Department of the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) Central Reform Committee launched an English-language magazine, which, for the next 75 years, would serve as a mouthpiece for Taiwan’s government. Initially titled the Free China Review, and later rechristened as the Taiwan Review, the magazine published its final issue in March. Former editor Richard Vuylsteke has described the magazine as Taiwan’s “landmark foreign language publication going abroad.” The magazine was not universally respected. Some international scholars, including a few contacted for this article, dismissed it as a “propaganda rag.” But others, including Shelley Rigger, a top US researcher at

On weekends, especially in the evenings, the site’s walkways are crowded with sunset watchers, its mudflats filled with people wading and taking pictures of the local wildlife. Birds, amphibious fish, crabs and other organisms flourish. A few hundred meters to the south Berth number 8 of the Port of Taichung juts inland, surrounded by chemical plants, cement factories, chemical storage sites, warehouses and wind turbines. Looking at Lee Hao-yu’s incredible season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:15 UTC
01:38:15 KST

One of the biggest stars on the Detroit Tigers’ Threads account is infielder Lee Hao-yu, with posts featuring the Taiwanese rookie rarely drawing fewer than 5,000 likes, far more than the 1,000 likes posts featuring other players only occasionally draw.
Behind much of that enthusiasm was the 23-year-old’s breakthrough season in MLB.
Lee finished with 87 hits, including 10 home runs and 46 RBIs in 114 games, setting Taiwanese single-season MLB records in all four categories. More importantly for Lee, he became a regular presence in Detroit’s lineup by the end of the season.
Photo: AFP
In separate interviews, anchor Martin Lin and Jacky Lee, an anchor for Videoland Sports, called it the best MLB season ever by a Taiwanese position player.
They pointed to the same obstacle to making that breakthrough last: his fielding.
‘BALANCED BATTING‘
Lee hit .264 with a .322 on-base percentage and .424 slugging percentage. His OPS+ of 107 put his offensive production 7 percent above league average after adjustments for ballpark and league conditions.
For Jacky Lee, statistics were only part of Lee’s story this year.
Taiwanese position players in the majors have often depended on injuries, specific matchups or defensive versatility to get playing time, but Lee increasingly gave Detroit a reason to find him a place regardless of circumstances.
“By the second half, you came to expect that if the Tigers were playing, you would see Lee Hao-yu,” the broadcaster said.
He contrasted Lee with Yu Chang, whose defensive versatility helped create opportunities for him across five MLB seasons but whose hitting was wildly inconsistent.
Lee’s ability to make contact, hit to the opposite field and make adjustments has given him a steadier offensive foundation, Jacky Lee said.
The right-handed hitting Lee impressed with his balance at the plate, finishing with a .263 average and .753 OPS against right-handers and a .265 average and .737 OPS against left-handers, giving him the chance to play every day.
Lin said the rookie’s success was owed to a combination of timing, opportunity and compatibility.
“The Tigers’ position-player group was clearly getting younger this year,” Lin said. “Lee Hao-yu happened to catch that wave.”
Injuries to second baseman Gleyber Torres opened up playing time, while Detroit’s fading postseason prospects created more opportunities for younger players.
Lee’s ability to drive the ball into the air suited Detroit’s offensive approach, Lin said.
That overall fit made Lee’s success difficult to emulate for other Taiwanese players, Lin contended.
“I don’t think you can use Lee Hao-yu alone as the standard. He is too unusual, too different,” Lin said. “His success is not necessarily something other Taiwanese players can replicate.”
‘PITBULL MINDSET‘
During August’s Players’ Weekend, Detroit’s lineup announcements displayed Lee’s nickname: “Pitbull,” evoking the strength and tenacity associated with the dog.
Lin credited Lee with staying focused when he initially was mostly used only against left-handers.
“He did not let that period of limited opportunities get him down,” Lin said.
Lee described his confidence in an interview video uploaded by sports news outlet Vamos Sports in August.
“They’re good, but I’m good too. I can hit them — why wouldn’t I be able to?” he said. “Whatever mindset I had in the minor leagues, I brought it to the major leagues.”
To Lee, pitchers were still pitchers, throwing the same fastballs, curveballs and sliders.
Maintaining confidence did not mean refusing to change. Jacky Lee said that the rookie’s return to Triple-A Toledo was a turning point. Detroit optioned him on June 2 and recalled him on June 13.
Upon his return, the broadcaster saw adjustments to his stance and hitting mechanics, a more aggressive approach early in the count, and a greater willingness to pull the ball.
Lee had previously struggled with his timing, often swinging late, Jacky Lee said, and the adjustments helped him use his power more effectively.
‘SERVICEABLE’‘
His bat has earned Lee opportunities, but the broadcasters said his glove could determine his fate.
Jacky Lee pointed to his minus-12 Outs Above Average, a Statcast measure estimating outs saved or lost relative to an average fielder. Lee recorded minus-five at second base, minus-six at third and minus-one in limited shortstop work.
Although Lee does not have to become an elite defender, Jacky Lee said he at least needs to become “serviceable.”
“He’s not even 25 yet. If he has to be moved to first base or designated hitter now, that would be very unfavorable for his long-term future in the major leagues,” the sportscaster said.
A major infield signing could squeeze Lee’s opportunities, particularly if his defense left Detroit with few other positions in which to play him.
Torres played this season on a one-year, US$22.025 million qualifying offer. Jacky Lee said his return was unlikely, saying that the Tigers might give the less expensive Lee a chance and spend elsewhere.
Lin said that range, reactions and ball handling were weaknesses for Lee, but he was firmer about Torres’ departure.
“The Tigers will definitely not sign Gleyber Torres back,” Lin said.
He expected Detroit to avoid another expensive veteran contract and give Lee substantial opportunities next spring, without the uncertainty over playing time he faced this year.
“Lee Hao-yu should be their first option at second base next year,” Lin said.

Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
Temperatures are expected to rise initially today, with highs of 30-31°C in eastern Taiwan and 32-35 °C in western Taiwan, he said.

US to assign liaisons in MND: sources

Unknown Publisher

16:38:14 UTC

Taiwan-US military cooperation is deepening, with the Pentagon expected to station personnel at the Ministry of National Defense (MND), sources said.
The NT$470 million (US$14.77 million) joint program is scheduled to run from this year through 2028, under which the Pentagon would dispatch representatives from the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy and the Institute for Defense Analyses, a senior military official said on condition of anonymity, adding that one representative from each organization would be stationed at the ministry’s headquarters.
The Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy is one of the US’ bodies responsible for formulating national security and defense strategy, and would help align policy coordination between Taipei and Washington, they said.
Photo: Reuters
The Institute for Defense Analyses is a defense think tank known for using data analysis and mathematical modeling to conduct complex defense simulations and operational assessments, they added.
The arrangement would place US personnel closer to Taiwan’s defense policymaking process and allow them to assist with policy coordination and combat capability assessments, elevating bilateral military integration to the highest level, they said.
The move supplements the presence of hundreds of US military instructors in Taiwan who have assisted with military training.
US defense personnel have long maintained a presence in Taiwan, usually in less visible roles, an anonymous military official said.
The American Institute in Taiwan’s (AIT) security cooperation and technical offices are staffed by active-duty US military personnel and civilian defense officials responsible for coordinating arms sales and logistics cooperation, they said.
The US’ Defense Innovation Unit has also over the past few years assigned liaison officers to the AIT to help integrate Taiwan’s drone and technology supply chains to address technological warfare and cross-strait tensions.
However, the new arrangement differs, because US representatives would work directly with Taiwan’s defense ministry rather than through AIT, the sources said.
That signals a shift in Taiwan-US military cooperation from tactical training to higher-level strategic planning and wargaming, they said.
US instructors usually focus on operational training and weapons employment, while the new arrangement would allow US experts to participate more directly in discussions on overall defense planning and asymmetric warfare tactics, such as providing on-site advice during the Han Kuang exercises and major weapons procurement evaluations, they added.
The move also reflects concrete efforts to institutionalize and normalize security cooperation between Taiwan and the US through legislation, such as the Taiwan Enhanced Resilience Act and successive US national defense authorization acts, they said.
However, the presence of US personnel within the core of Taiwan’s defense establishment would require stricter mechanisms governing the sharing of classified information, confidentiality procedures and cybersecurity protections, the sources said.

Iran army says prepared to face any scenario
TEHRAN– Iran’s Armed Forces are closely monitoring developments and remain fully prepared to respond to any scenario, the spokesperson for the Islamic Republic of Iran Army said on Saturday, as he referred to repeated threats by the country’s adversaries.
Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia made the remarks during a visit to the Army’s 65th Airborne Special Forces Brigade, a unit widely recognized for its specialized capabilities and role in missions requiring a high degree of operational readiness.
Highlighting the brigade’s position within Iran’s defense structure, Akraminia said its personnel, combining commitment, specialized training and operational capabilities, have turned the unit into an important asset for both the Army and the country.
He stressed that the missions assigned to the 65th Brigade extend beyond conventional tactical operations, arguing that the unit’s activities can produce consequences at the strategic level and affect Iran’s national security interests as well as the wider regional and international environment.
Against the backdrop of continued tensions and threats, the Army spokesperson said Iran’s military capabilities have been undergoing continuous development and that the Armed Forces are prepared to confront whatever circumstances may arise.
Akrami-Nia also addressed the calculations of the United States and Israel in the conflict with Iran, saying the resilience of the Iranian Armed Forces, coupled with the steadfastness of the Iranian people, had disrupted the adversaries’ calculations.
According to the Army spokesperson, the United States and Israel had initially anticipated that Iran’s defensive capabilities could be dismantled and their objectives achieved within a matter of days. He said those calculations did not materialize.
Akraminia further argued that the objectives pursued by Iran’s adversaries went beyond the country’s nuclear and missile programs or their confrontation with the Resistance Front. He said the broader objective was to undermine the Islamic Republic and fragment Iran as a country, but that none of those objectives had been achieved.
The remarks come as Iranian military officials have repeatedly emphasized the importance of maintaining a high level of readiness amid continuing regional tensions and threats of renewed confrontation. Iranian authorities have also stressed that the country’s defense posture is based on deterrence and the ability to respond to threats against its territorial integrity and national security.
The Army spokesperson attributed the Armed Forces’ ability to withstand the pressure to their faith, motivation and spirit of resistance. He also pointed to the role of public solidarity in sustaining the morale of military personnel.
Akraminia said the nightly presence of people in public squares during the conflict was not merely a manifestation of national unity and cohesion, but also had a direct psychological effect on servicemen stationed on the frontlines, strengthening their morale and determination.
His comments underscored the Iranian military’s continued emphasis on preparedness, national cohesion and the integration of specialized military capabilities into the country’s broader defense posture.

Investing in brain health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:04 UTC
01:38:04 KST

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has spread faster than any technology in modern history. Within three years of ChatGPT’s release, generative AI has been adopted by 53 percent of the world’s population — faster than the PC and the Internet — while organizational adoption hit 88 percent last year. Global corporate investment in AI has more than doubled, with much of that money going into physical infrastructure such as data centers and power grids.
Skepticism about AI is rising almost as quickly. A survey by S&P Global found that 42 percent of companies abandoned most of their AI initiatives last year, up from 17 percent the year before, and in a recent PwC poll, 56 percent of chief executive officers reported that AI has brought their firms no measurable benefit. Communities around the world are mobilizing to prevent data centers from being built in their backyards, while documented incidents of AI harms rose by more than 55 percent last year.
However, even as governments rewrite their industrial strategies around a technology whose value they cannot yet quantify, and as investors, insisting that this time is different, drive valuations reminiscent of the dot-com boom, calls for more responsible and ethical AI are growing louder. Everyone is trying to divine the future of AI in the hope of mastering whatever comes next.
Illustration: Tania Chou
The utopian and dystopian camps suffer from the same myopia. Both assume that the future of humanity depends primarily, perhaps exclusively, on the future of AI. It does not. While optimists and pessimists alike have trained their focus on the rise of AI, they have ignored the rapid decline in brain health and brain skills.
That decline is eroding the human capacity on which every system, including AI, depends. Mental and neurological conditions, substance-use disorders, strokes and self-harm account for about one-quarter of the global disease burden. The number of people who are 65 or older living with dementia rose to 49 million in 2021 from 18.7 million in 1991 and continues to climb. Governments allocate just 2 percent of their health budgets to mental health, even after the WHO declared loneliness a “pressing health threat” in 2023.
Brain skills are in freefall too. A majority of business leaders surveyed last year by the skills training company General Assembly said entry-level employees were less prepared for their jobs than they had been five years ago, especially when it came to soft skills. Likewise, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD) 2024 Survey of Adult Skills, the largest direct assessment of adult cognitive proficiency ever conducted, recorded declining or stagnant literacy across most participating countries. About 18 percent of adults in OECD countries lack basic proficiency in literacy, numeracy and problem-solving. Even among university-educated adults, proficiency fell or flatlined in most of the countries surveyed. New data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) show that student performance in reading, math, and science is declining across the OECD.
AI is fueling these trends. Emerging research suggests AI can reduce cognitive engagement, with studies finding less critical thinking and weaker neural connectivity during AI-assisted work. It can also foster over-reliance, as users sometimes accept incorrect AI outputs despite conflicting evidence or their own judgement.
Think about what this means. Just as humanity developed machines capable of taking on complex cognitive tasks, humans themselves have become less capable of performing them. The Global Brain Capital Index, which measures cognitive health and related skills, suggests that brain capital is declining at a time when trillions of dollars are being spent on AI infrastructure without a clear idea of what those investments should achieve. While a recent McKinsey Health Institute analysis estimated that the US spends about US$2.6 trillion a year on brain capital, from education to neurological care, less than 1percent of that spending goes toward disease prevention. Early intervention and research are underfunded, too.
Technological progress by itself does not make people healthier or more capable. However, the AI boom plays out, humanity would not fare well without a civilization-wide effort to rebuild brain health and cognitive skills. If AI becomes as powerful as its boosters predict, the premium on human intelligence would increase. As AI agents take over routine cognitive tasks, the value of human work would depend on qualities that machines cannot replicate, such as judgement, ethical reasoning, empathy and curiosity.
As the World Economic Forum’s employer survey last year showed, many of these human qualities are among those most in demand today and are expected to remain so through 2030. The survey also suggests that 59 percent of workers would require retraining, making investment in natural intelligence essential if human workers are to remain valuable in an AI-powered economy.
The current debate is largely focused on whether AI would save humanity or destroy it, but it could also turn out to be another technological fad. Even if the AI hype fizzles out like the metaverse craze of 2022, social and economic progress would still depend on rebuilding brain capital.
We do not need to start from scratch. Much of the necessary infrastructure already exists, thanks to those trillions of dollars already being spent on it. The challenge is to treat such investments as part of a larger system. Scaling interventions available today could give people around the world a combined 267 million additional years of healthy life by 2050 and add up to US$6.2 trillion to global GDP. Quality early-childhood programs can generate annual returns of 7 to 13 percent, while proactive investment in employee health could boost global GDP by as much as 12 percent.
That means investing in maternal and early-childhood development and shifting primary care toward preventing neurological and psychiatric disorders later in life. Workplaces can protect mental health without eroding cognitive skills, while education and professional training can be overhauled to promote lifelong learning. These are not moonshots, and there is plenty of evidence that they work.
AI itself can be part of the solution. It can enable early diagnosis of brain disorders and accelerate drug discovery. By democratizing knowledge, it can also feed curiosity and make lifelong learning easier.
The returns on brain capital do not hinge on the fate of the AI industry. Human ingenuity has economic value no matter which technology dominates the next decade. Investing in it is always a winning bet, because it is the one technology that will never become obsolete.
Harris Eyre is executive director of the Global Brain Economy Initiative. Lenny Mendonca, former chief economic and business adviser to California Governor Gavin Newsom, is senior partner emeritus at McKinsey & Company. Remington Tonar is cofounder of Cart.com.

Paris Fashion Week  illuminates the City of Light
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:38:04 UTC
01:38:04 KST

Saint Laurent sent out a river of gold, as giant chandeliers bathed a glossy black outdoor runway in golden light and the Eiffel Tower shimmered in the background.
The extravagant show was attended by Catherine Deneuve, Kate Moss, Hailey Bieber and Rami Malek, while elsewhere at Paris Fashion Week Jennifer Lopez watched from Stella McCartney’s rain-soaked gardens. Rihanna turned out for the upstarts at Matieres Fecales, a conceptual fashion house whose name translates as “fecal matter.” There, the finale sent a woman in a gold lame gown across a Paris protest square carrying two slumped dummies of white men in suits.
Whatever luxury’s financial troubles, Paris retained its ability to assemble stellar front rows and social media-ready staging.
Photo: Reuters
Midway through next year’s spring-summer season, shows crystallized into three stories: glamour on a grand scale; a great undressing that stripped all the way down to a pale pink thong beneath a coat that can top US$33,000; and an industry working couture technique into T-shirts and jeans — all while asking itself, nervously, who all of this is for.
SAINT LAURENT
“Was it an adieu?” one front row guest asked.
With a decade at the house, designer Anthony Vaccarello dispensed with his customary interviews and let a retrospective-tinged collection carry the occasion.
No departure was announced — but the guessing fit the mood of an industry swapping designers at a frantic clip in search of growth.
Last month, cosmetics giant L’Oreal overtook LVMH as France’s most valuable listed company. It is the first time since 2017 that a non-luxury company has topped the Paris bourse.
Saint Laurent’s parent Kering has returned to growth after a bruising downturn, but Balenciaga remains under pressure behind the runway gloss.
Saint Laurent on Tuesday night featured gold — and it was almost the whole story: brittle, fluid, translucent or densely worked.
Gold, of course, is exactly what Kering wants from this house.
Saint Laurent, the group’s second-biggest label, is growing again on strong US and European demand, hauling the load while Gucci struggles to reverse years of falling sales.
Safari jackets and trenches came in crinkled metallic cottons. Cocktail dresses featured glinting lace, cropped jackets in brocade. Stilettos stood on serpent-shaped heels.
Then came the black finale, led by model Anja Rubik — a reversal of Yves Saint Laurent’s all-gold closing sequence in 1991.
CHLOE
Two days later, Chloe approached excess through texture.
Chemena Kamali piled broderie anglaise with lace, pearls and tassels, and sent out rainwear and long-brimmed fishermen’s hats in vivid colors.
The question was how much decoration Chloe’s promise of easy dressing could carry.
McCartney’s show rewarded its damp audience with easy tailoring, coral-like knitted forms and airbrushed dolphins on denim.
Sculptural hems and peplums gave the clothes an underwater buoyancy, while naturalist David Attenborough’s voice supplied an ocean-conservation message.
The peplum was one of the week’s quiet constants, turning up sculpted here and stitched into shirting at Balenciaga.
Air was the week’s other quiet constant, and Issey Miyake built a collection on it: dancers opened Satoshi Kondo’s show on Friday by billowing a vast cloth to live piano, before balloon-twisted dresses and nylon forms that inhaled with every step floated past — what the house calls ma, “the space in between” body and garment.
UNDERGARMENTS
Underwear was doing an increasing share of the dressing.
At Tom Ford, Haider Ackermann staged a particularly playful display: sharp tailoring accompanied by bare chests, fishnet, severely reduced swimwear and silk robes. Black swimsuits were more geometry than garment.
A male model in a sweater and pale pink thong carried a vicuna coat — the world’s most expensive wool, which can cost more than US$33,000 a coat — draped over a weekend bag.
CORSETS AND CAGES
At Balmain, Antonin Tron built a stronger second outing around midcentury backstage photographs and their air of glamorous half-dress: corset bodices, garters swinging from miniskirts, bras under shrunken satin bombers, eel skin and animal-patterned jacquards.
Simulated rain lashed the covered windows of Karl Lagerfeld’s former mansion. Printing, embroidery and sequins gave the surfaces depth, although their richness sometimes competed with the sensual draping.
Even Rick Owens went boudoir, on his own terms: On a ramp across the Palais de Tokyo’s reflecting pool, he sent out stone-colored column gowns, spiked tulle, crystal-laden footwear and full-body constructions of tulle and elastic.
The cages turned literal at Courreges, where Drew Henry’s debut broke up its neon tailoring with floral bra tops, flower-dotted cage jumpsuits and hotpants.
LUXURY TRIMMINGS
The question beneath it all was harder to stage: in a downturn, how does luxury justify itself?
Pierpaolo Piccioli’s answer at Balenciaga was technique.
Dense rows of stitching shaped a white shirt into a fitted waist and flaring peplum.
A T-shirt received a similar treatment. Jeans were cut on the bias — diagonally across the fabric — to change their fall.
The collection made a persuasive case for putting couture knowledge to everyday use.
Loewe, entering its 180th year, answered more plainly still: fewer technical fireworks, more supple leather and glass-bead dresses — clothes made to be worn rather than talked about.
Luxury’s answer to the squeeze? Not lower prices — but craft moved into the clothes people live in, so the cost feels earned.
MATIERES FECALES
The new it-brand took over Paris’ protest area, Place de la Republique, for a show titled “The 99 Percent.”
The collection brought together sari-inspired draping, shredded denim and figures styled to evoke masked demonstrators.
While public access was part of the idea, the irony was hard to miss: 99 percent of the world cannot afford Matieres Fecales’ clothes.
The 99 percent have been voting with their wallets: Pinched by inflation and prices up some 20 percent in two years, about 60 million customers have abandoned luxury since 2022, said consultancy Bain & Company — which said that even the wealthy clients who remain feel “betrayed.”
Paris had demonstrated how to make people look, but it is the clothes, the industry hopes, that could persuade them to spend.
