Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s boyfriend found dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:49:17 UTC
23:49:17 KST

Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s boyfriend found dead
The partner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard, a prominent US true-crime figure known for her role in the 2015 killing of her abusive mother, has been found dead at his Louisiana home in a suspected drug overdose.
Ken Urker was discovered unresponsive at his Raceland residence on October 1, the day he turned 34 years old, after relatives requested a welfare check when he stopped answering calls and failed to show up for work. Family members said he had seemed depressed and upset the previous evening and later appeared on TikTok Live driving without speaking.
Relatives and Urker’s boss found him lying on his bed, cold to the touch and not breathing, before police arrived. Deputies later found syringes and a spoon near a “brown powdery substance” in the bathroom, along with another syringe, two shot glasses and a holstered handgun on the nightstand. The police report said Urker was “dead upon arrival.”
In a statement to the media on Friday, the local sheriff’s office said there were no signs of foul play but that the death remained under investigation.
Blanchard, who was out of state at the time, told People magazine she believed Urker had overdosed but did not know whether it was intentional. In an interview on Friday, she said he had “not been in a good state of mind lately.” In a later social media tribute, Blanchard called Urker her “soulmate,” and said he had endured “relentless cyberbullying” and intense public scrutiny, including over his relationship with her, which she believed had profoundly affected him.
The case that made Blanchard famous
Blanchard became the focus of intense media attention after the murder of her mother, Clauddine “Dee Dee” Blanchard, who had abused her.
According to well-documented accounts, Dee Dee portrayed her daughter as seriously ill and disabled for much of her childhood, isolating her and forcing her to use a wheelchair and undergo unnecessary medical procedures, while obtaining donations and other benefits based on her supposed illnesses. As she grew older, Blanchard began secretly communicating online and met her future boyfriend, Nicholas Godejohn, with whose help she plotted Dee Dee’s killing. Blanchard provided Godejohn with a knife he used to stab her mother to death at their home in Springfield, Missouri, on June 14, 2015.
The subsequent investigation exposed the extent of the abuse Blanchard had suffered, turning the case into a national media phenomenon, with public opinion split on whether Blanchard was a criminal or a victim. The abuse has been described as Munchausen syndrome by proxy, in which a caregiver fabricates, exaggerates, or induces illness in someone under their care.
Prosecutors took Blanchard’s circumstances into account when she pleaded guilty to second-degree murder in 2016. She was sentenced to ten years in prison and served more than seven before being released on parole in 2023. Godejohn was separately convicted and sentenced to life in prison without parole.
The case attracted widespread attention while Blanchard was still incarcerated and resulted in multiple screen adaptations, including HBO’s 2017 documentary ‘Mommy Dead and Dearest’ and Hulu’s 2019 drama series ‘The Act’. Interest further intensified after her release: she gained millions of social media followers, made numerous media appearances and became the subject of Lifetime’s reality show ‘Gypsy Rose: Life After Lock Up’, which followed her adjustment to life outside prison.
A relationship that began in prison
Urker first contacted Blanchard in 2017, while she was serving her sentence, after watching a documentary about her. He sent what she later described as a “supportive letter” along with his phone number. Their friendship eventually became romantic, and Urker proposed during a prison visit in 2018, but the couple called off their engagement the following year and later separated.
Blanchard rekindled her relationship with Urker in 2024. In December of that year, a year after she had left prison, the couple had a daughter. Blanchard earlier acknowledged that her relationship with Urker had faced difficulties, including the pressure of constant public attention.
By the time of Urker’s death, the couple had reportedly separated again. Accounts citing family sources claim they began living apart roughly two months earlier and ended their romantic relationship about a month before his death, though they continued co-parenting their daughter. Some reports attributed the breakup to Urker’s mental health struggles.

Writer: Netherlands still struggles to shake off narrative of Russia as Ukraine's “big brother”
She made these remarks in an interview with Ukrinform.
“In the Netherlands, it is still difficult to get rid of the narrative of Russia as Ukraine’s “older brother.” There are also many old Dutch books about the Soviet Union in which different peoples and countries are mistakenly described simply as “Russia.”” she said.
According to her, people in the Netherlands talk a lot about their own colonial past, but they hardly ever view Russia through the lens of colonialism. At the same time, history shows a long-standing policy of seizing territories, changing city names, rewriting history, and suppressing national elites, particularly in Ukraine.
“Despite the sanctions, money still reaches Russia through various countries and circumvention schemes, helping to finance its propaganda, among other things. In the Netherlands, there is still insufficient understanding of how Russian propaganda works, and Russia is too often perceived as an “incomprehensible” country with a unique “Russian soul.” These myths make it harder to understand Ukraine and other countries that, after the collapse of the Soviet Union, gained the opportunity to tell the truth about their own history and identity,” she said.
She also emphasized that “there is a huge knowledge gap, so together with Franka Hummel (a Dutch historian, freelance journalist, editor, and writer—ed.), we are now preparing a book for publication. It will be titled ‘Behind the Facade,’ because Russia is, for the most part, a beautiful facade.”
The writer noted that “on the outside, they still have the Hermitage and all those things. They have all this art, all of Swan Lake, and so on. There is still a feeling as if some kind of air bridge exists between the Netherlands and Russia. But in reality, there is a deep divide between them. We do not know Ukraine. People used to say: “It is a backward country. They are all barbarians there.” No, that’s not true. Back in 2016, there were internet access points and Wi-Fi at bus stops in Kyiv. It was incredible. We didn’t have anything like that back then.”
As reported by Ukrinform, the Dutch prime minister and the president of the European Parliament discussed support for Ukraine in The Hague.

The book bears witness to the deep bonds of friendship between Italy and Tanzania and serves as a tribute to the spiritual, cultural, and social contributions of the Franciscan family in Tanzania, often with the invaluable assistance of Italian Franciscan missionaries and Italian religious congregations. Furthermore, the book introduces the Tanzanian public to some of the prayers of St. Francis of Assisi, which are among the oldest expressions of Italian literature.

Kyiv is preparing pontoon crossings in case of bridge strikes and planning tunnel under Dnipro River – minister
The construction of several reserve pontoon crossings across the Dnipro River is scheduled to begin in Kyiv next week, and a long-term option of building a tunnel under the river is also being considered.
Source: Mykola Kalashnyk, Ukraine's Minister of Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport, in an interview with Suspilne
Details: Kalashnyk said a quick option for connecting the left and right banks of Kyiv in the event of bridge damage is currently being considered: building earth dams with pontoon crossings to maintain traffic across the Dnipro River.
Quote from Kalashnyk: "Urgent solutions include a dam and a pontoon crossing, which can be built quickly... This work has already begun. A corresponding coordination meeting was held by the president. We have received all the tasks taking into account their critical nature. The city did not deal with this on its own, so the decision was made for the ministry, the Agency for Restoration, and the military to tackle this together with the capital's authorities."
Details: The minister noted that the construction of the crossings could take up to three months, and the structures themselves should provide at least half the capacity of the existing bridges.
Quote from Kalashnyk: "Preparatory work is underway, and construction will begin shortly. All infrastructure will be involved to maximise the percentage of throughput. We have an average of about 600,000 cars crossing between the left and right banks per day. And the task is to preserve this capacity."
Details: The minister said the locations where construction will begin have been determined. The work is planned not only in Kyiv but also in other regions of Ukraine, and not just on the Dnipro River.
Furthermore, the ministry is considering other options, including the construction of quick-assembly concrete structures and, in the long term, a tunnel under the Dnipro River. However, such projects could cost tens of billions of hryvnias, so their implementation is only possible with the support of Kyiv's international partners.
Meanwhile, the main priority remains preserving the bridges and preventing their destruction. "The maximum amount of equipment has been deployed" for this purpose, the minister added.
Quote from Kalashnyk: "Obviously, each [bridge – ed.] has a margin of safety. And our first task is to provide protection from the sky, which we are doing in coordination with the military. So the first step is to prevent strikes. The second part is to provide protection. The third is rapid recovery. And the fourth is to make decisions regarding alternative reserve crossings, i.e., the construction of new alternative bridge infrastructure facilities."

Russia Adapted LMUR Missiles for Launch From Ground-Based System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:42:02 UTC
23:42:02 KST

During the Center-2026 strategic command-and-staff exercises, Russia unveiled a new ground-based missile system, Izdeliye 347, which uses the LMUR light multi-purpose missile.
This was reported by the Russian news outlet RIA Novosti, citing the Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation.
It was stated that the new system is designed for “high-precision strikes against stationary and moving targets at ranges of up to 20 km.”
“The main feature of the system is the ability for an operator to guide the missile to the target during the terminal phase of its flight path,” the Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation stated.
Judging by the published video, an armored 6×6 Ural truck was used as the platform, with a launcher for two missiles and a mast with an antenna for communications installed in the truck bed.
During the demonstration launches, the missile struck an ‘enemy artillery position’ at a range of 13.9 km. However, the missile missed the target in an open field, landing a few meters away from it.
The LMUR is a Russian multi-purpose air-to-surface guided missile, also known as Izdeliye 305 and Kh-39. It was developed by the Kolomna Machine-Building Design Bureau Research and Production Corporation, which is part of the High-Precision Systems holding company within the Rostec Corporation.
The LMUR is carried by Mi-28NM and Ka-52M attack helicopters, as well as specialized Mi-8MNP-2 helicopters. The Russian military has been using these missiles against Ukraine since at least 2022.
The basic version of the missile is 1,945 mm long, has a casing diameter of 200 mm, and a launch weight of 105 kg. It is equipped with a solid-fuel engine that provides a flight speed of up to 230 m/s.
The stated guaranteed range of guided flight is up to 14.5 km, and the flight altitude above the surface is 100–600 m. The missile carries a 25-kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead.
The guidance system combines inertial navigation with satellite correction during the cruise phase and a thermal imaging homing head during the terminal phase. A two-way radio channel transmits images from the missile to the operator’s screen in the helicopter and control commands in the opposite direction. This allows the crew to guide the missile beyond the helicopter’s field of view and take cover behind terrain features immediately after launch.
In June 2025, Russian sources reported on a modification of the UR-305UD with a flight range increased to 25 km. It is likely that this modification formed the basis for the Izdeliye 347 system.

Housing protests spread across Spain after parliament rejects tenant measures
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
17:40:23 EEST
23:40:23 KST

Tens of thousands of people marched in Madrid and other Spanish cities on Saturday to demand action on housing, a day after parliament rejected two government decrees covering evictions, rental contracts and property investment. The protests followed weeks of public anger over rising housing costs and the eviction of an 87-year-old Madrid resident.
Spain's government said about 70,000 people attended the Madrid demonstration. The city's Tenants' Union gave a figure of 500,000. The estimates could not be independently reconciled.
Around 50 demonstrations had been planned across the country. Protests in Barcelona and nearby L'Hospitalet de Llobregat were cancelled because of heavy rain, Reuters reported.
In Valencia, protesters clashed with police near the City of Arts and Sciences, where a property event was taking place. Reuters reported that police used rubber bullets and tear gas after about 30 demonstrators entered the complex. Other demonstrations were reportedly peaceful.
The protests followed Friday's defeat of two housing decrees proposed by the minority coalition government led by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and the second by 184 to 166. The conservative People's Party, Vox and the Catalan pro-independence Junts opposed both measures.
The proposals included a suspension of evictions involving vulnerable tenants until 2030, extensions to some rental agreements, measures affecting tourist accommodation and restrictions on purchases by investment funds. A separate decree included automatic renewal of rental contracts.
Juan Bravo of the People's Party defended his party's opposition by arguing that increasing supply offered the route to lower housing costs. "Housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes," he said during the parliamentary debate.
Junts lawmaker Miriam Nogueras argued that the measures had been prepared without enough rigour and would fail to prevent investment funds from buying homes or stop evictions.
The protest movement expanded after Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from the Madrid flat where she had lived for about 70 years. Accounts differ over the size of the rent increase she faced, with the supplied reports putting the rise between 230% and 275%. Following protests, the company that owns the flat reached an agreement allowing her to return at a lower rent.
Housing campaigners have continued demonstrations despite that agreement. The Tenants' Union is seeking talks with trade unions over a general strike, spokeswoman Valeria Racu told reporters in Madrid.
Housing costs have risen as construction has failed to keep pace with demand. The Bank of Spain estimates a shortage of about 700,000 homes. National statistics agency INE recorded a 12.2% annual rise in house prices in the second quarter of 2026.
The parliamentary defeat also exposed the limits of Sánchez's minority coalition. His Socialist Party and junior coalition partner Sumar need support from smaller parties to pass legislation.
Spanish media reported that Sánchez was considering an early election following the vote. Opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called on the prime minister to hold an election "as soon as possible".

From Startup Nation to R&D Nation: Israel’s next technological leap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:39:01 UTC
23:39:01 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel
- Technology & Science
- From Startup Nation to R&D Nation: Israel’s next technological leap
From Startup Nation to R&D Nation: Israel’s next technological leap
Record exports and multibillion-dollar deals underscore Israeli high-tech’s resilience under fire. The challenge now is keeping its talent, research and intellectual property at home
Over the past two years, Israel has faced one of the most complex and challenging periods in its history: a prolonged, intensive war on seven fronts, geopolitical uncertainty and global economic pressures. Yet from the turmoil has emerged one of the most impressive stories of resilience and strength in our national history. Israel’s high-tech industry, supported by determined, focused government policy, has not only weathered the upheaval but broken unprecedented records, returned to rapid growth and strengthened its position as a technological engine and strategic scientific hub for the Western world.
As missiles fly toward Israel, the world expresses its confidence with billions of dollars
An examination of official figures from the Israel Innovation Authority and government ministries turns economic statistics into a story of national triumph. In 2025, Israeli high-tech exports reached an all-time high of approximately $85 billion, accounting for around 58% of the country’s total exports. High-tech output soared to 352 billion shekels, or 18.3% of GDP, and the sector contributed roughly half of Israel’s overall economic growth.
Israeli companies raised approximately $15 billion, an impressive increase of around 30% over 2024, while the total value of exit deals surged to about $84 billion. Nearly 400,000 workers and technology leaders now stand at the forefront of the Israeli economy. The message from these figures is unequivocal: war and security threats have not broken Israel’s engine of innovation, and they will not do so.
An international vote of confidence: Mega-deals and record fundraising
The story goes beyond the figures themselves. It is also about the technology giants and international investors choosing to invest in Israel at this particular moment.
The Google-Wiz deal: In March 2025, Google announced its acquisition of Israel’s Wiz for $32 billion, the largest deal in the history of Israeli high-tech.
The Palo Alto Networks-CyberArk deal: Another major achievement, worth approximately $25 billion, reinforces Israel’s standing as the capital of cybersecurity and identity security in the AI era.
Leadership in the industries of the future: Alongside these deals, approximately 1,500 deep-tech companies now operate in Israel in fields including AI, semiconductors, quantum technology, robotics, life sciences and defense technology. These companies raised more than $28 billion between 2019 and 2025, making Israel the world’s leading deep-tech hub outside the US.
The new model: From Startup Nation to R&D Nation
For years, the “Startup Nation” brand rested on a model of founding companies, raising capital and selling them. Today, a shared vision across industry, academia and government is driving a historic shift in thinking. Success is measured by what remains in Israel after a deal: the talent, intellectual property, engineers, laboratories and research and development centers.
RealSense offers a striking example. Just 14 months after its separation from Intel, the company agreed in 2026 to be acquired by US-based Cognex in a deal worth more than $600 million including employee compensation. RealSense expects revenue of $80 million to $90 million in 2026, representing growth of more than 50% over the previous year.
The deal will retain the development center in Haifa, which employs most of the company’s workforce, and turn it into Cognex’s global R&D center for computer vision and robotics. This is the successful new model: the company is sold, but its talent, expertise and capital remain in Israel and put down deeper roots.
Israel now hosts more than 400 multinational R&D centers belonging to some of the world’s leading companies, including Intel, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, Apple and Amazon. They demonstrate every day that Israel is an indispensable part of the global technology industry’s research and development infrastructure.
Turning a challenge into an opportunity: A warning sign to guide national policy
Alongside these phenomenal achievements, a sober and responsible assessment shows that continued, active government involvement is necessary. The figures indicate that in March 2026, only around 62% of employees at privately held Israeli companies were based in Israel, compared with 69% in 2019. There has also been some decline in the number of locally based R&D employees.
These figures are no reason to lose heart. They are a call to action. The government must continue to lead a proactive national policy that shapes and supports the sector, ensuring that the technology created here remains a strategic national asset.
Vision and national policy: How Israel’s government can turn technological advantage into national strength
To secure Israel’s rise as a global R&D powerhouse over the coming decade, the country must continue to strengthen an active national policy that brings together government, industry and academia:
1. Set a strategic national goal: Establish Israel as a global R&D powerhouse in deep tech, AI, semiconductors, quantum technology, biotechnology and defense technology.
2. Create incentives to retain expertise and intellectual property: Develop tax and investment mechanisms that require and reward international companies’ expansion of development centers and intellectual property holdings in Israel.
3. Make transformative investments in research infrastructure: Accelerate the development of national supercomputing facilities, data and AI infrastructure, advanced laboratories and testing facilities that connect government, academia and industry.
4. Expand geographically and bring talent home: Extend innovation and R&D activity to the north, the south and the Negev, alongside attractive national programs to bring Israeli scientists and engineers back from abroad and draw international researchers to Israel.
5. Establish a national R&D coordinating body: Create a flexible government mechanism connecting the Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology, the Israel Innovation Authority, the defense establishment, academia and industry. This would support forward-looking regulation, rapid experimentation and regulatory sandboxes for breakthrough technologies.
Beyond survival: Leading and setting the rules of the game
Israel’s story under fire is about more than a small country that knows how to build successful startups. It is the story of a country developing the technological, scientific and defense capabilities that will shape the future.
Under fire on seven fronts, Israel has demonstrated national resilience, an enterprising spirit, operational capability and technological strength. Through the combined efforts of pioneering industry and forward-looking government policy, the transition from Startup Nation to R&D Nation is no longer merely a vision. It is a reality taking shape before our eyes.
Perhaps there is no better time to say this than during Sukkot and Simchat Torah. The sukkah symbolizes the ability to build, live and grow even in uncertainty. It reminds us that strength is measured not only in walls and material resilience, but also in a people’s ability to endure, unite and continue building its future even as storms rage around it.
Then comes Simchat Torah, the day when, after a period of soul-searching and reflection, we return to the Torah with song, dance and joy. “You shall rejoice in your festival … and you shall be altogether joyful.” This commandment does not ask us to disregard reality. It asks us to choose life, hope, creativity and faith in the future.
Perhaps this is the most powerful Israeli message of our time: not merely to survive the storm, but to grow through it. Not merely to defend what exists, but to build tomorrow. Not merely to respond to threats, but to develop the capabilities that will set the rules of the game.
From the simple sukkah to AI laboratories, from the joy of Torah to research laboratories, from the spirit of our people to the spirit of enterprise, the same age-old Israeli strength is at work: the ability to believe in the future and build it with our own hands.
Israel can and should be more than Startup Nation. It should be R&D Nation: a global powerhouse of knowledge, research, innovation and technology, generating economic, scientific and defense strength for generations to come.
This Sukkot, after years of war and challenges, the message is simple: we are here to build, create and lead.
Not merely to survive, but to flourish. Not merely to cope, but to overcome challenges through spirit and action. Not merely to dream of the future, but to develop it.
In the words of the Torah: “You shall rejoice in your festival … and you shall be altogether joyful.”
Happy Sukkot and Simchat Torah, and may the year ahead bring security, unity, innovation, growth and hope.
Dr. Eitan Lasri is an expert in governance, public policy and strategy. He previously served as an adviser to prime ministers and as chief of staff to the minister of science and technology. He is a senior media commentator.

He referred to an investigation which, he said, found discrepancies between people identified through the system as present at a student protest and records showing some of them were already in jail in connection with criminal cases.Kumar called for a time-bound inquiry into the use of force, alleged arbitrary detentions, concealment of identification badges, manhandling of protesters, deployment of plain-clothes personnel and use of facial-recognition systems.
He urged Shah to direct that people exercising their right to peaceful protest be protected and that police personnel deployed for crowd-control and detention duties remain identifiable.“Democratic dissent cannot be met with methods reminiscent of the British Raj police,” Kumar said.“Delhi Police must understand that its duty is to protect citizens and facilitate their constitutional rights, not to intimidate, assault or silence them,” he added.

Flydubai attack shines spotlight on Oman’s silence, Iran ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:35:32 UTC
23:35:32 KST

Oman has not reported on the attempted hijacking of the flydubai plane, nor on the identity of the attacker, co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, which was revealed overnight between Friday and Saturday. While the initial silence from other Gulf states has been broken, and the pilot who was stabbed, Smith Machachar, has also issued a statement, the Omanis are still choosing not to respond.
U.S. media outlets reported overnight that al-Hammami, who tried to crash the plane with all its Israeli passengers aboard, had previously worked for Oman Air but was dismissed over suspicions that he had become radicalized. The Wall Street Journal, which first reported his suspension from Oman Air, stressed that it remains unclear whether those concerns were subsequently conveyed to flydubai before the airline hired the terrorist.
On Friday afternoon, despite the various reports that had already been published by that point, Khalifa al-Hinai, an Omani lawyer and former judge, posted on X about the discussion surrounding the attempt to crash the plane.
In the post, which was divided into several points, he wrote: “The facts of the investigation and the nationalities involved — so far, no official body or authorized investigative agency has issued an accurate, official account of the circumstances of the incident or the nationalities of those involved. Despite the information gap, hostile accounts rushed to celebrate and spread unverified narratives, exploiting the opportunity to disparage Oman and attempt to defame its people.”
His second point concerned “individual and legal responsibility.”
“Even if, for the sake of argument, it is later confirmed that the co-pilot holds Omani citizenship or is of Omani origin, the established universal legal and ethical principle remains unchanged — criminal responsibility is individual,” he wrote. “Omanis are human beings like all other peoples. Among them are the righteous and those who err. The attempt to hold an entire society or nation responsible for the act of an individual is both wrong and morally bankrupt.”
In his third point, al-Hinai alleged an “excessive focus and rush to link the incident to Oman.” He said there were attempts to turn it into the dominant issue, adding that this would not “erase the criminal nature of Zionism and the atrocities it commits against innocent people.”
In the fourth and fifth points of his post, he added that from a legal standpoint, once the suspect’s identity is confirmed, Oman has the legal right to prosecute him under its domestic laws.
However, that does not negate the priority or right of the country where the airline is based to pursue the necessary legal proceedings.
He concluded: “We are all aware of the scale of the campaigns being waged against our country because of its positions and wisdom. We stand united behind our leadership and the government entrusted with managing the country’s political affairs. Oman, with its people and its wisdom, will remain impervious to all those with malicious intentions, under God’s watch and protection.”
Oman has played a central role as a mediator during months of negotiations between Iran and the United States, alongside other mediators, with meetings also held on Omani soil. However, when it comes to the conflict between Iran and the United States, it is difficult to describe Oman as a neutral party. The country lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, at the center of the confrontation.
That effectively makes Oman part of the story itself. In recent months, reports have said Oman and Iran have been holding talks aimed at reaching understandings over the future management of the Strait of Hormuz. Conflicting reports have also emerged regarding Oman’s position on collecting fees for passage through the strait.
Against the backdrop of those contacts, Oman also received a surprising threat from U.S. President Donald Trump, who warned that if it stood in the way of the United States, he would bomb it as well.
Despite the talks between Iran and Oman, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has made clear in recent weeks that any agreement with Oman would not mean the reopening of the strait. He said Iran’s condition for reopening the strategic shipping route is that the United States return to its commitments under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
Oman is ruled by Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said. The country is one of the Middle East’s key mediators and generally operates under the radar. It seeks to maneuver among the various regional players and maintain the best possible relations with them.
In 2018, reports said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Oman. Israel Katz, who was transportation minister at the time, also visited the country that year. Israeli officials also made diplomatic visits to Oman in the 1990s. Progress in relations stalled over the years amid the deadlock on the Palestinian issue.
Oman has a distinctive religious makeup. Most Omanis belong to Ibadi Islam, a relatively moderate branch distinct from both Shiite and Sunni Islam. Oman also has a significant Shiite population from various countries, including Iranians who have immigrated there, work there and maintain ties with their countries of origin.
Unlike other mediators, and as has again been evident in the days since the attempted downing of the plane, Oman generally does not issue major public statements — or, often, any statements at all.

Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on an oil facility near the Saudi capital on Saturday, where an AFP journalist saw flames and smoke, and accused the Gulf kingdom of striking Sanaa dozens of times.
The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen's Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait in a lightning offensive last month.
Houthi-affiliated channel Al-Masirah TV reported that "Saudi enemy aircraft" hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting "Saudi aggression" against the Yemeni capital, without providing details on the targets or casualties.
Two correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles at the city.
In neighbouring Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh, an AFP journalist said.
While the Saudi authorities are yet to comment, late on Saturday, the Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, adding that they sparked fires at the targeted sites.
The AFP journalist reported seeing firefighters attempting to extinguish a blaze at Aramco's Riyadh refinery, located south of the capital, while ambulances and police vehicles were stationed near the facility.
The Houthis' Al-Masirah channel earlier on Saturday also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen's northwestern governorate of Saada, one of the group's strongholds.
Read moreSaudi-led coalition accuses Houthis of striking Medina power station
It comes after the Houthis said that Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital itself on Thursday night for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July.
Hunger warning
After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war that month, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen including Sanaa, against Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country's south and east -- a region that is larger but much less populated.
Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation.
The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a practice in place for a decade.
Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022.
Since then, fighting has intensified with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab strait.
Read moreYemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
They have also struck multiple Saudi targets including oil infrastructure and the capital Riyadh while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.
The renewed fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, with the World Food Programme warning on Friday that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs.
Battle for Taiz
Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides.
The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died.
The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have conquered swathes of territory, they have yet to take control of Taiz city, which is Yemen's third-largest after Sanaa and Aden.
The Houthis also on Friday said Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours.
Saudi authorities meanwhile reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border.
Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump.
On Saturday US media outlet Axios reported that top cabinet members in the Trump administration met the day before to discuss Yemen as well as the Iran conflict, citing three US officials.
The meeting was not officially announced.

At least 17 people, mostly pilgrims, killed in Kenya road crash

At least 17 people, most of them Catholic pilgrims on the way to a prayer site, have been killed in a crash involving multiple vehicles on the highway to the Kenyan coastal city of Mombasa.
The crash in the Salama area, about 90 kilometres (about 55 miles) southeast of the capital Nairobi, happened after midnight, police said on Saturday.
The crash occurred when a truck driver tried and failed to overtake another truck; that caused a collision with vehicles including a van carrying pilgrims, police said.
Kenyan media reported that the pilgrims were travelling in a 14-seater minibus.
The van’s driver and 16 passengers, most of them women, died at the scene, police said.
The pilgrims were going to a prayer site in Nakuru County, west of Nairobi, said Martin Kivuva, archbishop of the Catholic Archdiocese of Mombasa.
The archbishop said in a statement that he and others were “saddened with lots of grief” over the deaths.
President William Ruto offered condolences to the families, friends, parishioners and the entire Catholic community “who are mourning this painful loss”.
Kenya’s National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) launched an investigation into the crash.
The NTSA said it dispatched investigators “to establish the full circumstances leading to the collision”.
But it noted that the stretch of road where the crash occurred is a known “black spot” and that “recommendations have been made to address safety concerns” regarding the route.
Road accidents are a problem across Africa. In Kenya and elsewhere in the region, the accidents are often blamed on poorly maintained vehicles, excess speed and poor road conditions.
Kenya recorded 5,009 road traffic deaths last year, while 2,150 deaths were reported in the first six months of 2026, local media reported, citing numbers from the NTSA.

What to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:23:55 UTC
23:23:55 KST

What to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential election
Polls show tight race between incumbent Lula and right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro amid concerns about crime and economy.
For the second election in a row, Brazilian voters face a choice between left-wing candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and a right-wing candidate from the Bolsonaro family.
The country’s fractious election is set to take place during a wave of successful far-right candidates across Latin America and a sensitive time in Brazil’s modern political history.
Former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence over his role in a coup plot following his loss to Lula in 2022. The conviction of Jair Bolsonaro and several military officers raised questions about the resilience of Brazilian democracy, revived several decades ago following a period of rule by a United States-backed military dictatorship.
An explosive corruption scandal has implicated prominent figures and institutions across the political spectrum, and observers have expressed concern about possible US intervention.
Polls suggest Lula, the current president seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, are in a virtual tie in a simulated run-off.
Who are the candidates, what issues have been front and centre, and what could the election mean for Brazil? Here’s what you need to know about Brazil’s 2026 presidential elections.
When is the election?
The first round of voting in the Brazilian presidential election will take place on October 4 from 8am to 5pm Brasilia time (11:00 to 20:00 GMT).
If no candidate wins the first round outright, the top two candidates will proceed to a run-off vote on October 25.
Who is Lula?
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, better known simply as Lula, is the country’s current president and the candidate for the Workers’ Party, or the PT.
The 80-year-old has been a central figure in Brazilian politics for decades, serving two four-year presidential terms between 2003 and 2011, and his current term, which began in 2023.
His time in office has been defined by an effort to pair political democracy, restored after a US-backed military dictatorship that ruled the country for several decades until the 1980s, with material improvement for the country’s poor through a series of social programmes meant to address inequality.
Lula has also sought to forge ties between developing, non-Western countries on the global stage.
“He has come to embody the institutionalisation and consolidation of Brazilian democracy since the end of the dictatorship,” Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and the author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera in a phone call.
Who is Flavio Bolsonaro?
Flavio Bolsonaro has emerged as the heir to his father’s status as leader of Brazil’s political right and Lula’s main challenger in the 2026 election. Bolsonaro is running as the candidate of the right-wing Liberal Party.
The 45-year-old is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
Flavio has pledged a hard stance on crime and insecurity and close collaboration with the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has designated several criminal groups in Brazil as “terrorist organisations”.
He has also promised to rein in inflation and government spending, with an adviser stating that he would implement a debt ceiling if elected.
Flavio Bolsonaro has also sought to turn his father’s conviction into a story of political persecution, denouncing his trial as illegitimate and seeking his release from prison.
“I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro, so that he may place the presidential sash across my chest,” he said at a campaign event in September.
“The Bolsonaro family’s pitch is that the institutions that Brazilian democracy has erected since the end of dictatorship are either rotten and unresponsive, and that we need a sharp turn away from this status quo,” said Pagliarini.
“The stakes of this election are incredibly stark because the candidates stand for such opposing visions about what Brazil’s recent history means,” he added.
What issues have defined the race?
As with many recent elections across the region, crime, insecurity and cost of living issues have dominated the Brazilian election. Corruption and concerns about US intervention in the country’s domestic affairs have also loomed over the campaign.
A Quaest survey from September 7 found that 31 percent of respondents cited violence as their biggest concern, followed by 20 percent who said corruption, 19 percent who said the economy, and 12 percent who said health.
While Brazil has seen decent economic growth and low unemployment and inflation during Lula’s third term, those mild gains have been paired with explosive levels of household debt and concerns about the rising cost of living.
A report from the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a left-leaning US-based think tank focused on economic issues, found that extreme poverty in Brazil fell by about 40 percent between 2022 and 2024, unemployment dropped to historic lows, and the country’s economic growth significantly outpaced that of most of its neighbours. But the analysis also found that households were strained by a sharp uptick in the cost of servicing debt. All in all, analysts say they amount to a view of the economy that is neither catastrophic nor particularly satisfying.
Pagliarini says that both candidates have tried to steer the election onto more favourable terrain for their issues of choice, with Lula portraying Flavio Bolsonaro as a willing accomplice in US efforts to undermine Brazilian sovereignty, and Flavio Bolsonaro accusing Lula of being corrupt and weak on crime.
What do the polls say?
Analysts say that polls reflect the state of Brazilian politics: deeply polarised but unenthusiastic.
“The general vibe is that this is a very downbeat campaign,” said Pagliarini. “There’s not a lot of enthusiasm either way, and it’s hard to tell at this stage who that favours.”
Most surveys show a close race, with Lula holding a marginal advantage over Flavio Bolsonaro that tightens further in a hypothetical run-off.
A Quaest survey from September shows Lula with 37 percent of voter intention against Flavio Bolsonaro’s 33 percent, while an AtlasIntel survey from the same period showed Lula winning 46 percent to Flavio Bolsonaro’s 43 percent.
A Datafolha poll found Lula with 40 percent and Flavio Bolsonaro with 36 percent.
Polls also show Flavio Bolsonaro favoured over Lula on issues of inflation, combating corruption, and crime and drug trafficking, while Lula is seen more favourably on issues of poverty and inequality, foreign affairs and health.
What challenges has each campaign faced?
An explosive corruption scandal, focused on disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro, has raised questions for both campaigns and implicated members of the country’s political and economic elite across the political spectrum.
Reports found that Flavio Bolsonaro had solicited substantial funds from Vorcaro, ostensibly to finance a documentary – The Dark Horse (or O Azarao) – about his father.
Lula’s former finance minister, Guido Mantega, has also said he helped arrange a meeting with Vorcaro, Lula and the head of Brazil’s central bank to discuss banking policy. Lula has said he told Vorcaro there would be no political interference in his bank’s case, only a “technical investigation conducted by the central bank”. The Reuters news agency confirmed the meeting.
The scandal has also embroiled the country’s Supreme Court, with Alexandre de Moraes, whose central role in Bolsonaro’s coup trial turned him into a subject of ire for the political right, facing questions about his own links to the banker.
De Moraes has in turn accused a justice appointed by Bolsonaro of wrongdoing, with the court considering probes into the conduct of both justices.
What are the concerns about US intervention?
Concerns that the Trump administration could intervene or seek to influence the outcome on behalf of Bolsonaro have also loomed over the election.
The US president has frequently threatened to cut off economic assistance to Latin American countries if his preferred candidate fails to win. Trump had also used sanctions to target members of the Brazilian judiciary involved in the case against the elder Bolsonaro, which he portrayed as a “witch-hunt”. Trump also placed heavy tariffs on Brazil in a bid to have the case thrown out.
The country’s government denied visas to two US officials who sought to travel to Brazil, saying they planned to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazilian elections. Lula’s government has warned the US against meddling in the country’s domestic affairs.
Trump has himself used false claims of rampant fraud to justify efforts to remain in office despite his election loss in 2020.
A group of 31 Democratic US Congress members recently sent a letter to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticising “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazilian elections.
The Reuters reported that Brazilian intelligence officials also briefed a French and German delegation in September about possible interference in the election by outside powers such as the US and Russia. The officials said that US interference ranged “from lawfare to interference that is openly acknowledged”.

Meta has opened Muse for creating custom AI gadgets

Meta has opened Muse for creating custom AI gadgets
Kyiv • UNN
Meta has launched the open Muse Gadgets project with firmware and an SDK for developers. The company is also giving away 5,000 Home Link devices for free.
Meta has introduced Muse Gadgets, an open-source project that allows developers to create their own devices for connecting to the Muse AI agent. The company has provided open-source firmware and an SDK for Linux, as well as suggested initial gadget ideas. TechCrunch reports, writes UNN.
Details
Meta’s Muse—a personal AI agent that books trips, fills out forms, and makes purchases on behalf of the user—has already become popular among a broad audience. However, the company’s new side project may be of particular interest to enthusiasts who enjoy experimenting with technology.
On Friday, the company introduced Muse Gadgets, an open-source project that enables developers to create their own hardware that connects to Muse.
Meta is providing open-source firmware—the low-level software that runs directly on a device—as well as an SDK for Linux. The company has also suggested several ideas for initial projects. These include equipping Muse with a color e-ink display or installing the system on a dongle-like device that connects to a TV via HDMI.
Users can take an inexpensive enthusiast computer, such as a Raspberry Pi, or a ready-made ESP32 board, and then connect Muse "to displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and anything else you have on your desk," Meta notes.
The company has also created a Discord channel to support users.
Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, said in a post on X that the company had created a device called Muse Home Link. The device is powered via USB-C and enables Muse to connect to a home network and interact with smart devices connected to it, including speakers and smart TVs.
According to Friedman, Meta made 5,000 of these Home Link devices and is giving them away free of charge to Muse subscribers while supplies last. Given that Friedman’s post about Home Link garnered nearly 30,000 views within a few hours, it can be assumed that these free devices have already been claimed. Friedman said that Home Link will be ready to ship in a few weeks.
Muse Gadgets may not be of interest to a broad audience, but the project fits well with Meta’s strategy of turning Muse into something more than just a standalone chatbot. Meta is not limiting itself to promoting Muse among ordinary consumers—the company is also seeking to attract small businesses and large enterprises.
Earlier this week, the company introduced Muse for small businesses. The service is free, but has usage limits and connects to tools such as Shopify, Dropbox, and Slack. Meta has also launched a new Meta Enterprise Platform division, which is intended to help the company promote its artificial intelligence-based solutions among businesses and corporate clients.

‘This can’t go on’: tens of thousands protest against housing crisis in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:19:46 UTC
23:19:46 KST

Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Madrid and other Spanish cities as they step up demands for action to tackle a mounting housing crisis after government measures were struck down by the opposition.
Demonstrators on Saturday waved posters calling for a general strike after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid, and other housing issues, were rejected in parliament on Friday.
Authorities said 70,000 people were protesting. Organisers put the figure at 500,000.
“It’s a shame,” Nando de Anguulo, 26, who joined the protest in Madrid, told Reuters. “It only proves that it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, may call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass, Spanish media reported on Friday, and would be watching the strength of Saturday’s protests before making a decision.
The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta.
Protests on Saturday were peaceful in 50 Spanish cities. In the south-eastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and teargas to break up the protests.
About 30 people managed to get inside the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural building in the city, before they were ousted by police.
One protester in Madrid, Marcos Sainz, a librarian, 26, said he used to rent a two-bedroom apartment with friends for a monthly rent of 900 euros ($1,000) but that a one-bedroom flat often now cost 1,000 euros – or half the median monthly salary in the capital.
He told AFP he would protest rental spikes “until someone dares to regulate it all, as (otherwise) we’ll all have to leave Madrid and that would be a shame as I am from Madrid”.
Javier, 31, a solar panel installer, said: “We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project.” He added: “I spend half of my salary on a tiny room.”
“What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, an energy that is showing that eight days of people power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government,” Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants’ Union organising the protest, said in a statement.
“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” she said.
Late on Saturday groups of far-right protesters, some of them performing Nazi salutes, tried to get to the camp in Madrid but were blocked by police.
One video posted on the website of Spanish daily El País showed police chasing some members of the group through the streets and the newspaper also reported that officers had made three arrests.
On Friday, Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
Despite the anger of the protesters outside parliament, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees.
The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.
News of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.
The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years. The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report.

Teaching is just the start: The crushing burden on India's college teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:18:24 UTC
23:18:24 KST

According to a survey on higher education, while recommended student-teacher ratio (STR) targets in higher education range between 15:1 and 20:1, the national average hovers between 24:1 and 27:1.
In a brightly lit classroom at an engineering college in Bengaluru, a fourth-year Computer Science lecture is underway. At the front, a professor moves through a technical lesson while also keeping track of attendance sheets and administrative requirements.In the middle rows, a student sits quietly, mentally calculating train schedules between Bengaluru and Pune. He is trying to work out how to explain to a corporate employer that a career-launching Pre-Placement Offer (PPO) could be at risk because of a mandatory offline attendance requirement for a single elective subject.The scene captures a growing tension inside India’s higher education system.For final-year students, college is no longer only about completing a degree. With competition for jobs intensifying, students are increasingly focused on internships, practical skills, early employment and mental health support. But the institutional framework around them remains tied to attendance thresholds, credit requirements, standardised evaluation and administrative compliance.Caught at the centre of these competing pressures is the college teacher.According to data from the All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE), while recommended Student-Teacher Ratio (STR) targets in higher education range between 15:1 and 20:1, the national average hovers between 24:1 and 27:1.
In public and state institutions, that figure can rise to 35:1 or 50:1, with individual undergraduate lectures accommodating 80 to 120 or more students per section.The pressure is compounded by faculty shortages. Central universities report faculty vacancy rates between 29% and 34%, while senior professor vacancies frequently exceed 50%. Across technical institutions such as the IITs, NITs and IIITs, unfilled positions range from 30% to over 50%.This leaves teachers performing several roles at once: academic instructors, institutional policy enforcers, career advisers and, often, informal listeners when students are struggling.At the same time, they have to manage UGC Academic Performance Indicators, NAAC and NIRF documentation and heavy teaching loads.
Modern classroom: More than academics
For today's students, particularly those in their final year, the classroom is closely linked to the question of what happens after graduation.“A student may come because he is confused about an internship, worried about placements or simply doesn't know how to deal with something happening at home. We try to listen, but there is a limit to what a subject teacher can realistically handle,” Prakash, a college faculty member at an engineering college, says.From the student's perspective, the final year can feel like a race against time, with academic requirements running alongside internships, placements and preparations for entering the workforce.Pranav Vats, a final-year Computer Science and Engineering student in Bengaluru, describes what students prioritise:“Whenever a guy comes to a college, he eventually wants to get placed. He doesn't want to get a 9-plus CGPA every semester. He just wants to get placed in a good company and do well in his career financially and also growth-wise... I have been doing internships from the first year itself. And whatever interviews I have been going through, nobody asked me about what my CGPA is. Everybody just asked, okay, how much do you know, how much practical skills you have, and how well you understand the market and how well do you understand your business in which you are going to work now.”That shift creates a difficult balance for teachers. Students may see practical experience as more directly connected to employment, while faculty members remain responsible for ensuring that students complete prescribed courses, credits and attendance requirements.
When attendance collide with career
The tension becomes particularly visible during placement and internship season.Pranav describes a situation in which he had secured an internship opportunity in Pune after clearing an interview:“Two, three months back, I got an interview. I've cleared it. I went to Pune. And at that time, I got permission from college. They gave me this letter of acknowledgement that you can go and pursue your six months internship, and all. But all of a sudden, after two months, they are saying that no, you have to fulfil your academic requirements and all... This company is very good. I'm doing very well there. And they are giving me the PPO for it. I could have got placed. But right now, this company is not giving away. College is saying that you have to attend weekly once class. As a student, it is not possible for me to come from Pune to Bangalore every week to attend some stupid class that is not even relevant to my coursework, which is not even relevant to my computer science degree... It is just an open elective subject.”He says discussions with his mentor, department head and other authorities did not resolve the problem. Pranav says similar situations have affected other students, including those with jobs or internships in Bengaluru itself.He says, “A guy got placed in Bangalore itself. And he said, ‘Sir, I can't attend this class this week because I've got placed.’ They said, ‘You have to fulfill this academic thing’.”For teachers, however, understanding the student's situation does not necessarily mean being able to change the rule.“The final year is particularly difficult because everything seems to happen at once. Students are completing projects, dealing with attendance and examinations, and at the same time worrying about placements and what they are going to do after graduation. You can see that pressure building up, especially when a student's plans don't work out,” the faculty said.The faculty member explains the dilemma, “There are situations where a student gets an internship or an opportunity outside the college and genuinely needs flexibility. As a teacher, you may understand why that opportunity matters to him. But you are also responsible for implementing the academic requirements. That can put the teacher in an uncomfortable position because you may sympathise with the student without having the authority to change the rule.”
Teacher becomes institutional buffer
The teacher is therefore often caught between three sets of expectations.The administration expects attendance, syllabus completion and documentation for institutional requirements. Students expect empathy, career guidance and flexibility. Parents expect academic performance, safety and career outcomes.The teacher may have to explain an institutional decision to a student without having any authority over that decision.“Sometimes the student is upset with the institution, the parents are worried about the student's performance and the department is concerned about academic requirements,” the teacher explains. “The teacher ends up sitting in the middle. We are expected to explain one side to the other, even though we may not have control over the decision ourselves.”For students, this can reinforce the perception that teachers are primarily there to enforce attendance and award marks.Pranav puts it bluntly, “They don't care, they just want these things to attend classes, they want attendance, they want marks, that's it... If you go to an off-campus thing, where majorly everybody is applying right now, nobody asks you about your CGPA. They just want you to have your practical skills. But this CGPA thing or whatever coursework they are teaching us in college, it is not even relevant to what we will work in our offices.”
When personal problems enter classroom
The pressure is not limited to academics and placements.Teachers are also increasingly expected to recognise when students are struggling emotionally, even though they may not be trained to provide professional mental health support.“You spend enough time with a class to notice changes,” the faculty member observes. “If a student who is normally interactive suddenly stops speaking, misses classes or stops submitting work, you notice it. The difficult part is deciding whether to ask, ‘Is everything okay?’ because you don't know whether the student wants you to enter that part of his life,” Prakash say.The teacher describes the boundary involved, “There is a very fine line between being concerned about a student and becoming intrusive. If I ask too many questions, it may seem intrusive. If I don't ask anything, I may miss something important. Teachers are constantly trying to judge where that line is.”At the same time, faculty members recognise their own limitations.“I want my students to know that they can approach me, but I also have to be honest about my limitations. I can listen, I can help them think through a problem and I can direct them towards the right person. But I am not trained to provide therapy, and pretending otherwise can be harmful,” Prakash says.
Counselling gap, a stigma problem
Many institutions have counselling cells or mentor-mentee systems, but having a service does not necessarily mean students will use it.Pranav says his mentor-mentee system is largely focused on academic issues:“For every 20 or 30 sets of people there is assigned one mentor. So whatever the issues you have regarding the college, you can talk with them and they can get a resolution about it... [But] there is nothing like that through which we can discuss our career... They are strictly for the subject.”He says students also face peer pressure around seeking counselling.“We have one basically like they have hired a person... if you have any emotional issues or something like that, then you can go schedule a session,” Pranav says. “[But] if you suppose you go to a counsellor there is this peer pressure. If you go to a counselor, or maybe you're discussing things with the teacher, you would seem like a weak person.”“This thing is very very disturbing to the students and nobody talks about it because everybody feels that okay, if I talk about it I can feel weak about it and people will think that okay he's not mature enough to deal with his own problem on his own... I talk to some of my friends about it who are eventually on the same path... but majorly I work with my pressure on my own,” Pranav adds.When behaviour changes significantly, teachers also have to balance intervention with confidentiality.“If I feel that a student's behaviour has changed significantly, I cannot just say, ‘That's his personal matter.’ There are situations where you have to involve the appropriate support system. But you also have to be careful about confidentiality and about not turning a student's difficulty into a public issue,” Prakash says.
Emotional burden on teachers
While student stress receives increasing attention, the pressure on faculty can remain largely invisible.A teacher managing a class of 80 to 120 students may also have to deal with staff shortages, administrative work, evaluations, meetings and institutional documentation. A difficult conversation with a student does not necessarily end when the class does.The faculty member says teachers need institutional support if they are expected to take on these additional responsibilities.Prakash says, “I don't think teachers are unwilling to take on a larger role. Most teachers care about what happens to their students. But if the expectation is that we should identify emotional distress, provide career guidance, handle academic problems and support students through personal crises, then the institution also has to give teachers training and a proper support structure.”
Beyond the classroom
The experiences of both students and teachers point to a larger structural problem.When colleges rely on individual teachers to enforce academic rules, handle administrative requirements, guide students through careers and respond to emotional distress, the teacher becomes the point where multiple pressures meet.
The solution therefore cannot rest entirely on individual faculty members.As colleges respond to changing job markets and rising student pressures, the system would require clearer boundaries for faculty responsibilities, greater flexibility for final-year students navigating legitimate career opportunities, and stronger professional support systems.For the teacher standing at the front of the classroom, the challenge is no longer simply teaching the subject. It is managing everything that happens around it, often without the authority, time or institutional support required to do so.
Vijaya Srivastava is a journalist and feature writer whose expertise lies in covering human-centred developments. Her stories explore how policy, technology, economic shifts and social change influence people's everyday lives. Her work also focuses on bringing depth, context and a human perspective to complex issues.
Her reports primarily cover society, healthcare, safety, public policy and emerging trends, alongside other political developments.
