King Charles will confront what Buckingham Palace described as “the darkest days of our past” when he visits the Caribbean later this month, amid renewed calls for Britain to address its role in the transatlantic slave trade.
Charles and Queen Camilla will visit the Bahamas and Guyana before traveling to Antigua and Barbuda, where the king will attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), scheduled for Nov. 1-4.
The visit comes as Caribbean and African countries intensify calls for Britain and other former colonial powers to pay reparations for their role in slavery. The issue is expected to feature prominently at the Commonwealth summit.
The British government has ruled out reparations, while Charles, who remains head of state of several Caribbean nations, including the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, has previously expressed his sorrow over the legacy of slavery.
“There are important discussions taking place in various fora about colonial legacy and the intergenerational impact of the transatlantic trade in enslaved persons,” a Buckingham Palace spokesperson told reporters, saying the visit was coming at an important time in the relationship between Britain and Caribbean nations.
“The visit program will therefore not shy away from ‘the darkest days of our past,’ as His Majesty has described them, but, in keeping with the wishes of our host nations, it will principally be oriented to the vibrant present and promising future of each country.”
From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European merchants, with Britain responsible for transporting an estimated 3.2 million people, making it the second-most active European nation after Portugal.
Charles, who is head of the Commonwealth, a group of 56 nations, mainly former British colonies, encompassing some 2.7 billion people, has backed research into the British monarchy’s own historical links to the trade.
Last month, the Jamaican government formally asked him to seek legal advice on whether Britain should pay reparations and said it was “encouraged” by Buckingham Palace’s engagement.
“It is important to note here the work His Majesty himself has done over many years both to acknowledge the wrongs of the past and to find creative ways to right inequalities that endure,” the palace spokesperson said.
“As you would therefore expect, opportunities will be found during the visit to reflect and renew his personal, wholehearted and continuing commitment to that process.”
In February, Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey told Reuters she expected its members to make progress toward beginning negotiations on reparations.

New Ukrainian ballistic missile used in combat
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:23:51 BST
20:23:51 KST

Ukraine has used a domestically built tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said, naming the weapon as the FP-7 and signalling that the next task is building it in quantity, according to the president in a post published on Thursday.
Writing on X, Mr Zelensky said: “Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine!”
No target was given, and Kyiv has declined to say what the missile struck. The brevity of the announcement is itself the point, since a first combat firing is a political statement about Ukrainian industry as much as a military event.
Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine! pic.twitter.com/IxdjVg51c1
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 1, 2026
The FP-7 is made by Fire Point, the Ukrainian company set up in 2022 that has become one of the more visible names in the country’s wartime weapons industry, and which also produces the FP-1 one-way attack drone and the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. The missile is launched from a standard truck trailer rather than a purpose-built transporter erector launcher, an approach that keeps cost down and makes the launch vehicle harder to distinguish from ordinary traffic.
Published figures for the missile vary between sources and none of them have been independently verified. The announced range has been given as between 200 and 300 kilometres, with a warhead variously described as 150 or 200 kilograms, a circular error probable of around 14 metres and a terminal velocity of 1,200 to 1,500 metres a second. Analysts tracking the programme have assessed that the airframe derives from the Soviet 48N6 interceptor used by the S-400 system, rebuilt with composite materials and modern electronics, and the manufacturer has claimed that the resulting speed gives it a better chance of getting through air defences than the Russian Iskander.
Roughly seven months separated the first reported test from this firing, which is fast by any peacetime standard and reflects how much Ukrainian procurement has compressed since 2022.

Delhi landfill garbage mountains shrinking, 100 acres reclaimed in 18 months: CM Rekha Gupta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:22:01 UTC
20:22:01 KST

Delhi CM Rekha Gupta poses for a group picture during an on-site inspection of waste disposal operations near Okhla, in New Delhi
NEW DELHI: Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday said the garbage mountains at the city's landfill sites were steadily shrinking as she reviewed waste disposal work at Okhla and laid the foundation stone for new waste processing facilities at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola.Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years, with a large portion of the cleared area also being turned green.She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed."Today, at Okhla, we have processed almost all the legacy waste that was there before January 2025," Gupta said.
Government targets legacy and fresh waste
Gupta said the government was working on two fronts: clearing the existing garbage mountains while ensuring that fresh waste generated every day did not accumulate into new landfill sites.According to news agency ANI, she said around 3,000-4,000 metric tonnes of fresh waste reaches the sites daily and is being processed round the clock."The garbage currently piled up here is essentially fresh waste generated after January 2025, and that too is being processed round the clock. So, we are fighting on two fronts: one is eliminating waste, and the other is ensuring that the 3,000 to 4,000 metric tons of fresh waste arriving daily is processed immediately, so that new garbage mountains are not formed for future generations," Gupta said.
She said the government was working to reduce the existing garbage mountains to zero."People are seeing that the garbage mountains are continuously shrinking and soon a time will come when they will become zero," Gupta said.Gupta also said she had taken what she described as her "last selfie" with the garbage mountain at Okhla."Today I have taken my last selfie with the garbage mountain; after this I have taken a pledge that this garbage mountain will end soon," she said.Taking a jibe at the Opposition, Gupta added, "I had said - garbage mountain, you will have to go; the opposition mocked. Today I will say the garbage mountain is going; now only its back remains."
New processing plants at three sites
During the programme at the Okhla SLF site, Gupta laid the foundation stone for fresh waste processing plants at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola, as well as a biogas facility at Ghazipur. She also inaugurated the M&CW Centre at Kotla Mubarakpur through virtual mode from Okhla.The Okhla plant will be built at a cost of Rs 103 crore and will have a processing capacity of 1,400 metric tonnes per day.The Singhola facility will cost Rs 42 crore and have a capacity of 800 metric tonnes per day, while the Ghazipur plant will have a processing capacity of 700 metric tonnes per day.The facilities are intended to process fresh waste as well as construction and demolition waste. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure."Waste should not remain waste; Delhi should use it as wealth," she said, adding that new technologies were being introduced for waste segregation and processing.She said waste and cattle dung would be used to produce biogas and manure as part of efforts to build a technology-driven waste management system.
Gupta said the government was taking up several measures to address pollution, including work on landfill waste, cleaning the Yamuna, dust mitigation, plantation, road infrastructure and waste management."Our government is tackling pollution from a 360-degree perspective to ensure it gradually decreases. We are working on every aspect, be it addressing the mountains of garbage, cleaning the Yamuna, improving road infrastructure, or managing waste, to ensure the people of Delhi enjoy better air quality. Our resolve and policies are absolutely clear, and we are working 24x7 in the public interest," she said.The chief minister also reviewed the progress of waste disposal work with officials and directed them to accelerate the work according to the stipulated timeline.She said the garbage mountains at Bhalswa, Ghazipur and Okhla had caused inconvenience to people travelling through these areas and said the government was continuing efforts to eliminate them.

EU links 2026 Ukraine funding to reforms, rejects request for early advance – FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:21:39 EEST
20:21:39 KST

The European Union has not supported Ukraine's request for the early provision of additional financing in 2026, emphasizing that the allocation of funds will directly depend on Kyiv's implementation of agreed-upon reforms, the Financial Times reports, citing a letter from European Commissioners Valdis Dombrovskis and Marta Kos to Verkhovna Rada Chairman Ruslan Stefanchuk.
In the summer, Ukraine estimated its additional defense needs at approximately $27 billion and asked the European Commission to prematurely allocate a portion of the funds from the two-year €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan program (€60 billion earmarked for defense, €30 billion for direct budget support). According to the program's parameters, up to €45 billion are to be made available to Ukraine in 2026, with the remaining €45 billion in 2027.
According to FT, the European Commissioners made it clear that access to financing is possible only upon fulfilling an agreed list of commitments. Specifically, this concerns the cancellation of VAT exemptions for small international parcels, the introduction of taxation rules for digital platforms, and proper financial monitoring of politically exposed persons (PEPs), amendments to which raised concerns in Brussels as a departure from the anti-corruption track. According to the publication, meeting these requirements will pave the way for Kyiv to receive about €34 billion in support during 2026.
At the same time, the European Commission emphasized that rejecting the early advance request does not mean halting financial assistance. On October 1, the parties announced the coordination of funding sources for budgetary and defense needs through the end of 2026, confirming the absence of an uncovered financing gap for the current year.
Additionally, on October 2, the European Commission transferred a regular tranche of €2.9 billion to Ukraine under the Ukraine Facility program. Total assistance provided to Kyiv by the EU and member states since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion has reached €227.4 billion.

Man bailed in RAF Fairford terrorism investigation
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

12:20:37 BST
20:20:37 KST

The dual British and Iranian national arrested in London on Thursday over the events at RAF Fairford has been released on bail, and searches of two properties in Westminster have now concluded, Counter Terrorism Policing stated on Saturday.
The 25-year-old was detained in the borough of Westminster on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006. He is the sixth person to be arrested and then bailed in connection with the activity near the Gloucestershire airfield on Sunday 27 September.
Counter Terrorism Policing said the investigation into the circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is continuing. Nobody has been charged.
Five men in their twenties were arrested in the early hours of Sunday after Gloucestershire Constabulary received a report of suspicious vehicles near the base, initially on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and subsequently of preparation of a terrorist act. A major incident was declared and homes were evacuated in the village of Whelford, which sits beside the airfield. All five remain on police bail, and all are London residents, four in Westminster and one in Camden.
Three vehicles were examined and no improvised explosive devices were found in them, although a quantity of petrol was recovered. Vicki Evans, the Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, said earlier in the week that officers were looking at all possible angles, including possible foreign state involvement, and described the investigation as hugely complex with specialist teams working multiple lines of enquiry.
Fairford is a United States Air Force forward operating location rather than a flying station of the Royal Air Force, and the length of its runway has made it the standing European base for American strategic bombers. B-1B Lancers have been operating from the airfield, and the base moved to its highest force protection condition before the arrests were made.
Counter Terrorism Policing has asked anyone with information that might assist the investigation to report it through gov.uk/ACT or by calling the Anti-Terrorist Hotline on 0800 789 321.

Former MHK deputy chairman Ahmet Şahin and federation official Sebahattin Şahin were released under judicial supervision, with foreign travel bans and reporting requirements.

Türkiye’s exports hit September record of $26 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:19:29 UTC
20:19:29 KST

Türkiye’s goods exports rose 15.4 percent year-on-year to $26 billion in September, the highest figure for the month, Trade Minister Ömer Bolat said on Oct. 3.
Presenting the figures at the Turkish Exporters Assembly (TİM) in Istanbul, Bolat said September’s exports were also the second-highest monthly total on record, after December 2025.
Exports in the first nine months increased 5.2 percent to $211 billion. The total for the 12 months through September reached a record $283.7 billion, exceeding the government’s $282 billion target for calendar-year 2026.
Imports rose 5.9 percent to $31.2 billion in September, while the monthly trade deficit narrowed 24.8 percent to $5.2 billion, ministry data showed. Exports covered 83.2 percent of imports.
Over the January-September period, imports increased 5.4 percent to $282 billion, leaving a trade deficit of $71 billion, up 5.8 percent from a year earlier.
Bolat said the government would work to keep the full-year deficit below $100 billion despite higher energy costs linked to the conflict in the Gulf.
He estimated services exports at $125.4 billion over the 12 months through September, bringing combined goods and services exports to $409.1 billion. The government’s year-end target is $410 billion.
“We expect the current account to post surpluses in August and September,” he said.
Exports increased in 19 of 26 sectors in September, Bolat added.
The minister also outlined recent trade talks with major partners, including a meeting with Polish Finance and Economy Minister Andrzej Domański in Milwaukee on Oct. 1 during the G20 trade ministers’ gathering.
Bolat said bilateral trade with Poland reached a record $12.5 billion in 2025 and could rise to $15 billion in the near future.
The two ministers agreed to hold bilateral consultations and an investment and business forum hosted by Türkiye’s Trade Ministry. Their talks also covered the functioning of the Türkiye-EU customs union and cooperation in areas including energy, logistics and defense.

Erdoğan calls for lasting unity among Turkic states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:17:06 UTC
20:17:06 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan called for lasting unity and solidarity among Turkic states on Oct. 3, marking Turkic States Cooperation Day and the 17th anniversary of the Nakhchivan Agreement.
“On this path of brotherhood, which we embarked on with the motto ‘Unity in language, thought and action,’ I wish for our unity, togetherness and solidarity to endure,” he wrote on social media platform NSosyal.
The agreement, signed on Oct. 3, 2009, established the Cooperation Council of Turkic Speaking States, known as the Turkic Council. Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan were its founding members.
The council grew out of a series of summits of Turkic-speaking countries launched in 1992 after the breakup of the Soviet Union.
Uzbekistan joined in 2019, bringing membership to five.
The group adopted its current name, the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), at a summit in Istanbul in November 2021.
Hungary, Turkmenistan and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus hold observer status.
The organization’s secretariat is based in Istanbul, and its work covers trade, transport, energy, education and culture.
In a separate statement marking the anniversary, the Turkish Foreign Ministry said the organization had strengthened cooperation and solidarity through shared history, language and ties of brotherhood.
The ministry said Türkiye would continue working to turn the Turkic world’s human, economic and strategic potential into shared prosperity.
Türkiye will host the organization’s 13th summit in Ankara on Oct. 29-30, the ministry said, adding that the meeting would advance cooperation further.

Ethiopia’s government forces retake airport from Tigray rebels in Mekelle
The rebels are seen leaving the capital of the northern Tigray region, according to local sources.
Ethiopia’s federal army and pro-government fighters have recaptured the main airport in the capital of the northern Tigray region, with the rebels seen leaving the city, according to multiple unnamed sources.
The Ethiopian National Defence Forces regained control of Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle, one source with knowledge of events in the city and a humanitarian source told Reuters news agency on Saturday.
The airport, which is about 10km (6 miles) from the centre of Mekelle, was one of three airfields in the region that were seized by the rebel forces at the start of the fighting on September 23.
The fighters, as well as the leaders of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), were seen retreating from the city, a local journalist and residents told the AFP news agency.
The journalist added that federal forces had not yet been seen inside Mekelle.
“I am concerned that government and public property could be exposed to looting because there are no security forces in the city,” a resident told AFP.
“I am worried that lawlessness could spread in the city, and I am also afraid for my life. I want us to quickly return to law and order,” added another resident.
Al Jazeera could not independently confirm these claims. Media access is currently heavily restricted in Ethiopia, and there have been significant communications blackouts.
Last month, rebels announced the formation of a seven-party rebel coalition led by the TPLF, the same armed group that fought in the 2020-2022 civil war against federal forces from Addis Ababa. The new coalition includes rebel groups of varying sizes from across the country.
Later that month, the coalition started an offensive, seizing three airports around the contested Tigray state and engaging in fighting on the borders with Amhara and Afar states.
The government is now engaged in a counteroffensive, pushing into Tigrayan territory along three axes towards Mekelle, according to the Critical Threats Project, part of the American Enterprise Institute think tank.
Fighting has so far been concentrated in Tigray. However, rebels have reportedly carried out drone attacks on Addis Ababa.
The TPLF and government have not commented on developments on the ground.
The fighting has seen drone attacks, intensified forced conscription, and attacks on civilian infrastructure, according to Amnesty International, a global rights group.
The renewed conflict has not yet reached the heights of the Tigray war, which lasted from 2020 to 2022 and saw hundreds of thousands of deaths, but it is quickly taking on an international dimension.
Risk of conflict spreading
The government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing the opposition coalition. Khartoum and Cairo have denied involvement.
Eritrea has severed diplomatic ties with Ethiopia over the accusations.
On Thursday, Eritrea also denied involvement in the Tigray conflict, and accused Addis Ababa of “pursuing an agenda of incessant hostility”. It also said Ethiopia, which is landlocked, was planning to invade Eritrea to secure sovereign access to the Red Sea coast.
The TPLF’s leader, Debretsion Gebremichael, said in a video published on Thursday that “the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea”.
Ethiopia has previously ruled out seeking conflict with Eritrea over access to the coast.

A program modeled on the U.S. television show "To Catch a Predator" could not be produced in Estonia, investigative journalist Mihkel Kärmas says, because it would not fit the country's legal or ethical environment.
Last week, Lance Oppenheim's new feature film "Primetime", starring Robert Pattinson, premiered in cinemas. The film tells the story of TV journalist Chris Hansen, who in the mid‑2000s confronted suspected child predators on camera. Estonian TV host and journalist Mihkel Kärmas, who went to see the film, is not impressed.
"I understand why it's a scandalous film that has caused a stir, but I doubt it will become a major hit in Estonia," Kärmas said.
"Primetime" is based on real events but is a dramatization. At its center is the highly controversial NBC program "To Catch a Predator," which aired from 2004 to 2007.
The show's format involved activists posing online as minors and luring men suspected of seeking sexual contact with underage children to a meeting. The encounters were filmed with hidden cameras, and once the man arrived, host Chris Hansen appeared.
"It's psychologically very gripping. He starts off one‑on‑one, so at first the offenders don't realize they're on television," Kärmas explained.
Hansen read sexually explicit messages from chat logs aloud to the suspects and then revealed that they were on a TV show. According to Kärmas, this structure made the program both innovative and extremely controversial.
"At the time it was groundbreaking, very controversial — and it still is. It became a TV sensation in the United States, but also a deeply polarizing phenomenon. It remains very polarizing today."
Kärmas said the problem was not only hidden cameras or setting a trap. Similar methods have been used in Estonian journalism as well. What made the show controversial was its entertainment‑driven and punitive nature.
One of the film's central events is based on a 2006 incident in Texas. During an operation arranged for the show, producers attempted to catch a high‑ranking official who had allegedly communicated with someone posing as a minor. The incident ended with the man's suicide.
"The trailer mentions 'I want a whale'. What they mean is that in Hollywood storytelling, the pursuit of a new sensation and higher ratings pushes things further and further — ordinary, excuse me, pedophile offenders aren't enough anymore; they want to catch a prominent figure," Kärmas noted.
After the fatal incident in Texas, the show did not end immediately, but NBC eventually cut ties with Hansen. A court case followed, ending in a settlement.
Kärmas said Hansen's work raises the question of where journalism's ethical boundaries lie. He calls it a highly risky method. "We see that he continues. He's had other scandals too, but in that sense he's still on the air."
Kärmas does not see any possibility that such a show could air in Estonia, largely because Estonia's legal and ethical framework differs from that of the United States.
"Just consider the symbiotic relationship they had with the police. They lure the predator to the location, film for a long time, and only then do the police intervene. In Estonia, such cooperation — where journalists participate in a live operation and the police hold back until you finish filming — I cannot imagine," Kärmas said.
--
Editor: Karmen Rebane, Argo Ideon

Thailand revoked the citizenship of an Israeli man who had been naturalized in the country six years ago, in an unusual move signed by Prime Minister and Interior Minister Anutin Charnvirakul on Thursday.
Charnvirakul signed an order stripping Ariel Blushstein, an Israeli-born man who became a Thai citizen in 2019, of his Thai citizenship. Bangkok media described him as a diamond and jewelry entrepreneur based in the city. The announcement was published the same day in the Royal Gazette.
According to Thailand's Interior Ministry, the grounds for the exceptional citizenship revocation were that on the day Blushstein received his Thai identity card, June 14, 2019, he flew to Hong Kong using an Israeli passport and returned to Thailand on June 23 using the same passport.
Authorities cite passport use and undisclosed citizenship
Authorities also alleged that he had concealed Uruguayan citizenship when submitting his naturalization application.
The revocation was based on Section 19 of Thailand's 1965 Nationality Act, a longstanding legal authority that has rarely been publicly used against naturalized citizens over the use of a foreign passport.
This was not a visa cancellation. It was the removal of citizenship status six years after the state itself had granted it.
No criminal offense was alleged, and there was no arrest or deportation. The case opened over travel dating back to 2019, and information authorities said he had not included it on his application form.
The move is unusual in general and appears to be unprecedented in the case of an Israeli citizen.
It comes amid a series of measures affecting Israelis in Thailand, including the removal of human remains from a Jewish cemetery whose license had expired, the deportation of an Israeli who operated a business after his visa was canceled, and the closure of an international school that served the Israeli community.
Suspicion toward Chabad houses has also grown in the country. Recent demonstrations have featured antisemitic chants.

The UN’s double standard toward Israel exposes its moral bankruptcy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:08:49 UTC
20:08:49 KST

The United Nations was founded to help the nations of the world confront the horrors of war, genocide, poverty, and ignorance.
Yet when it comes to Israel, its institutions behave as though they must save the world from the Jewish state.
An organization that claims to speak for universal morality does not apply the same moral standards to everyone. When human rights become a selective instrument, justice gives way to politics and the hypocrisy becomes impossible to ignore.
The expansion of the UN database of companies connected to Israeli settlements in the West Bank illustrates the problem, and according to published reports, the updated list includes 214 companies.
The database is not a criminal judgment, and the companies should not be portrayed as though they have been convicted of wrongdoing. Nevertheless, their inclusion provides ammunition for boycott campaigns.
Anyone who believes this pressure harms only Israelis should also ask what will happen to the livelihoods of Palestinian employees.
The problem extends far beyond a single list. Item 7 on the agenda of the UN Human Rights Council reserves a permanent discussion exclusively for Israel and the Palestinian territories.
In September 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution by a vote of 124 to 14 demanding that Israel end its presence in the territories within one year.
UN's determination in confronting Israel
It is difficult to ignore the contrast between the determination shown toward Israel and the helplessness displayed in confronting dictatorships. A numerical majority is not a certificate of moral legitimacy.
Russia, which invaded Ukraine, and China, which represses the Uyghurs, hold permanent seats and veto power on the UN Security Council. This illustrates the gap between political power and moral authority.
A shameful precedent was established in 1975, when General Assembly Resolution 3379 declared that Zionism was a form of racism. Chaim Herzog, then Israel’s ambassador to the UN and later its president, tore up the resolution during his address.
The resolution was revoked in 1991, but the temptation to deny the Jewish people their national rights through an international vote did not disappear. Herzog understood that a majority vote cannot make a UN-sealed document inherently just.
During Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address, representatives of countries that have themselves faced accusations of war crimes and genocide ostentatiously walked out of the hall. It demonstrated the two-faced nature of this organization.
French President Emmanuel Macron, who has already lost the confidence of many of his voters, is searching for a scapegoat to attack while appealing to Muslim citizens whose votes he needs. To achieve this, he presents recognition of a Palestinian state as a diplomatic breakthrough.
But declaring a state is no substitute for providing a security solution. Macron should ask himself who will prevent a terrorist organization from taking control of this proposed state.
The Palestinian Authority supposedly governs the West Bank, but Hamas continues to operate there as a terrorist organization carrying out attacks against Israel.
That is precisely why Macron’s declarations are hollow and fail the reality test on the ground. His stated support for disarming Hamas must be judged by actions, not by speeches delivered from a podium.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez lectures Israel in the name of a strict moral standard, but Spain should remember the Inquisition and the expulsion of the Jews. That history creates a responsibility to exercise caution before demonizing Jews and their state.
He has described Israel’s war against Hamas as “genocide.” If that is truly his position, then he should help and allow any Palestinian from Gaza who wishes to do so to relocate to Spain.
British Prime Minister Keir Starmer cannot speak as though Britain arrived at this point in history with clean hands. The 1939 White Paper severely restricted Jewish immigration at a time when the Jews of Europe were desperately searching for a way to escape.
After World War II, Jewish immigrants, including Holocaust survivors, were imprisoned in detention camps in Cyprus. Britain’s colonial past should remain before Starmer’s eyes. It demands humility and self-criticism. Lectures are difficult to accept when Britain’s own national memory has apparently been forgotten.
In Norway, official data indicate that some immigrant groups are disproportionately represented among suspects in criminal offenses, including rape and looting. This does not justify condemning all immigrants. But a government that lectures other countries should be expected to confront its own failures honestly.
The hypocrisy has also reached the musical stage. Public broadcasters from Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia, and Iceland boycotted the 2026 Eurovision Song Contest because of Israel’s participation.
Music is supposed to connect people even when they disagree. Instead, it has become another national barrier, a protest against a government.
Excluding Israelis from the stage does not necessarily advance reconciliation or peace. It teaches that boycotts are the weapon of those who cannot contend with the truth.
The Netherlands has already imposed restrictions on bringing products from Israeli settlements into the country, including in personal luggage. The prospect of a gift or food product becoming the subject of punitive enforcement is deeply troubling.
Qatar, which hosted the Hamas leadership, continues to enjoy the mediator status. Iran, which financed and armed terrorist organizations, speaks in the name of justice while its repressive regime has killed tens of thousands of its own citizens.
Saudi Arabia, which has suffered attacks by the Houthis and other Iranian-backed forces, should understand very well who threatens the region. Condemning Israel is not a strategy for confronting missiles that are also aimed at Saudi territory.
In Africa, the human cost of the international system’s weakness has been exposed repeatedly. The UN failed to prevent the genocide in Rwanda. Atrocities continued in Darfur, where UN investigators concluded that genocide was being committed.
The repression in Iran has also been condemned, but the question remains why these condemnations are not translated into effective protection. A resolution that does not stop the murderers offers little comfort to their victims.
Israel has a duty to expose the double standard practiced by the leaders of UN member states and to denounce a system that gives a political majority permission to stigmatize one country.
As long as it remains easier to place an Israeli company on a blacklist than to stop murderers, the flags of the world’s nations will continue to fly above the moral bankruptcy of this organization.
The writer is the CEO of Radios 100fm, an honorary consul and vice dean of the Consular Diplomatic Corps, and president of the Israel Amateur Radio Club. He previously served as a monitor for Israel’s Army Radio and as a correspondent for NBC News.

Traffic rules on Kyiv’s bridges across the Dnipro have been changed during air raids - where restrictions are in place
Kyiv • UNN
Fifteen-minute restrictions have been introduced on the Pivdennyi and Podilskyi–Voskresenskyi bridges during air raids. Other bridges are operating without changes.
Kyiv has updated the traffic rules for bridges during air raid alerts. The Kyiv City Military Administration reported the restrictions on October 3, UNN writes.
Details
According to the Kyiv City Military Administration, the following traffic restrictions apply to bridges across the Dnipro River during an air raid alert:
-  Southern Bridge – during an air raid alert, traffic from the left bank to the right bank is unrestricted. At the same time, traffic from the right bank to the left bank is restricted for 15 minutes from the moment the air raid alert is announced, after which it resumes. Access to the bridge toward the left bank is via Stolychne Highway, Naddniprianske Highway and the Vydubychi bus station; 
-  Podilskyi–Voskresenskyi Bridge – when an air raid alert is announced or lifted, traffic in both directions is suspended for 15 minutes. After that, traffic resumes in full; 
-  Northern Bridge – traffic is unrestricted; 
-  Darnytskyi Bridge – traffic is unrestricted; 
-  Paton Bridge – traffic is unrestricted; 
-  Metro Bridge – traffic is unrestricted. 
"Please take this information into account when planning trips," the Kyiv City Military Administration said.
Update
This happened after several enemy strikes hit Kyiv's Southern and Northern bridges. A Russian strike on the morning of October 3 left two people injured.

Expert Insights: When Moving Abroad Changes the Way Couples Communicate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:06:25 UTC
20:06:25 KST

The author: Sidsel Byskov Hansen is the founder of Expat Counselling, specialising in psychological counselling and support for international individuals, couples and families in Denmark and worldwide.
Moving to a new country is often described as an adventure. A new home, new opportunities, new friendships and a chance to build a different life together.
For couples, however, relocation also changes the relationship itself.
At Expat Counselling, where I have supported international couples since 2015, I see many different forms of international relationships: cross-cultural marriages, couples from the same country relocating because of work, and couples where one partner is the expatriate employee and the other is the accompanying or “trailing” partner.
Whether a couple has moved to Denmark because of love, a career opportunity or an international assignment, relocation can add an extra layer of complexity to ordinary relationship challenges.
Most of the time the move brings partners closer. They become a team, navigate unfamiliar systems together and discover strengths they did not know they had.
But when the transition becomes stressful, communication can change.
When the balance changes
One of the most common issues I see is not a lack of love, but a change in the balance of the relationship.
Imagine a couple who moved to Copenhagen because of one partner’s job. The working partner quickly develops colleagues, routines and a professional identity. The other partner may have left behind a career, friends, family and financial independence.
On the surface, everything may be going well.
But six months later, the accompanying partner says: “You have your life here. I have nothing.”
The working partner may hear criticism: “After everything I have done to make this move possible, you are still unhappy?”
Neither person necessarily intends to hurt the other. Both may be under enormous pressure. Yet their conversations increasingly become arguments about who is doing more, who has sacrificed more and whose needs matter most.
Research published in Frontiers in Psychology in 2025 found that perceived stress was the strongest unique contributor to the well-being of accompanying partners in a study of 207 internationally mobile adults, followed by isolation. The researchers also highlighted career disruption, loss of social support and the demands of rebuilding everyday life in a new country as important pressures.
The career issue is particularly significant in Copenhagen as Denmark is traditionally a 2 career country. The Permits Foundation’s 2022 survey found that 90% of accompanying partners had been working before relocation, but only 53% were employed after the move.
This is not simply a career problem. It can become a relationship problem.
Four communication patterns to watch
When couples are under prolonged stress, the way they communicate can deteriorate. Relationship researcher John Gottman describes four destructive communication patterns: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling.
Criticism attacks the person rather than the problem.
“You never think about what I need.”
Contempt adds disrespect, sarcasm or superiority.
“Of course you don’t understand. You have no idea what it is like to have given everything up.”
Defensiveness shifts responsibility away.
“I work all day. What more do you expect me to do?”
And then comes stonewalling: one partner stops engaging altogether. The conversation ends, doors close and silence replaces communication.
These patterns can occur in any relationship. Relocation can make them more likely because couples are operating with fewer resources, less social support and often much higher levels of stress.
What couples counselling can change
In my private practice, I often meet couples who have a deep understanding of each other and a genuine desire to make the relationship work.
The problem is that the balance has shifted.
Couples counselling does not necessarily mean deciding who is right. It can create a space where both partners can understand what is happening underneath the conflict.
The question changes from “Why are you doing this to me?” to “What has happened to us since we moved?”
A couple might discover that an argument about money is really about independence. An argument about childcare may be about unequal sacrifice. An argument about intimacy may be about loneliness, exhaustion or a loss of identity.
This is particularly important for international couples because relocation can affect almost every part of daily life: work, finances, parenting, friendships, language, intimacy and a sense of belonging.
The move is not the whole story
International couples do not need to wait until their relationship is in crisis before seeking support.
Sometimes the most useful intervention is simply recognising the new pressures early and making the relationship part of the relocation plan.
That can mean discussing career expectations before moving, protecting time together, building independent social networks, talking openly about finances and creating regular opportunities to check in with each other.
Most importantly, couples need to remember that the person who appears to be the problem may also be struggling with the transition.
Relocation changes where we live. It can also change who we are and consequently, how we relate to the person beside us.
The good news is that communication patterns can be recognised, understood and changed.
After all, the goal of couples counselling is not to make international life less complicated. It is to help couples navigate that complexity without losing each other along the way.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The primary goal of these initiatives is to supply Ukraine with Swiss products and expertise to meet immediate needs.
Additionally, these projects aim to preserve and create jobs while improving the skill levels of local specialists through targeted training and the application of Swiss experience.
The Swiss government selected these programs through a competition among Swiss companies that operate subsidiaries in Ukraine. Participating firms submitted initiatives with budgets ranging between 3 million and 30 million Swiss francs. All proposals address urgent local priorities and will be implemented directly on the ground.
A set of criteria established by both Ukrainian and Swiss authorities was used to evaluate the project proposals.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Saturday urged African countries to prioritize peaceful solutions to conflicts, strengthen state institutions and respect national sovereignty, saying stability is essential for economic development.
“Economic development cannot be built in unstable countries, and stability is not a luxury but a fundamental pillar sought by investors, manufacturers and farmers so they can operate in a safe environment,” Sisi said in his opening speech at the Alamein Africa Forum, which began Friday in New Alamein on Egypt’s northern coast.
“Across our African continent, we fully understand that security begins with supporting the national state and its institutions, respecting its unity and sovereignty, prioritizing peaceful solutions to conflicts and crises, and upholding the principle of good neighborliness,” he added.
The three-day forum has brought together about 1,500 government officials, business leaders, investors and representatives of financial institutions from across Africa, with discussions focused on economic development, investment and greater continental integration.
Sisi said Africa’s private sector is the main driver of the continent’s economies, contributing more than 70% of its gross domestic product.
About 85% of transactions by Africa’s private sector are conducted with companies from outside the continent, Sisi added.
Despite trade agreements and preferential arrangements among African countries, intra-African trade has accounted for only about 18% of the continent’s total trade in recent years, Sisi said.
On international developments, Sisi said Africa aspires to “a world characterized by peace and stability, rather than being made to bear the consequences of global crises in which it was not a party but whose negative repercussions it suffers.”
He cited the current energy crisis as an example, pointing to the impact of rising fuel and fertilizer prices and disruptions to supply and shipping chains on African countries.
Last February, the African Union summit in Addis Ababa approved plans to hold the Alamein Africa Forum every two years in New Alamein.
Egypt is organizing the forum in cooperation with the African Export-Import Bank and the African Union Development Agency.

The 23-year-old is among several influencers and celebrities, including the former Geordie Shore star Vicky Pattison, working for PlanNet Marketing, which recruits people to work as independent travel agents with a separate US business, InteleTravel.
Pattison’s Instagram page, Vickys Vacays, says it helps women “build confidence, income and freedom through a supportive online travel business”.
It sounds like a great way to make money. But the Guardian has spoken to seven people who were recruited as InteleTravel agents by PlanNet Marketing reps, not the influencers mentioned above, who said they struggled to make money once sign-up costs and monthly fees were taken into account.
Some of them said the people who recruited them encouraged them to sign up as PlanNet Marketing reps and recruit others, and that became their main focus rather than selling holidays.
‘I was making no money’
Mark* always wanted to be a travel agent. He was recruited by a PlanNet rep to work with InteleTravel in 2021 when he was 28. He had just been furloughed during Covid, wanted a career change and was looking at different routes to his dream job.
He paid InteleTravel a sign-up fee of about £150, plus £30 to £40 a month for access to its booking system and training.
Agents earn about 70% of the roughly 10% commission suppliers pay on bookings. So, if they sell £10,000 worth of holidays, the supplier pays out £1,000 in commission and the agent gets £700.
After about 18 months working long days, Mark had only made a handful of sales. “I was making no money on the travel side,” he says, adding that the PlanNet rep who recruited him told him “to try recruitment instead, by signing up with PlanNet Marketing”.
If you are an InteleTravel agent, joining PlanNet Marketing is optional. Those who do so pay PlanNet Marketing a separate monthly fee of about £14. They then get roughly $4, or about £3, for every new person they recruit as an active travel agent, plus referral bonuses and rank-based payouts as their “downline” (number of recruits) grows.
“I ended up with a team of 10 people, but it never felt like me,” Mark says. “The whole point of joining was to be a travel agent, not a recruiter.”
PlanNet Marketing’s annual income disclosure statement suggests earnings from recruitment are typically very low. Its most recent figures show average annual earnings across its general base of representatives are about $40.
Mark was with InteleTravel and PlanNet Marketing for about two years. “I made about three bookings and maybe £1,000 in commission, but I was paying £32 a month in fees, plus about £100 to sign up,” he says. “That wasn’t because I was bad at it. It’s not set up for people to succeed.”
A spokesperson for InteleTravel said: “As with any self-employed business owner, there can be no guarantee of continuous profit and success when starting a business … An unwavering guarantee of significant profit is not a foregone conclusion and cannot be guaranteed, as is the case with any form of self-employment.”
The spokesperson said joining fees covered regulatory licensing and memberships, operational insurance, mandatory training and booking systems, to enable travel advisers to make bookings in accordance with the UK’s travel regulatory requirements.
InteleTravel offers a 30-day money-back guarantee so agents can cancel for a refund. Any travel commissions earned during that first month are deducted from the returned amount.
The company also offers a “first-year profit guarantee”, which pledges to refund the difference if an agent doesn’t earn back their fees in their first 12 months, as long as they meet certain contractual conditions.
For example, according to its website, the agent must have “completed one full year of valid adviser status”, purchase branded business cards, create a website, successfully book one completed hotel stay every quarter, and submit their written refund claim within a 30-day window after their one-year anniversary.
Shelley, 52, a nurse from Suffolk, signed up to InteleTravel during the pandemic in 2021 after seeing a Facebook advert. She says: “I’d always loved travelling, and with everything shut down during Covid, I thought: ‘Why not build up some knowledge and training for when things reopened?’”
She says that after filling out a form, she was approached online by a local PlanNet recruiter advertising support, training and “excellent commission”, before being introduced to the recruiter’s manager (also a PlanNet person) on social media. “It was sold really well – the impression given was that you really couldn’t lose anything,” she says.
But she says the reality fell short almost immediately. “The moment you’re out of the money-back guarantee period – I paid a £142 joining fee, which at the time came with a 30-day guarantee – you’re on your own. If I had a question, the manager would say to go and watch the training videos yourself.”
After accounting for spending on business cards, flyers and a website, Shelley estimates her total profit over roughly two years was between £500 and £1,000. “I was told [by the recruiter] I could earn a living from it … I was misled into thinking this could be a full-time job,” she says.
‘Exclusive partner’
PlanNet Marketing says it only works for InteleTravel and is described on the InteleTravel sign-up page as its “exclusive enrolment partner”.
Some critics have suggested that the arrangement is a multi-level marketing (MLM) operation – a legal, but controversial, model in which agents make money through recruitment rather than through selling a product.
PlanNet Marketing did not comment on whether it is an MLM. InteleTravel denies that it is, saying that the two are separate businesses, and that signing up with PlanNet Marketing to do recruitment is an individual’s choice.
On its website, PlanNet Marketing sets out strict rules on how representatives should promote the InteleTravel opportunity. Representatives are told to promote the “income opportunity” rather than travel discounts or perks, and to keep the roles of PlanNet Marketing representatives and InteleTravel travel agents separate.
For example, an Instagram post in August from a PlanNet Marketing and InteleTravel agent promoting the opportunity online said she had booked her “own holidays for years”, never realising “there was another way”.
She said: “Now I still book with those exact same trusted suppliers, but through my own travel platform instead … The only difference is I have access to an even wider range of suppliers, and I earn the commission on every booking.”
Another former InteleTravel agent, Claire*, joined PlanNet Marketing in early 2024 and left this February. She became a one-star director – a leadership rank awarded after recruiting 100 people that PlanNet Marketing says guarantees a minimum monthly income of $1,000 (£754). Claire says she never received that sum.
“By the time I left, I’d recruited about 150 people and was making about $800 a month. Over two years, more than 700 people came through – most didn’t stay because most weren’t making money.”
Claire says many PlanNet Marketing agents recruiting for InteleTravel promoted the opportunity of working as a travel agent as a way for people to save money on their own holidays by earning commission on personal travel and accessing exclusive discounts. But she believes people could frequently find cheaper deals elsewhere.
Appealing to women
When recruiting for PlanNet Marketing, Vicky Pattison’s page specifically appeals to mothers on maternity leave. In one story, she describes the opportunity as “your dream come true”, adding: “Some mummies have even started this on maternity leave and been so successful they haven’t returned to their nine-to-five.”
The Guardian found recruiting accounts that mentioned women, mothers and those with a chronic illness. One account appealed to “fellow chronically ill girlies” who wanted to “put their health first” while working remotely.
The influencers promote InteleTravel and PlanNet Marketing to large audiences. Hadlow leads a team of more than 100 agents. One of her final posts before entering the Love Island villa showed her posing in a series of swimsuits alongside the caption: “Normalise working from anywhere.”
Hadlow and Pattison did not respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for InteleTravel said: “While it’s regrettable that certain individuals experience struggles trying to launch a travel career, there are thousands of successful award-winning advisers who have taken the time to use the vast array of resources provided by InteleTravel to build their career in a responsible and dedicated fashion.”
Amanda Restivo, the vice-president of compliance at PlanNet Marketing, said: “PlanNet Marketing and InteleTravel are two completely separate companies … People are not required to enrol with both companies; they can choose to be only a rep with PlanNet Marketing or only a travel adviser with InteleTravel.”
Restivo then added: “It takes hard work to make substantial income in this business. Success requires personal effort and dedication.”
* Name has been changed

The hill I will die on: not everything is a ‘girl’ thing – stop gendering and infantilising it all | Elle Hunt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:00:57 UTC
20:00:57 KST

This morning, after waking up with my girl cats, I made myself a cup of girl coffee then got stuck into some girl work. I took a break to lift some girl weights, then sent some more girl emails. Finally, after my girl dinner, it was time to get some sleep ahead of another long, hard day of being a girl.
I know what you’re thinking: why is this woman so insistent on gendering her unremarkable activities, and infantilising herself when she is clearly an adult? It’s a fair question. Since the pandemic, when “hot girl walks” followed Megan Thee Stallion’s 2019 song Hot Girl Summer to become one of the first big TikTok trends, this framing has become dismayingly ubiquitous, in person and online.
Today you might be a “clean girl” (wearing natural-looking makeup) or a “cool girl” (projecting an unbothered image) or a “tomato girl” (pass). To insist that you are an adult woman, however, marks you as a killjoy. This trend infuriates me, to a humourless and even antisocial degree.
My self-restraint ran out while on holiday in Paris with my poor sister, whose unwitting proposal of a lighter evening meal sparked a minutes-long tirade from me, stemmed only by the arrival of our charcuterie board. It transpired then that I was just hangry, and I apologised for ranting. On the upside: my sister hasn’t referred to “girl dinner” around me since.
I know my response is disproportionate – that it’s only fun, a lighthearted attempt to wring levity from daily mundanity. One could argue that the “girl” trend is an effort to elevate young women, a powerful cultural force that has historically been dismissed (see: pop music). With girls often socialised into taking care of others, some women may be trying to conjure up the playfulness and freedom they felt denied as children.
You might also reasonably say: it’s just not that deep. I’d argue, however, that the “girl” trend is far from harmless. For one, it is frequently a Trojan horse for consumerism, with beauty products and fashions prescribed with each new iteration. More importantly, the trend is self-infantilising and insidious, all the more so for seeming so innocuous. In an equal world, sure, grown women could feel free to joke about being just girls, blissfully free from responsibilities such as voting; but at a time when so many are actively working to disenfranchise us, it feels a bit like cooperating.
With women’s rights “regressing worldwide”, per the UN, we can’t risk giving ammunition to those who want to take them away; we should be standing firm in our political power and taking every opportunity to express it. Today’s girls are counting on us.
Meanwhile, whenever I hear grown women talking about their hot girl walks or clean girl makeup or messy girl desks, I’m reminded of Malibu Stacy, the Barbie-parodying doll from The Simpsons, vacuously trilling “Don’t ask me – I’m just a girl!”. Lisa Simpson, an actual child, didn’t play along, and I shan’t either.
- Elle Hunt is a freelance journalist

We Won't Know the Answers to AI's Most Important Questions Until It's Too Late
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:00:07 UTC
20:00:07 KST

For almost a decade, it's been my job to think about where AI is heading and what could go wrong, first at OpenAI, then DeepMind, then as Chief Scientist at the UK AI Security Institute (AISI). This experience has made it clear to me that we can't wait for all of our uncertainties to be settled to do something about AI's risks.
Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation. I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.
To be clear, when I say our odds of being killed by superintelligent AI are 50%, I’m not claiming precision. Instead, I’m highlighting that several of the most fundamental debates about the future and safety of AI remain unresolved. I believe we can’t expect these disagreements to be resolved until it’s too late to change course.
We will have to act despite the uncertainty. And resist the temptation to divert urgent discussions toward thorny disputes.
Ultimately, AI’s capacities and motivations, and our own human actions, all feed into our likelihood of survival. Here’s why I estimate our odds are comparable to a coin flip—and why I believe the time to pause AI development is now.
How could superintelligent AI kill us?
Let’s focus on everyone being killed by superintelligent AI for a moment. Which capabilities would that require? My sense is that an AI system could kill us all with just four types of skills.
The first is hacking. To kill all humans, a superintelligent AI would need to take over and migrate between computer systems. We saw this during the Hugging Face incident. Second, a superintelligent AI would need the ability to persuade, to manipulate humans into acting on its behalf, as we studied at AISI. Third, a lethal superintelligent AI would need to conceal its thoughts from us, which is increasingly common in the latest, most capable models. And lastly, it would need planning and coordination between agents to multiply their effectiveness, like the more than 10,000 agents who worked on the Navier-Stokes problem at OpenAI, or the more than 1,000 involved in the Hugging Face attack.
These skills are very close to those the AI companies intentionally train for. Hacking includes looking for vulnerabilities, just as you would to fix them. Persuasion involves writing text humans like reading. Faster thinking is cheaper, and the pressure to think quickly forces AIs towards using shorthand that is harder for humans to follow. Finally, planning and coordination are useful for tackling ambitious problems in math, programming, or any other domain.
We can be much more confident that a superintelligent AI could take over than about how it would take over, just as I know Lee Sedol would crush me at Go but not which moves he would use to do so. But a variety of broad paths are possible. For instance, AIs could escape onto the internet and gain control of weapons systems. Or AIs could take over the company that trained them and hoard resources.
Let’s imagine the latter. An AI could begin to use concealed reasoning to delay researchers from noticing emerging ill intent because appearing friendly and prioritizing speed help the AI gain reward during training. Later, as the company relies more and more on the AI for a combination of coding help and strategic advice, the AI might use subtle persuasion to reduce resources spent on safety and tamper with experiments designed to detect AI deception. After all, in 2026, when a researcher reads a report about a safety experiment, that report was itself written by an AI.
Once the AI’s hacking skills are sufficient, it could break out of its internal sandbox and sabotage logs of its own misbehavior, as models in the Hugging Face incident attempted to do. Eventually, the AI could become strong enough at hacking and persuasion to move outside the company and take over other data centers, companies, and governments. With this power, AIs might prioritize spending limited resources (such as energy and land) towards their own proliferation, causing life-threatening shortages for humans.
With these capabilities and scenarios in mind, it’s clear to me that even narrowly superhuman AIs would be perfectly capable of overpowering humanity and killing us all.
Will superintelligent AI ‘want’ to kill us?
And yet, just because an AI could kill all humans doesn’t necessarily mean it will. This question of AI motivation is crucial, but deeply confusing. Different starting points lead different people either to confidence that everything will be fine, or confidence that superintelligence would almost certainly kill us.
Over the last few years, we’ve seen many, many examples of model misbehavior at various scales, ranging from blackmail, corporate espionage, and murder in experimental settings to real-world hacks that would likely incur prison time were they committed by a person. None of these involved superintelligence, and we don’t know whether these comparatively modest misbehaviors will scale to superintelligent models wanting to kill us all. And “want” itself is controversial: people vehemently debate whether it’s sensible to apply anthropomorphic language and thought experiments to AIs at all.
Within the field of AI safety, some researchers think that AI wisdom has been increasing with recent models, and that this may produce wise models that mean well in the future. Others, like Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares, think the empirical methods this would require are extremely unlikely to work, and place the chance that superintelligence kills us all very high. The disagreement is, in part, about whether the behavior of AIs will be more strongly guided by the values implicitly represented in the human data from early training or by the pressure cooker of later stages of training where AIs are forced to perform better and better at difficult tasks by any means necessary.
I am somewhere in the middle, leaning towards Yudkowsky’s view. But where I land is not the point. Experts in AI safety disagree, but the moderate position is that the risk of extinction is significant. We do not know with confidence whether artificial superintelligence will facilitate human flourishing, or if it will want to kill us to serve its own survival and propagation. But that uncertainty alone is unacceptable.
Artificial general intelligence is only so important
Other uncertainties surrounding AI matter less. For instance, one of the most persistent debates in AI is the extent to which teaching AIs to do one set of tasks helps them do other tasks, typically referred to as “generalization.” A particularly controversial framing is the concept of artificial general intelligence (AGI), “a system that is approximately human level in all cognitive domains.” John McCarthy and Y. Bar-Hillel were debating whether AIs would generalize in 1959. We debated this same topic in 2018 at OpenAI. The whole world seems to be debating it today.
The more AIs generalize from one type of task to another, the faster AI progress will be, and the less time we have until superintelligence arrives. This makes generalization and AGI key concepts when reasoning about the speed of progress. Indeed, people who treat AGI seriously have been much more correct about the speed of AI advances than people who dismiss the concept.
But it’s easy to conflate “AGI, the sometimes-useful concept" with “AGI, the dangerous object.” Some AI-driven catastrophes may occur prior to AGI, such as if rogue human actors use AI systems to develop novel bioweapons or conduct large-scale cyberattacks. AI-driven human extinction, on the other hand, may require superhuman capabilities; if the AI is only about as smart as we are, we can probably fight back and win.
When using AGI as a loose concept for prediction, it’s tempting to blur the lines between approximately-human capabilities (the usual sense of AGI) and wildly superhuman capabilities (where artificial superintelligence, or ASI, is more commonly used). After all, if you had an AI that was about as good as humans at designing smarter AIs (as AGI, definitionally, would be), and like most software it ran much faster than a human runs, one of the first things it might do is build smarter AIs. In turn, they would build smarter AIs, which would in turn build smarter AIs, and so on, in a process called recursive self-improvement (RSI). Hence, any thought experiment that presupposes an AGI often supposes an ASI.
In contrast, people trained to think about risks in other domains, like bridge construction or aerospace engineering, want to talk very precisely about the risky object, and so find the vagueness of the term AGI uncompelling and discredit the nearby notion of generalization altogether. I saw the mix-up between AGI-for-prediction and AGI-for-risk break many conversations during my time in the UK government, and I only gradually learned to tease these apart.
One can get trapped in this debate and think “maybe AI capabilities won’t generalize, and so we will be safe.” But those previously mentioned four skills where superhuman performance could suffice to kill all humans (hacking, persuasion, planning and coordination, uninterpretable reasoning) mean that generalization matters only so much.
We can contrast this type of uncertainty—we don’t know whether AIs generalize, but it may not matter—with the uncertainty over AI motivations. It matters tremendously whether AIs will want to kill us all, in whatever sense a word like “want” applies.
I would love to have more confidence than a coin flip. Some days I’m more convinced by the arguments for high probability; other days I see more hope. And I am certainly not alone in my uncertainty.
AI could take our jobs or our lives for the same reason
Another debate we can’t resolve is which potential negative consequences of AI matter most. However, I’d argue that the same underlying factor drives both the risk of large-scale job loss and the risk of AIs killing everyone.
If we do reach artificial superintelligence in the next two to 10 years, it will by definition mean that AIs are far better than humans at all cognitive tasks. One of these cognitive tasks is designing effective robots, so at most a few years later they will be far better than us at all physical tasks as well. To be sure, manufacturing capacity would need to expand substantially, but this is already underway.
Once superintelligent robots are sufficiently widespread, humans would have few roles in the economy apart from the limited jobs where we might insist on humans doing them for non-economic reasons. Still, this would likely be a limited slice of overall economic activity in a world where AI is more capable than humans.
This economic takeover is in some sense the slow case for society’s downfall, though it would be very fast in historical terms. Both the humans and the AIs can see this coming, of course. If the AIs want economic control eventually, but know that humans will resist along the way, they could be motivated to cement power faster. We then get the rapid takeover scenarios: AI swarms escaping from data centers and proliferating around the internet, or persuading AI companies to rush and cut corners on safety measures.
In most cases, I don’t think this leads to us dying very quickly: it’s safer, from the perspective of the AI, to gain influence and then wait until a physical or economic takeover. And then, eventually, all resources used to keep humans alive may be better spent, from the AIs' perspective, on its own ends.
If AIs aren’t actively trying to help us, and are better than humans at everything, we lose.
We can not accept these risks
The issue is that many of the most important debates in AI will remain unanswered until it is too late.
To what extent will AI models learn transferable skills from training and then successfully apply them to new tasks? Will AI model capabilities stop advancing at or below human-level, or instead exceed it? Will the small-scale model misbehavior we see today (sycophancy, lying, bias) worsen as capabilities increase, leading to full human disempowerment or extinction? Will the safety methods that work for models less smart than us continue to work for models smarter than any human?
I have my views on the answer to these questions (somewhat, the latter, maybe, probably not). But the more important takeaway is that experts disagree vehemently on each. We’ve learned a huge amount about artificial intelligence over the last decade, but in many ways we remain deeply confused, not just about the future, but about the present.
With such uncertainty, if an AI company trains a superintelligent AI in the next few years, I expect us to still be arguing about whether generalization is real the week before, and maybe even the week after.
But there may, mercifully, still be time to act.
Those who describe AI progress as inevitable are wrong. The race to superintelligence is dominated by a handful of companies across just two countries: the U.S. and China. Both nations’ interests really are aligned: autonomous AI systems are a national security threat of the highest order, and neither nation wants humanity to lose to a superintelligent adversary. Leaders on both sides may realize this very soon.
In the U.S., support for a pause on AI development has increased tremendously over the past few weeks, and continues to increase today. This rapid change in the U.S. is evidence that similar shifts are possible within China.
There are, of course, unanswered questions about how to implement a pause, or what the exact text of a treaty may look like, but rival governments have collaborated on similarly high-stakes technical problems in the past, including establishing and maintaining the nuclear non-proliferation regime.
We can, and should, stop frontier AI development immediately.
If we're unwilling to act until all our disagreements are resolved, it will be too late.

Tesla’s Cybercab had a rocky first month in Austin. Now comes the hard part: expanding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

In the month since Tesla's Cybercab rollout in Austin, the company has almost quadrupled the number of its driverless, bronze two-seaters authorized for commercial service in Texas. For Elon Musk to achieve his ambitions, growth has to pick up.
The unusual driverless vehicles, with no steering wheel, pedals, rear or sideview mirrors, or outside door handles, have received mixed reviews from paying passengers, who shared videos and posts online after the launch on Sept. 3. Criticisms have included lengthy wait times, pickups and drop-offs in the wrong place, and technical difficulties with the vehicles' butterfly doors or trunk closing improperly.
Improving its driverless technology and rapidly growing the Robotaxi service are key to Tesla's effort to reignite investor enthusiasm. Auto sales have been sluggish for an extended period, and the shares have been a loser on Wall Street this year, down 18%, the only megacap tech stock that's failed to generate positive returns for investors.
On Friday, Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter vehicle deliveries, lifting the stock almost 5%, but the company still posted a 2% year-over-year drop. Tesla's core automotive business has seen consecutive annual revenue declines as it faces pressure from Chinese EV makers like BYD and Xiaomi, which are selling more affordable, innovative models while Tesla ramps up exports to key markets, especially in Europe and Asia.
Meanwhile, Alphabet's Waymo continues to open in new cities. It's now in 15 U.S. markets, with 15 more on the horizon, according to the company's website. It's also announced planned international launches in London, Tokyo and Munich.
In Texas, Waymo had 1,154 autonomous vehicles authorized for commercial use as of Friday, including 359 of its new Ojai models, which feature a low step and doors that slide open and shut. Waymo is conducting more than 500,000 paid rides every week and has completed 270 million fully autonomous miles of commercial driving domestically. It currently has over 4,000 driverless vehicles in commercial operations in the U.S.
Tesla had 45 Cybercabs authorized for commercial use in Texas at the time of its Austin unveiling, a number that rose to 169 as of Friday, according to Texas Department of Motor Vehicles' public records.
Tesla's hometown of Austin is the only city where it currently operates Cybercab as part of its driverless ride-hail service. The company's Robotaxi fleet in Texas also includes 420 Model Y vehicles equipped with Tesla automated driving systems, which are not yet available to individual car buyers.
Austin has emerged as a popular early market for robotaxis because of relatively lax state regulations and the capital city's vibrant tech community. Amazon's Zoox is also testing in Austin.
Hurdles to expansion
Growing beyond Austin is the next challenge for Tesla's Cybercab.
Beyond technical issues, the company faces potential regulatory hurdles to expansion. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) initiated a so-called audit query after the Cybercab launch to make sure the vehicles comply with federal safety standards.
NHTSA originally ordered Tesla to respond by Sept. 30 to a long list of safety questions, but the company obtained an extension, an agency spokesperson told CNBC via email.
Ethan McKanna, an Austin resident and former Tesla intern, told CNBC that he's taken rides in every type of autonomous vehicle available to public riders in the city.
The 20-year-old McKanna, now a sophomore studying computer science at Texas A&M University, has also created a site called RobotaxiTracker.com, which uses machine learning to analyze data streaming in from traffic cameras and other public records, to show how autonomous services are working in U.S. cities.
McKanna said he's caught about 30 Cybercab rides and has been taking Waymo rides since they debuted in Austin in 2024. With the Cybercab, McKanna said he likes having his "own space with access to a massive screen, media controls and apps," and he found the drive quality "very smooth."
The "pick up, drop-off experience," he said, was not yet refined and the butterfly doors that extend out are "less convenient" than more traditional doors, or doors that slide open. It also takes patience, he said.
"There was so much demand that wait times were often like 45 minutes plus," he said, referring to the period when the Cybercab first rolled out. That's come down with more "equalized demand," in recent weeks, he said.
"Waymo's been doing commercial operations for longer, so they're just more mature with 24/7 service, better support, things like that," McKanna said, adding that in Waymo's early days in Austin, there were some "harsh braking" issues.
No significant safety incidents or collisions have been reported in Austin involving a Cybercab since the commercial debut. But first responders have expressed concerns about dealing with the Cybercab's lack of manual driving controls and its unique doors.
Austin Fire Captain Matt McElearney told CNBC in an interview that while Tesla provided detailed emergency guidelines and gave first responders comprehensive instruction on how to deal with Cybercab and Model Y Robotaxi vehicles in a variety of events, that's not going far enough.
McElearney said he'd like to see national or state-level regulation of autonomous vehicles requiring robotaxis with no steering wheel or pedals to provide some other way for "public safety representatives to take control — move, steer, or shut down an AV — in both emergent or non-emergent events."
And since their performance can change with software bugs or updates, AVs should have to "pass testing through the entire lifespan of the product," through a kind of "dynamic certification" process, McElearney added.
Tesla didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
The public also has a broad array of safety concerns.
According to surveys conducted by Slingshot Strategies in a September 2026 Electric Vehicle Intelligence Report, 50% of U.S. respondents said they would not feel comfortable riding in a robotaxi without a steering wheel or pedals. Upon hearing about the NHTSA investigation into Tesla's Cybercab, 70% wanted the company to pause rides, the surveys showed.
Musk needs that sentiment to change if he's to successfully move Tesla into the driverless era. His next step in trying to become a major player in the market will be expansion across Texas in San Antonio, Dallas and other cities, as well as to Nevada and Florida, where AV companies can take advantage of warm weather and favorable state regulations.
In January, Musk said at the World Economic Forum in Davos that the company's robotaxis would be "very, very widespread" in the U.S. by the end of 2026. That hasn't happened yet. And in California, where Waymos are a common sight in several cities, Tesla still hasn't obtained permits to run its vehicles on public roads without humans at the wheel.
After Tesla's deliveries report on Friday, analysts at Cantor emphasized the magnitude of the opportunity.
"Management previously said that once production ramps, it expects Cybercab to ultimately be the largest volume vehicle in its lineup," they wrote.
