Collision course: Are Israel and Turkey headed for confrontation?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:17:20 UTC
19:17:20 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this week ordered the Justice Ministry’s International Law Department to prepare a legal case against Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan at the International Criminal Court. The case, according to several Israeli media reports, will focus on Turkey’s treatment of its Kurdish minority, and its ongoing support for and domiciling of Hamas.
The case is unlikely to have major consequences. Neither Israel nor Turkey has ratified the Rome Statute, meaning that neither recognizes the authority of the ICC. Israel’s move appears to come in response to a Turkish effort to secure an Interpol red notice intended to lead to the arrest of Netanyahu.
Still, the Israeli initiative is notable for several reasons. It is the first time that Jerusalem has sought to make use of Turkey’s treatment of its Kurdish minority as a counter-pressure tool against Ankara. Israeli ministers have made statements relating to this issue in the past, but nothing practical has resulted.
Instead, the latest move represents a picking up of the gauntlet by Israel in the field of lawfare. It is the first sign that Jerusalem aspires to do something more than play defense in this area. The Israeli initiative was enthusiastically hailed by several politically engaged, Turkish-born Kurds who spoke with this writer.
The initial maneuvers form part of a more general picture in which Israel and Turkey find themselves increasingly on a collision course across a broad spectrum of issues of strategic interest across the region. In addition to the lawfare field, the areas in question are: Syria, the eastern Mediterranean, Jerusalem and the West Bank, and the Red Sea/Horn of Africa.
In all these friction points, Israel and Turkey have clashing interests and ambitions. The emergent dynamic is zero-sum. Turkey’s extensive regional ambitions can only come at Israel’s expense, given the religious and ideological underpinnings of Turkey’s stance.
Erdogan and his party are making use of the powers available to them
This has been a long time coming. Prescient Middle East analysts such as my colleague, the late Barry Rubin, flagged the coming Israel-Turkey confrontation as far back as 2004, shortly after Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party (AKP) came to power.
Rubin did what Western observers of the Middle East don’t do often enough: listen carefully to statements by Erdogan, Ahmet Davutoglu, and other AKP leaders; read their writings; and extrapolate their likely behavior.
At the time, the bon ton was to see the AKP and Erdogan as likely to be moderated by the experience of government, or bound to be constrained by Turkey’s “objective” strategic interests. Subsequent events have shown that neither constraint applies.
Rather, Erdogan and his party are making use of the powers available to them to advance a regional strategy that comfortably combines a neo-Ottoman nationalism with an outlook deriving from Sunni political Islam.
Regarding the specific areas of tension: Syria is without doubt the most volatile and combustible. Turkey was a key element behind the victory of the Sunni Islamist regime now in power in Damascus.
Ankara is energetically engaged in building up the armed forces of the new regime. Israel is deeply suspicious of the long-term intentions of the emergent new power. Specifically, Israel is concerned at the possibility that Turkish assistance in rebuilding Syrian air defenses could impact Israel’s need to maintain freedom of operation over Syria’s skies, in order to act against Iran.
The Israeli air raid on Syria’s Abu Duhur Air Force Base on August 18 demonstrated Jerusalem’s determination to enforce its red lines in this regard. Turkish Foreign Minister and former intelligence chief Hakan Fidan, while in Damascus earlier this month, described Israel as the “greatest potential threat to Syria’s stability” and announced that Erdogan would visit Damascus “in the near future.”
Syrian sovereignty remains partial. Both Israel and Turkey are in de facto occupation of parts of the country, with diametrically opposed ambitions for its future.
The agreement ignores the maritime jurisdiction and continental shelf rights of Greek islands
Elsewhere, the eastern Mediterranean is similarly an arena for directly opposed Israeli and Turkish ambitions. Turkey, in a 2019 maritime boundary agreement with Libya, declared an exclusive economic zone extending from southwest Turkey to northeast Libya.
The agreement ignores the maritime jurisdiction and continental shelf rights of Greek islands, including Crete and Rhodes. In so doing, it also cuts directly across Israel’s and Greece’s own intentions regarding exploitation of gas resources in this area, and their plans to lay a power cable linking the electricity grids of Israel, Cyprus, and Greece.
In a statement issued on September 24, the Turkish defense ministry explicitly stated that it was “closely monitoring military developments on the island of Cyprus,” and that cable-laying on “our continental shelf must be coordinated with our country in advance… unauthorized activities… are not permitted.”
Regarding the West Bank and Jerusalem: Israel is also cognizant of Turkey’s continued maintenance of an active Hamas office in Istanbul. This office has a track record of direct operational activity, including violent attacks, in the West Bank. The activities of the Turkish Cooperation and Coordination Agency (TIKA) in the West Bank and Jerusalem are also of concern.
Israeli intelligence notes that TIKA funds and supports religious and social institutions closely affiliated with Hamas and Muslim Brotherhood networks in the West Bank. Alongside Turkish efforts to play a role in Gaza and Lebanon, Jerusalem sees all such efforts as part of a Turkish attempt to build influence and leverage in areas that have direct impact on Israel.
In the strategically vital maritime corridor of the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa, Israeli-Turkish competition is reflected in alignments with rival local forces. Israel recognized Somaliland as an independent country in December 2025 – the first UN member state to do so.
Jerusalem plans to build a military base on Somaliland’s territory to observe and counter Houthi activity on the other side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Turkey, meanwhile, strongly opposes Somaliland’s independence and maintains a major training base in Mogadishu, Somalia’s capital.
Ankara has also signed agreements for oil and gas exploration off Somali waters, creating an additional potential point of tension.
A review of all the relevant information, alongside the stated goals and ambitions of the Turkish government, indicates that the Israeli-Turkish contest across the region is one of the most important geopolitical realities of the emerging Middle East.
The net result of the dramatic events of the last three years appears to be the weakening (though not the destruction) of the Iran-led regional alliance, and the growing sense among all regional players that anything resembling a Pax-Americana in the region is largely defunct.
In the changed power environment deriving from these developments, powerful local players are seeking to extend influence. Turkey is weaponizing the forces of Sunni political Islam in a manner that, in some ways, is reminiscent of Iranian practices. Opposition to Israel is an inherent and integral element of this strategy. Further and increased friction seems inevitable. Watch this space.

Crime scene: The Black Sea. How the war is poisoning the water, killing wildlife and changing landscapes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:15:00 EEST
19:15:00 KST

Crime scene: The Black Sea. How the war is poisoning the water, killing wildlife and changing landscapes
On 19 July 2026, Odesa-based environmentalist and hydrobiologist Vladyslav Balinskyi was relaxing on the beach. It was a Sunday, warm and dry – too nice a day to stay at home. It was around 17:00 when he heard a powerful explosion. Smoke began billowing from a vessel about eight kilometres away – a distance he would later check on a map.
Then came another explosion. The final strike occurred after rescue workers had already begun approaching the damaged vessel.
That day, the Russians launched three Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles at the Golden Leo, a bulk carrier sailing under the flag of Guinea-Bissau, that had departed the port of Chornomorsk loaded with maize. Eight crew members were taken to hospital and ten people were killed, including a Ukrainian pilot.
A week later, the Golden Leo capsized and sank in Odesa Bay at a depth of around 22-24 metres. The maize remained in its hold.
Ukraine's Economy Ministry and scientists warned of serious environmental risks from the sinking of the bulk carrier. A potential fuel leak could cause surface pollution, while the fermentation and decomposition of the grain could affect seabed ecosystems.
Having witnessed the attack, Balinskyi became even more convinced of two things. Firstly, he believes the Russian military's objective is not simply to stop civilian vessels but to kill as many people as possible – which, he argues, is the purpose of the tactic of double and triple strikes. Secondly, paradoxical as it may seem, he says Ukrainian strikes on Russia's shadow fleet tankers cause less environmental damage than Russia's destruction of civilian bulk carriers.
"I compared it with Operation MoLoChKa. Most of the vessels struck during that operation were disabled but did not sink. They lost propulsion, and there were no follow-up strikes that could have caused a major oil spill. In other words, the apparent aim was to put the vessels out of action without sinking them: they could no longer move under their own power but remained afloat. There were some exceptions – for example, one vessel caught fire and burned for about two weeks. But in most cases, the vessels simply lost propulsion without sinking or spilling their cargo," Balinskyi argues.
MoLoChKa, the operation Balinskyi is referring to, is an operation by Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces which, as of mid-September, had resulted in Ukrainian forces "hunting down" 285 vessels belonging to Russia's shadow fleet in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.
The Russia-Ukraine war has long since extended beyond the mainland. The fighting is affecting not only the course of the war itself, but also the environment for years – perhaps even decades – to come.
Balinskyi, a researcher at Tuzly Lagoons National Nature Park and head of the Odesa branch of the National Ecological Centre of Ukraine, is one of those tracking and documenting this environmental impact.
Russia has opened a criminal case against him and placed him on an international wanted list over what it calls "fake news" about the Russian military and damage to Soviet memorials in Odesa. Balinskyi himself is convinced, however, that the main reason is his professional activities. Among other things, he works with the Environmental Evidence Platform, which helps document environmental damage caused by Russian aggression, and is involved in investigating the destruction of the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant.
Ukrainska Pravda spoke to Balinskyi about how the war is changing the Black Sea, why some of its consequences may remain invisible for a long time, what is happening to the ecosystem following the destruction of the Kakhovka dam, and whether we will only understand the true scale of the environmental damage caused by the war years from now.
When vegetable oil is just as dangerous as petroleum products
Before the Golden Leo, there was the Golden Lion. That was the name of a bulk carrier sailing under the flag of Antigua and Barbuda that was attacked by Russia in autumn 2024. It was around that time that Russia shifted from sporadic strikes on vessels in the ports of Greater Odesa to systematic attacks on participants in the maritime corridor and on port infrastructure. In some cases, the environmental consequences were extremely serious. [Greater Odesa is a logistical and industrial hub in Odesa Oblast that combines three major ports – Odesa, Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi – ed.]
In December 2025, for instance, the Russians struck tanks containing vegetable oil, causing it to spill into the sea. Scientists recorded a slick covering 60 sq km and stretching for 25 km. "Oily patches were observed along the coast from Lanzheron Beach to Station 16 at Velykyi Fontan," the Ukrainian Scientific Centre of Ecology of the Sea reported.
"Imagine this: one morning, I suddenly start getting call after call from people saying something is happening to the sea. It's December, it's freezing cold, and they're telling me the entire sea is covered in some kind of yellow substance. The whole surface is yellow, and so is the entire coastline. Then they start sending me photos – and what I see is horrific. There are birds floundering in it.
People were taking off their clothes in that freezing weather to go into the water and rescue the birds. And it was all done entirely by volunteers," Balinskyi recalls.
Vegetable oil forms a film on the surface of the water that disrupts gas exchange and oxygen levels. Over time, it can sink to the seabed and form a dense layer that remains there for years.
Balinskyi has counted at least four incidents over the past two years that caused large-scale pollution of the sea. The most recent occurred in April 2026, when tonnes of sunflower oil entered the water following a Russian strike on the port of Chornomorsk.
In terms of some measures of environmental impact, the expert stresses, vegetable oil is even worse than fuel oil.
Spills of fuel oil and other petroleum products are another consequence of the war that is devastating for the sea. And Ukrainian attacks on Russian facilities are not the only issue.
Russia transports petroleum products in small tankers across the Sea of Azov before transferring them near Kerch or Taman to larger vessels capable of travelling onwards through the Black Sea. The very operation of this logistics hub creates a risk of pollution in the surrounding waters.
Balinskyi monitors the number and size of oil slicks using satellite data and says the situation has deteriorated significantly since the start of the full-scale invasion.
In December 2024, for example, two Russian tankers, Volgoneft-212 and Volgoneft-239, were caught in a storm and broke in half in the Kerch Strait. Several thousand tonnes of fuel oil spilled into the water. This year, as the sea warmed, Balinskyi observed significant releases of fuel oil from the wreckage of the tankers.
"You look at the satellite images and it seems as though the ships have only just sunk, because the plumes spreading from them are so large. There is a fairly stable cyclonic current in the area that carries the pollution directly towards us. Following the coastline, it's about 600 km from the site of the accident to Tuzly Lagoons National Nature Park. Yet within a month, we were already finding clumps of fuel oil in the park. And we're still finding them today," he says.
The war's biggest environmental disaster
When Balinskyi saw what had happened to the sea after Russian forces destroyed the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant in June 2023, he was stunned. He still considers that disaster the most painful environmental consequence of the war.
"You'd walk down to the sea and hear frogs croaking. Entire islands of reeds were floating in the water, some with roe deer stranded on them. You'd walk along the shore and come across a Danube crested newt – a species listed in Ukraine's Red Book – lying there. Everything that had lived and grown along the Dnipro had been swept all the way here. This was freshwater wildlife that couldn't survive once it reached the sea.
And there was an appalling amount of debris: refrigerators, pieces of roofs, trees, pillows. I didn't even know breeze blocks could float until I saw them washed up here. Later, the sea carried much of that rubbish away again. But it didn't actually disappear. A lot of it simply sank and is now lying on the seabed," Balinskyi recollects.
Read also: Everything you need to know about the Kakhovka HPP disaster
The enormous quantity of pollutants that entered the Dnipro-Buh Estuary and adjacent bays continues to affect the local ecosystem. Balinskyi is convinced that restoring it to its previous state is now impossible.
Shortly after the disaster, in July 2023, Ukraine's Cabinet of Ministers approved an experimental project to construct the Kakhovka hydroelectric complex and rebuild the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant. Clearly, under current wartime conditions, the project cannot progress beyond the design stage. Balinskyi nevertheless criticises the idea of restoring the reservoir in the future, regarding it as a continuation of what he sees as the Soviet Union's damaging approach to nature.
In the three years since the disaster, the vast river floodplains known as the Velykyi Luh, which were submerged in the 1950s during the construction of the Kakhovka Reservoir, have begun to recover. Today, forests and meadows are spreading across the area. In some places, there are as many as ten trees per square metre.
This is one of the few pieces of good news to emerge from the disaster: not all of the dire predictions have come true. Three years ago, environmentalists feared erosion and dust storms, but nature's drive to regenerate has proved stronger.
The visible and invisible scars of war
Almost 100,000 bottlenose dolphins, common dolphins and harbour porpoises have died in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov since 2022, according to estimates by Tuzly Lagoons National Nature Park. Dolphin carcasses occasionally wash up on the shore. In June 2026 alone, scientists found 56 dead animals in the area around the national park.
The problem is not limited to the enormous volume of chemical pollutants entering the water as a result of the fighting. Balinskyi points out that dolphins use echolocation to navigate and hunt. Military sonar and regular explosions interfere with their ability to find food and avoid danger.
Chemical and acoustic pollution are not the only traces the war has left in the sea. Some of its consequences can literally be picked up. The day before his interview with Ukrainska Pravda, Balinskyi saw a video of a boy swimming in the sea using a piece of foam from a Russian Gerbera drone as a makeshift boat.
During his own dives, Balinskyi sees enormous quantities of drone debris, mainly carbon-fibre wings and tail sections. These remnants are not the greatest danger, however. Mines and other munitions also end up in the sea, which are occasionally washed up on the shore by currents and storms.
This means that once the fighting ends, the seabed will have to be cleared of mines and unexploded ordnance before any broader clean-up can begin. Balinskyi says these consequences of the war will continue to affect both the marine environment and human life for decades.
***
Which of Russia's major environmental crimes is the least documented and receives the least attention?
Balinskyi answers without a moment's hesitation: what is happening to the land along the line of contact – the way the war is changing soils and landscapes.
He has previously seen what happens to an area after phosphorus munitions are used.
"You have to understand: all the humus, all the fertile material in the upper layer of soil, is burned away. It's not simply a mineral component. It's a living ecosystem containing hundreds of thousands of different bacteria, soil-forming organisms, fungi, insects, crustaceans and worms.
After the impact of shells and extreme temperatures, after the blast wave has simply lifted all of this up and thrown it into the air, the structure and density of the soil change. Fine particulate dust is created, and its structure is completely different from that of soil. And beyond that, the landscape itself changes," he explains.
What does this mean? Even after the fighting ends and the battlefield has been cleared of mines, nature will be unable to recover there on its own.
Without human intervention, Balinskyi believes, these areas are unlikely to turn into either wild vegetation or steppe. Their only future will be desertification.
Rustem Khalilov, Ukrainska Pravda

Ukraine’s Partners Speed Up F16 Maintenance to Keep Fighter Jets Flying

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

To counter these persistent air threats, Ukrainian defense operations relied on a combination of tactical aviation—including F-16 fighter jets—ground-based air defense systems, interceptor missiles for Patriot units, and mobile MANPADS, while emphasizing the urgent need for long-term partner support and scalable domestic production.

China opens anti-dumping probe into EU days before Beijing trade talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:09:07 UTC
19:09:07 KST

Running a €1 billion-a-day deficit with China, Brussels has nearly tripled the rate of its own trade investigations and is warning of "harsher measures" unless Beijing offers something concrete.
China has opened an anti-dumping investigation into a chemical imported from the European Union, less than a week before the bloc's trade commissioner arrives in Beijing for talks meant to stop a dispute from escalating.
The commerce ministry in China said on Saturday it would examine whether low-priced p-nitrotoluene from the EU was flooding the Chinese market. A spokesperson said domestic producers had asked for the probe, complaining of "damage to production and operations".
The chemical is used to make dyes, pharmaceuticals and pesticides and the investigation is due to conclude within 12 months, with a possible six-month extension.
It follows an investigation by the EU, opened in September, into polyvinyl chloride imports from countries including China. Beijing denies that its manufacturers owe their competitiveness to state support and has threatened countermeasures against EU moves to block its firms.
"China has repeatedly reiterated that the EU needs to face its own economic and trade problems directly and resolve mutual concerns through dialogue and consultation," the spokesperson said.
What is dumping?
Dumping is when a company exports a product for less than it charges at home, or for less than it costs to make. World Trade Organization rules allow the importing country to respond with extra tariffs, known as anti-dumping duties, if an investigation finds that the cheap imports have injured its own producers.
Brussels is reaching for the tool far more often. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in August that the EU had opened 30 trade defence investigations in a year, nearly triple the usual rate, as Chinese imports rose 45% in five years.
Sefčovič heads to Beijing
EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Sefčovič will be in Beijing on 8–9 October to co-chair a session of the EU-China Trade and Investment Council and meet Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. The visit marks the deadline Brussels set in June for the first tangible results from its dialogue with Beijing.
Brussels wants assurances that China will curb exports to the EU and extend a truce on rare earth exports, with the bloc's trade deficit running at €1 billion a day. Beijing has already warned it would respond firmly to any new EU restrictions on Chinese companies or products.
In an exclusive interview with Euronews last month, Sefčovič described the talks as highly political and said negotiations had to produce concrete results. Without them, he warned, there would be "a strong political movement to push for, I would say, harsher measures".
He also told Euronews that if he had nothing to show EU leaders, "the political interest would be to look for the solution through other instruments". Those leaders meet in Brussels on 15–16 October, a week after his trip.

Women declare #IamJaneDoe in solidarity with Cornell University rape accuser

Women declare #IamJaneDoe in solidarity with Cornell University rape accuser
- Women are showing support for the Cornell rape accuser by using #IamJaneDoe on social media, sharing their own experiences to reduce stigma.
- The accuser sued seven fraternity members and Cornell, prompting renewed criminal investigation and official criticism of initial police handling.
- Online attempts to reveal her identity have caused distress, leading supporters to defend her privacy and emphasise survivor solidarity and resources.
AI generated
Women, some citing their own experiences of sexual assault, are posting on social media that they are Jane Doe, in solidarity with the woman using the pseudonym in accusing fraternity members of raping her at Cornell University in 2024.
In a case that has drawn national attention, the woman is suing seven fraternity members and the Ivy League school in Ithaca, New York, among others.
And although New York law allows “Jane Doe” anonymity for sexual assault lawsuits, the Cornell student has become distressed at attempts by some online sceptics of her account to discover her name and publish it, her lawyer said.
“I want us to support Jane Doe in coming to her own way of identifying herself in her own time,” said Twanna LaTrice Hill, a writer and actor in Denver who has declared #IamJaneDoe on social media in recent days.
“And if she never does, that’s fine. But the flip side of that is that the people like me need to speak up if we are able to.”
Backlash
The woman, who was 20 at the time of the alleged 2024 gang rape, filed suit on Sept 16, prompting prosecutors to reopen a criminal investigation they had initially closed without charges.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state’s attorney general as special prosecutor in the case and on Oct 2 faulted police and prosecutors, saying they had not fully investigated the woman’s allegations.
The accused men have denied all wrongdoing, the New York Times reported. Cornell has defended its handling of the matter.
Since the woman filed her lawsuit, some commentators have sought to learn and publish the accuser’s identity online, efforts that her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, called an attempt to shame her.
“She’s not doing well,” Giuffra told CNN. “She's under siege on social media.”
He said some women have been incorrectly identified as his client.
“That’s been really difficult,” he said. “And she’s gone through a lot.”
Much of the online support for her has criticised independent journalist and commentator Michael Tracey, who has expressed sympathy for the accused men over what he says is the harassment they have since faced.
Tracey has also questioned the accounts of victims of the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Tracey, who did not respond to a Reuters request for an interview, describes his effort to identify the Cornell student as journalistic diligence protected by constitutional free speech protections.
“Let’s see if anyone has the ‘b***s’ to name this Jane Doe so we can all evaluate her veracity, and that of her lawyers, since her lawsuit didn’t hesitate to name and shame seven of her peers as gang-rapists,” Tracey posted on social media on Sept 29, one of multiple messages on the case.
Early on Oct 2, he posted what he believed to be the accuser’s name, which Reuters was unable to verify, before quickly deleting it, saying his point had been made.
“But please do not harass her, her family, or anyone else associated with her,” he wrote after deleting the name. “I’m serious. I wish her no harm. I feel bad for her in a way.”
Outrage
A post by Amee Vanderpool, who publishes an online newsletter on Substack, was typical of a number of messages and videos shared by those outraged at Tracey’s efforts.
“To anyone who is looking to find out the identity of Jane Doe in the Cornell rape case, look no further, because it’s Amee Vanderpool,” she wrote. “I am Jane Doe.”
Hill, 62, the writer in Denver, posted on Facebook this week about speaking publicly in 1990 about being raped when she was a teen by a youth minister who had counseled her.
“I was in absolutely no way trying to get other survivors to come forward or to go public if they did not feel ready,” she wrote. “But I had hoped that as more of us coming forward, the stigma would be reduced. Perhaps it has in some small way, but not nearly enough.
“So I stand before you today simply to say: #IamJaneDoe.”
Katy Jacobson, a 35-year-old San Diegan who works with children with disabilities, said the hashtag can help survivors of sexual assault feel less alone.
“Because oftentimes you feel like you’re on an island," said Jacobson, who added she felt fortunate to find support on campus when she was raped during college by a former boyfriend.
Some 21% of women in the US report being survivors of completed or attempted rape, according to the most recent figures from the US CDC’s National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence Survey.
At Cornell, 35% of undergraduate women reported experiencing non-consensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation since arriving on campus, according to a university survey conducted in 2025 and published on its website. That was up from 20% in 2021.
Jacobson’s posts direct people to organisations such as RAINN, which operates the National Sexual Assault Hotline.
“Even today, if you looked at my story, it has resources,” Jacobson said. “I’m not posting about the men. I’m posting about Jane Doe.” REUTERS

Congress resets Team Uttar Pradesh: 5 clear messages for BJP and Akhilesh Yadav
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:07:25 UTC
19:07:25 KST

Congress replaced Ajay Rai with Aradhana Misra Mona as Uttar Pradesh Congress chief.
NEW DELHI: Congress has overhauled its Uttar Pradesh organisation ahead of the 2027 assembly election, replacing Ajay Rai with three-time Rampur Khas MLA Aradhana Misra Mona as state unit president and appointing Saharanpur MP Imran Masood as working president. The party has also named Chaudhary Virendra Singh as Congress legislature party leader.The reshuffle brings together a prominent Brahmin leader from eastern UP, a Muslim leader with influence in western UP, and Dalit and OBC representation in senior organisational positions. Rajendra Pal Gautam, a Dalit leader, is already the party's Uttar Pradesh in-charge. With these recent appointments, Congress may be trying to widen its social and regional reach after years of electoral decline in the state.Taken together, the appointments suggest that Congress is trying to do two things at once: strengthen its bargaining position with the Samajwadi Party while rebuilding an independent political identity in Uttar Pradesh.The timing is important. The 2024 Lok Sabha election revived Congress's presence in UP through its alliance with Akhilesh Yadav. But Akhilesh’s party remains the much larger organisation in the state. In the 2024 polls, SP moved 32 seats up and won 37 seats, registering a 15.73% gain in vote share.
On the other hand, Congress also slightly improved its Lok Sabha tally with 6 seats and a jump of a little over 3% vote share.Congress is now trying to turn that electoral revival into a more substantial organisational base before the 2027 assembly election in a state which has been long associated with Congress's political success story.Here are the five messages embedded in the reset.
1. A bigger, but amicable, say at seat-sharing table
The appointment of Aradhana Misra Mona as UPCC president, along with the elevation of Imran Masood, suggests that Congress wants to push for a larger share of assembly seats while keeping its relationship with the Samajwadi Party workable.
What Mona Misra said after her appointment as UP Congress chief
Masood has been unusually vocal about Congress' seat demand. On September 3, he argued that if Congress' electoral performance continued to improve, its share of seats should also increase."Hum koi bhikhari hain jo Samajwadi Party se bheekh mangenge? ... Party formula tay karegi, lekin jo formula Lok Sabha election mein tha, woh formula nahi hoga. (Are we beggars who will beg from Samajwadi Party? ... The party will decide the formula, but it will not be the same formula used in the Lok Sabha elections)," he had told ANI.Congress' UP in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam has also spoken of seeking an equal number of seats with the SP, while Masood has backed a 50:50 formula.The rhetoric sharpened on September 28, when Masood directly declared: "If Akhilesh Yadav is unhappy (with seat-sharing discussion), the loss will be his own... We fail to understand what the anger is even about."Mona's elevation, on the other hand, sends a somewhat different signal. Unlike the more combative rhetoric around seat-sharing, her appointment gives Congress a state president who is seen as having a more workable equation with the SP leadership. Her political experience and close association with the Congress leadership also give her a role in managing the alliance even as the party pushes for greater space.The numbers give Congress some basis for making that argument. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, the SP won 37 of UP's 80 seats while Congress won six, taking the INDIA bloc's combined tally to 43. The SP's 37-seat tally was a dramatic rise from five seats in 2019.However, going by the numbers, Congress cannot negotiate from the position of higher power and will most likely have to settle for the junior partner role.But how "small" the partner role it gets will be crucial.
2. Rebuilding old social reach, but with a new mix
One of the clearest messages in the new team is social and regional balancing.Mona is a prominent Brahmin face from eastern Uttar Pradesh. Masood brings a prominent Muslim face from western UP. Devinder Nishad gives the organisation an OBC, riverine-community face, while Alok Prasad brings Dalit representation into the senior state team. Rajendra Pal Gautam is already the party's Dalit in-charge for Uttar Pradesh.The choice of Mona is particularly significant because she replaces Ajay Rai, a Bhumihar leader, with another upper-caste leader from a different community. The switch from Rai to Mona could be read as an attempt to reconnect with Brahmin voters who were traditionally associated with Congress but have, over time, moved substantially towards the BJP.
What Ajay Rai said after being replaced as UP Congress chief
This rejig comes at a time when the upper-caste groups (Rajputs, Brahmins, Tyagis) reportedly feel increasingly sidelined by BJP's aggressive outreach toward non-Yadav OBC and Dalit vote banks. Tensions stem from ticket distribution cuts, perceived administrative favour toward Rajputs over Brahmins, and farmers' issues.Mona's appointment, however, is not simply a return to Congress's old social formula. The new team combines upper-caste, Muslim, Dalit and OBC representation, while also distributing the leadership geographically between eastern and western UP.The BJP has built a broad social coalition of its own in Uttar Pradesh. Congress' organisational response now appears to be an attempt to create multiple social entry points into the party rather than rely on a single caste or community bloc.
3. Not conceding Muslim vote
Masood's elevation carries another particularly important message for western Uttar Pradesh.The Saharanpur MP is one of Congress' most prominent Muslim leaders in the state, and his appointment puts a western UP Muslim face in the second-most important position in the state organisation. His appointment seems to be a direct attempt to attract and consolidate Muslim support.That matters because the SP has traditionally been the principal opposition party competing for the Muslim vote in UP. The 2024 Lok Sabha election demonstrated the strength of that relationship.
What Imran Masood said after UP Congress organizational reshuffle
A post-election CSDS-Lokniti analysis estimated that 77% of Muslim respondents in Uttar Pradesh voted for the SP and 15% for Congress, while 2% reported voting for the BJP. These are, of course, survey estimates and not absolute vote counts. However, it may reflect the trend.The actual election results also showed the importance of Muslim-heavy constituencies to the opposition's performance. Congress won Saharanpur and Sitapur, while the SP and its allies captured several other such seats.Masood's promotion therefore gives Congress a prominent vehicle to seek Muslim support directly rather than relying entirely on the SP to bring that constituency into the alliance.
4. Congress wants credibility
Mona's appointment is significant because she brings an electoral record to the top of the state unit.She first entered the Uttar Pradesh assembly through a bypoll in 2014 and subsequently retained Rampur Khas in the 2017 and 2022 elections. She has therefore won the seat three times. Before entering the assembly, she served as block pramukh of Sangramgarh from 2002 to 2014 and held positions in the organisation and cooperative sector.Her 2022 victory was particularly notable because Congress was reduced to just two assembly seats across Uttar Pradesh. She defeated BJP's Nagesh Pratap Singh by 14,741 votes, polling 84,334 votes, or 50.27%, according to Election Commission data.That gives Congress a state president who is not merely an organisational appointee but an incumbent with a repeated assembly-winning record.
5. Women power at heart
The appointment of Aradhana Misra Mona also gives Congress a prominent woman at the helm of its Uttar Pradesh organisation, at a time when BJP too is putting renewed emphasis on its women leaders in the state.The timing is notable. The BJP has recently brought back Smriti Irani into a more prominent organisational role, signalling that women leaders continue to have an important place in its political strategy. Irani, who beat Rahul Gandhi and represented Amethi in the Lok Sabha from 2019 to 2024, remains one of the BJP's most recognisable women faces in Uttar Pradesh.The Mona-Priyanka Gandhi combination will give Congress a big women power picture it can easily put on its posters.
The wider electoral numbers also underline why women matter. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, the Election Commission recorded female voter turnout in Uttar Pradesh at 57.22%, compared with 56.46% among men. Women therefore turned out at a slightly higher rate than men in the state.As a bonus, Mona's elevation also gives Congress a combination of representation and political substance: a woman leader, a Brahmin face, a three-time assembly winner and someone with an established organisational network.The new UP team combines experience with caste, community, regional and gender representation, giving Congress multiple entry points in the voter base. The real test now will be whether the reshuffle can translate into stronger grassroots organisation and enough bargaining power ahead of the 2027 assembly election.

Swiss space firm Beyond Gravity target of cyberattack
Beyond Gravity, the Swiss state-owned aerospace supplier, has fallen victim to a targeted cyberattack.
According to the company, a highly professional actor is believed to be behind the attack.
+ In space exploration, Switzerland punches above its weight
Beyond Gravity announced on Friday that it had received the first indications of malicious activity in its IT environment on August 12. The investigation is being carried out in collaboration with the Federal Office for Cyber Security and the IT security firm Mandiant.
As of Friday, it was not known who was behind the attack. The company has filed a criminal complaint and stepped up its security measures, the statement added.
Experts were specifically searching for the attackers’ activities and carrying out forensic analyses of the affected devices, a company spokesperson told the AWP news agency.
+ Swiss parliament prohibits sale of Swiss space company Beyond Gravity
The company did not issue a statement until several weeks after first indications of an attack emerged. In the case of cyberattacks, thoroughness takes precedence over speed, said the spokesperson. Issuing a statement prematurely would have jeopardised the forensic investigations.
Beyond Gravity is owned by the Swiss state. The company was spun off from the defence group Ruag in 2022.

Iran Intel. Min. dismantles 4 sabotage networks, 31 arrested
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:05:20 KST

In a statement on Saturday, the Iranian Ministry of Intelligence announced that members of four organized networks, comprising 31 mercenaries of the American-Zionist enemy in Sirjan County were identified and arrested following public reports and intelligence monitoring by the intelligence forces of the ministry at the General Department of Intelligence of Kerman province.

Best Mosquito Repellents for Your Yard: What Works and What Doesn’t (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:03:00 UTC
19:03:00 KST

Mosquitoes suck. Literally, figuratively, and every other way. These bloodsuckers have been a worldwide menace since the beginning of recorded history. A popularly reposted infographic lists them as—by far—the world’s deadliest animal, thanks to the parade of nasty diseases they can transmit. West Nile, Zika, chikungunya, malaria, dengue—these are no longer illnesses confined to the global south. In recent years, all have been discovered in bugs in the United States.
Ridding your property of mosquitoes is a decidedly Quixotic effort. You can stem the tide for a while, but you can’t ever win the war. Once whatever abatement method you use has worn off, they swoop back in, thirstier than ever. Nevertheless, you have to do something. Left unattended, mosquitoes can quickly turn from a nuisance to an epidemic that makes your outdoor space completely unusable.
Outside of wide-scale community mosquito spraying programs, most personal and home-based mosquito abatement tools focus on repelling them rather than trying to outright kill them. Insecticides like DEET work by being rubbed onto the skin, while metofluthrin and allethrin work in vapor form, creating a cloud of repellent that works without you having to make physical contact with the chemicals. Trapping mosquitoes is another potential option, luring them into a chamber from which they can’t escape.
For years I’ve tried innumerable technologies and tactics to rid my property—and my very susceptible skin—from mosquitoes. Here’s what I’ve uncovered to date that works—and what doesn’t.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Featured Products
Best Personal Repellent Gear
This pint-sized repeller weighs a little more than a pound and recharges via a USB-C cable. Power it up and a heating element inside warms a vial of metofluthrin, releasing mosquito-repulsing vapor in your immediate vicinity, about 10 feet in every direction. It’s simple and extremely portable, making it easy to move from one area to another.
The system works. It warms up in just a few minutes and effectively keeps bugs at bay, provided you keep the repeller close by. Best of all, I was able to take it with me as I moved around the yard—but be warned, there’s some lag time for the vapor cloud to reform each time you relocate. A small chemical replacement cartridge lasts for about 36 hours; refills are $39 for a 2-pack.
Note that Thermacell markets myriad versions of this product, including a unit with a built-in light, one with a docking station for easier charging, one with longer battery life, and one that is ruggedized and can be worn around the neck on a lanyard. Any of the above will get the job done (and done well) in functionally the same way.
This butane-powered device offers a twist on the E-ZoneGuard line, containing no battery at all, which may be preferred in some exceptionally off-the-grid environments. Instead, a butane cartridge twists into the system. When activated (no flame needed), it heats up a replaceable chemical mat that slides into a groove on top of the device, this one using allethrin instead of metofluthrin. One downside: The vapor shield promised by the Fuel-Zoneguard stretches only about 7½ feet in each direction, more restrictive than the E-Zoneguard, and a butane canister will only get you about 12 hours of operation. Allethrin may also be less effective than metofluthrin against pests. That said, I experienced great results with this product and found the freedom from cables to be liberating. Refills run $19 for 24 hours of extra fuel and insecticide mats (sold together).
The Fuel-Zoneguard is also sold as part of a lantern or in a handheld form, designed for use on the go. (As with E-Zoneguard products, the underlying technology is identical.)
Best Large-Scale Repellent Gear
Take Thermacell’s E-Zoneguard system and make it yard-sized, and you’ve got LIV, a semi-permanent solution that uses the same repellent chemical (metofluthrin) but dramatically expands its coverage potential.
The system is built around a hub that plugs into wall power and connects to your home’s Wi-Fi. Up to 10 freestanding repellers connect to this hub via cables. You string them in a chain to surround your deck, your pool, or whatever else you want to protect from mosquitoes. Arranged in a rough circle, the resultant cloud of repellent serves as a large-scale barrier that can protect the whole family from being attacked. It’s all controlled via a mobile app (with Alexa support allegedly in the works), so you can fire the system up before you even head outside.
It’s one of the most effective systems I’ve tested, in large part because it pumps out so much repellent at precise locations. While nothing is perfect, LIV is about as close as it gets, protecting my entire swimming pool and deck at the touch of a button on its mobile app.
The only catch is that LIV is far from inexpensive, and Thermacell no longer sells it as a DIY solution; you’ll need a professional installer to complete the job. If saving your skin (and potentially your health) from mosquitoes is important to you, it could be worth it.
Tiki BiteFighter—from the company that makes the iconic torches—is an ingenious twist on the wider-scale repellent concept that takes advantage of wiring you may already have. The system works with string lights: Just remove a bulb from your lights and screw the Plug & Repel into the socket. When the lights are on, the device heats up a vial of metofluthrin that attaches to the bottom of the repellent unit, protecting the immediate vicinity from mosquitoes. (In theory, you can also use it with any overhead light socket.)
Naturally, the device comes with some caveats. The biggest is that it requires a (standard size) E26 socket to connect to; many string lights, including mine, use much smaller E12 candelabra bulbs, so compatibility can be a problem. Second, the range of BiteFighter’s vapor is considerably smaller than Thermacell’s: Tiki recommends plugging in a repeller every 12 feet. That can require a significant investment in hardware, mar your lighting aesthetic, and require lots of maintenance. (The system ships with a 12-hour metofluthrin pod; 48-hour replacement pods cost $10 each.)
Still, if you have the right environment, with compatible string lights surrounding or criss-crossing your outdoor space, the solution is much more affordable than a hard-wired system like LIV. If you only plan to use the system occasionally, the math is even more compelling.
Just OK: Mosquito Traps
These devices may look like old-school bug zappers, but they’re actually traps, designed to lure bugs in with a purple light, then sequester them in a chamber thanks to the tiny fan that sucks them in. Mosqitter's and Dynatrap’s devices work almost exactly the same way, boasting coverage that spans up to an acre, depending on the model you choose.
I tried both of these products—in Mosqitter’s case for months, letting it run all summer long—and found that while they were both effective at capturing insects, neither one attracted many mosquitoes. In both cases, I returned after a few weeks to find the trap chamber filled almost exclusively with moths. I don’t really love moths, either, but I don’t feel like I need to go out of my way to kill them.
I spoke to Mosqitter about my results and they suggested adding a packet of mosquito attractant to the device ($25, lasts a month), but this didn’t have any result on my mosquito catch rate. Again, mostly moths at the end of the testing period.
So, why am I saying these might be worth a try? As Mosqitter pointed out to me, there are countless species of mosquitoes—3200 globally, 174 in the US—and they don’t all behave the same. The ones around Austin may be resistant to the attractant and blasé about purple light, instead preferring to dine exclusively on human flesh. (This certainly tracks.) So while my results were lackluster, I’m willing to concede that users in other parts of the world, where the bugs are less hearty, may have better luck with it. If you don’t get good results, you can always return the gear for a refund.
If You Do Get Stung
Less effective
I’ve tried plenty of products that promise to kill or repel mosquitoes. These have not been effective—or, at least, not worth the money and effort involved.
This oddity arrives as a plastic bucket that you fill partway with water, mimicking a mosquito breeding site. A chemical-laced band hovers over this water, slowly contaminating it with a poison that kills adult mosquitoes and their eggs. The band must be replaced monthly. I tested this system for two months but found that the water evaporated much too quickly and, more importantly, the whole thing became an attractant for mammalian wildlife like racoons and opossums, which periodically tossed it around, maybe in the hopes of getting at the water. It’s a cheap option at $35, but not something I was keen to leave on my patio long-term.
The lowest of low-tech anti-mosquito solutions, Mosquito Dunks are small discs that you can drop into any amount of standing water, either natural (water feature like a fountain) or man-made (a bucket you intentionally fill with water as a trap). These contain a bacteria that’s toxic to mosquitoes but won’t hurt other wildlife, slowly releasing into the water as they dissolve over the course of a month. The only problem: They smell awful, and of course you need a reliable source of standing water for them to work at all. That’s fine if you have a handy pond that you don’t want to drain. Much less exciting in the average backyard.
$100/treatment and up
If you live in mosquito country, chances are your neighborhood is teeming with companies that promise to repel the bugs by spraying chemicals into the trees and foliage around your property, warding them off. I paid for a service to spray my property for years, and found that a very familiar routine developed: Immediately after each spray, my yard would be almost devoid of bugs, and my family would have two or three days of bite-free bliss. After that, the spray would wear off and the bugs would return, leaving us another 18 days or so until the next triweekly treatment. (Any amount of rain would also wash away all of the treatment chemicals even quicker.) Given the cost of over $2,000 per year, I’ve never been happier with a decision to cancel a service.
Mosquitoes just aren’t attracted to shiny lights the way other insects are. You’ll hear plenty of satisfying pops if you hang a bug zapper near your pool, but you won’t likely find many of the dead to be mosquitoes. Skip ’em.

‘I have to dodge them all the time’: Rome locals incensed by rise in golf cart tours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:00:56 UTC
19:00:56 KST

On the edge of Piazza Navona, one of the grandest squares in central Rome, Barry and Linda, visitors from Texas in the US, stepped out of a golf cart. They planned to cross the square on foot, perhaps stopping to admire Lorenzo Bernini’s 17th-century Fountain of the Four Rivers, before being picked up by their driver at the opposite end.
The couple had already done a walking tour on day one of their trip, and had been so exasperated by a stifling three-hour shuffle along a corridor towards the Sistine Chapel on day two that by the third day they wanted to give their tired feet a rest.
“When I first heard you could do golf cart tours in Rome, I thought to myself: that sounds a little weird,” said Barry. “But then we decided to try it out.” He said the most enjoyable thing about the experience was “feeling the breeze”.
Rome is a difficult city to navigate, noted Linda, especially its ancient narrow streets in the centre. “There are no sidewalks,” she said. “Our feet were hurting and we needed a break.”
For visitors, golf cart tours offer respite from the heat, crowds and cobbles. For residents, however, their proliferation in recent years has become another source of frustration in a city already wrestling with traffic and overtourism.
Taxi drivers are especially incensed, accusing golf cart operators of stealing their business, while one local newspaper said the city had been “taken hostage” by the vehicles.
Now Rome authorities are cracking down on the burgeoning trade. Police intensified checks this week after the news agency Adnkronos reported that 90% of the roughly 500 golf carts circulating in the city were operating without authorisation.
In recent days, police stopped 131 carts around Piazza Navona, the Pantheon, Circo Massimo and the Spanish Steps, issuing €38,000 of fines for offences ranging from unlicensed driving to illegal parking.
Rome’s leaders are pushing for regionwide measures to properly regulate an activity that “risks spiralling out of control”, Eugenio Patanè, a councillor for mobility, told the news agency Adnkronos.
Prices vary based on the type of tour and duration, but the cost per person can start at €100 and exceed €400 for a half-day trip. Barry and Linda paid €310 for their three-hour ride. “But it’s worth it,” said Barry.
Rome’s traffic problem is hardly new. Julius Caesar tried to tackle the issue more than 2,000 years ago by banning private vehicles and commercial carts from the city’s streets during the day. Today, pedestrians, cars, scooters, delivery vans and the occasional rogue horse-drawn carriage all jostle for space.
Tourists can also take tours in Fiat 500s, on Vespas with sidecars, and even in tuk-tuks. But the golf carts seem to have drawn a special kind of wrath.
“There are too many of them,” said Nora Fahmi, who works at Trevimage, an art photography shop behind the Pantheon. “We’ve had this shop for 13 years and have seen all sorts of things, but the golf cart situation is kind of wild.”
Nearby, two teenagers from Israel were taking a rest on a parked cart. “We just want a lift to the Colosseum but you have to book online,” said their mother, Miri. “Rome is too crowded and it’s difficult to walk.”
Elisa Isacco, who lives in the Monti area, spares no sympathy for the weary tourists. “What do they actually see or learn about Rome when they are on one of these things?” she said. “I find myself having to dodge them all the time – Rome is chaotic, it’s like a jungle.”
Amid the clampdown, several golf cart tour operators have banned staff from speaking to the press. But Leo Pavoncello, a driver for an operator in the Jewish Ghetto area, was happy to publicly defend the trade.
“Golf carts are silent and eco-friendly,” he said. “Rome is not an easy city to visit but these vehicles allow people with disabilities and families with children to see the sites in a comfortable way. On top of that, they provide jobs for young people.”
Pavoncello, who was subjected to the police checks and was found to be operating fully legitimately, argued that a few rotten apples were giving the business a bad name.
“I don’t understand why they are targeting us,” he said, although he suspects “taxi lobbies” are piling on the pressure. “But Rome is a touristic city that has always been full of traffic, and the golf carts are simply another mode of transport.”

====================================================================================================

Outgoing prison chief in Christa Pike case oversaw five ‘botched’ executions, lawyers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:00:56 UTC
19:00:56 KST

Tennessee’s prison chief is resigning after the failed execution of Christa Pike, which lawyers say was the fifth “botched” execution under his leadership across two states since 2022.
Frank Strada, the commissioner of the Tennessee department of correction, has faced mounting questions about the state’s highly secretive death penalty protocols since Wednesday evening when Pike became the first death row prisoner in the US to to be injected with lethal drugs and survive.
Witnesses said Pike, 50, was heard choking and struggling an hour after receiving the first injection of pentobarbital, a sedative, and after a second dose failed to kill her she was hospitalized in critical condition.
The scrutiny on Strada comes as Pike’s failed execution has sparked international outrage, with lawyers and advocates calling for a national halt on executions in the US. Pike’s lawyers have called the process “cruel and torturous”, and one death penalty expert said it was the worst botched execution in modern history.
Bill Lee, Tennessee’s Republican governor, on Saturday announced that Strada would step down from his role this month, the Associated Press reported. Lee also suspended executions in the state until the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry.
Strada said in a statement that stepping aside would “be in the best interests” of the state as the independent review was carried out to determine why Pike’s execution failed on Wednesday.
Lee called the case “deeply disturbing”, but when a reporter asked him about Strada’s leadership on Friday, Lee responded: “So far as we know, the department of correction followed exactly the protocol that was outlined.”
The journalist was pressing the governor on Strada’s history, which includes another failed execution in May of this year, when Tennessee officials struggled for more than an hour to locate Tony Carruthers’ vein, prompting the procedure to be called off. And when Strada was a deputy prison director in Arizona in 2022, the state carried out three executions that experts and attorneys said were prolonged and “botched”.
Death penalty lawyers said there were common threads in the five problematic executions under Strada, including the prisoners’ protracted suffering and questionable injection procedures, and argued that Lee should never have appointed Strada given his Arizona record.
Tennessee department of correction spokespeople declined to answer questions about Strada’s record on Friday and said the commissioner was unavailable for an interview. A spokesperson for Lee did not respond to inquiries.
‘Botched’ executions in Arizona
After joining Arizona’s corrections department in 2020, Strada oversaw executions, which included forming the teams that carried out the procedures, monitoring the practices and obtaining lethal injection drugs, he said in a deposition.
In the May 2022 execution of Clarence Dixon in Arizona, a media witness said the execution team struggled to place IVs to administer the lethal drugs, ultimately requiring them to make an incision by his groin to insert the IV. That process, according to his attorneys, took roughly 40 minutes.
In June 2022, a witness said Frank Atwood, a death row prisoner, had to help executioners find a vein after officials repeatedly struggled to kill the 66-year-old, who had a degenerative spinal condition.
And in November 2022, Arizona officials struggled to find a vein in Murray Hooper, forcing them to insert a catheter into his groin.
The Death Penalty Information Center, a non-profit organization that studies capital punishment, classified all three Arizona executions as “botched”, based on researchers’ analysis. “Botched” is not a legal term, but the group says executions can be botched when there is a breakdown in protocol or unexpected problems or delays that cause needless suffering.
Dale Baich, who represented Arizona death row prisoners during Strada’s tenure, said the fact that execution officials’ struggled to find veins suggested they were not qualified: “If your job is to access veins, you should be able to do that ... to me, it indicated the department of corrections did not properly vet those team members.”
In a 2023 declaration in a court case, Arizona’s corrections director said his review of execution procedures identified “several critical issues”, including “inadequate knowledge and expertise” of the people involved in executions, concerns about the IV team’s procedures, and concerns about the efficacy of the drugs.
Trouble in Tennessee
Despite reports of three botched Arizona executions, Lee appointed Strada to head Tennessee’s prisons in early 2023. That appointment came while Tennessee was grappling with its own scandals around lethal injections, with a 2022 state-commissioned independent report finding that Tennessee had failed to follow protocol in several executions, not properly tested drugs and had a “tunnel-vision, result-oriented” approach to executions.
Death row attorneys have argued that Strada has failed to address the problems raised in that report.
Under Strada, Tennessee removed a key training requirement for people involved in lethal injections, according to Kit Thomas, a death row attorney. Before Strada joined, execution team members were directed to practice catheterization with saline, records show. But training guidelines put in place under Strada eliminated that requirement, saying: “No IV is inserted into the person playing the role of the inmate.”
“He reduced the training requirements and we’ve seen disastrous results,” said Thomas. “He oversaw executions in Arizona which involved prolonged, torturous attempts to establish IV lines, and he brought a similar practice here.”
After Strada left Arizona, corrections officials made changes to the state’s lethal injection process, including increasing the number of people on the IV team responsible for injections and requiring more rigorous training, records show. But Strada has not overseen similar changes in Tennessee, instead implementing a protocol that mirrored the older Arizona policy of requiring only two people on the IV team that does injections, Thomas noted.
Thomas also provided excerpts of a November 2025 deposition where Strada was questioned by death row attorneys. When Strada was asked what he considered to be a successful execution, he responded: “The condemned is put to death.” When a lawyer followed up, asking: “Anything else?”, Strada replied: “No.”
Thomas said Strada’s response suggested he had “no regard for the experience of the individual being executed other than that they end up dead”. The response, she added, echoed the same “tunnel-vision” approach to executions that investigators had called out in the Tennessee-commissioned report in 2022.
In the 2025 deposition, Strada further acknowledged he had not followed some of the recommendations of the 2022 report, including failing to hire a full-time employee or consultant with a pharmaceutical background to provide guidance on the lethal injection process and failing to hire a full-time employee or consultant to assist with locating lethal injection sources.
“What good is an independent investigation if those investigators provide recommendations that are ignored?” said Thomas.
Questions mount over lethal drugs
Questions about how the state acquires, maintains and administers lethal injection drugs are critical following the botched killing of Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 at age 20 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
Pike’s lawyers said Friday that she remained unconscious and on a ventilator. Prison officials have not addressed questions of what might have gone wrong, but some outside experts have questioned whether the pentobarbital could have been degraded or may have failed to properly enter her bloodstream and instead seeped into surrounding tissue.
Tennessee keeps secret the identities of people involved in executions and basic facts about the drugs it uses in executions. Thomas pointed to a number of questions that Strada previously declined to answer, including whether he was using the same drug supplier he used in Arizona, whether Tennessee’s supplier had complied with Food and Drug Administration rules and regulations, and whether he had any procedures or checklists to ensure the lethal injection chemicals had not been adulterated.
Stephen Ferrell, federal defender and one of Pike’s attorneys, expressed skepticism about the governor’s call for another independent inquiry, noting the last independent investigation on the state’s death penalty system resulted in continued secrecy.
“We are kept in the dark,” he said in a press conference Thursday, noting that reporters who served as witnesses to Pike’s botched killing also raised concerns about the secrecy surrounding the execution procedure: “Our predictions are downplayed, and yet they continue to come true. Tennessee should not be torturing its citizens in the name of justice.”
As the governor sidestepped questions about Strada, candidates running to replace Lee said they would not keep Strada in the job if they were elected in the November midterms.
Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said Tennessee officials should answer questions about Strada’s involvement in multiple botched executions. She also raised concerns about the lack of transparency or accountability after Carruthers’ botched execution in May: “We saw no information about why this had gone wrong and no explanation or corrective action to ensure that wouldn’t happen another time.”
“Governor Lee should urge his officials to be forthcoming about all the mistakes that may have been made and to accept responsibility for whatever went wrong with these executions,” she continued.
Ed Pilkington contributed reporting

A billionaire is one of Trump’s loudest critics. Will Democrats send him to the White House?

When Donald Trump returned to power, 20 long months ago, some state leaders wrung their hands, worrying what explicit resistance might cost their citizens – and their careers – during the second term of a vengeful president. JB Pritzker was not among them.
Two days after Trump’s re-election, the Democratic governor of Illinois warned the president would need to “come through me” to reach the people of his state. He waited all of 30 days after the inauguration before drawing a comparison with Nazi Germany.
“All I’m saying”, Pritzker declared during his State of the State address in February 2025, “is when the five-alarm fire starts to burn, every good person better be ready to man a post with a bucket of water if you want to stop it from raging out of control”.
Not everyone grabbed a bucket.
While Pritzker is willing to cede that he was not entirely alone in standing up to Trump in those early months, prominent figures alongside him could be counted “on each of your digits”, he suggests in an interview at his campaign headquarters in Chicago.
Several of his counterparts – from Gavin Newsom, who launched a legislative blitz to curb immigration enforcement in California, to Janet Mills of Maine, who told Trump she would see him in court over his bid to deny state funding over transgender athletes – could legitimately claim a digit.
Others have taken an altogether different tack. New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani is among those who have sought to strike a productive working relationship with the president. And in Washington, Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer faced fierce criticism after some Democratic senators reached a bipartisan deal to end the longest-ever US government shutdown.
Now, Pritzker suggests, the number of elected leaders willing to speak out aggressively against the administration is “finally” growing. “For one reason or another, people have chosen to come on board with Team Fight, and get off of Team Cave.”
Trump and Pritzker have a few things in common. Both are billionaires who inherited enormous wealth from their families. Both worked in business before entering politics. Both – no, the comparison pretty much ends there, says Pritzker, who, according to the governor’s campaign, has not spoken to Trump since the Covid pandemic.
“He’s a wannabe authoritarian, and I don’t say that rhetorically,” argues Pritzker, a philanthropist who helped build his state’s Holocaust Museum before entering office and spent time with survivors. “One thing that they would tell you is that you cannot give an authoritarian an inch.”
The governor is regularly cited as a potential contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee – encouraged, however implicitly, by his self-appointment as captain of Team Fight in Illinois. Amid visceral anger among voters over the political status quo – not just at one party, or one president, but the sustained failure to fix big problems and improve their lives – could he do this job nationwide?
He has another election to win first.
Illinois is one of 36 states with gubernatorial elections coming in November. Pritzker is widely expected to become the state’s first three-term governor in more than three decades. (His Republican opponent, state senator Darren Bailey, finished 12 points behind last time around.)
Pritzker, first elected during Trump’s first term, says his tenure has been dominated by four crises: a fiscal quagmire inherited from his Republican predecessor; the Covid-19 pandemic; Texas governor Greg Abbott’s move to send tens of thousands of migrants to Chicago; and Trump’s return.
All the while, he says, he has focused on affordability and the rights of Illinoisans, from raising the state minimum wage to codifying reproductive rights. After a string of credit rating upgrades, Pritzker likens alleviating the state’s financial woes process to reorienting an aircraft carrier 180 degrees – something he claims to have done, although critics note Illinois retains one of the lowest ratings in the country.
With Democrats hoping to use November’s midterm elections to mount a significant fightback against Trump, Pritzker launched a $20m political action committee to support party campaigns nationwide, recently flew to Texas to help counter-program the Republican convention, and will soon head to South Carolina, the first state in Democrats’ next presidential nominating process, to address the NAACP state conference.
His job might be in the state of Illinois, but his career aspirations sure look national.
Time is slowly but surely ticking on the Trump era. With the president barred by the US constitution from running for a third term, the searing political spotlight will soon shift, whether he likes it or not, on to those vying to succeed him.
As Democrats search for a candidate who could win back the White House and confine this chapter to the history books, speculation around Pritzker’s aspirations stepped up a level last week when he disclosed he has been using a GLP-1 medication to lose weight over the past two years.
Pritzker “knows what a lot of people may be thinking”, reported CBS News, which broke the news. “Eyeing a 2028 Bid, He Used a Weight-Loss Drug to Drop 80 Pounds,” ran the New York Times headline. “Ahead of Possible Presidential Bid, JB Pritzker Says He Is Taking Weight-Loss Drugs,” offered the Wall Street Journal.
Just how many times has he been asked if he’s running for president? For the first time in our hour together, Pritzker hesitates. “I’m not sure the connection,” he replies. “National political reporters can’t help yourselves,” he adds, referring to the way the announcement about his health was covered. “I’m not sure the question. You’re asking … what are you asking me?”
How many times has Pritzker – a politician who argues Democrats should campaign nationally on issues he so happens to have championed in his state – been asked if he’s running for president? “Reporters that don’t know me” continue to ask “very often”, he concedes. “I understand why people ask the question,” he continues, pointing to his record in Illinois. The conspicuous lack of a firm answer might also have something to do with it.
He is more open to discussing what exactly went wrong at the last election, and the factors behind the crushing defeat suffered by Kamala Harris in 2024.
Beyond the “entire setup” of Joe Biden’s withdrawal 15 weeks before polling day, Pritzker wishes the campaign had focused more on “putting money in people’s pockets”, citing an increase in the national minimum wage, which has stood at $7.25 per hour since 2009. “People need to hear that you’re going to do something tangible for them today, immediately.
“I think the campaign should have entirely been about working families, the middle class, people striving to get there, and the most vulnerable,” says Pritzker. “And I often say those things – I mean, I talk about those people – because that’s why I’m a Democrat. And it’s why, I think, most people are Democrats, or would vote for a Democrat.”
It is also, perhaps coincidentally, one of the key areas where Pritzker says he has delivered in Illinois. From the outset as governor, he took the view that he should be “fighting for the things that in your everyday life are challenging, fighting to overcome those challenges, and fighting for things that make it a little easier”, he says. Even in campaign mode, he acknowledges one failure: his signature plan to overhaul the state’s tax system from a flat rate to a graduated levy, which was rejected by voters in 2020.
While Pritzker has endured his fair share of attacks and potshots as governor, not least from Trump, a presidential run would bring a whole new layer of scrutiny – of his record, his background, and his wealth.
An heir to the Hyatt hotel chain who ran an investment firm with his brother before running for governor, Pritzker’s personal fortune currently stands at about $4.2bn, according to Forbes: significantly more than Trump’s fortune before his return to office, albeit significantly less than Trump’s fortune today.
In 2024, Pritzker made more than $1.4m while playing blackjack on vacation. “I was incredibly lucky,” he said at a press conference at the time. “It was in Las Vegas, and I like to play cards,” he added as an explanation. We’ve all been there.
(The governor’s campaign said he donated the winnings to charity.)
This year’s Democratic primaries have been dominated by headlines about anti-establishment, anti-elite candidates – including some members of the Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA – clinching the party’s nominations, from Michigan and Pennsylvania to New York and Florida. Pritzker has been watching closely.
“I think there is a desperate need for elected officials to address affordability,” he says. “And the candidates that are winning are the ones who are communicating their passion for the issue, and their articulation of the policies that will bring that. I think if you’re not showing up with that, then you’re missing the point.”
Sure, Pritzker cedes across the boardroom table; “some national reporters” have “focused” on DSA victories. “But I will just point out to you that that’s a very, relatively small percentage of the results in primaries,” he suggests. “Although they’re notable.”
“The more outspoken people, even if they weren’t DSA members, I think won,” he adds. “And they won because that is what people are feeling. People are hurting, genuinely pained, right now.”
A notable number of Democratic candidates won the party’s nomination by speaking out not only for those struggling to make ends meet – but also against those at the other end of the spectrum, with extreme wealth.
Is today’s Democratic party really prepared to send a billionaire to the White House?
Pritzker allows a brief chuckle. “Could we rephrase that question? Because you’re trying to single me out, I think,” he says. “How about if we say it a little – I’ll just answer it the way I want to.”
“When I ran in [the Illinois gubernatorial] Democratic primary in 2018, people asked the question, do we really want a businessman billionaire to be our Democratic candidate for governor? I think a legitimate question, given … what people were seeing,” he says, pointing again to Trump, but also Bruce Rauner, the former Republican Illinois governor – a mere multimillionaire at the time – whom he went on to defeat.
“Legitimate question today,” acknowledges Pritzker. “Look at Elon Musk. Look at Sam Altman. Look at – we could make a list, whoever you want to fit in what sometimes people refer to as ‘the oligarchs’ in that group. I understand the skepticism that people have about wealthy people.
“But what I can tell you is that, over the course of the last eight years – and I think over the course of my life, really, but certainly as people have paid more attention over the last eight years – I’ve proven that I have, in fact, done more for working people in this state than maybe any governor in the country, and … restored services for the most vulnerable people in our state.
“And so the real question is, what are your values? Not how much money do you have, but what do you believe?”
