We live in a rape-prone society. The horrific Cornell case reveals what that looks like | Rebecca Solnit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:00:55 UTC
19:00:55 KST

Sometimes a story is so so appalling, it captures the public’s attention, including the attention of people who don’t focus on the issue otherwise. Such is the case with the alleged 2024 gang rape at Cornell University.
For feminists who focus on violence against women or anyone who has ever cared about campus rape, the claims made in Jane Doe’s civil lawsuit against the alleged perpetrators may be unusual in its severity – but we know the statistics that show that somewhere between 20% and 25% of women college students will be the victim of a sexual assault (no statistics tell us what percentage of men students will be rapists).
This makes the public outcry to punish seven male students miss the point, which is that there are tens of thousands of campus rape stories, few of which make the news.
We know that nearly every campus in the US has a plethora of rape victims and rapists. We also know how it often happens. The Johns Hopkins University “student well-being” blog summarizes a key aspect:
“The ‘Red Zone’ is a period of time that lasts from the start of the fall semester through Thanksgiving break when the majority of sexual assault occurs on college campuses ... It’s a six-to-10-week time frame when many students are going to parties, gatherings, and other social events to celebrate their return to campus. Data shows that over 50% of sexual assaults that occur on college campuses occur during this time. New students can be especially vulnerable during this period, due to their unfamiliarity with the campus, new social experiences, and the resources available to survivors.”
We know that the Greek system that sets the rules for most sororities and fraternities does not permit alcohol at sororities, which makes fraternities the hosts of the alcohol-saturated parties, which sends young women into enemy territory, which is where they are sometimes manipulated to get them drunk and stranded and abused.
The Hopkins blog notes: “Alcohol is the tool that is most commonly used by perpetrators in cases of sexual assault ... A person who is incapacitated by drugs or alcohol is not able to consent.” We know that fraternities often make the news for their excesses and abuses, including sometimes-harmful-to-fatal hazing of their own potential members.
We know the Cornell student newspaper editorial that brought this case to light declares that 15% of all students there have experienced “nonconsensual sexual contact” and a disproportionate fifth of those incidents took place at fraternities.
The Cornell fraternity in question was suspended from campus for a period, as a November 2024 Guardian piece about the incident reports. Meanwhile, campus rape is a nationwide issue, and the Trump administration’s assault on Title IX continues.
The non-profit organization Human Rights Campaign reports that the Department of Education just rescinded a Biden-era Title IX rule: “Specifically, this move puts back in place rules for colleges and universities from the first Trump administration that suppress the voices of survivors of rape and sexual assault and make it easier for their perpetrators to get away with their actions.” It also affects LGBTQ+ students.
The Trump administration appears comfortable in the company of alleged perpetrators. Last year, it intervened on behalf of Andrew Tate, who is charged with several counts of rape, trafficking and assault against women. This past week, administration members selected Russell Brand, likewise awaiting trial on multiple charges of sexual assault, to co-moderate a panel at a Maha conference on 29 September, and then there’s Trump, who has been held liable for sex abuse, and the allegations against the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. (All of the men deny wrongdoing.)
While the criminal justice system should address reports of rape, we know that rates of conviction are appallingly low for a number of reasons. Although, thanks to feminist interventions, the legal system is better equipped to understand this crime and less prejudiced against victims, we will not change the world through that means.
Sexual assault arises in part through both the entitlement and the desire to abuse and dehumanize women, which is in part about definitions of both masculinity and femininity: masculinity in that domination, violation and degradation are seen as status-enhancing, femininity in the perception that women’s bodies are for men to use, women’s voices and rights to be ignored.
The most compelling thing I’ve read in response to the Cornell case is in an essay by feminist writer Soraya Chemaly. She cites anthropologist Peggy Sanday, who told her that there are “rape-prone” and “rape-free” societies: “She found that in rape-free cultures, women have far more authority, status, safety and freedom.”
They’re societies in which women’s rights to bodily and social self-determination are respected, and a man who violates those rights would face severe consequences. “Rape-prone cultures, on the other hand, treat rape as an entitlement in a system that revolves around masculine contests and hierarchies.”
Sanday also wrote a book titled Fraternity Gang Rape, documenting “daily life in the fraternity, highlighting the role played by pornography, male bonding, and degrading, often grotesque, initiation and hazing rituals”. In 2020, an 18-year-old Cornell freshman died from an alcohol-intensive hazing ritual at the Phi Kappa Psi fraternity, neighbor to the fraternity where the 2024 gang rape allegedly took place.
The only effective, lasting, far-reaching solution is the political, legal, economic and cultural equality of women. This requires the liberation of men from the kind of misogynistic male supremacy Sanday describes in the fraternities, which may give them power and status in the context of that supremacy, but also corrupts and distorts their psyches into the kind of dehumanized grotesquery described in the Cornell case.
- Rebecca Solnit is a Guardian US columnist. She is the author of Orwell’s Roses and co-editor with Thelma Young Lutunatabua of the climate anthology Not Too Late: Changing the Climate Story from Despair to Possibility

Left-wing justifications partly shield antisemitism from liberal disapproval, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:00:49 UTC
19:00:49 KST

A recent study published in American Psychologist suggests that while political liberals generally harbor a strong distaste for prejudiced individuals, they tend to evaluate people expressing antisemitism more positively when those remarks are accompanied by justifications related to human rights or criticism of Israel. The research provides evidence that these specific justifications act as social signals, and liberals tended to view the speaker as a political ally who is not broadly bigoted.
Antisemitism involves prejudice or hatred directed toward Jewish people. In social psychology, researchers also study how prejudices are expressed in daily life, noting that people rarely state a prejudice outright without offering a justification. A justification is a reason or rationale provided by a speaker to make their prejudiced views seem more socially acceptable or grounded in a legitimate concern.
Hate crimes against Jewish people in the United States spiked following the onset of the Israel-Hamas war in October 2023, rising from 11% of all hate crimes in the year before the war to 27% in the year after. Historically, political liberals have been fiercely protective of minority groups and quick to condemn discrimination. In fact, a study covered by PsyPost in 2022 found that, before the war, agreement with overtly antisemitic statements was two to three times higher on the American far right than on the far left.
“Part of our motivation came from observing political discourse,” lead author Jordan W. Moon, a lecturer in the School of Psychology at the University of Southampton, told PsyPost. “There has been a sharp rise in antisemitic rhetoric and incidents, but it seemed to us that the people who were otherwise most concerned about protecting minorities were somewhat unconcerned or even dismissive of this rise.”
Moon and his team wanted to investigate this apparent contradiction. “We wondered whether some types of prejudice and discrimination were more tolerated by different audiences—in this case, whether antisemitism was tolerated by political liberals,” he added. “We wanted to know, first, whether liberals indeed currently tolerated antisemitism, and second, whether there are certain ways of expressing antisemitism that are more accepted by liberal audiences.”
Antisemitism and criticism of Israel are related but distinct attitudes. A study covered by PsyPost in 2025, for example, found that antisemitic attitudes were linked to greater support for political violence, while criticism of Israel on its own was linked to legal activism but not to support for violence.
The researchers aimed to understand whether specific political rationalizations help explain why liberals might tolerate certain expressions of anti-Jewish prejudice. They noted that by 2025, 75% of Republicans but only 21% of Democrats said their sympathies lay with Israelis, which they argued may make criticism of Israel a marker of liberal identity. They proposed two potential psychological mechanisms: ingroup favoritism, where a justification signals shared political views, and alliance politics, where a justification implies the speaker is not indiscriminately hateful toward other groups.
To test these ideas, the research team conducted three preregistered online experiments between October and December of 2024 involving 979 American adults. The samples were recruited via Prolific and quota-matched to the U.S. population on age, gender, ethnicity, and political party; the number of Jewish participants was negligible. In their analyses, the researchers treated political views as a continuous scale running from 0 (extremely liberal) to 100 (extremely conservative). They then estimated each effect for someone somewhat liberal, around 17 or 18 on that scale, and someone somewhat conservative, around 79 to 81.
In the first experiment, 270 participants read profiles of individuals expressing prejudice against Jewish people, Black people, or Muslims. Each participant saw all three prejudiced profiles mixed among five unrelated distractor profiles. Participants were randomly assigned to see the prejudice stated plainly without explanation, or accompanied by a socially common justification.
For antisemitism, the justification was a strong disapproval of Israel and its war in Gaza. For anti-Black prejudice, the justification was a belief about crime rates, and for anti-Muslim prejudice, it was a belief about conflicting cultural values. After reading the profiles, participants rated how much they liked or disliked the individual on a 7-point scale, and estimated the speaker’s likely political orientation and how likely they were to be a bigot.
The results showed that without any justification, liberal participants disliked all prejudiced individuals more than conservative participants did. But when the anti-Jewish prejudice was justified by a disapproval of Israel, liberals liked the speaker 1.1 points more on the 7-point scale. This particular justification did not have an effect on how conservative participants evaluated the speaker. The justifications used for anti-Black and anti-Muslim prejudices did not increase liking among liberals.
The researchers emphasized that this relative increase in liking did not mean these participants suddenly endorsed prejudice. “On a scale of ‘Dislike Extremely’ toward ‘Like Extremely’, the prejudiced targets were largely disliked by both liberals and conservatives, regardless of which prejudice they expressed and how it was justified,” Moon noted. “That is, liberals did not ‘like’ antisemites, but certain justifications did make them feel relatively more positively toward them.”
To test if left-leaning justifications work for other types of prejudices, the scientists conducted a second experiment with 277 participants. They expanded the targets of prejudice to include Jewish, Black, Muslim, Chinese, and Russian Americans. This time, they tested justifications appealing to liberal values, such as accusing the targeted group’s ancestral home country of human rights violations. They compared these to justifications appealing to conservative values, such as claiming the targeted group threatens traditional American values.
Once again, liberals strongly disliked all prejudiced individuals when no justification was provided. However, when prejudices against any of the five groups were justified by citing human rights violations, liberals evaluated the speakers more positively, by roughly half a point to a full point on the 7-point scale.
Conservatives also liked some of these speakers more, including those prejudiced against Muslim and Chinese Americans, so only for the anti-Jewish speaker did the effect differ reliably between liberals and conservatives. Justifications centered on traditional American values mostly had no effect for either group, raising liberals’ liking only for the speaker prejudiced against Russian Americans and conservatives’ liking only for the speaker prejudiced against Chinese Americans.
The authors pointed out that this finding addresses a common misperception that their results only apply to antisemitism. “Although we focused our writeup on antisemitism, we found similar effects for other prejudices,” Moon clarified. “A person who expresses prejudice toward Black Americans or Chinese Americans was liked a bit more by politically liberal observers when they appealed to human rights abuses by African countries or China. This process seems to be a general notion of ‘prejudice is more acceptable when expressed by someone in my group’ than something that is unique to a single type of prejudice.”
A third experiment with 432 participants focused exclusively on anti-Jewish prejudice but tested a wider variety of rationalizations. These included disapproval of Israel, conspiracies about Jewish power and influence, historical beliefs about genetic inferiority, and religious blame. Each participant saw only one profile.
As in the earlier experiments, liberals disliked the unjustified antisemitic speaker more than conservatives did. When the speaker justified their prejudice using a disapproval of Israel or conspiracies about Jewish power, the negative social penalty for expressing the prejudice was reduced relative to when no reason was given. Unlike in the first two experiments, however, these two effects did not differ between liberals and conservatives, and neither reached statistical significance when the researchers examined liberals and conservatives separately. The authors say they are cautious about treating these results as definitive.
Justifying the prejudice with claims that Jews are genetically inferior lowered liking overall, and both liberals and conservatives saw that speaker as more likely to be a bigot. The religious justification had no statistically significant effect.
Moon said the team was surprised by how participants responded to a conspiracy trope long associated with the political right. “One of the justifications we included was the trope that Jews hold too much power and influence over financial markets, governments, and the media,” he explained. “Historically in the U.S., this has been a right-coded justification. However, in our experiment, participants thought the profile uttering this trope was more politically liberal than the profile expressing unjustified antisemitism, and this trope had a similar effect in licensing antisemitism as the disapproval of Israel and the war in Gaza justification.”
Across the experiments, the authors found evidence for two psychological processes that statistically accounted for why liberals liked speakers who used left-leaning justifications. First, liberals viewed these speakers as being politically closer to themselves, indicating a type of ingroup favoritism. Second, liberals inferred that a speaker focusing on human rights was less likely to be generally bigoted, which the authors interpret as making them less of a threat to the broader liberal political coalition.
Dylan Selterman, director of research and resource development at Heterodox Academy and an SNF Agora Faculty Affiliate at Johns Hopkins University, was not involved in the research. (He noted that these views are his own and do not represent his employer, Heterodox Academy.) He told PsyPost that “this research shows how people who in some cases eschew group-based ethnic prejudice may yet condone it in other cases, if such prejudice is accompanied by a moral justification.”
“This is an important fact because many people believe that they are immune to negative prejudices,” Selterman added. “However, this is not always the case.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The specific justifications tested across different marginalized groups in the first two experiments were not perfectly identical, which makes direct comparisons between prejudices somewhat difficult. The study also relied on statistical models to test the psychological mechanisms, meaning future experimental designs would be needed to establish exact cause and effect. Additionally, the research measured how people react to brief written profiles, which might not fully capture the complexities of real-world social interactions.
“My confidence is high,” Selterman said. “The authors appear to have done some elegant experiments, with sound statistical tests. Experiment 3 was somewhat inconsistent with the results of Experiments 1 and 2 but the authors reported it anyway,” he noted. “That makes me feel more confident in the results that did emerge.”
“Condoning prejudice is not the same as expressing prejudice,” Selterman explained. “The authors did not find that respondents held prejudice; rather, they studied how people view others who hold prejudices. These studies highlight how third-party judgment works. However, even though these studies did not examine prejudicial feelings directly, the findings are still very important because they show how prejudice can become more socially acceptable, which can lead to increases in discrimination and even violence.”
The authors suggest that efforts to combat antisemitism should consider not just the underlying prejudice but the language used to package it. They speculate that a prejudiced statement made in the service of a social cause might signal especially strong commitment to that cause, and to the political group associated with it.
“This kind of justification communicates that one is part of the liberal political coalition,” Moon said. “Because of ingroup favoritism, liberals were more tolerant of the person expressing antisemitism in this way. If we want to understand why some prejudices become socially acceptable, we should consider the guises they take, and what information they communicate to others.”
As for next steps, Selterman said he would want to better understand “(a) whether people are aware that they are using a justification to morally license bigoted attitudes, (b) what specific political attitudes (beyond simply being liberal or conservative) are associated with this kind of licensing, and (c) what kind of interventions would get people to have consistent moral standards against prejudice, without any justification.”
The study, “Justifying Antisemitism: Political Liberalism and Perceptions of Prejudices,” was authored by Jordan W. Moon, Michael Barlev, and Steven L. Neuberg.

Studio Armitage creates Field Shelter for people tending allotments in Nara

Studio Armitage creates Field Shelter for people tending allotments in Nara
A water tank ballasts this wooden pavilion in Nara, Japan, designed by London practice Studio Armitage as a shelter for people working in the surrounding rice fields and allotments.
Named Field Shelter, the demountable structure addresses the absence of a rest spot for locals tending their allotments in the Amagatsuji neighbourhood.
Studio Armitage developed the design while spending time at Space Department, a nearby creative hub, and noticing how these fields doubled as an important social space for locals.
The ambition was to provide an unobtrusive rest spot for people, complementing the other simple agricultural structures and sheds in the fields that were "assembled from whatever materials are readily available".
"I was spending a lot of time walking and cycling through the rice fields and allotments around the studio and became interested in the small sheds, field stores and other structures scattered amongst them," studio founder Freddie Armitage told Dezeen.
"I also noticed that there was almost nowhere to stop. The summer sun in Nara is incredibly strong, and the rain can be sudden and heavy. At the same time, the allotments clearly had an important social life," he continued.
"The idea for the shelter grew directly from that. We found a plot that sat at a natural meeting point within the fields and approached the owner about building a small communal structure there."
Field Shelter comprises a deliberately simple wooden structure formed from standard timber sections and battens, raised above wet ground on impermanent concrete blocks.
The overlapping roof structure is topped with polycarbonate corrugated sheets, sheltering two benches that flank the central water container.
There is no obvious front or back, or division between inside and outside. The shelter is fully demountable, and its pared-back design means another version could be easily made.
Alongside the agricultural structures, this design also draws on local temples and storehouses around Nara that are raised on platforms, have deep eaves and legible construction.
"I was interested in how little we needed to build in order to make a recognisable place," reflected Armitage.
"The shelter is essentially a raised floor, a roof and two benches. Those elements are enough to give some protection and a sense of enclosure without separating you from the fields," he continued.
"Everything was deliberately based around standard dimensions and materials that we could obtain locally. There is no specialist fabrication and very little equipment is required to build it."
Studio Armitage deliberately placed the benches facing opposite directions. One looks east for the morning light, while the other faces west for evening light.
"There is no fixed way that it has to be occupied," said Armitage. "Somebody can stop there alone while working on their plot, two people can sit facing out across the water, or a larger group can gather around it in the evening."
The water butt that ballasts Field Shelter serves "a spatial role", Studio Armitage said, forming a divider between the two sides.
It also acts as a shared water store for the locals. If periodically filled, it means people do not have to struggle to carry water to their allotments on each visit.
Other design details include the blue-painted end grain of the timber sections, providing additional weather protection while making "the individual pieces of the construction very legible".
Studio Armitage's hopes the structure will remain in the allotments for as long as locals find it useful. However, its structure is easily demountable, meaning it can be rebuilt or repurposed elsewhere.
"It might remain where it is for a long time, move to another group of allotments or appear somewhere completely different," reflected Armitage.
"A small piece of overlooked ground in a town could need exactly the same things as a field in Nara – somewhere dry to sit, a little shade and a place where people can meet."
Other shelters recently featured on Dezeen include a whimsical dog-like structure in London, built by Assemble from wood and thatch, and The KinShip EcoLab by Fuinneamh Workshop Architects in Ireland, which has rammed-earth walls and a thatched roof.
The photography is courtesy of Studio Armitage.

Why I Bring My Kids to Vote with Me
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:00:08 UTC
19:00:08 KST

Every election, when I head to the polls, I try to bring my kids with me. They love to get their “future voter” sticker. Well, maybe not my oldest anymore.
My kids are 11 and 9 years old now, which means they’re old enough to understand that something important is happening when we vote, and curious enough to ask plenty of questions.
I want them to ask those questions.
I’ve spent nearly 30 years at the League of Women Voters, helping people understand how they can shape our democracy, participate in elections, connect with elected leaders, and make their voices heard. I care deeply about this work. Becoming a parent made my work feel even more personal. I want my children to understand they have the power to influence the decisions that shape their lives.
My kids can’t vote yet, but the consequences of democratic decisions already affect nearly every part of their lives. Those decisions shape the funding available for their schools, parks, playgrounds, and pools, as well as the libraries and community resources available to them. They determine the safety of the bike lanes and roads we use daily. The choices our elected leaders make today will shape the opportunities available to all our children tomorrow.
Kids don’t vote for the officials meant to represent them, but that doesn’t mean kids shouldn’t understand how decisions are made—or how, one day, they can have a say in them.
That’s why I bring my children with me when I vote—and to rallies and community meetings. In nearly three decades at the League of Women Voters, I have seen how powerful it can be when people understand that democracy belongs to them. I’ve also seen why we can’t take that understanding for granted.
I want my kids to see democracy in action: something people do, not just something they learn about in school. When we walk into a polling place, they see neighbors and community members showing up. They see me check in, receive my ballot, and make my choices. And they see that participating in our democracy is a normal part of being a member of a community.
For me, these trips also lead to bigger conversations. Both pre-teens, my kids are at slightly different stages in understanding how government and elections work. Their interests are different, so their questions are different. But both have very clear ideas of what is fair and just, and they recognize when something happening in the world affects them, our community, and the people they care about.
I want them to know what they can do about it. Voting is important, but it’s not the only answer. Democracy gives us many ways to use our voices. We can learn about issues. We can ask questions until we’re satisfied with the answers. We can contact our elected officials. We can speak up at a school board or city council meeting. We can organize with other people who care about the same thing.
And, when we’re old enough, we can vote for those we want representing us. No one wakes up on their 18th birthday automatically knowing how to participate in democracy. We have to teach it. More importantly, we have to model it. Our kids watch how we treat people, how we respond to problems, and how we care for our communities. They watch how we participate, too.
Let me be clear: this doesn’t mean telling our children what to think or whom they should someday vote for. In fact, I want the opposite for my kids. I want them to grow into people who ask questions, seek out reliable information, listen to others, and reach their own conclusions.
When they exchange their “future voter” stickers for “I voted,” I hope that, in addition to being momentous and exciting, the experience also feels familiar. I hope they know how to find reliable information. I hope they ask questions. And I hope they understand that they don’t have to agree with me—or anyone else—about every issue.
Most of all, I hope they understand the power of their voice and how to use it.
Decisions being made today will have consequences our children will have to live with tomorrow. And part of teaching kids about democracy is about reminding them that they don’t have to be passive observers in their own lives. They can learn, participate, speak up and, eventually, vote for the kind of world they want to live in, not one they were handed.
That’s why I bring my kids with me to the polls. There may be extra questions, and it may take me a little longer to cast my ballot. Someday, these decisions will be theirs to make. And I want them to be ready to use their voices when it’s their turn.

"It does not mean that there is no problem": Marchenko explained where the budget lacks funds following the EU statement
Kyiv • UNN
By the end of the year, Ukraine needs to receive $29.5 billion from its partners for non-military expenditures. The EU guarantees €17 billion for defense, but the additional need amounts to $27 billion.
Following new statements from the EU regarding funding for Ukraine this year, Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko explained on October 3 what is happening with the budget deficit and funds from European partners, UNN writes.
Details
"In light of recent media reports citing statements by EU representatives, I consider it necessary to clarify several points regarding the budget situation as of today," the minister said on social media.
According to Marchenko, "it is worth separating the budgetary and military funding tracks."
"First. International financing for the needs of the state budget. These are funds that we use to cover non-military expenditures. By the end of the year, we urgently need to receive $29.5 billion from our partners (more than $3 billion of which was received yesterday). And we will receive it if we fulfill all the commitments agreed upon on our side. Parliament and the government will fulfill them jointly. Laws and resolutions. There will be no financing gap if we fully do our homework regarding our commitments," Marchenko stressed.
"Second. Guaranteed EU funds under the USL for defense needs (the purchase of weapons and drones). They are unconditional. That is, we will definitely receive them. As of today, €17 billion remains available for drawdown through the end of 2026. With regard to these funds, we agreed with the European Commission to accelerate work on the fastest possible approval of the requests submitted by Ukraine," the head of the Finance Ministry said.
"Third. In August 2026, the Ministry of Defense declared an additional defense need amounting to $27 billion (even after the full drawdown of funds under the USL. See point 2.). This week, together with representatives of the Ministry of Defense and the European Commission, we held meetings in Brussels where we discussed possible ways to cover this need. We developed a plan and presented our vision, but this does not mean that the problem does not exist," Marchenko stressed.
He noted that "through internal resources, Ukraine will cover more than $7 billion of this need. This involves savings and the redistribution of expenditures." "We expect to find a solution for another approximately $12 billion through joint efforts," the minister said.
The remaining funds are a critical need, and we are working jointly with the Ministry of Defense to determine the source of coverage. The European Commission will not be able to cover it due to the lack of appropriate instruments on its part this year
"We continue working around the clock with our partners to ensure all the needs of the Ukrainian budget. We will provide updates on progress," the minister said.

How to Have More Self-Control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:00:07 UTC
19:00:07 KST

The ability to manage one’s thoughts, regulate emotions, and restrain impulses is key to a happy and healthy life. People who have good self-control often have higher psychological well-being, more academic and on-the-job achievements, and healthier relationships. Low self-control, in contrast, is a core contributing factor to numerous problems, including substance abuse and impulsive buying.
Any of us can succumb to the limits of in-the-moment willpower. We see that box of cookies on the counter and we reach for one, and then two. Most of us can learn how to think before we act and even engage in self-restraint in high-stress situations. But if we aren’t taught to practice self-control early in our lives, it can be harder, though not impossible.
Walter Mischel, a psychologist who taught at Stanford and Columbia, conducted some of the most famous studies on delaying gratification in the late 1960s and 1970s. Decades later, he published a book expanding on this research: The Marshmallow Test: Mastering Self-Control. For those unfamiliar with the original study, in brief, children ages three to five were presented with a marshmallow and given two options. They were told they could eat the marshmallow immediately, or, if they waited for 20 minutes and didn’t eat the marshmallow, they could have two marshmallows.
Mischel and colleagues followed those children and continued to study them over time. What they found was remarkable. The preschoolers who had a tough time delaying gratification— who ate the first marshmallow—were less academically and socially skilled, eloquent, attentive, and not as good at managing frustration in adolescence.
Over time, large-scale replication and extension studies of the marshmallow test with more diverse socioeconomic and racial samples found more nuanced findings. While similar findings on wait times and outcomes were found, additional analyses showed that children’s ability to delay gratification and wait for a second marshmallow was more strongly related to parents’ education and children’s home environment. This showed that self-control is not a fixed trait, and that circumstances greatly contribute to children’s ability to delay gratification.
In addition, when the marshmallow test was administered to adults, it did not predict their functioning. That makes sense. Few of us are going to struggle with not eating a marshmallow. But if it was a more suitable enticement for adults, like a salted caramel cheesecake or immediate access to our social media or news feeds, we might.
Angela Narayan, a clinical psychologist and associate professor at the University of Denver, conducts research and works clinically with low-income families to identify resilience processes that protect against the intergenerational transmission of trauma. I asked her how she helps support highly stressed parents to engage in effective emotion regulation, self-control, and distress tolerance.
“I encourage adults to try to notice the negative feeling in the moment—pausing and reflecting and then try to sit with it for a moment to notice how, with simple coping skills, the intensity of the feeling passes,” she said. “Even if the feeling itself doesn’t pass, it becomes weaker and less bothersome. If you ride the wave of the negative feeling, as opposed to lashing out at someone, yelling at a loved one, or sending an angry email, the worst of it will pass and you will be able to think more clearly and have better control over what to do next.”
In other words, when we recognize that our impulses are temporary, they become less powerful.
As I tell my patients, we are never too old to learn new skills, as long as we are open and motivated to learn and then practice the techniques. Most of the people I work with struggle with impulse control because they experienced severe and prolonged trauma experiences and have significant hyperarousal and difficulties managing their emotions.
Among other things, I try to teach them that often when they engage impulsively, they, in a sense, give their power away. Their intense emotions get the best of them. They say or do something they deeply regret. I explain that it’s in their best interest to thoughtfully respond rather than react. That way, they have a better chance of keeping their power and self-respect.
I am a very visual person, so I like imagery. My patients sometimes laugh at me when I tell them to picture themselves riding a horse and pulling back the reins on their strong emotions. If this or a related visual grounds them from taking negative action, I’ll take their laughter as a good sign.
We are all likely to engage in forms of instant gratification from time to time, but if we immediately satiate all our impulses, we miss the bigger rewards. We need to create a little psychological distance from our impulses and stay focused on the prize. We get bigger rewards when we manage our impulses well. We get to look at ourselves in the mirror and like our behavior.
To be fair, some of us have a harder time reining ourselves in. We may be risk-seekers who pursue activities that give us an adrenaline rush. We might have inherited, by no fault of our own, genetic factors that contribute to being more impulsive. It’s harder for us to pull ourselves in. But it’s not impossible.
Learning, practicing, and engaging in self-control is essential to leading a good life. Why wouldn’t we want that for ourselves?

Trump is campaigning in reliably red states, a sign of midterm concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- President Trump is holding midterm rallies in GOP strongholds to energize supporters as Republican concerns grow ahead of midterms.
- Rather than visiting competitive districts, Trump has been traveling to Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama.
DURANT, Okla. — David Coleman doesn’t know much about the Republican candidates who are running in November. But he knows President Trump, and he trusts that the president won’t steer him wrong.
The 54-year-old Oklahoman made his way to Trump’s midterm rally in Durant, Okla., on Thursday planning to support whomever Trump brought onstage with him.
“I am going to ask ChatGPT what their name is and vote for them,” Coleman said as he and thousands of others waited for the president to appear.
Voters like Coleman — who are fiercely loyal to Trump but only loosely attached to the rest of the Republican ticket — are part of those whom the president is trying to target in the final stretch before the Nov. 3 election.
Rather than prioritizing visits to battleground districts, which will decide which party controls Congress, Trump is rallying in Republican strongholds such as Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama, betting that his presence will be enough to energize a base that may be thinking about sitting out the election because his name isn’t on the ballot.
In Oklahoma, Trump told the crowd to imagine he is on the ballot because the future of his “America First” agenda depends on Republicans getting out to vote. He then urged them to vote for GOP candidates like Senate candidates Ken Paxton of Texas and Kevin Hern of Oklahoma.
“You have to get out and vote,” Trump said. “You can’t assume they are going to win.”
The red-state itinerary is a departure from what Trump initially promised to do in the 30 days leading up to the midterms. At a Rose Garden dinner with Republican lawmakers last month, he pledged to campaign in the country’s 35 most competitive districts. But in many of those races, the president is proving to be a political liability as his his approval dwindles, even among Republicans.
In Texas, Paxton, who is locked in a tight race against Democrat James Talarico, has lamented that Trump’s GOP convention in Dallas hurt him, according to a recording obtained by the New York Times. Since the report, Trump has told supporters to vote for Paxton “whether you love him or not” even while he said that “he can be a pain in the ass.”
“We need Ken so badly, that’s why I am here,” Trump told a crowd in Texas on Thursday, while noting that it would be a “horror” if Republicans lost the Senate seat to Talarico.
Democrats, meanwhile, are making heavy investments in winning back voters they lost to Trump in 2024, including Latino voters in south Texas. Some of those voters have said they feel betrayed by Trump’s policies on immigration and the economy.
Trump has dismissed the poll findings that he is losing the Latino vote. Asked what his message was to Latino voters who are dismayed by his policies, he said: “We have to do what we have to do.” The president has also brushed off comments that his unpopularity among Americans may be hurting Republican candidates, saying that “everybody that has me wins.”
But in recent days, Trump has publicly said Republicans are “worried” about several races, including those in Michigan, Texas and “a few other states.” These concerns come as even the most ardent Trump supporters grow concerned about the economy, particularly the cost of gas.
Ronnie Smith, 77, has voted for Trump every time he has been on the ballot, and his support for the president has not wavered. But, he said, “the only thing that I think is hurting him is the cost of diesel.”
Gas prices in the U.S. have soared during the seven-month Iran war, with the national average for a gallon of diesel reaching $6.37 on Friday, according to AAA. The cost of diesel hit a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.
Smith says he regularly hears complaints about the cost of fuel from trucker friends who have long commutes for work. But he said he is sure Trump can “take care of it.”
On Friday, Trump announced that the world’s wealthiest industrial nations had agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and fuel products from their strategic stockpiles in the coming weeks, a move that he is expected to tout in his upcoming midterm rallies.
In these rallies, Trump has repeatedly said that he believes his administration has been doing a “tremendous” job with the economy, the problem is that “we’re doing an extremely poor job at promotion.”
A Republican source close to the White House said the president visited Durant because of its proximity to the Texas border, with the hope of helping candidates in both states. The strategy is similar to his Friday visit to Mobile, Ala., which is near Florida’s Panhandle.
Trump’s swing through GOP strongholds is seen as a way to get the word out to his base.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters this week that Republicans “need the president to turn out voters that are his voters.”
“In a non-presidential year, in a midterm election, that challenge is always voter turnout,” he said. “In this case you have a lot of voters out there who may not be inclined to go out there and vote.”
Sylvia Sigler, 66, a school cafeteria worker who attended Trump’s Oklahoma rally Thursday, said she normally votes in local elections but has not voted in a federal election since 2016.
When asked what would motivate her to get out and vote this November, she contemplated what to say.
“I haven’t thought about it, but maybe the economy,” she said. “I don’t even know who is running because I don’t keep up with it.”
But she was curious to attend Trump’s rally and see what the buzz was all about. Asked whether she thought his message would make a difference for her, she once again paused.
“It could,” she said. “But I am not making any promises.”

At Oktoberfest, nonalcoholic beer is no longer a punchline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Nonalcoholic beer, once a curiosity, is now being increasingly accepted at that temple of beer — Munich’s Oktoberfest.
- At this year’s festival, sales of nonalcoholic beer are on the rise, reflecting a broader decline in beer drinking in Germany, the U.S. and across the globe.
- Some Oktoberfest visitors, however, are unconvinced. ‘Nonalcoholic beer doesn’t make any sense to me,’ says a reveler.
MUNICH, Germany — Can you have a smashing time at Oktoberfest without getting smashed yourself? Increasingly, the answer appears to be “jawohl.”
A global shift toward nonalcoholic drinks — driven by greater health consciousness from California to Cologne and beyond — has reached even the world’s biggest celebration of beer.
Not long ago, ordering a nonalcoholic beer at Oktoberfest could draw puzzled looks. Or disdain. But now Oktoberfest is a proving ground for one of the most profound changes sweeping the global drinks industry as more consumers cut alcohol from their lives.
“When I was growing up and coming here about 20 years ago, if someone ordered a nonalcoholic beer, everyone would look at you and say, ‘What’s wrong with you?’ or ‘Oh, you must be the designated driver,’” said Joerg Biebernick, chief executive of the Paulaner Brewery Group, one of Germany’s largest brewers. “But now it’s totally socially acceptable if you want to drink beer without alcohol.”
In the tents erected in Munich for Oktoberfest, the atmosphere can be intoxicating enough without the alcohol. Brass bands pound out songs and pop anthems with thumping beats such as Neil Diamond’s “Sweet Caroline” and Robbie Williams’ “Angels” as thousands of voices roar along.
Waiters weave through packed aisles carrying foaming one-liter mugs, and strangers at long wooden tables quickly become friends. Revelers lock arms and sing together, climbing onto benches to dance as entire sections of a tent seem to move as one. Few people lifting a stein here would guess that beer consumption is down worldwide.
Celebrants from the U.S., where slugging back brews is also on the decline, are a sizable part of the spectacle. About 285,000 attended last year, making the United States the festival’s largest source of overseas visitors. Former California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger is a regular and was back this year, conducting a band and thousands of singing beer drinkers.
This year’s Oktoberfest will end Sunday. At the halfway point of the 16-day festival, sales of nonalcoholic beer were up 4.5% from a year earlier. Sales of the traditional Festbier brewed especially for Oktoberfest — which contains about 6% alcohol, meaning a one-liter mug packs about as much alcohol as three and a half 12-ounce American beers — slipped 1.4% even as attendance rose.
Last year, nonalcoholic beer accounted for nearly 8% of reported beer volume, with more than half a million liters served.
The trend extends beyond the festival grounds. Germany’s annual per capita consumption of traditional beer has fallen about 40% since 1990 to 77 liters now — an alarming development for an industry whose origins reach back to the Middle Ages.
In 2025, global beer consumption fell 0.7% to 1.896 billion hectoliters — about 50 billion gallons — according to the British Guild of Beer Writers. Germany’s output fell nearly 6% to 79.2 million hectoliters, or about 2.1 billion gallons — a mark below 80 million hectoliters for the first time.
At the same time, nonalcoholic beer has been one of the few hot segments of the global beer industry.
“I really like that there are options and that there’s something for everyone and everyone can enjoy it here,” Amanda Nguyen, a 34-year-old worker with a nongovernmental organization from Los Angeles, said as she took in the scene — thousands dressed in lederhosen or colorful dirndl, the eye-catching dresses with fitted bodices that have become almost as synonymous with Oktoberfest as the beer itself.
Nguyen said she planned to stick with nonalcoholic beer.
1. Annabelle Beyer, 25, sells souvenir “Trachtenhut” hats at Oktoberfest. Vendors like her are informally known as “Schatzis,” German for “sweethearts.” 2. Along with alcohol-free beer, other non-alcoholic drinks sold at Oktoberfest include water, apple spritzer, Spezi (a cola-orange soda) and lemonade.
Oktoberfest did not even begin serving nonalcoholic beer until 1986. What was then widely regarded as a poor imitation of the real thing has since moved into the mainstream.
One reason is simple: The beer got a lot better.
Christian Dahncke, Paulaner’s director of brewing, said important breakthroughs in technology have allowed producers to preserve much more of the flavor and aroma while removing the alcohol, just as increasingly health-conscious consumers began demanding better alternatives to alcoholic drinks. No one is sure which came first in this “chicken-or-the-egg” story — greater demand for more nonalcoholic beer or better quality offerings.
“People want to live healthier nowadays, and that’s especially true for the younger generations,” Dahncke said. “It’s not just Bavaria or Germany but everyone around the world. They want to look and feel as good at 80 as they did when they were 50. Getting rid of the alcohol is all part of that trend.”
Germany has a surprisingly long history of trying to remove alcohol from traditional drinks. As early as the 19th century, vintners began experimenting with dealcoholized wine using a process known as vacuum distillation.
Today, nonalcoholic wine is widely available in Germany, including at some Oktoberfest beer tents and festival stands, though it is far less prominent than nonalcoholic beer.
Not everyone is ready for a dry Oktoberfest.
Felix Heide, a German-born engineer and computer scientist at Princeton University who regularly returns to Munich for Oktoberfest, said he could not understand the attraction.
“Nonalcoholic beer doesn’t make any sense to me,” Heide, 39, said while celebrating in the 8,250-seat beer hall. “Beer is so deeply ingrained in our culture. We know exactly what it is. You don’t need to change a thing.”
Brian Oswald, a 69-year-old retired forestry professor from Nacogdoches, Texas, came straight to Oktoberfest after landing on an overnight flight from the United States.
“I love beer,” he said. “I’m sure nonalcoholic is getting better, but I’m not at the point where I have to worry about that.”
France Salvosa, a designer from Knoxville, Tenn., was even more emphatic as she celebrated her 50th birthday with her sister, gripping a frothy mug after watching security carry away a young man who appeared too inebriated to walk straight.
“I like to drink, love the beer here, love the taste, and like the way it hits me right away after the first two sips,” she said.
Her sister, Duch, was celebrating just as enthusiastically — but without the alcohol.
“I want to participate, want to see how this culture works and still want to be here,” she said. “But I’m OK without the alcohol, without a headache the next day.”
Kirschbaum is a special correspondent.

Candidates line up to replace Swiss government minister Parmelin
The process to replace Guy Parmelin in the Swiss government has started after the economics minister announced on Friday that he is stepping down at the end of the year.
Numerous names are already being bandied about ahead of a parliamentary vote on appointing a new government minister on December 9.

Tsar Samuel’s Remains Return to Bulgaria After Decades of Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:58:21 UTC
18:58:21 KST

Greece returned the remains of Tsar Samuel to Bulgaria in exchange for 48 ecclesiastical relics taken by Bulgarian troops at the end of World War I, in a ceremony in Thessaloniki attended by Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis.
The exchange, which the two leaders said concluded more than 50 years of negotiations between Sofia and Athens, took place at the Museum of Byzantine Culture. The agreement was signed by the countries’ culture ministers, Evtim Miloshev and Lina Mendoni.
Efthymia Moutsopoulou, widow of the late Greek archaeologist Prof. Nikolaos Moutsopoulos, was also present. He discovered the remains of Samuel and members of his family in a family tomb inside a church on the island of Agios Achilleios in Lesser Prespa Lake in 1964. The church was built during Samuel’s reign, from 997 to 1014.
Bulgarian guardsmen carried the sarcophagus, draped in the national flag, to the Spartan military aircraft for its flight to Sofia. A solemn ceremony and burial at the medieval Saint Sophia Church in the center of the capital were planned. The government provided free rail travel for Bulgarians wishing to attend.
"We are going to bring our Tsar home," Radev told Bulgarian National Television (BNT) journalists shortly after arriving in Thessaloniki. BNT had exclusive rights to broadcast the event live, covering every stage of Samuel’s final journey.
Greece also returned the bones of 10 other people buried alongside Samuel. Eight were children, while the other two are believed to have belonged to Samuel’s son, Gavril Radomir, and his nephew, Ivan Vladislav. Genetic and anthropological examinations are to be conducted.
At the ceremony, Radev said, "It is a tremendous honor for me to be back at the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki and, on behalf of the Bulgarian state, to receive the mortal remains of the Bulgarian Tsar Samuil - remains that Professor Nikolaos Moutsopoulos entrusted to your magnificent museum, and to whom we Bulgarians owe eternal remembrance."
He said Bulgaria had sought the return of the remains since Moutsopoulos found them in the basilica on the island of Saint Achillios in the 1960s, adding that the state had continued its efforts throughout the following six decades. Radev said the return fulfilled the archaeologist’s moral legacy and thanked the political leaders whose decisions had made the agreement possible.
"If Tsar Samuel once divided us, today he unites us. Today, he strengthens our strategic partnership and solidifies the bonds between our two peoples," Radev said. He added that shared EU membership enabled both countries to understand each other’s concerns and aspirations.
Radev also said the two countries were entering a new phase in their relations after a thousand years of conflict, and described their current levels of political, economic and cultural cooperation as exceptionally high.
"Today, we are forging a very deep bond with Bulgaria and not merely a cultural one. The return of significant ecclesiastical artifacts transforms difficult historical moments into new opportunities for dialogue," Mitsotakis said.
The Greek prime minister said the agreement had required time, determination and the will to overcome past challenges. He described the cooperation as being at an early stage and expressed hope that it would lead to further collaboration and the return to Bulgaria of other relics held in Greece. Mitsotakis also said cultural diplomacy worked quietly but productively.
The event, called "historic" by participants and commentators on BNT, took place during Bulgaria’s presidential election campaign. The second part of the program included an official ceremony and a procession to the Church of St. Sophia in Sofia.
Before the flight, two pairs of Bulgarian fighter jets, F-16s and MiG-29s, were scheduled to escort the Spartan aircraft carrying Samuel’s remains from the Greek border to the skies above Sofia.

Economic Watch: Extended breaks, richer experiences add momentum to China's holiday travel boom
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
17:56:26 CST
18:56:26 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's National Day travel market kicked off on a strong note, as many travelers linked the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day breaks with their annual leave. This trend has led to longer trips and a surge in bookings for long-haul journeys, multi-city itineraries and experience-based travel products.
LONGER BREAKS, FARTHER JOURNEYS
With the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day separated by only three working days this year, some travelers used three days of leave to link the two breaks into a 13-day holiday. Trip.com Group data showed that one in every 10 travelers combined the two holidays into an extended break.
Cao Shuai, CEO of Tongcheng Travel's destination business division, said strong demand for the 13-day break has lengthened the overall consumption cycle and helped release demand for long-haul and in-depth travel.
Data from online travel platform Qunar showed that by Oct. 1, the first day of the National Day holiday, 20 percent of travelers had already reached the second city on their itineraries. Nearly 30 percent had booked hotels in at least two cities, while bookings involving stays in four or more cities surged 53 percent year on year.
For Yuan You, who works for an internet company, the 13-day break made it possible to split one holiday into two distinct stages. She planned to first spend three days in Jiuzhaigou, a UNESCO-listed scenic area in southwest China's Sichuan Province known for its turquoise lakes and waterfalls, before continuing to Chengdu for the remainder of the break.
"With such a long break, spending the whole time either resting or sightseeing can become monotonous, so I opted for a mix of both," Yuan said. In Chengdu, she chose to spend part of that extra time learning woodworking.
Longer breaks are encouraging people to travel farther. Flight bookings for journeys of more than 2,000 km rose 76 percent year on year during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day period, accounting for more than a quarter of all flight bookings, according to Meituan.
Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said the extended break has encouraged more people to start traveling earlier, spreading trips over a longer period rather than concentrating them within a few peak days. That, Wang said, could help sustain demand across tourism, accommodation and catering services for longer periods of time.
China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said that China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on Oct. 1, setting a new single-day record.
RICHER EXPERIENCES, MORE TO EXPLORE
The surge in mobility has translated into demand for richer experiences at destinations. At the National Maritime Museum of China in north China's Tianjin Municipality, 19,000 visitors streamed through the doors on the opening day of the National Day break.
Among the new draws is "Echoes of the Whale Song," the museum's first customized full-sensory virtual reality experience. Unlike conventional walk-through VR attractions, visitors remain seated as the experience unfolds around them, allowing for a more immersive encounter.
Under blue lights, visitors see a giant whale entangled in discarded fishing nets and take part in a virtual rescue, learning along the way about the impact of marine debris on ocean life.
Such experience-oriented products are gaining traction well beyond one museum. On Fliggy, Alibaba Group's online travel platform, domestic attraction ticket bookings on Oct. 1 rose nearly 30 percent year on year, while the number of users purchasing products for natural scenic areas and villages increased by nearly 50 percent.
Searches on Qunar for "immersive performances," "fireworks shows" and "night tours" also climbed more than 50 percent year on year.
The growing demand for interactive travel experiences can be seen at Changchun Zoological and Botanical Park in northeast China's Jilin Province. There, a nighttime immersive show inspired by the Chinese classic "Journey to the West" has drawn large crowds into a vibrant fantasy world, with costumed performers mingling with visitors and transforming the park into a stage after dark.
Yang Han, a researcher with Qunar's big data research institute, said travelers are increasingly setting out to "enter a story" rather than simply view static scenery, with content-driven experiences gaining popularity and bringing new opportunities to less traditional tourism destinations.
Bu Xiting, an associate researcher in the School of Cultural Industries Management at Communication University of China, contrasted the current trend with the previously popular "special forces-style tourism," a fast-paced form of travel in which people try to pack as many sights as possible into a short period, and city walks, which offer smaller-scale urban experiences during pockets of free time.
By linking public holidays with annual leave, travelers now have more time to shape their trips around what they want to experience, Bu said. Tourism consumption, Bu noted, is shifting from a focus on "time efficiency" toward greater "experience density." ■

Verstappen takes dominant pole for F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
17:56:02 CST
18:56:02 KST

by F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
SEPANG, Malaysia, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Max Verstappen claimed his first pole position of the 2026 Formula 1 season on Saturday with a dominant qualifying performance for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, as F1 returned to the Sepang International Circuit for the first time since 2017.
The Red Bull driver topped all three qualifying sessions and produced a best lap of one minute, 35.130 seconds in Q3, finishing 0.298 seconds clear of Lewis Hamilton.
Kimi Antonelli took third for Mercedes, ahead of Charles Leclerc and the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.
Red Bull's strong showing was underlined by Isack Hadjar setting the third-fastest time, though the Frenchman will start eighth after receiving a five-place grid penalty for fitting his seventh power unit of the season.
Verstappen had appeared the man to beat from the start of qualifying, topping Q1 in 1:36.477 before going fastest again in Q2, 0.263 seconds ahead of Antonelli. He led Hamilton by 0.308 seconds after the opening runs in Q3 before improving on his final attempt.
The Dutchman will now chase his first victory of the season at a circuit where he won the most recent F1 race nine years ago. That 2017 Malaysian Grand Prix victory was only the second of his career.
Antonelli managed third despite having only one fresh set of soft tyres available in Q3, while teammate and closest championship rival George Russell could manage only seventh.
Russell had dominated qualifying and the race at the previous round in Baku, but Mercedes struggled for pace at Sepang despite bringing a major upgrade package to Malaysia.
Pierre Gasly and Gabriel Bortoleto also impressed by reaching Q3, qualifying ninth and 10th respectively.
The return to Sepang, widely regarded as one of the standout circuits designed during F1's expansion into new venues around the turn of the century, came about because of upheaval to this year's calendar.
The Bahrain and Saudi Arabian Grands Prix had originally been scheduled for April but were canceled in March. Bahrain subsequently pushed for its Grand Prix to be staged elsewhere, with negotiations resulting in Sepang hosting the event.
Despite being held in Malaysia, the race has retained Bahrain's naming rights and is officially the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. The Bahrain Grand Prix trophy will be presented after Sunday's race and rosewater will be sprayed on the podium instead of champagne.
F1's return to Sepang has presented teams with a problem: extreme heat and an unusually abrasive track surface.
Track temperatures reached 57 degrees Celsius during qualifying, with Piastri comparing the experience to "driving on sandpaper."
The combination of tropical heat and the abrasive asphalt has produced severe tyre degradation, raising the prospect of a two- or even three-stop race on Sunday.
Several drivers were shown the black-and-white flag during qualifying for driving too slowly on their cool down laps as they attempted to protect and cool their tyres.
Both Aston Martins progressed from the opening session for the first time this season after a trying year, but Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll were eliminated in Q2 along with Liam Lawson, Carlos Sainz, Franco Colapinto and Arvid Lindblad.
Nico Hulkenberg, Oliver Bearman, Esteban Ocon, Alex Albon, Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez were the six drivers to be eliminated in Q1. ■

The Russians have developed a jet-powered version of the Garpiya strike drone.

“The Garpiya still has no mesh modems or cameras. Only INS + SNC and, occasionally, a laser sensor for air-to-air detonation,” said a source at ‘Colonel GSH.’

This will allow the occupiers to launch attack drones from virtually any location without using drone ports or airfields, which are regularly attacked by the Ukrainian Defense Forces in an effort to reduce Russian strike capabilities.
Russia is promoting an export version of the Garpiya-A1 strike UAV on the international market under the designation Garpiya-A1E.
The manufacturer claims to have sufficient capacity to fulfill both domestic and export orders simultaneously.
In addition, it is prepared not only to export the drones but also to localize their production in countries friendly to Russia.

"Flash": Russian repeaters may be operating in Kyiv to guide Shaheds
Kyiv • UNN
Serhii Beskrestnov suggested that 1–3 MESH repeaters are operating in Kyiv for short-term control of Shaheds. The theory is still being verified.
MESH radio repeaters may have been installed in Kyiv, which Russian forces use to create temporary communication channels with Shahed-type attack drones and adjust their flight immediately before an attack. This version was voiced by Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, the President’s adviser on the development of technological areas of defense and a radio technology specialist, reports UNN.
Details
According to the expert, a small number of such devices are involved, probably between one and three. He assumes that the repeaters may provide a short-term drone control channel as the drones approach their target.
"I now insist that the enemy’s MESH radio repeaters are being switched on in Kyiv, providing a temporary short-term control channel for Shaheds to adjust strikes. Not many. Perhaps 1–3," Beskrestnov wrote on social media.
In his view, such devices are difficult to detect, but they need to be sought out, since if they are present, countering the drones solely by means of electronic warfare may be insufficiently effective. As one of his arguments, the expert cited the strike on an SBU facility, noting that there were no other "Shaheds" nearby during the attack that could theoretically have performed the function of repeaters. He also said that he had analyzed strikes on Kyiv’s bridges and the possibility of creating long-range MESH channels from the territory of the russian federation.
At the same time, Beskrestnov emphasized that this was specifically his technical theory, which requires further verification.
The expert also drew attention to the circulation of photographs of air-defense systems on Kyiv’s bridges in Russian information resources. According to him, it is practically impossible to completely conceal such systems from observation because of the large flow of people. He added that without stable online control right up to the moment of impact, it is difficult to hit narrow structures precisely, including bridge supports or stay cables.
Beskrestnov added that specialists are carefully examining the wreckage of downed Russian drones; however, according to him, they have not yet detected any other unknown communications equipment, including LTE or systems such as "Rassvet."

Earlier, UNN reported that Russia uses repeaters for UAVs in Belarus.

Publishers say using AI to translate classics is ethically wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:50:00 UTC
18:50:00 KST

Publishers say using AI to translate classics is ethically wrong
Publishers Krista Kaer and Piret Lemetti warn that AI-assisted re-translations of literary classics appearing on the market are unethical, unfair to readers, and devalue the work of human translators.
Varrak Editor-in-Chief Kaer said that the overall situation for translated literature in Estonia has not improved from the viewpoint of publishers.
"Print runs of books have dropped sharply, and translated literature is expensive to publish. In addition to purchasing rights, there is the translation cost, which is very significant for larger books. Overall, the amount of valuable translated literature has decreased. With the classics, everything is fine — the Hieronymus series publishes books very nicely, and what should have appeared long ago is well covered. However, the situation is bad with contemporary quality literature," Kaer admitted.
"Books are published that are more or less a sure bet. There is nothing to be done; a large part of the world is still uncovered for Estonians, and this situation will not change in the near future either. The Cultural Endowment helps, thank God," Kaer laughed.
"I look with great envy at the French and Germans, where very important works published all over the world appear very quickly and continuously. In Estonia, books that appear quickly tend to belong to the field of entertainment and crime fiction," she noted.
Eesti Raamat Editor-in-Chief Piret Lemetti agreed.
"Often you look at a book that you would very much like to publish, but you know that publishing it would be a very big risk. Especially if it is English-language literature, because people read a lot in English. If you cannot publish the book at the same time it appears in English, then you have already missed the train," Lemetti admitted.
"The share of translations from English is decreasing in other European countries as well because many people read in English. For Estonia, translating literature published in the Nordic countries is becoming more important, as is Central Europe. Of course, Asia is still half-undiscovered for us. South Korean literature is currently making a huge breakthrough, but we simply do not have enough translators," Kaer added.
"It is also very difficult to introduce unfamiliar foreign names to Estonian readers because there is a deep distrust — people prefer to take a book by a well-known author or at least someone who can be associated with something," Kaer noted.
Lemetti added that a point of comparison is crucial for readers. "If readers cannot associate authors with someone or something, they are not very inclined to buy the book," she said.
"If print runs drop by another couple hundred, there will actually be no point in publishing these books anymore," Kaer said, expressing hope that books people hesitate to buy will still be borrowed from libraries, provided libraries have enough money to purchase them.
"At the same time, all agents are gradually raising author fees and translation-rights fees. One can fight this and negotiate down, but these costs are becoming higher and higher. For some reason, there is an opinion that books are being bought more and more and publishers are doing better and better, which of course is not true," Kaer laughed.
The publishers added that exciting niche works remain untranslated because, in Estonia, their target audience would only be 300 to 400 people.
At the same time, older translations are also being updated. Varrak has published Dostoevsky texts, and Kaer herself has retranslated Yeats.
"These are probably needed, but new mystical translations have appeared — for example, of Conan Doyle — that are clearly made with artificial assistance and are completely terrible. Such things are very bad: taking classics to which copyright no longer applies and for which one does not have to pay, and then simply throwing them onto the market in a way that they cannot even be called translations or books," Kaer warned.
Lemetti added that she has encountered such books herself. "It is actually written on the title page that artificial intelligence assistance has been used in translation. I do not understand why this has been done," she noted.
Kaer believes the driver is a quick cash grab.
"This is unfair toward the author, and it is unfair toward buyers and readers. Doing such things is simply ethically wrong," Kaer said.
"This is also the devaluation of the translator's work. Essentially, the translator is reduced to a glorified editor. I do not understand what the point of this is," Lemetti added.
--

An attack by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) killed more than 25 civilians in the Umm Badr area of Sudan's North Kordofan state, according to the Sudan Doctors Network.
In a Saturday statement, the non-governmental network said a video circulating online shows RSF members executing civilians in the area.
The gravity of the incident is compounded by indications that the killings were carried out on ethnic grounds, under the pretext of accusing the victims of siding with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), the statement said.
"The unlawful execution of civilians constitutes a grave crime and a flagrant violation of international humanitarian law and human rights standards,” the network said.

The doctors urged the UN and rights groups to launch an independent investigation and hold those responsible accountable.
The RSF did not immediately comment on the statement. However, the group typically maintain that they do not target civilians—a claim disputed by Sudanese authorities and international human rights groups.
Sudanese army retakes nearly a dozen areas
The Sudanese army has made advances across large parts of North Kordofan recently, following fighting with the RSF and announced that it has taken control of 11 areas in the state.
Since late July, the SAF has taken control of large areas of North Kordofan after retaking the strategic city of Bara, as well as the areas of Jabra al Sheikh and Umm Siyala, and securing the national road linking Bara with Omdurman, west of the capital Khartoum.
The three states of the Kordofan region—North, West and South—have witnessed clashes between the SAF and the RSF since last October.
Sudan has been embroiled in a war between the Sudanese army and the RSF since 2023, which has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Flavio Bolsonaro: In the name of the father, sons, and holy ideology
