Flavio Bolsonaro: In the name of the father, sons, and holy ideology
The first round of Brazil’s presidential election on Sunday pits two well-known names in the political ring: Lula vs. Bolsonaro. But it’s not former president Jair Bolsonaro facing off against the incumbent head of state – it’s his eldest son, Flavio Bolsonaro. He’s less charismatic than his father but just as ideologically radical as the family patriarch.
Will “Son No. 1” become the second president from the Bolsonaro family? Flavio, the eldest of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro’s five children, is neck-and-neck in the polls with incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva as the country heads to the polls Sunday in the first round of the presidential election.
Jair Bolsonaro is likely following his 45-year-old son’s campaign closely. For the patriarch, this is not just a matter of family pride. Sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison after his convicting for plotting a coup following his 2022 election defeat, the former president is surely rooting for his son. “Bolsonaro Junior”, the Liberal Party’s candidate, has promised to grant his dad a pardon as soon as he assumes Brazil’s highest office.
But first, the eldest son must defeat incumbent President Lula. That is not a foregone conclusion.
Brand Bolsonaro
Flavio Bolsonaro is widely considered a shadow of his father. He is not a “charismatic and popular leader", said Andreza Aruska, director of the Brazil Institute at King’s College London. “He’s not a great orator either and he can come across as lacking in self-confidence,” added Corneel Weyers, a Brazil specialist at the Paris-based Center for International Studies (CERI) at Sciences Po.
While he is running under the Bolsonaro banner, the son has also had to maintain some distance from his convicted and jailed father on the campaign trail. “Jair Bolsonaro is no longer as popular, and slightly more than half the population believes he should serve his full sentence,” noted Georg Walter Wink, a Latin America specialist at the University of Copenhagen who has studied the foundations of Brazil’s far right.
But it’s still the power of the family name that has managed to catapult Flavio Bolsonaro into a statistical dead heat with Lula in the opinion polls.
At the official launch of his campaign in July, an AI-generated video of his jailed father endorsing the son was screened on stage. The video sparked a storm, with Brazil’s Supreme Court demanding an explanation about the appearance of the AI clone of Jair Bolsonaro, who is barred from making public statements while serving his sentence. The former president had to deny authorising the use of his image and voice for the deepfake video.
Read moreBrazil's Jair Bolsonaro denies authorizing deepfake for election message
Opting for a legally risky video screening in a country where the use of deep fakes is as widespread as it is strictly regulated does not exactly signal a break with Bolsonaro senior.
Watch moreFocus: What's real and what's fake? How AI is impacting Brazil's election race
But Flavio Bolsonaro is no stranger to public scrutiny. Last month, it emerged that Candidate Bolsonaro was under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering linked to the upcoming film “Dark Horse”. He is accused of seeking funding for the biopic glorifying his father, played by Jim Caviezel, a US actor linked to far-right circles. The film was originally scheduled for a September 11 release, but it was postponed indefinitely.
Political schizophrenia
Flavio Bolsonaro actually has little choice but to campaign on the strength of his family name. “He has almost nothing else to legitimise his candidacy,” noted Aruska.
In a political environment as polarised as Brazil’s, he “cannot afford to truly distance himself from his father without the risk of losing votes among his electoral base, which would accuse him of betraying ‘Bolsonarism’”, said Chris Lyon, a Brazil specialist at the University of Birmingham.
In Brazil, it is also perfectly natural to claim affiliation with a political dynasty. “People often talk about the three ‘B’s – Bible, bullets, and beef to describe the major [conservative] political blocs,” said Wink, referring to the Christian Evangelicals, the military, and landowners. “But there is also a fourth: family,” he noted.
During his campaign, Flavio Bolsonaro engaged in a balancing act between showcasing his father’s legacy and distinguishing himself from the patriarch that smacked of political schizophrenia. While he claimed to have his father’s support and blessing, the son also “removed his name from several campaign materials in recent months", noted Weyers.
He is also “much less blunt in his manner of speaking, and unlike his father, Flavio Bolsonaro avoids any misogynistic or homophobic remarks; he is also careful not to be as aggressive towards the press", explained Wink.
There is also a shift in tone in the way he presents himself. Whereas Jair Bolsonaro “played the role of the angry outsider challenging the system, the son is more willing to don the mantle of a mainstream politician who favours compromise and knows how to build coalitions", said Lyon.
The question now is whether Flavio Bolsonaro is willing to politically “kill” his father to make Bolsonarism appear more respectable. In reality, the far-right candidate is responding to “a tactical imperative to expand his electoral base,” said Aruska. While the extreme political polarisation has certainly whittled down the ranks of undecided voters in Brazil, “there are still some left, and Flavio Bolsonaro is primarily seeking to win over a segment of women who haven’t yet made up their minds", explained Lyon. It’s no coincidence, in fact, that he often makes public appearances with his wife, Fernanda Bolsonaro.
A family affair
But the imaging upgrade is “pure media spin", according to Weyers. “We must be careful not to give in to the temptation to believe that Flavio Bolsonaro is more moderate than his father,” he said. “The ideological substance is exactly the same.”
The 2026 Flavio Bolsonaro campaign is a sort of “family joint venture to bring Bolsonarism back to power", said Aruska. Behind Flavio are his younger brothers. “There is a very clear division of labour within the clan: Carlos plays the role of the pit bull on social media; Eduardo, who has gone into exile in the US, is responsible for forging international ties with other far-right movements; and Flavio was chosen to lead the campaign because he comes across as the most diplomatic member of the family,” explained Wink.
Flavio Bolsonaro’s political career also demonstrates that he is ideologically in perfect alignment with his father. As a state senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019, “he has championed the same values as his father — he promotes a highly repressive security policy, defends family values, advocates an economic policy inspired by the model implemented by Javier Milei in Argentina, and opposes any environmental regulations,” said Lyon.
As a Congressman, Flavio Bolsonaro was implicated in a number of scandals. He is notably accused of having close ties to the “milicias", paramilitary groups made up of former law enforcement officers. Senator Bolsonaro was also linked to a case involving the embezzlement of civil servants’ salaries, which was closed in 2025 without convictions.
The stakes for Brazil’s democracy are even higher in this presidential election, said Weyers. “The first time with Jair Bolsonaro, we wondered how seriously we should take him. This time, we know. And the fact that Flavio Bolsonaro presents a more technocratic profile makes the threat even greater.”
Lyon agreed. “His ability to negotiate and play the game of alliances could make him even more effective at advancing the Bolsonarism agenda,” he warned.

Russia’s Shturm robotic tank debut ends stuck in the mud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:47:58 UTC
18:47:58 KST

- Russia's Shturm uncrewed tank repeatedly lost its control link at Tsentr-2026 and was driven by a crew driver for Putin's demonstration.
- The vehicle still got stuck in mud, and armor expert Andrei Tarasenko said its engine compartment and turret roof are nearly unprotected from drones.
Russia’s new Shturm uncrewed tank failed in its first major outing, losing its control link again and again during the Tsentr-2026 strategic exercise and finally getting stuck in mud, even with a human driver at the controls.
The remotely operated vehicle, built on a T-72 tank chassis, repeatedly dropped the radio link that connects it to its separate control vehicle during the drills at the Chebarkul training range in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region, Russian sources said. For the demonstration in front of President Vladimir Putin, the tank was not driven remotely at all. A crew driver-mechanic took the controls because of fears of a technical failure.
Even that did not save the show. A photo from the exercise shows the Shturm tilted nose-down in a muddy ditch beside a dirt track, its tracks and front hull sunk into the soil.
The failure comes after Russia presented the system as one of the highlights of Tsentr-2026. The Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 2 that Putin had been shown the new uncrewed combat vehicles, built on the T-72B3M chassis in tank and BMPT versions, and that they provided fire support to assault units during the main stage of the drills, The Defence Blog reported.
The Shturm heavy robotic assault system, developed by Uralvagonzavod, pairs remotely controlled combat vehicles with a crewed control vehicle that also sits on a tank chassis. The main version carries a shortened 125 mm gun for urban fighting, a bulldozer blade and extra armor against shoulder-fired anti-tank weapons. Operators steer each vehicle from inside the control vehicle, which has to stay within a few kilometers to keep the link.
Russian armor expert Andrei Tarasenko said the vehicle has several technical flaws, including an engine compartment and turret roof that are almost unprotected. Those are the areas drones most often target when attacking armored vehicles in Ukraine.
He also questioned the whole concept.
“The idea of this vehicle seems unsuccessful to me: dependence on a command post that has to be 3 to 4 kilometers away and in direct line of sight. Without proper communications like Starlink, or something similar, there is no point in such a vehicle,” said Andrei Tarasenko.
The link problem goes to the core of the system. Without a stable signal, the Shturm cannot fight as an uncrewed vehicle, and the crew in the control vehicle still has to stay close to the front line in an armored vehicle of its own. On the battlefield in Ukraine, both sides jam drones and ground robots daily, which makes a steady radio link even harder to hold than on a training range.
Uralvagonzavod began work on Shturm around 2018. The first test vehicle was spotted at the company’s plant in Nizhny Tagil in July 2025, with a crew on board.

Ukrainian woman detained in Kazakhstan after alleged FSB trap over grandson's return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:46:31 UTC
18:46:31 KST

Ukrainian woman detained in Kazakhstan after alleged FSB trap over grandson's return
Kazakh authorities detained Ukrainian citizen Liubov Rozhanska at Astana airport at the request of Russian authorities, her lawyer, Alexei Pryanishnikov, told The Insider, an independent Russian investigative outlet, on Oct. 2.
She had traveled to Kazakhstan to collect her eight-year-old grandson and bring him back to his father in Odesa under an agreement reached in advance with the boy's Russian relatives.
According to Pryanishnikov, the boy is on Ukraine's list of children abducted by Russia. Ukraine’s Supreme Court ruled in 2025 that he should be handed over to his father.
Rozhanska arrived in Astana on a flight from Istanbul on Oct. 1 and was detained immediately upon landing. The Russian request was reportedly conveyed through the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), a Moscow-led security alliance that includes Kazakhstan.
According to the lawyer, the case dates back to 2021, when it began as a family dispute. Alla Andreeva (née Sochnik), a Ukrainian citizen, was living in Odesa with her son, who was born in 2018 during a previous marriage.
She married Russian sailor Vitaly Andreev in 2020. Pryanishnikov said Andreev pressured her to move to Russia. In August 2021, Andreeva traveled with her son and husband to Kaliningrad to visit his parents. They never returned to Ukraine.
According to Pryanishnikov, the boy's father had agreed to the trip on the condition that his son be returned. After repeated delays, Andreeva renounced Ukrainian citizenship for herself and her son in 2022, and both later obtained Russian citizenship.
The father's attempts to maintain contact with his son led to court proceedings in Kaliningrad. Pryanishkov said psychologists opposed contact because the father was Ukrainian. A court eventually allowed the father, a Ukrainian serviceman, to visit his son during summer holidays, but only in Kaliningrad Region.
In 2023, an agreement was reached to return the boy to Ukraine, but two Ukrainians who traveled to Kaliningrad to collect him were detained, accused of attempted abduction and espionage, and sentenced to 15 and 16 years in prison. A Russian court also named Rozhanska as the alleged organizer of the "abduction."
Talks over returning the child to his father in Ukraine resumed in summer 2026, Pryanishnikov said. He now believes the negotiations were conducted under FSB control, citing the Russian family's insistence on Kazakhstan, repeated delays to the handover, and the fact that the meeting in Astana was scheduled at the same time a Kaliningrad court, at the FSB's request, ordered Rozhanska's arrest in absentia.
"Everything suggests she was being lured there," Pryanishkov said.
The lawyer said the case could ultimately result in Kazakhstan extraditing a Ukrainian citizen to Russia for the first time since the full-scale invasion began.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry press service told journalists in a chat on Oct. 2 that the Ukrainian Embassy in Kazakhstan had asked the Kazakh authorities not to grant Russia's extradition request immediately after learning of Rozhanska's detention.
Ukrainian consular officials also requested permission to visit Rozhanska, who is currently being held in a detention center, and received preliminary approval, the ministry said.
Russia has abducted tens of thousands of Ukrainian children since the start of the full-scale invasion. As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation, though Ukrainian officials estimate the real total could number in the hundreds of thousands.

Elections to Latvia’s 15th Saeima take place in Latvia and abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:42:23 UTC
18:42:23 KST

On Saturday, 3 October, elections to Latvia’s 15th Saeima are taking place in Latvia and abroad, with voters electing 100 members of parliament for the next four years.
There are five constituencies in the Saeima elections: Riga (38 seats), Vidzeme (26 seats), Latgale (12 seats), Kurzeme (11 seats) and Zemgale (13 seats). Voters abroad cast their ballots for candidate lists in the Riga constituency. As in previous elections, voters may vote at any polling station.
On election day, polling stations in Latvia and abroad will be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time. Latvian citizens aged 18 and over are eligible to vote. Voters must bring a valid Latvian citizen’s passport or national identity card (eID card). Further information about voting procedures at polling stations is available here.
“Every vote is equally important. Our task is to ensure a secure and transparent election process so that every voter can express their choice freely and by secret ballot. I encourage Latvian citizens, both in Latvia and abroad, to exercise their right to vote and take part in the elections,” said Māris Zviedris, Chair of the Central Election Commission (CVK).
Polling station addresses, opening hours and information about accessibility for people with mobility impairments are available at iecirkni.cvk.lv. An additional 82 off-site voting locations will also be available on election day.
In Latvia, votes cast in the Saeima elections will be counted manually at polling stations during the evening and overnight after voting closes. Results will be available at cvk.lv.
At the polling station, each voter will receive a set of ballot papers and a stamped ballot envelope. Alone in a voting booth or screened area, the voter must select the ballot paper for one candidate list. They may leave it unchanged or indicate their preferences regarding individual candidates by filling in the oval in the “PAR” (“FOR”) column if they particularly support a candidate’s election, or in the “PRET” (“AGAINST”) column if they oppose it. Candidates’ names and surnames should not be crossed out. The selected ballot paper must be placed inside the ballot envelope, which must then be sealed and deposited in the ballot box.
Voters who cannot attend a polling station for health reasons, as well as carers of people who are ill, may apply to vote at their current location. The CVK encourages voters to submit a written application in good time, preferably by noon on 3 October. Applications received later will be fulfilled if the polling station commission can reach the voter before voting closes.
If a voter has already cast an advance ballot but votes again on election day, only the most recent vote will be counted.
After voting closes, polling station commissions will begin counting ballots. Votes will be counted manually at open commission meetings, which authorised observers and media representatives may attend. Preliminary results will be published progressively as vote-counting data are received from polling stations.
Further information about the elections is available on the CVK website, cvk.lv, and by calling the information line on +371 67019999.

"The Ombudsman's Office carries out the return of Ukrainian children from deportation, forced displacement, and foreign countries in cases where documents are missing and there are various legal aspects. After all, an independent trip to Russia or an attempt to pick up a child through third countries can create serious risks for the relatives themselves and jeopardize the further return of the child!" Lubinets summarized.

Drones Strike Russian Tsymbulovo Jet-UAV Base in Oryol

Can anything politicians say at Sunday’s election stop young people from leaving Bosnia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:35:06 UTC
18:35:06 KST

On a perfect October morning in Sarajevo, the motivation for young people to be leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina in droves is not immediately apparent. The country’s capital is basking in the autumn sunshine and the pavement cafes in the shadow of the Sacred Heart Cathedral are packed. People lingering over coffee and cigarettes mix peacefully with the Swedish football fans in town for their team’s Nations League match.
But Sarajevo’s many charms have not been enough to keep young people in Bosnia. One local organisation that tracks emigration estimated that more than 600,000 people had left the country in the decade after the 2013 census, when the official population was 3.5 million.
“If I weren’t optimistic, maybe I would also move out,” said Timur Ilic, a 28-year-old municipal councillor in Sarajevo, who is standing on Sunday for election to the cantonal government. He represents Our Party – a multi-ethnic, non-nationalist, liberal movement that he admits faces a struggle to appeal to voters in a country dominated by ethnonationalist parties.
“People are not ready for a significant change,” he said. “They’re afraid of uncertainty. I think there needs to be a new generation which doesn’t understand why people are willing to put up with this situation and who are willing to maybe vote for us to try something different.”
The problem for Our Party – and other non-nationalist movements – is that the young people who make up their support base are voting with their feet, rather than making their mark on ballot papers. In theory, Sunday’s vote should be one of the great European festivals of democracy, with the election of no fewer than 14 prime ministers and five presidents. But the plethora of posts on offer reflects a fiendishly complicated system of governance.
The Dayton agreement’s creation of two powerful regional “entities” – with a weaker central government – was intended as a stopgap to ensure peace after the ruinous conflict of the 1990s. Instead, it has perpetuated the divisions in the country. Most Serbs live in the Republika Srpska (RS), while the Federation is home to most of Bosnia’s Croats and Bosniak Muslims. There is no incentive for the ethnonationalist leaders to change that situation – or to appeal to young people who see a brighter future outside the country.
“They don’t want young people to be interested, and young people are not interested in politics,” said Sarah Ćato, gesturing over her shoulder to a banner of the unsmiling leader of the Bosniak SDA party looming over the cafe tables in central Sarajevo. The 19-year-old student of political science and international relations is eligible to vote on Sunday for the first time – but she says that her age group feels unseen by the political mainstream.
“Young people don’t know how to vote or who to vote for because nobody’s standing for us,” she said, adding that the reluctance to engage in politics reflects its status as a “taboo subject” after the end of the conflict in 1995. “I think educating youth from middle school on how to be a good citizen should be mandatory.”
But there seems little chance of that happening, given that Bosnian children learn different versions of their country’s recent history depending on whether they are Serbs, Bosniaks or Croats. Indeed, the curriculum in the RS now celebrates Radovan Karadzic and the late Ratko Mladić – both convicted of genocide by an international tribunal in The Hague – as “national heroes”.
East Sarajevo is just a short drive from the centre of the capital – but it is on the other side of the “entity line” that divides the Federation from the RS. The road signs are written in Serbian Cyrillic, and young people grow up “surrounded by murals of war criminals”, as 23-year-old local resident Dijana Papaz put it. She worked on an exhibition with Sarah Ćato called What If the Border Is Within You?, looking at the divisions between Sarajevo and East Sarajevo – and how young people overcome them.
Papaz rejects ethnic labels, referring to herself as “Bosnian”, but she concedes that the glorification of Mladić following his death in August reflects both enduring divisions and the need for change.
“We need to do something about our constitution, because Dayton wasn’t supposed to last 30 years,” she said. “It was supposed to be a temporary thing after the war while we made the country better, but that never happened.”
People born since 1995 may have no memories of the conflict or its causes, but they do hear plenty about it from family members. And Ajna Mešić from the Youth Initiative for Human Rights says the continuing exodus of Bosnia’s brightest prospects can also be put down to pressure at home.
“Our parents tell us to go,” she said. “Growing up, my destiny was to be a lawyer in Germany. Then somewhere in high school, I remembered I have free will. But a lot of parents will tell you that they fought the war for nothing and they don’t want us also to live here.”
Young faces were thin on the ground at a pre-election rally for the non-nationalist Social Democratic party (SDP) opposite Sarajevo’s historic city hall, with red flares reflecting off the Miljacka River as party activists put on a show. But 23-year-old Benjamin Ahmedbegovic, the vice-president of the local branch of the SDP’s youth forum, admitted he did not expect the polls to change the country’s situation – or the propensity of its young people to leave.
“Political instability has been one of the main drivers of migration from Bosnia and Herzegovina,” he said, pointing to the phenomenon of people “voting for their own” as an aggravating factor. “Everyone just wants someone who has the same ethnic label to be in power, rather than judging whether they do something well or not.”
That means the elections are unlikely to bring any surprises – or any reasons to make young Bosnians who are thinking of leaving change their minds. They may, as Ilic puts it, “miss the coffee”. But they certainly will not feel the same way about the divisive politics that leave their country stuck in the past.

In Russia, military exercises rehearsed the seizure of territories and the creation of a &quot;security zone&quot; outside the country
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:34:44 EEST
18:34:44 KST

In Russia, military exercises rehearsed the seizure of territories and the creation of a "security zone" outside the country
Kyiv • UNN
Russia and its allies conducted exercises involving the seizure of territories and the creation of a security zone outside the country. 47,000 military personnel took part.
Russia, as part of the Center-2026 military exercises, which it is conducting with the participation of, among others, China, practiced the "creation of a security zone" on the territory of a neighboring state. This was reported by Vazhnyye Istorii, UNN writes.
Details
Russia involved fewer units in the exercises than previously. The exercises are taking place from October 28 to October 3. They involve 47,000 personnel and 2,000 pieces of military equipment, 90 aircraft, and 77 ships and vessels. Six countries—Belarus, China, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Tajikistan—sent their military contingents; Kazakhstan and Congo are present in the form of operational groups.
The Kremlin stated that units not participating in the war in Ukraine were involved in the exercises. This is likely why significantly fewer service members are taking part than in previous years, the publication notes.
Previously, similar exercises were held in 2019 and 2015, with 128,000 and 95,000 service members participating, respectively.
"As part of the exercises, they practiced not only repelling a strike, but also capturing foreign territories," the publication writes.
"The main objective of the exercise is to improve the skills of the command staff of headquarters at all levels in managing troops while repelling external aggression," said Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin, who, according to the Kremlin, attended the exercises.
He emphasized that all tasks are being addressed with consideration for the experience of conducting the war in Ukraine.
Officially, the exercises train the repelling of aggression in the Central Asian direction and the provision of security in the Caspian region, the publication writes.
At the same time, Russian Deputy Defense Minister Yunus-Bek Yevkurov, reporting to Putin on the course of the exercises, said that the troops were not only practicing repelling a strike, but also the "creation of a security zone in adjacent territories."
"The coalition grouping of troops and forces is repelling the main strike in the South Ural direction, has restored the situation, and has been conducting offensive operations since October 2 to liberate the captured territory and create a security zone in the adjacent territory," he said.
The exercises, the publication notes, are taking place against the backdrop of an unprecedented deterioration in relations between Russia and European countries. This week it became known that Russia sent NATO an informal memorandum threatening to use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to blockade the Kaliningrad region.
NATO responded to Russia's nuclear threat over Kaliningrad30.09.26, 16:30 • 5746 views
"This is the first time since the Cold War that Russia has threatened us in this way. Therefore, it is serious," a high-ranking Reuters source in the defense ministry of one of the European countries said.
Putin's press secretary, Dmitry Peskov, said that the exercises were planned and were not related to challenges near Russia's borders.

The reports came as the first flight carrying Israelis home from the United Arab Emirates landed in Tel Aviv after services were suspended following the attack, according to Israel's airport authority website.
"The co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist act" and had "attacked the captain in the cockpit with the emergency axe and tried to take control of the aircraft", WAM quoted UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi as saying, referring to initial findings of an investigation.
The co-pilot is still in custody in the UAE. Multiple media outlets overnight identified him as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami and said he had been banned from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views.
During the flydubai flight, the plane's Indian captain was assaulted by the co-pilot but the captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the attacker and force an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Passengers described rushing the cockpit and a fight for control after the plane plummeted -- losing around 17,000 feet of altitude in the span of a minute, according to the Flightradar24 website.
'Radical indoctrination'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed the suspect had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination" and had attempted to crash the plane.
The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that Omani authorities had banned the pilot from flying over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views, citing people familiar with the matter.
CNN, citing two sources familiar with the matter, reported the pilot was removed from a job at Oman's national airline last year over concerns about extremist views.
Al Arabiya, citing an informed source, also reported that Omani authorities determined that the co-pilot held extremist views.
The broadcaster said he had spent time in Syria, raising concerns he may have been influenced by radical groups there.
ABC News, citing senior intelligence and law enforcement officials familiar with the investigation, reported the suspect had allegedly been found in possession of extremist materials while he was a trainee.
US President Donald Trump warned on Thursday that if Iran was found to be linked to the attack the country would be "hit very hard".
Netanyahu has said Israel would check how he had been cleared to work on flights to the country.

On Friday, 2 October, Raivis Bremšmits, State Secretary at Latvia’s Ministry of Economics, met with Ieva Jāgere, Director of the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), to review progress during the first nine months of 2026 in attracting investment and using state financing and capital instruments, as well as the results of LIAA’s trade missions to Germany and the United States.
During the first nine months of 2026, the total value of investment projects attracted by LIAA reached €886.8 million, equivalent to nearly 90% of its investment attraction target for the year. This figure represents the total planned value of the projects secured. Actual investments are made gradually, with implementation taking between one and five years, depending on the project. The projects cover energy, real estate, defence and dual-use technologies, financial technology, logistics and other sectors.
“In nine months, we have reached nearly 90% of our annual investment attraction target. This means that most of the work planned for the year has already been completed. Equally significant is the fact that investment projects are being implemented across various sectors of the economy, while state financing instruments are helping companies undertake increasingly large and strategically important projects,” said Raivis Bremšmits, State Secretary at the Ministry of Economics.
The trade mission to Germany, led by Minister of Economics Viktors Valainis, brought together 54 Latvian companies and organisations. During the mission, work continued on advancing German companies’ investment projects in Latvia worth more than €600 million. A memorandum of understanding was also signed between LIAA, the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK) and the German-Baltic Chamber of Commerce (AHK). It provides Latvian companies with access to contacts and services through Germany’s international chamber network at 150 locations in more than 90 countries, as well as the establishment of a Latvian export support contact point at AHK.
Meanwhile, 44 Latvian companies and organisations participated in the trade mission to the United States. Memoranda of cooperation were signed in defence technology and genomics, and discussions began on new research, investment, manufacturing and export projects. The mission strengthened cooperation with US companies, investors and research institutions, creating opportunities to expand Latvian exports and attract new investment.
“LIAA will continue to focus on developing concrete investment and export opportunities. We will help Latvian companies strengthen their position in foreign markets and support investors in implementing projects in Latvia. The results achieved in nine months demonstrate that focused work with companies and investors delivers results. The agreements reached during the missions to Germany and the United States open up opportunities for Latvian companies to join international supply chains and develop technologies alongside foreign partners. The priority now is to turn these agreements into joint projects and export deals,” said LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere.
Financing instruments offered by the development finance institution ALTUM also make a significant contribution to the implementation of major investment projects. Across four funding rounds, the Large Investment Fund has approved 36 investment projects worth €894.7 million. These projects are expected to create 1,645 new jobs, increase exports by €516.2 million and generate an additional €668 million in tax revenue by 2035.

UAE says FlyDubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe in “terrorist” act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:27:47 UTC
18:27:47 KST

The FlyDubai co-pilot who nearly crashed the Tel-Aviv bound flight is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami. He was barred from flying by Oman amid concerns he showed signs of extremist views. The incident threw the already hard-hit regional travel industry into crisis.
The co-pilot accused of attacking the captain of an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight used a crash axe against the captain and “attempted to carry out a terrorist attack”, the United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said on Saturday, while the UAE president's diplomatic adviser Dr Anwar Gargash called the incident "a dangerous terrorist act". A crash axe is a tool in the cockpit for the pilots to use in an emergency.
In the first comments by Emirati investigators on Saturday, UAE prosecutor general Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said the co-pilot of FlyDubai flight FZ1073 tried to take control of the aircraft and that the investigation continues “to uncover all the circumstances of the incident, its motives, and related connections, in addition to completing technical examinations and examining physical and digital evidence”, according to UAE state news agency WAM.
The co-pilot who nearly crashed the Tel-Aviv bound flight with 182 people aboard is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami, according to Associated Press’ sources who also reported, alongside the Wall Street Journal, that he was banned from flying by Oman over concerns that he held radical ideological views. The UAE and FlyDubai did not publicly identify the co-pilot yet as their investigations continue.
The co-pilot was then hired by UAE-based airline FlyDubai, a source told the Associated Press. A FlyDubai spokesperson said on Saturday that the incident was still under investigation, without releasing further details.
The co-pilot was born in the UAE and worked with Oman’s national airline but was removed from flying because of concerns that he showed signs of extremist views, the AP reported quoted officials, and he was moved to an administrative job at Oman Air. Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted. Oman did not yet comment on the incident.
How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning, being allowed to fly the sensitive route to Israel is a central question for investigators. Israel says has it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don’t maintain diplomatic relations with it. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.
Both the captain and the co-pilot were taken to the UAE after their immediate medical treatment in Saudi Arabia as the UAE is leading the investigation. Security agencies from four regional countries including Israel were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments, according to the AP.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalization,” but provided no evidence. He said Israeli investigators were looking into whether the co-pilot acted alone and that anyone involved would pay "a heavy price".
The FlyDubai captain, Indian national Smit Machchhar, who suffered wounds to his head, hands and neck, told India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modhi in an emotional video from his hospital bed in Saudi Arabia that he used his remaining energy while being attacked to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to come in, subdue the co-pilot and stabilise the plane.
Hailed as a global hero for saving the passengers, the 17-year aviation veteran said "I was fighting for my life," adding that "when I was lying on the floor I could feel the aircraft was going down. I knew exactly that this would be the last push. I told myself that if I didn't get up, there would be a problem. I managed to open the door, and then everyone else came in."
Passengers who entered the cockpit described scenes of blood everywhere, while a phone video showed Machchhar covered in blood on the floor while being helped by passengers and crew. The passengers arriving in the cockpit subdued the co-pilot and stabilised the plane, while a back-up pilot on the flight then made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia with a damaged rudder as part of it broke off during the steep descent during the pilots fight in the cockpit.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said “the Indian pilot at FlyDubai, Smit Machchhar, deserves every bit of appreciation, for he embodied the meaning of courage and responsibility in the face of a dangerous terrorist act and a potential disaster. His professionalism and moral sense in the darkest of circumstances make him a true hero.”
“Far from the easy reduction of what happened or the adoption and promotion of conspiracy theories, vigilance and caution remain essential in confronting the risks of extremism and terrorism,“ Gargash added.
Amid shock and disbelief within the UAE’s sprawling pilots community, the attack left the region’s travel industry in crisis, raising questions about aviation security and further unsettling a Middle East already shaken by the US-Iran war.
The UAE cancelled all flights to Israel, while Israel’s El Al airline cancelled its scheduled flights to the UAE following the incident. Israel and the UAE agreed on repatriation flights to bring back passengers.

G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel, will it curb prices?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:27:38 UTC
18:27:38 KST

G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel, will it curb prices?
Global energy prices have soared due to the US and Israel’s war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine.
The Group of Seven (G7) countries have agreed to release 100 billion barrels of crude oil and diesel from emergency reserves over several months in an effort to reduce soaring energy prices after pressure from United States President Donald Trump.
The US and Israel’s war on Iran, as well as Russia’s war on Ukraine, have triggered a spike in global oil and diesel prices.
“The emergency release by G7 members will put some downward pressure on prices, particularly global diesel prices. However, the impact would be short-lived given that this is just a temporary solution to the supply crunch,” Hamad Hussain, a climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told Al Jazeera.
Oil prices jumped on Thursday and settled up more than $4 a barrel. Global diesel prices also hit a record high last Friday with the average price for a gallon (3.79 litres) of diesel at $6.50, up from $5.61 a month earlier, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
In a statement on Thursday, the G7, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the US, with the European Union also represented, said there will also be a “substantial diesel release within the first 20 days” and discussions over “additional diesel releases as necessary” will be held in the coming days.
Will the G7’s energy release stabilise the global energy market?
Here’s what we know:
What has the G7 announced?
After a video conference of G7 leaders chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday, the group said in a joint statement: “Taking into account commitments that have already been fulfilled, we will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels.”
Earlier this week, the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Executive Director Fatih Birol said that members had released about two-thirds of the 400-million-barrel agreement.
The G7 energy release will begin immediately and last for four months and will include a substantial diesel release for 20 days. It is not clear how many oil and diesel stocks each member of the group will release.
“We will convene in the context of the IEA in the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary,” the statement said.
“We will coordinate maintenance schedules across G7 refineries to prevent simultaneous capacity shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where feasible,” it added.
The G7 also urged member countries to refrain from imposing export restrictions on energy products among themselves.
Earlier this week, the Trump administration had threatened to impose a ban on US diesel exports and also pressured Europe to release its emergency diesel stocks to help ease soaring diesel prices.
Why are oil and diesel prices so high?
Global energy prices have been soaring due to the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which has disrupted energy exports from the Gulf. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy installations have also disrupted global energy supplies.
The former head of the International Energy Agency’s Oil Industry and Markets Division, Neil Atkinson, told Al Jazeera that there are three key factors contributing to the decline in global diesel supply.
First, “there isn’t diesel coming out of the Middle East to Europe, and Europe took quite a lot of diesel from Saudi Arabia and from Kuwait”.
Second, “Russia has now ceased to export diesel at all” due to “the attacks by Ukraine on Russian refineries”.
“And China is no longer exporting diesel,” he added.
“We’re in a situation where demand remains relatively high and is likely to stay high because of the agricultural harvesting season.”
According to data from the Joint Organizations Data Initiative (JODI) and the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), the US is the world’s largest producer and exporter of diesel. It produces about 240.5 million tonnes and exports around 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day.
Russia is the world’s second-largest diesel exporter, supplying 783,400 barrels per day (bpd) to the global market. Saudi Arabia is the world’s second-largest producer of diesel at 58.4 million tonnes, but it consumes a large portion of its diesel domestically.
Will the G7 energy release bring prices down?
After the G7 announcement, French President Macron, who had co-chaired the meeting, said the group’s move to release the oil will “bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.
The price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, briefly dropped below $100 a barrel after the G7 announcement, but rose to about $102 in the evening.
Naeem Aslam, chief investment officer at Zaye Capital Markets, told Al Jazeera that the G7 energy release was “very much needed”, but the group’s announcement was just to ease off pressure on the energy market.
“The actual structure changes about who is going to release [the energy stocks] and what and where the bans will be lifted, remains an important component in terms of the market,” he said.
Aslam added that by Sunday night, especially before the markets open, the added pressure on energy prices will come off. “But going into Monday morning … we could potentially see the reversal in the market,” he added.
Atkinson, the energy expert, said the G7’s fuel release is welcome but “doesn’t deal with the fundamental problem that the global supply remains lower than normal”.
Atkinson told Al Jazeera that “seven months after this war started in the Middle East, we are still in a situation where the global supply of crude oil or products remains significantly below pre-war levels”.
“We are now in a situation where the focus is on end use of products, mainly diesel, which is what we’re talking about here,” he added.
What has Trump said?
Soaring diesel prices have been a source of tension for the Trump administration and Republicans who fear this will cost them votes in the upcoming November midterm elections.
Last week, Trump pressured Ukraine to stop attacking Russian diesel facilities amid the war.
Then, on Thursday this week, the US president told reporters that his administration “may” ask European countries to release diesel stocks, shortly after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Europe to “immediately” tap its reserves.
Trump also threatened to ban US diesel exports if Europe did not release emergency diesel stocks.
But on Friday, Trump told reporters at the White House that Washington would not impose a diesel export ban. He said the plan was never really on the table.
“Europe has a lot of diesel, and they’re going to be making a major world contribution, and so are we. And we’re not going to be doing the export ban. We’re going to be doing what we’re supposed to do,” Trump said.
“Trump is scared by diesel prices above $6, which is a price jump of 70 percent compared to before he started the war. This is likely to get worse with US diesel inventories at their lowest seasonal level since records began in 1982.
“So if there is not enough diesel being produced because of the US-Israeli war on Iran, and diesel reserves have been used up, the only way to bring more diesel to the US market is by exporting less,” Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, told Al Jazeera on Friday.
After the G7 announcement, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform: “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately.”
The White House is also reportedly preparing an executive order to tackle record-high US diesel prices that could be unveiled as early as next week, two people familiar with the process told the Reuters news agency.
Schneider noted that countries are also concerned about high energy prices since diesel and gasoline are important for economies and fulfil different roles.
“While gasoline fuels cars, diesel fuels anything from trucks, freight trains, ships, tractors, harvesters, construction machinery, mining equipment and backup generators. This means gasoline is used more by consumers while diesel is mostly used by producers, meaning a diesel price shock spreads into the price of almost everything else, most prominently food, building materials and anything delivered by truck,” he added.
Farmers are hit twice because diesel prices are rising at the same time as fertiliser prices, both of which have been pushed up by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
“A higher diesel price therefore acts like a tax on production and logistics, while higher gasoline prices act like a tax on consumers directly. Like higher gasoline prices, higher diesel prices risk stagflation by pushing up inflation while simultaneously squeezing margins in transport and agriculture, meaning central banks find [themselves] in a dilemma between cutting rates [helping producers] and raising rates [cutting inflation],” he said.

“Someone else decides for you” – Latvian president urges voters not to stay home on election day

Making a choice in an election is certainly not easy, but it is always possible to find a party that feels closer to your values, President of Latvia Edgars Rinkēvičs told journalists on Saturday after casting his vote.
Rinkēvičs said he had carefully considered his choice, adding that he follows on a daily basis what has and has not been accomplished, while also closely assessing party programmes, track records and, quite critically, their promises.
“To tell the truth, it really isn’t that simple,” the President stressed.
He explained that he has his own list of criteria that guided him both in his first election in 1993, when the 5th Saeima was elected, and today.
The President said it is important to him that Latvia remains firmly anchored in the Western European space. Security and defence, demographics, economic development trends and healthcare are also important issues at present, he stressed.
“It is absolutely essential that people come out and make their choice. If you don’t go to the polls, someone else decides for you, someone else gives their representatives a mandate of trust, and someone else ensures that their ideas are put into practice,” Rinkēvičs said.
He noted that Latvian society is highly diverse and holds many different views. People often have radically opposing ideas about what the economy and politics should look like, as well as differing positions on issues that matter to various groups of voters, he said.
“I definitely disagree with those who say there is no one to vote for. No person, no party and no politician is perfect. That has never been the case and never will be. But you can always find something that is closer to your heart – whether it is a large or a small party. Someone may find one choice or another unacceptable, but it is our own ability to decide, our own choice,” Rinkēvičs stressed, adding that his work would begin on Monday.
As reported, polling stations across Latvia will remain open until 20:00 on Saturday.
Once voting ends, polling station commissions will begin counting the ballots. Votes will be counted manually during open commission meetings.
Preliminary results will be published gradually as vote-counting data are received from polling stations.

Who is the mystery co-pilot behind the Flydubai attack?

Who is the mystery co-pilot behind the Flydubai attack?
The pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani citizen, according to multiple reports.
A Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking the captain of a flight bound for Israel has been identified as an Omani national previously barred from flying in his home country over concerns about alleged extremist views, according to media reports.
There has been no official confirmation of the pilot’s identity or his beliefs.
The United Arab Emirates on Saturday described Wednesday’s incident on board Flight FZ1073 as an attempted “terrorist operation”, saying the co-pilot attacked Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, with an emergency axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft.
But investigators are still working to establish the motive and whether anyone else was connected to the attack, which has raised concerns about pilot vetting and aviation security.
Here is what we know:
What do we know about the accused pilot?
The co-pilot suspected of attacking the captain of the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight carrying 174 people has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf diplomat and a Western diplomat, told AP news agency.
All spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media. The Gulf diplomat said investigations are under way to establish whether he acted as a “lone wolf or had any connection with any extremist groups”.
US media outlet CNN, quoting a source and an Israeli official, reported that al-Hammami is an Omani citizen who was born in the UAE to a Syrian mother and spent several years in the Emirates.
Questions have emerged about his previous aviation career and whether warning signs had been raised before he joined the Dubai-based low-cost carrier.
The Wall Street Journal, quoting unnamed sources, reported on Friday that Omani authorities had previously barred the accused co-pilot from flying in the country because of concerns that he had held extremist views.
Nevertheless, it remains unclear what those alleged views were or whether Oman informed other countries or airlines about its concerns.
CNN separately quoted a regional diplomatic source as saying that al-Hammami had been removed from flight training over similar concerns and was subsequently reassigned to another position.
The US-based network also reported that a LinkedIn profile bearing al-Hammami’s name said he had spent seven years at Oman Air before leaving in February 2025. The profile said he joined Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and left in January 2026.
It has now been confirmed that al-Hammami studied at a UK university.
In a statement to the Press Association, a spokesman for Buckinghamshire New University said: “Our thoughts are with the injured pilot, crew and passengers involved in this incident.
“Hamam al-Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management. “He did not undertake any pilot training at the University.”
What happened on flight FZ1073?
At 7:05am (03:05 GMT) on Wednesday, Flight FZ1073 departed Dubai for Tel Aviv, climbing to 34,000ft (more than 10,000 metres), according to Flightradar24. A little more than two hours later, it suddenly began to descend, plunging before rising and then descending again.
Flight-tracking data showed the plane plunging more than 17,000 feet in about two minutes, before climbing and descending again.
Meanwhile, a fight had begun in the cockpit between the two pilots. The co-pilot had attacked the Indian captain of the plane, Smit Machchhar, by stabbing him.
Machchhar later described finding himself seriously wounded on the cockpit floor as the aircraft descended.
“When I was down, I could feel that the aircraft was plummeting, and I knew this is the last chance to do something,” he told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi from a hospital in Abu Dhabi.
“I knew that the aircraft was going down … I had fallen to the ground. I told myself that the door is right there, just open it. I managed to do it and people entered,” he said.
Passengers and crew members entered the cabin and overpowered the co-pilot. The aircraft eventually levelled out at about 15,000 feet. Its transponder was subsequently switched to code 7500, signalling unlawful interference.
Two reserve pilots who were on board took control of the jet and landed it in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia. The plane landed safely at 9:45am (06:45 GMT) local time. Saudi authorities said both pilots were taken to hospital. They were later transferred to Abu Dhabi after being medically cleared.
What has the UAE said about the attack?
UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said on Saturday that investigators had determined that the co-pilot had begun carrying out what he described as a “terrorist act”.
According to al-Shamsi, the co-pilot attacked the captain inside the cockpit using the aircraft’s emergency crash axe and “attempted to take control of the aircraft’s controls”.
A crash axe is a tool kept in a cockpit to help pilots cut through the plane in emergencies.
On Thursday, al-Shamsi had ordered investigators to determine whether the incident was connected to “terrorist activity or intent” or involved prior planning or direction.
The UAE has not yet publicly established a motive or announced whether investigators believe al-Hammami acted alone.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash on Saturday said that the latest ‘terrorist’ attack is new warning that region’s fight against extremism is not over.
“This underscores the importance of the UAE’s early and firm stance: no tolerance for extremism and no leniency towards its rhetoric. Security begins with confronting hatred and drying up the sources of extremism,” he posted on X
What is the latest in the investigation?
Abu Dhabi is now leading the investigation, with prosecutors examining the circumstances of the attack, its motive and any possible connections to others.
Previously, al-Shamsi said UAE judicial authorities have jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag, adding that UAE law applies to crimes committed on board “even if they occur outside the country’s territory”.
On Saturday, al-Shamsi said investigators are working “to uncover all the circumstances of the incident, its motives, and related connections, in addition to completing technical examinations and examining physical and digital evidence”.
The final results will be announced as soon as the necessary procedures are completed, he said.
Meanwhile, Flydubai flights to Israel remain suspended amid the investigations.

Philippines urges ASEAN talks after 50 killed in Myanmar airstrike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:17:00 UTC
18:17:00 KST

The Philippines, which holds the 2026 chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, has expressed concern over a deadly airstrike in Myanmar’s Rakhine state and offered to facilitate regional discussions on how ASEAN can help address the country’s worsening crisis.
Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary for ASEAN Affairs Ana Marie Hernando said in an email response Saturday that Manila was closely monitoring developments after the Sept. 28 attack in Kyauktaw, where the death toll rose to 50 and at least 58 people were wounded, according to local aid workers and the Arakan Army, the ethnic armed group that controls the area.
“The Philippines is closely monitoring developments and expresses concern over the attacks which resulted in destruction, loss of lives and injuries to those affected,” Hernando said.
Manila said it would remain mindful of the positions of ASEAN’s member states and follow the bloc’s consensus-based approach.
The Philippines also said it was prepared to facilitate discussions on ways to assist Myanmar, in line with ASEAN’s stated goal of finding a solution that is “Myanmar-owned and led.”
The statement came days after the airstrike hit a busy market area and a nearby bridge in Kyauktaw, a town in western Rakhine state near the Bangladesh border.
The Arakan Army said a military fighter jet dropped two bombs near the market around midday, when the area was crowded with vendors, shoppers and other civilians. The military has not publicly commented on the attack.
Local rescue officials initially reported 33 deaths and 36 injuries. The death toll later climbed to 50, while 58 people were reported wounded, with some in critical condition. Local sources said fires caused by the bombing badly burned some victims and complicated efforts to recover and identify bodies.
The attack was among the deadliest recent airstrikes in Rakhine, a state that has endured some of the fiercest fighting since Myanmar's military seized power in February 2021.
The United Nations expressed alarm over the reported casualties and said the violence underscored the continuing danger facing civilians and displaced people in the region.
The airstrike came as fighting between Myanmar’s military and the Arakan Army continues to reshape control of Rakhine.
The Arakan Army has captured large areas of the state during an offensive that began in late 2023, while the military has increasingly relied on air power and artillery in areas where it has lost ground.
The broader conflict began after the military overthrew the elected government in February 2021.
The coup triggered mass protests and an armed resistance movement that expanded as ethnic armed organizations and pro-democracy forces fought the military across much of the country.
The conflict has created one of Southeast Asia’s most severe humanitarian crises. The U.N. estimated nearly 3.8 million people were internally displaced across Myanmar by June 2026, while 16.2 million people, including 4.9 million children, required humanitarian assistance.
Conflict monitors have estimated that more than 100,000 people have been killed since the 2021 coup. Rakhine has been particularly hard hit, with hundreds of thousands of people displaced and humanitarian access severely constrained.
Myanmar's crisis has tested ASEAN's ability to respond collectively.
The bloc's engagement has centered on its Five-Point Consensus, adopted in 2021, which calls for an immediate end to violence, dialogue among the parties, the appointment of a special envoy, humanitarian assistance, and an envoy visit to Myanmar.
Implementation has made limited progress, with the military authorities resisting meaningful engagement with their opponents.
ASEAN has also struggled to maintain a unified position as member states have differed over how strongly the bloc should pressure Myanmar's military leadership.
The Philippines assumed the ASEAN chairmanship for 2026 and has emphasized a Myanmar-owned and Myanmar-led process while maintaining the organization's consensus-based approach.
Manila's response to the Kyauktaw strike reflects that cautious diplomatic position.
Rather than announcing a new collective measure, the Philippines expressed concern, reiterated ASEAN's established approach and offered to convene discussions on possible assistance.

In the Chelyabinsk region, the Russians conducted exercises to ‘repel external aggression’ and ‘establish a security zone’ on the territory of a Central Asian country.
The exercises at the Chebarkul training ground, attended by Russian President Vladimir Putin, were named Center-2026 by the Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation.
The scenario was not limited to defense.
After repelling the main assault in the South Ural direction, the troops launch an offensive to “liberate the occupied territory and establish a security zone in the adjacent territory.”
“The coalition force repelled the main strike in the South Ural direction, stabilized the situation, and has been conducting offensive operations since October 2 to liberate the occupied territory and establish a security zone in the adjacent territory,” — stated Russian Deputy Defence Minister Yunus-Bek Yevkurov to Putin.
The exercises involved the T-14 Armata tank, armored vehicles, drones, artillery, and aircraft.
At the same time, the Caspian Flotilla was conducting an anti-landing operation.
As part of the operation, four long-range aircraft are striking ‘critical enemy targets.’
According to Putin’s statement, more than 47,000 military personnel are participating in the Center-2026 exercises across 11 training grounds and in the Caspian Sea.
This is significantly fewer than the reported number of participants in the two previous exercises: approximately 128,000 people took part in Center-2019, and about 95,000 in Center-2015.
Kazakhstan best fits the description of an aggressor country in the exercise scenario; it is located in Central Asia, has access to the Caspian Sea, and borders the Chelyabinsk region.
Prior to this, Kazakhstan also conducted military exercises in Central Asia, involving 7,000 military personnel.

Source: Beskrestnov on Facebook

He also said that if the drones can be controlled in real time, not only bridges but also nearby air defence systems could be at risk.
Quote: "As long as there is online control of Shahed drones, not only bridges but also air defence assets will be at risk."
Details: Beskrestnov added that Ukrainian experts are examining the wreckage of Russian drones and have found no other communications equipment that could explain this type of control.
There is currently no independent confirmation that Russian MESH relays are operating in Kyiv.
Background: On the night of 2-3 October, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 157 drones, including Shaheds, Gerberas and decoy drones. Strikes were recorded at 12 locations.

"It's about time we prioritize that in this department, and we're fixing it right here, right now," he added.

The Swiss Federal Council approved a funding package of 135 million Swiss francs (approximately $162 million) on Friday, Oct. 2, to finance eight reconstruction projects in Ukraine managed by Swiss enterprises operating locally.
According to United24, the capital allocation is designated to reinforce Ukraine’s energy grid, public transit systems, and municipal water management infrastructure as the country confronts compounded damage from sustained Russian air strikes ahead of the winter heating season.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The program is structured to supply Ukrainian municipal authorities with specialized Swiss equipment and technical expertise to address urgent recovery requirements.
In addition to physical repairs, the initiatives focus on workforce stabilization, aiming to preserve existing employment, create new domestic jobs, and train Ukrainian engineering specialists through direct technical cooperation with Swiss industry.
Project selection was conducted through a competitive tender open to Swiss corporations maintaining active operational subsidiaries in Ukraine.
The approved initiatives carry individual budgets ranging between 3 million and 30 million Swiss francs ($3.6 million to $36 million respectively), with all projects designed for immediate, on-the-ground implementation across Ukrainian municipal centers.
Corporate tender
The evaluation of bids was conducted under a joint regulatory framework established by Swiss and Ukrainian government authorities.
Ukraine Denies Reports Western Embassies Plan Kyiv Relocation
Proposals were reviewed against standardized benchmarks assessing local relevance, technical feasibility, demonstrable socioeconomic impact, risk management, and overall cost efficiency.
Under the statutory terms of the program, winning corporate contractors are required to provide a minimum co-financing share of 10 percent of their project’s total cost, ensuring commercial alignment and operational accountability.
The final portfolio of eight initiatives was formally approved in coordination with the Ukrainian government to ensure that resource distribution aligns directly with prioritized state reconstruction schedules.
The initiative expands Bern’s direct economic assistance for Ukrainian public utilities, utilizing the footprint of established private enterprises to navigate wartime supply chain bottlenecks and expedite the delivery of critical components for water sanitation, district heating, and urban transit rolling stock.
Neutrality referendum
The Federal Council’s funding decision follows a national referendum on Sunday, Sept. 28, in which Swiss citizens rejected a proposed constitutional amendment that would have strictly codified the country’s traditional neutrality policies.
Official referendum results showed that 70 percent of voters across all 26 Swiss cantons rejected the initiative, which was sponsored by the national-conservative group Pro Schweiz and supported by the right-wing Swiss People’s Party (SVP).
The proposed amendment would have prohibited Switzerland from participating in non-UN sanctions regimes and strictly barred military cooperation with foreign nations unless Swiss territory came under direct armed assault.
Rejection of the measure preserved the federal government’s legal authority to align autonomous foreign policy measures with European partners and sustain economic assistance for Kyiv. Following the referendum outcome, the SVP announced it would not pursue further legislative efforts to restrict Swiss sanctions policy.
In recent years, Bern has aligned domestic regulations with successive EU sanctions packages targeting the Russian Federation’s financial system, defense industry, and fossil fuel revenues.
In February, Swiss authorities enacted a full prohibition on the purchase and import of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG), mirroring provisions within the EU’s 19th sanctions package.
The reconstruction package also complements a comprehensive security blueprint approved by the Federal Council in September, which established 10 strategic goals and 46 operational measures to enhance critical infrastructure resilience and defend against state-sponsored hybrid warfare and cyber disruptions across the European continent.

Kenneth Ruut: Average Estonian university student lives in an educational paradise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:10:00 UTC
18:10:00 KST

Kenneth Ruut: Average Estonian university student lives in an educational paradise
The fact that Estonian students consider the free and internationally integrated European model a crisis only demonstrates how isolated the debate here has become. Much of this isolation stems from the fact that the claims fueling student protests are largely based on exaggerations, writes Kenneth Ruut.
As is typical at the start of the academic year, recent weeks' media coverage has focused on teachers' salary negotiations and the 24 September student protest "Läbipõlev Eesti tulevik" (Burning Out Estonia's Future).
The student demonstrations in Tallinn and Tartu portray today's university life not as a normal, effort‑demanding stage of life, but as a failure of Estonia's higher‑education system. Reading headlines in social media, newspapers, and university newsletters, one might get the impression that Estonian higher education is on the verge of collapse.
But stepping back from daily news and looking at the bigger picture reveals a very different reality: the local tragic narrative is unfolding in the most favorable and student‑friendly conditions in human history. Put simply, in the broader context of today's world and recent history, the average Estonian university student lives in an educational paradise.
This becomes especially clear when comparing Estonia's model with other international systems. In the United States, obtaining a bachelor's degree often results in a six‑figure student‑loan burden, forcing young people to begin their working lives with serious financial obligations. Loan repayment can take decades after graduation, and these obligations are nearly impossible to escape — even bankruptcy does not free one from repaying student loans.
In Asia, entering and staying in university requires years of exhausting 12‑ to 16‑hour study days in an extremely competitive environment that leaves no room for free time, extracurricular self‑development, or part‑time work.
It is also worth looking at Europe. In Germany, some courses pack more than 2,000 students into a single lecture; professors do not know your name, and courses are structured so that more than 70 percent of participants fail.
Adding fuel to the fire is the practice of expelling students after repeatedly failing exams, along with the possibility of a nationwide ban (bundesweite Sperre) that prevents continuing studies in the same field at any German university.
Against all this, the average Estonian student receives fully funded, free higher education in a country that ranks at the top of European education tables, taking courses where lecturers are significantly more accessible and often offer personal guidance.
The high quality of Estonia's higher‑education system is further illustrated by Europe‑wide programs like Erasmus+. Estonia's system not only provides a free domestic degree — it practically pays students to travel.
Through such programs, Estonian students can receive substantial monthly living stipends that allow them to live in major European cities, study at top universities, and experience different cultures.
Government‑guaranteed free education, Estonian universities' agreements with international institutions, and fully funded mobility are a tremendous political achievement, not a systemic failure.
The fact that local students consider the free and internationally integrated European model a crisis only shows how isolated domestic debate has become. Much of this isolation stems from claims fueling student protests that are largely exaggerated — especially those concerning academic workload.
For example, the official standard states that one credit point requires roughly 26 hours of work. This metric, originating from the early 2000s, is often cited by students to mathematically prove they are overworked.
It is important, however, to recognize when theory and practice diverge. On paper, one credit point indeed corresponds to 26 hours of work, but this calculation ignores the reality of modern digital efficiency. With contemporary technology, digital tools, and smart use of artificial intelligence, tasks formally estimated at 26 hours can often be completed and submitted in a fraction of the time — sometimes in as little as three hours.
For students who have even minimal familiarity with technology — today, a significant majority — academic workload is surprisingly manageable. Therefore, arguments about excessive credit‑point workload lose credibility for the average student and instead raise questions about the complainers' study methods.
Naturally, academic workload is only one part of the protest rhetoric, which largely revolves around living costs and the fact that state support may not fully cover market‑rate rent in Tallinn or Tartu. Rising rents and inflation are real economic factors, but treating them as structural problems of the university system ignores the nature of becoming an adult.
Working part‑time alongside studies is not inherently a tragedy or a sign of oppression — it is a perfectly normal part of independent adult life. Expecting consolation prizes and pats on the back for time management and holding a part‑time job is appropriate for a child, not a young adult becoming independent.
A free degree provides an educational foundation; it does not promise a fully subsidized private luxury lifestyle at taxpayers' expense. Managing a personal budget, working to cover one's expenses, and balancing competing responsibilities are universal milestones of adulthood that rarely warrant lengthy negotiations or unprecedented sympathy.
The truth is that most students already do exactly this. They work part‑time, save reasonably, keep their expenses under control, and manage their lives perfectly well. This is the everyday reality of thousands of young people. Labeling routine adult life as systemic oppression is unreasonable.
Instead of a genuine structural deficiency, the recent rise in campus activism may be better understood through youthful solidarity. One constructive explanation is that protests serve as events that give young people a chance to engage in shared discussion, express identity, and belong to a group of peers. Participation provides a tangible sense of community and shared identity during a transitional period.
Many students, however, do not participate in these actions because they are satisfied with the existing system or successfully navigate it in their daily lives without major complaints. Meanwhile, protest rhetoric turns ordinary economic adjustment into an existential crisis, amplifying a vocal minority over a quiet and content majority.
Although public systems and societal institutions must indeed be constantly evaluated and improved, we must not lose sight of the bigger picture. Estonia's higher‑education system offers world‑class knowledge, unprecedented opportunities for self‑development, and international mobility. How students engage with and benefit from this system remains a matter of personal initiative, discipline, and character.
Looking beyond local alarm bells and replacing them with a global and historical perspective reveals that Estonian higher education remains a remarkable launchpad for young people willing to adopt a healthy outlook, take responsibility for their future, and work toward it. Previous generations achieved success under far more difficult conditions, so it is worth using every opportunity available today and giving one's best.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon
