Former director of the Molodyi Theater Bilous, suspected of sexual violence against female students, released from pretrial detention center - lawyers
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:06:15 EEST
18:06:15 KST

Former director of the Molodyi Theater Bilous, suspected of sexual violence against female students, released from pretrial detention center - lawyers
Kyiv • UNN
Former director of the Molodyi Theater Andrii Bilous was released from pretrial detention after bail was posted. He is suspected of sexual violence against female students.
Former director and artistic director of Kyiv’s Young Theatre, Andrii Bilous, who is suspected of sexual violence against female students, was released from pretrial detention on October 2 after bail was posted. This was reported by UNN, citing the director’s lawyers and case materials.
Earlier, the court reduced the amount from almost UAH 5 million to UAH 1.3 million.
Details
Bilous’s defense lawyers reported his release from the pretrial detention center. Earlier, the court ordered that the director remain in custody but set bail as an alternative preventive measure. Initially, the bail amount was UAH 4.992 million. The defense appealed the decision, stating that Bilous’s family was unable to provide such a sum. At the end of September, it became known that the bail amount had been reduced to UAH 1.3 million. This was reported, in particular, by the director’s wife, Iryna Bilous. After the funds were deposited, he left the pretrial detention center.
At the same time, release on bail does not mean that the criminal proceedings have been discontinued. Bilous must comply with the procedural obligations set by the court, and the case is ongoing.
What Bilous is accused of
Andrii Bilous was notified of the suspicion in October 2025. The criminal case materials were subsequently transferred to court.
According to investigators, starting in 2017, Bilous allegedly used his authority in the theater community, as well as his status as a lecturer and theater director, to sexually harass female students and commit violent acts against them. Five injured parties are involved in the case. According to investigators, two of them were minors at the time the alleged offenses were committed. Bilous is charged with criminal offenses under Parts 2 and 3 of Article 152, as well as Parts 1 and 2 of Article 153 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. These concern rape and sexual violence under aggravating circumstances.
As part of the investigation, law enforcement officers questioned the injured parties and dozens of witnesses, conducted searches, and seized mobile devices and other physical evidence. The prosecutor’s office had previously stated that witnesses reported sexualized behavior, demands to send intimate photographs, sexually explicit correspondence, and physical harassment.
In addition, according to the prosecution, psychological examinations documented trauma-related consequences in the injured parties.
The defense’s position
Andrii Bilous himself denies the accusations against him. He previously stated that he had caused no one physical or moral harm and described the situation as a campaign aimed at discrediting him. According to the man, his relationships with the people involved in the case were friendly and based on trust.
The director’s lawyers also drew attention to certain procedural aspects of the case. In particular, the defense claimed that some materials from covert investigative actions had been destroyed and that they may have contained information important to the defense’s position.
The prosecution, for its part, insisted that Bilous needed to remain in custody because of possible risks of influencing the injured parties or witnesses or obstructing justice.
How the scandal unfolded
The public controversy surrounding Andrii Bilous began in early 2025. In January, former student Sofiia Sapozhnyk stated that the director had allegedly asked her to send intimate photographs, discussed sexual fantasies with her, and forwarded images of other female students. After that, new public testimonies from other women emerged. The Karpenko-Karyi Kyiv National University of Theatre, Cinema and Television announced that it was conducting an internal investigation and had forwarded the relevant information to law enforcement authorities.
Against the backdrop of the scandal, Bilous was suspended from teaching and temporarily removed from managing the Young Theatre. In March 2025, after the suspension period ended, he returned to work at the theater, prompting protests from some members of the theater community. In May, Bilous submitted a resignation from the position of director and artistic director of the Young Theatre by mutual agreement. At the time, he explained his decision by saying that he wanted to reduce tensions within the organization.

Christa Pike unconscious as Tennessee execution goes awry: Lawyers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:05:00 UTC
18:05:00 KST

Convicted killer Christa Pike was left critically ill, unconscious and on life support after Tennessee's failed attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers said Friday, providing the first detailed account of the injuries she sustained.
Hospital staff were working to save Pike's life and remove the drug pentobarbital from her system, her attorneys said in an emergency motion seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence from Wednesday night's botched execution.
Pike remained in critical condition, intubated and dependent on a mechanical ventilator to breathe, her lawyers said. Two doses of pentobarbital were administered intravenously at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital.
The bungled attempt to establish intravenous lines also left both of her arms "swollen, burned and blistered," apparently because pentobarbital, a highly alkaline and caustic substance, seeped into the tissue beneath her skin, according to the court filing.
The lawyers accused Department of Correction officials of disregarding prior warnings from Pike's doctors that pre-existing medical conditions, including small veins and a blood disorder called thrombocytosis, would make placing IV lines especially difficult.
"At no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike's body," her lawyers said in a filing in the Chancery Court for Tennessee's 20th Judicial District.
Witnesses to the execution attempt could hear Pike "crying, whimpering and breathing loudly throughout the procedure," the filing said.
The filing provided the fullest picture yet of the medical consequences of an attempted execution that Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said followed the state's established protocol.
It was the state's second botched execution this year, prompting Lee to halt any further attempts to carry out the death penalty for the rest of 2026. He also ordered an independent review of what went wrong.
Pike, 50, was convicted three decades ago of first-degree murder for her role in the torture and killing of 19-year-old vocational school classmate Colleen Slemmer at the University of Tennessee campus in Knoxville in 1995, when Pike was 18.
She had been scheduled to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than two centuries and the only person in the modern era of U.S. capital punishment to be executed in the state for a crime committed as a teenager.
Pike's then-17-year-old boyfriend was tried as an adult and convicted of murder but received a life sentence with the possibility of parole. A third schoolmate, who was 18 at the time and acted as a lookout for the other two, testified for the prosecution and received probation.
Lee earlier this week rejected a clemency petition seeking to commute Pike's death sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The petition argued for leniency, in part, based on her childhood history of severe neglect, sexual abuse that included two rapes and untreated mental illness.
The clemency petition also cited evidence that Pike's mother drank heavily during pregnancy, which the petition said contributed to impaired brain development that made it difficult for Pike to control her impulses.
The U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday lifted an 11th-hour stay of execution issued earlier that day by a federal appeals court to allow more time to consider Pike's claim that her childhood trauma had not been properly considered during sentencing.
In their filing Friday, Pike's lawyers urged the state Chancery Court to order the preservation of evidence they said would show that state prison personnel violated her constitutional rights by subjecting her to cruel and unusual punishment.

The joint U.S.-Ukrainian Recovery Investment Fund has signed its first critical minerals agreement and approved four other projects, Conor Coleman, head of investments at the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), told Reuters.
According to him, the total volume of the fund's current project portfolio is estimated at approximately $70 million.

Ten monumental brutalist buildings in Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:00:59 UTC
18:00:59 KST

Ten monumental brutalist buildings in Asia
From a modernist church in South Korea to a geometric post office in Qatar, editor Bob Pang selects 10 of his favourite projects from the recently released Brutalist Asia book.
Edited by Pang with Blue Crow Media founder Derek Lamberton, Brutalist Asia contains photographs and essays of 140 buildings in 28 Asian countries.
It aims to shine a light on the continent's contribution to the brutalist movement and offer insight into the varying ways local and international architects interpreted the architectural style.
Read on for Pang's top picks of buildings in Brutalist Asia:
Inter-University Seminar House, Japan, by Takamasa Yoshizaka, 1965
"Alongside Kunio Maekawa and Junzo Sakakura, Takamasa Yoshizaka was one of the three key Japanese architects who trained directly under the modernist master Le Corbusier in his Paris Rue de Sèvres studio.
"Takamasa was a main figure in importing modern architecture theory to his own country by translating key Le Corbusier texts into Japanese, including Towards an Architecture and The Modulor.
"Inter-University Seminar House is a radical academic complex in Hachioji, Tokyo, featuring an inverted pyramid main hall and scattered student pavilions embedded in the hillside. It remains in use today."
Sacred Heart High School for Girls, Taiwan, by Kenzo Tange, 1967
"Kenzo Tange's first architectural design outside of Japan was the Sacred Heart Girls' High School located in the Bali District of New Taipei City, Taiwan.
"It is also the only surviving work in Taiwan by this master of modern Japanese architecture."
Round Building at the Faculty of Science, Mahidol University, Thailand, by Amorn Srivong, 1968
"Amorn Srivong grew up in a Chinese merchant family but ventured out on his own to work as a general labourer on construction sites, which eventually led him to a job as a draftsman at structural engineer Veekorn Veeranuvat's firm.
"Having received no formal architectural training whatsoever, Amorn began designing small-scale projects for clients in the 1950s. By the 1960s and 1970s, as universities were being established across Thailand, Chiang Mai University, Khon Kaen University, and Thammasat University became his architectural testing grounds.
"This round building fully demonstrates his architectural talent with challenging cantilevered structures and organic geometry."
Dafineh Museum, Iran, by Nezam Ameri, Kamal Kamooneh and Hormozdyar Khosravi, 1978
"Iranian architect Kamal Kamooneh established his firm in the 1960s alongside Nezam Ameri, a former student of Frank Lloyd Wright.
"At the time, their designs were heavily influenced by Wright's work. The Dafineh Museum, located in Tehran, is their masterpiece."
National Cooperative Development Corporation, India, by Kuldip Singh, 1980
"Educated both in New Delhi and at UCL in London, Kuldip Singh's architecture is highly stylised with bold forms, geometry and challenging structures.
"His collaboration with the legendary Indian structural engineer Mahendra Raj, who worked on Le Corbusier's Chandigarh project, pushed the boundaries of modern Indian architecture."
St Stephen's College Special Room Block and Tang Shiu Kin Hall, Hong Kong, by Tao Ho, 1981
"Founded in 1903, St Stephen's College is a prestigious British-style institution with a long history. Designed by Tao Ho, the Special Room Block and Tang Shiu Kin Hall brutalist additions to the school were completed in 1981.
"Upon taking on the project, Ho noted the scattered and unstructured layout of the campus and proposed positioning the new addition as a focal point.
"After careful planning, the site was finalised in front of the historic School House. Ho's project included three classroom blocks and a standalone indoor sports hall connected by three arched staircases and elevated walkways."
Kyungdong Presbyterian Church, South Korea, by Kim Swoo-geun, 1981
"Kim Swoo-geun was the first modernist architect in Korea, and was dubbed the 'Lorenzo de' Medici' of South Korea by Time magazine.
"The Kyungdong Presbyterian Church concept was inspired by the Korean and Asian gesture of praying with two hands.
"The vertical volumes of the church are an abstraction of fingers, while the interior resembles a whale's belly."
General Post Office, Qatar, by Twist and Whitley Architects, 1985
"The General Post Office was designed by British architects Twist and Whitley, whose work includes the Arts and Social Sciences Library at the University of Bristol and the Science Library at Queen's University Belfast.
"The building is a refined example of how foreign architects adapted the brutalist style to local climates and evolved a brand of brutalism which blends with the domestic language of traditional Gulf and Qatari architecture."
Cua Tung Writers' House, Vietnam, by Le Huu Thang, 1992
"The house was sponsored by the regional Literature and Arts Association, Hội Văn học Nghệ thuật, during the early post-Đổi Mới transition era.
"Le Huu Thang approached the design as a sculpture rather than a conventional architectural form."
Interdesign Building, Lebanon, by Khalil Khoury, 1973–97
"The building took 23 years to complete due to the outbreak of civil war in the country, and it has never been in full use.
"However, it is widely regarded as one of the most remarkable brutalist and modernist structures in the Middle East."

====================================================================================================

What do Britain’s death-penalty cheerleaders have to say about Christa Pike? | Maya Foa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:00:56 UTC
18:00:56 KST

In recent months, there has been a resurgence of interest in the death penalty among rightwing politicians in the UK. The leader of Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe, has made a manifesto commitment to holding a legally binding referendum on bringing back capital punishment. The Reform MP Lee Anderson is also in favour of a referendum, arguing that the public would vote in favour of the death penalty.
Such supporters of capital punishment in Britain point to polls such as this “bombshell survey” that supposedly showed 47% of students favoured bringing back the death penalty. But these headlines are misleading, as surveys rarely include details about the grim administration of capital punishment and only present a binary choice of the options.
The more information you give the public about the reality of the death penalty, the less support it enjoys. In the UK, when people are offered specific alternative punishments, the death penalty has historically failed to get majority support, regardless of the crime. Only 35% of respondents believe it should be available as a punishment in all cases of murder, according to YouGov. And in the US, support for capital punishment has steadily declined, from 80% in 1994 to 52% in 2025.
The horrific failed execution of Christa Pike is only the most recent state-sanctioned killing that has gone badly wrong. Lethal injection commands higher support than other methods of execution because it has a medical veneer that makes it seem more “humane”. This myth has sustained the death penalty in the US. Polling suggests that if states were to switch methods, support would decline.
Pike is a woman who suffered horrific trauma from a young age and ended up being tortured by prison officials for more than an hour in a failed attempt to kill her. Campaigners have long argued that Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 at the age of 20, shouldn’t be on death row. At trial, she was presented to jurors as a dangerous killer, rather than a teenager who had suffered extreme, violent abuse since she was a child, including being raped by several strangers.
Her ordeal in the execution chamber was a visceral demonstration that there is nothing medical or humane about execution by lethal injection. What we saw was the awful, ugly, indefensible reality of the death penalty. It should make pro-capital punishment politicians in the UK urgently reconsider their positions.
Great Britain abolished the death penalty for murder in 1965, in the outcry that followed a fatal miscarriage of justice when Timothy Evans was hanged for murdering his wife and daughter. They were actually both victims of the serial killer John Christie, who lived downstairs. This was not an anomaly. Countries that have the death penalty inevitably execute innocent people: one study estimates that at least one in every 25 people sentenced to death in the US is likely innocent.
British supporters of the death penalty look to the US as the model of a democratic society that practices capital punishment. But the case of Christa Pike should force them to pause. More than 200 people have been exonerated from death row in the US – one for every eight people executed. And there is clear evidence that capital punishment does not deter crime: in 2024, of the eight most-violent states in the US measured by the murder rate, seven had the death penalty.
In April, the US Department of Justice published a death penalty report that brazenly claimed that all methods of execution available to US states are humane, from lethal gas to the electric chair, the firing squad to lethal injection. This is despite decades of evidence to the contrary, both statistical and found on the bodies of those tortured to death.
Proponents of capital punishment often claim that it will be reserved for the “worst of the worst” mass murderers. Research shows that in reality the death penalty is disproportionately reserved for the most vulnerable, including people with mental illness and intellectual disability, and people who can’t afford a lawyer.
Ruth Ellis, the last woman executed in the UK, in 1955, was punched, pushed down the stairs and threatened with murder by the man she shot dead. This summer, she was granted a conditional pardon by King Charles in light of evidence that she was a victim of domestic abuse and coercive and controlling behaviour. It was a tiny measure of justice, 71 years too late, for a woman who should never have been executed.
In 1956, as parliament debated abolition, public opinion was divided. Lord Mancroft told peers that one poll showed 73% support for capital punishment in 1953, while another, after the execution of Ellis, found only 50% in favour. In the Commons, Sydney Silverman MP summed up the moral obligation of politicians to lead, not follow, opinion, asking MPs if they would kill a man “whom they knew it would be wrong to kill … if there were violent public pressure” to do so.
As the list of countries rejecting capital punishment grows ever-longer, it is increasingly used as a tool by authoritarian regimes. The overwhelming majority of global executions last year were carried out by China, Iran and Saudi Arabia. Iran reportedly executed more than 2,000 people – many for participating in protests calling for more equal rights for women. Is this the kind of company Lowe and Anderson think the UK should be keeping?
In the US, numerous top lawyers and doctors are demanding a moratorium on the death penalty in the wake of Pike’s botched execution. Here in the UK, each time Lowe, Anderson or any of their fellow travellers say they want to bring back a debate about capital punishment, they should be forcefully reminded of the horrific reality of what it means in practice.
- Maya Foa is the CEO of the human rights charity Reprieve
- Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.

Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:00:56 UTC
18:00:56 KST

Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in western Libya have upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country.
Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.
But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.
Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors.
Donald Trump’s Africa adviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister.
Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.”
But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces.
Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.
On 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar.
Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said.
The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change.
Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.”
He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war.
The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east.
Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance.

‘It’s been hard’: families await the return of the USS Abraham Lincoln
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:00:55 UTC
18:00:55 KST

A mother in San Diego is counting down the days until her son comes home.
“I had a big sign made, welcoming him back,” she said. “I can’t wait to see him.”
Her son is one of roughly 5,000 sailors and marines onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, the US aircraft carrier that has been deployed for nearly a year, and since late February was supporting US military operations against Iran.
What began as a deployment bound for the Pacific, anticipated to return in the spring, became something entirely different after the United States launched its war with Iran. The Lincoln was diverted to the Middle East, and the deployment became what one military official described as “one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era”.
The months that followed were marked by combat operations, deployment extensions, a record-breaking stretch at sea, and reports of shortages of food and basic supplies and deteriorating mental health among some crew members, including reports that several crew members had attempted to jump overboard.
Senior Trump administration officials pushed back against accounts of poor conditions, but some families and veterans warned that the length and intensity of the deployment were taking a toll on both those serving onboard and their loved ones.
As reports of conditions leaked out, the Lincoln soon became a flashpoint in the increasingly contentious debate over the war and, for some, a symbol of the strains and pressures the conflict has placed on the US military and the people serving in it.
Now, after months at sea, the Lincoln is in the final stretch of its journey back to San Diego, where it is expected in the coming days.
But as the carrier heads home, the toll of the deployment has come into sharper focus. In late September, the navy disclosed that during the deployment, eight service members from the Lincoln and its accompanying strike group had attempted to take their own lives.
When the Lincoln left San Diego last November, its deployment was expected to be relatively routine. The carrier was scheduled to spend several months in the Pacific region before returning home to California in the spring.
Instead, as the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, the carrier was redirected to the Middle East.
The Lincoln and its strike group, carrying approximately 6,000 to 7,000 sailors across roughly a half-dozen ships, were soon pulled into combat operations, which would see them shoot down “more than 200 Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps drones threatening international shipping and US forces”, according to Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command. The group’s guided-missile destroyers, he said, engaged in “arguably the most intense combat at sea the navy has seen” since the second world war while the carrier’s air wing carried out hundreds of “decisive strikes on IRGC targets”.
The crew worked long hours as the carrier remained at sea for months without a port visit. The war disrupted regional resupply routes and traditional hubs, making it harder to replenish the ship and rotate personnel, especially after Iran damaged a US navy base in Bahrain.
By August, the Lincoln had spent more than 250 consecutive days at sea.
Armen Kurdian, a retired US navy captain who served on the Lincoln in 2005, described the carrier as a “giant floating city” where sailors live in close quarters, and “you’ve got aircraft smacking down on decks repeatedly, hundreds of times per day, and that rattles the ship”.
The strain of this deployment was compounded by uncertainty over when the sailors would come home. Some familiessaid they went weeks without hearing from their loved ones, and for stretches of time, they said, those onboard did not receive letters and care packages from home.
Then reports began to emerge about conditions on the ship.
In April, photographs purporting to show poor-quality meals on the Lincoln circulated widely online. The US navy denied reports of food shortages, calling such claims “false”.
But by August, some families began describing a more troubling picture of what their loved ones onboard had told them about the conditions: shortages of food and basic supplies, plumbing problems, and exhaustion and deteriorating mental health among the crew. Two leading military newspapers also reported that there had been two attempts by sailors to jump overboard, causing concern among families and military health experts.
That month, it was reported that more than 200 family members attended a virtual town hall with navy leaders to discuss their concerns. One spouse reportedly said her husband, a sailor onboard, had texted her that day, saying: “He hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow.”
One mother whose 19-year-old son is onboard the carrier said this week that there were periods when she went a month without hearing from him. When they did communicate, she said, he sometimes sent photographs of the food, which she said looked “horrible”.
At one point, he told her about a power outage on the ship, but assured her that he was doing OK. He would tell her how other sailors had begun “to not be themselves” and were “losing themselves”.
“It’s been hard knowing the conditions and the type of food they’re being fed, and just not having any contact for long periods of time, and them being gone so long,” the woman, who requested anonymity, said. “It’s just been difficult.”
The reports of supply shortages and declining morale and mental health prompted outrage from Democrats, and swift pushback from senior officials in the Trump administration.
Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary who has pledged to restore the “warrior ethos” to the US military, said the conditions on the Lincoln had been “completely misrepresented”. Navy officials acknowledged that the war had disrupted traditional supply networks, but maintained that the carrier had adequate food, medical care and supplies.
When reporters asked Donald Trump whether the families were concerned about the reported conditions on the vessel, he claimed, “No, they’re not,” and when asked if he thought the deployment had gone on too long, he responded: “Not nearly long enough.”
For some naval families, that comment was difficult to hear.
One mother whose son was onboard the Lincoln said she became angry when she heard Trump’s comments.
“I thought, you know, this guy has never served a day in his life,” she said. “Neither has his family, none of his children have – how would he feel if it was his kid on that ship?”
She said she understood that the sailors were at war, but what troubled her was how long the deployment had lasted, with no opportunity to leave the ship and little sense of when the crew would return.
“For a long time I didn’t hear from him because he didn’t have internet or whatever,” she said. “So it was hard not knowing what’s going on, and then listening to news reports about all this stuff that’s going on, I was very worried.”
When she was finally spoke with her son after the reports of the suicide attempts and poor living conditions emerged, she asked whether he was eating, and if he was OK. She said he told her he was eating three meals a day, and sounded well. But from thousands of miles away, it was impossible to know for sure.
The picture emerging from the Lincoln was complicated, and worried families scrambled to try to piece together what was happening through brief phone calls and text messages, as well as news reports relaying what other relatives had heard.
Some families weren’t surprised by the reports, saying that their relative onboard had described similar conditions. Others, however, said their relative had described nothing of the sort, which led them to believe that some of the accounts circulating online had been overblown or just the experience of a handful of sailors.
One mother, herself a navy veteran, said she believed some reports about food and plumbing had been “blown out of proportion”. Food on these vessels in general, she said, could be “pretty disgusting”.
Her bigger concern was the length of the deployment, the lack of port visits, and the inability of sailors to receive mail and care packages from home for extended periods.
“I can’t imagine not feeling the ground under my feet for that amount of time,” she said. She also worried about sailors on their first deployment and whether such an experience might influence their decision to re-enlist.
For some families, the feeling of helplessness became overwhelming.
In August, Jefferson Kelley, whose son is onboard the Lincoln, wrote to his senator, Bernie Moreno, a Republican from Ohio, offering to take his son’s place on the ship for the remainder of the deployment.
In the letter, shared with the Guardian, Kelley proposed what he called a “parent swap”.
“If there is any lawful way for me to serve in his place so that he may return home, I am asking for that opportunity,” he wrote.
His son had never complained to him or his family about conditions on the ship, Kelley said, adding that he often responded that he was doing fine, but as a father, he said he couldn’t help by worry about his son, especially as the reports continued to emerge.
“I was trying to show that I am someone that is willing to do more than just sit at home and say somebody should do something or complain on social media,” Kelley said, describing his son’s deployment amid the war in Iran as a “very, very difficult experience” for the family.
On 15 August, as headlines about conditions on the Lincoln intensified, and as Democratic lawmakers demanded more information from the Pentagon, Adm Cooper, who heads Central Command, visited the carrier.
Not long afterward, he released a statement, claiming that of the US navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, the Lincoln “currently has among the lowest number of cases related to mental health”. But, he added, “this doesn’t mean that all is perfect”.
A long deployment at sea, Cooper said, “is uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways”.
In an opinion piece in the Wall Street Journal that week, Cooper wrote that “the crew is tired, but they continue to fire on all cylinders”.
“History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era,” he said. In the essay, Cooper said that “recent media reporting has portrayed varying perspectives on operational tempo, crew morale and the realities facing our deployed forces”, adding: “What I found aboard the Lincoln is that many elements of those stories are old news.”
That same month, for one sailor, the strain of being away from home was compounded by events happening there. In a post on social media, Joshua Aviles, a sailor onboard the Lincoln, wrote that he had just learned that his father was detained by federal immigration authorities.
Aviles said his father had a driver’s license, social security card and work permit, and that the family “had done everything through immigration to get his green card approved, and we are just waiting”.
“I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal,” he wrote in a Facebook post.
US immigration officials said at the time that Aviles’ father had entered the country illegally, and that “having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws”.
Several days later, Aviles said his father was released.
In late August, it was finally announced that another US aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, had arrived to relieve the Lincoln, and that the Lincoln would be heading back to San Diego.
On the journey home, the Lincoln docked in Thailand for several days, giving sailors a chance to walk on land and rest before beginning the final passage home.
In Thailand, the Guardian spoke with several sailors, who requested anonymity, who described eating “uncooked beef” and sliced-up, uncooked potatoes during the deployment. One sailor said that in his opinion, the decline in living standards was down to the battle conditions imposed during the combat operation, dubbed Operation Epic Fury, rather than the unprecedented length of deployment.
Another of the sailors said that the hardest part of the deployment was “pushing through, keeping the mentality”, while another serviceman hinted at the toll the long deployment had taken: “Some people adapt to it, but not everyone.”
Shakeria Fairfax, whose daughter, Jada, is onboard the Lincoln, couldn’t pass up the chance to be reunited with her daughter after such an intense deployment. She flew to Thailand, and still, to this day, Fairfax struggles to describe the moment they saw each other.
“The best way I could describe it is just kind of like when I first looked at her it was the overwhelming sense of love after having had so much time apart,” Fairfax said in an interview this week. “There was such a sense of pride, love and pride.”
For two days in Thailand, they played their favorite card game, went shopping and did what Fairfax called “girly things” – manicures, pedicures, facials and massages.
“It felt like we had some normalcy back in our lives after having been apart,” she said.
Like several other families the Guardian has spoken with, Fairfax did not want to disclose details of her daughter’s experience on the vessel, but described her as “extremely resilient”.
The deployment was Jada’s first, her mother said. She had completed basic training in October before she was deployed in November. When Fairfax woke to the news in February that the US and Israel had launched their war against Iran, she “couldn’t believe it”.
“We don’t come from a military family, and now my child is at war and I don’t know what that looks like,” she said.
Not long afterward, Fairfax lost contact with her daughter for several weeks, receiving only a handful of emails saying that she was OK. Then, on Easter weekend, Jada finally FaceTimed her mother. “It was beautiful,” Fairfax said.
Over the months that followed, Fairfax remembers only one occasion when her daughter told her she was feeling discouraged. Fairfax said she felt powerless, and asked her what she could do to help. Jada, who turned 25 onboard the ship in June, asked her mother to tell her stories about when she was growing up, she said.
So she did. “I told her stories. I sent her photographs,” Fairfax said. “Some of them she received, some of them she didn’t.”
Jada told her mother about some sailors onboard the ship who did not have the same kind of support system – people who did not receive care packages or have family members sending them reminders of home. And as the deployment continued, Fairfax said she could only imagine how difficult that must have become for those sailors. She and her daughter have since talked about finding a way to help those who do not have that support, she said.
For Fairfax, there was never much of a question about whether she would go to Thailand to see her daughter when she docked, as to her: “It was really about showing up for my daughter.”
Now she hopes to be able to head to San Diego to welcome her home.
The most serious disclosure about the deployment came after the Lincoln left Thailand.
In a letter responding to questions from the Democratic senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, acknowledged that eight navy personnel in the Lincoln strike group had attempted to take their own lives during the deployment, but said that no sailor had died from the attempts.
Cao said one sailor assigned to the air wing went overboard from the ship in early August but was “quickly recovered by an air wing search and rescue helicopter”. The sailor was treated by the vessel’s medical department and transferred off ship for follow-up care, Cao said, and the sailor’s family was notified.
Another sailor, he said, attempted to go overboard in March, but was stopped by his shipmates. That sailor was “also provided immediate medical care and subsequently returned to home port”, he added.
According to US Department of Defense data, there were 356 attempted suicides recorded in the navy in 2024. There were 287 in 2023, and 282 in 2022. This month, NPR reported that a 21-year-old sailor onboard the USS Fort Lauderdale, which had been deployed in the Caribbean as part of the Trump administration’s operation around Venezuela, died by suicide in June, a month before the vessel returned to Virginia.
Cao said that the navy launched a suicide prevention and response taskforce earlier this year, and also said in the letter that the Lincoln had deployed with five chaplains, an embedded integrated prevention counselor, a psychologist, a clinical social worker, three behavioral health technicians and a facility dog.
Cao said that the Lincoln “maintains adequate food supplies” but that due to the ship’s “participation in major combat operations with limited opportunities for resupply in a combat ‘environment, the number of main entree options served during regular meal hours was reduced from two to one for a short time”.
“Four meals were served daily, and all meals provided were nutritionally balanced, with adequate calories per day made available to every sailor,” he said.
The navy also acknowledged that earlier in the deployment the ship had experienced “localized piping failures” and temporary issues with its desalination units but that “shipboard engineering teams successfully completed repairs, and the potable water supply remains safe and tested daily”.
The new information prompted further calls from members of Congress for investigations and greater transparency.
In a statement, Gillibrand, who is a member of the Senate armed services committee, criticized the Trump administration’s handling of the reports from the vessel.
“What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members,” she said, adding: “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect.”
In response, a White House spokesperson said that Trump has “rightfully restored a focus on readiness, lethality and supporting our war fighters at the Pentagon”.
“The president cares about our troops more than anyone, and he is ensuring our brave service members have all the resources they need to be successful as the United States military continues to economically strangle the Iranian regime,” they added.
Richard Blumenthal, the Democratic senator from Connecticut, also requested that navy leaders provide an “accounting of the eight suicide attempts”, including when they occurred and when senior navy leaders were informed of the incidents. He has also asked navy leaders to “detail the steps you will take to protect sailors’ mental health and wellbeing during future extended deployments”.
In an interview with the Guardian, Donald Guter, a retired navy judge advocate general, described the eight reported attempts as a “tremendously concerning number” but said that “given the operational tempo and the total lack of opportunity for port calls, in a way, it shouldn’t have surprised people”.
He described the Lincoln’s deployment as “extraordinary”, saying that spending “that long at sea without any breaks, at that operational tempo, is stressing on anyone”.
Carl Schuster, a retired US navy captain, said that during his long deployments, which lasted between six and seven months, it was not unusual to have one or two suicide attempts.
But, he said, “keep in mind, the Lincoln spent over 250 days at sea in a nine-month deployment, which is a much longer deployment and much more time entirely at sea than I ever did, so I’m not surprised at the additional stress and the additional attempts”.
“We’re asking the crews to sacrifice much more than was normal in my day,” Schuster said. “All of us have a breaking point.”
Lory Manning, who served more than 25 years in the navy, said that given the size of the strike group and the unprecedented length of the deployment, she didn’t think it was that “far out of bounds to have that many attempts” across thousands of people who “have been bottled up on ships for 10 months”, particularly amid prolonged uncertainty, deployment extensions and intense combat conditions.
“I’m very glad that nobody succeeded,” Manning said.
John Cordle, who retired from the navy in 2013 after 30 years of service and served in a carrier strike group, said he could remember only one suicide attempt onboard a ship of the two that he was in command of, so to him, “eight seems like a lot”.
Cordle said that his longest deployment had been seven and a half months and his longest period without a port call had been 110 days.
“I never had to deal with conditions this extreme,” he said of the Lincoln’s deployment.
He urged the navy in the future to be more transparent earlier about the conditions onboard, especially with the families, and said that he hoped the leaders learned from the Lincoln’s deployment.
Several veterans also cautioned that the strain of these deployments could potentially affect enlistment in the future.
“Given the history of what does and doesn’t make people re-enlist, it’s certainly quite possible that none of them want to go through that again,” said Manning, “and maybe not the sailors, maybe it’s their families that don’t want to have to go through it again.”
During a town hall in late August, Adm Daryl Caudle, the chief of naval operations, warned that long deployments could become more common. That warning came as, earlier this year, the USS Gerald Ford returned from a record-breaking 326 days at sea, marking the longest deployment by a US warship since the Vietnam war.
“In the short term, until I can grow the navy we need, I hate to admit it, but longer deployments are going to be probably part of that,” Caudle said.
Matthew Brown, a US navy reserve commander and former captain of the USS Scout, said he visited the Lincoln in mid-September.
Brown runs Chimney Trail Health, a behavioral healthcare company that specializes “in creative adaptations of cognitive behavior theory”. He said the Lincoln’s captain had invited him to provide his company’s cognitive readiness training program to the sailors as the carrier headed home.
He said he delivered an in-person seminar, “sort of like a tabletop workshop-type thing”, to those onboard, and that it was “well received”.
At that time, the crew were on their journey home, and Brown said he observed that their “morale was that they were obviously quite tired because it was a very like rigorous deployment” but that “they were resolute”.
The sailors, he added, “were strong, and many of them maintained a very good sense of humor”.
For future deployments, Brown said that having more personnel onboard trained in the basics of cognitive behavior theory and equipped with evidence-based materials could help when it comes to addressing some of the mental health challenges that may arise.
Later in September, the congresswoman Sara Jacobs, a Democrat representing California’s 51st district, which includes San Diego, said she joined a bipartisan delegation for in-person oversight of the Lincoln as it journeyed back to San Diego.
“I raised my concerns directly with the ship’s command and received a briefing on logistics, supply issues and lessons learned for future deployments,” she said. “I also met with sailors and marines onboard who painted a very different picture of this war; they shared stories of the deployment and their struggles to wash clothes, get medicine and healthcare, and eat enough food.”
Jacobs said that she didn’t blame the ship’s leadership, saying they had done the best they could under difficult circumstances. Instead, she said she blamed the president, whom she accused of “knowingly launch[ing] a war without the required planning and strategy needed”.
She said she would push for an investigation into the conditions and a House armed services committee hearing to hear directly from service members once they returned.
Meanwhile, another US carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, was just recently dispatched to the Middle East.
In a video statement in early September, navy leaders said that they were learning from the Lincoln’s deployment, and had loaded the Roosevelt up with additional food, hygiene products and other supplies before it got under way.
“We’re also focused on quality of life,” they said, adding that they will provide additional entertainment and fitness equipment onboard, and said that they were improving communication with families throughout the deployment.
“To the Lincoln team, thank you for what you accomplished, and for what you taught us, and to the Roosevelt team, we’re doing everything we can to make sure you are ready for the mission,” they said. “You and your families.”

‘It’s not just about getting drunk!’ How Oktoberfest took over the UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:00:54 UTC
18:00:54 KST

Under a sea of Bavarian bunting, vendors hand out steins of pilsner, dunkel and weissbier, alongside platters of bratwurst, pork knuckle and pretzels. The lederhosen-clad Bettesteiner Footstompers lead the cheering crowd in a boisterous oompah singalong: “Eins, zwei, g’suffa!” (“One, two, drink up!”) Foot-tapping, glass-clinking and swaying soon turn into dancing, and eventually a full-blown conga.
The spirit of Oktoberfest is well and truly upon us – but Munich is more than 500 miles away. My friends and I are at Wünder Harbour in Folkestone, Kent, a homage to the German event. Wünder Harbour has been held since 2023, first over one weekend, and now four as its popularity has rocketed. It is just one of scores of Oktoberfest tributes all over the UK, from tiny bars to enormous marquees in pretty much every major city.
The original Oktoberfest was held in Munich in 1810 to celebrate the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria, later King Ludwig I, and Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen. It involved a horse race and a five-day party; the latter was such a hit it has been repeated every year since – except during wars and pandemics – and now lasts more than two weeks. Despite the name, Oktoberfest mostly takes place in September (19 September to 4 October this year).
Munich’s Oktoberfest is the world’s biggest beer festival: last year, 6.5 million people drank 6.5m litres of the stuff. Brits tend to associate the event with bratwurst, but by far the most eaten dish is Wiesnhendl, or roast chicken. It’s not just about boozing, either. According to the official report on 2025’s event, “The festival audience was a colourful mix of families with children, groups of work colleagues, young people and senior citizens – all coming to the Theresienwiese [the festival grounds] to stroll around for a few hours, try out the rides, eat, drink and celebrate in the festival tents and beer gardens.” About 30% of visitors were from abroad, with Britons in third place after Americans and Italians.
In the UK, the Campaign for Real Ale and other drinking enthusiasts have long held autumn beer festivals inspired by Oktoberfest. But outright copycat events – German-themed, often held in large tents – are a newer phenomenon. Belfast was one of the first UK cities to host one, in 2008, followed by London in 2011, Edinburgh in 2013 and Cardiff in 2014. Now they are everywhere, in city squares (such as Newcastle), parks (Cambridge, Chichester), racecourses (Beverley, Doncaster) and town halls (Portsmouth). Southampton claims to hold the UK’s biggest Oktoberfest.
Some are daytime, family-friendly affairs, like Folkestone’s. Dan Johannsen, the marketing manager for Folkestone Harbour Arm, tells me it was deliberately named Wünder Harbour rather than Oktoberfest to give it a broader appeal. There are certainly as many families eating fish and chips and ice-cream, and enjoying the free entertainment, as there are groups getting stuck into the steins. “The world needs more of this!” one man tells the band after a rousing chorus of Edelweiss.
Elsewhere, things can get a bit boozier. British beerhalls have got in on the action, such as Albert’s Schloss, whose branches in Manchester, Liverpool, Birmingham and London celebrate Oktoberfest for five weeks. I braved the opening night at another, the Bermondsey Bierkeller, which claims to host “London’s wildest Oktoberfest”. Within minutes my friends and I were standing on the table, beers in hand, singing along to an oompah version of Don’t Look Back in Anger by Oasis.
“We’re a German-themed bar, so it would be criminal not to celebrate Oktoberfest,” says Jim Gallivan, the Bierkeller’s general manager. He says the event started after Covid and has got busier every year since. He estimates that on Saturday nights, about half the crowd is in fancy dress, and we certainly spotted plenty of lederhosen and dirndls. Why does he think it is so popular? “It’s immersive, with actors, stilt-walkers and a seven-piece band. There are no airs and graces – it gets pretty rowdy,” he says. “People are looking to get as much as they can from a night out.”
Perhaps that’s it. With socialising now so expensive, people want more for their money. “I think it’s partly down to social media,” adds Beth Heath, the co-owner of Shropshire Festivals, which runs an Oktoberfest in Shrewsbury. “A themed event works as an Instagram moment.”
Heath organised the first Shropshire Oktoberfest in 2017 for her husband. “I’d been running events for years and he moaned there was nothing for blokes,” she says. “We had a festival for kids, a food festival for me, so I decided to do a beer festival for him.” About 6,000 people came – about 40% of whom were women. “There weren’t enough toilets! You need a lot more loos than you think at a beer festival.” By last year, attendance had doubled to 12,000 (the facilities have been scaled up accordingly).
Heath says the festival is especially popular with groups of friends. “We get big groups of about 15 people, such as university reunions,” she says. “They can drink, dance and party, and still be in bed by 11. People come from all over the UK. Accommodation in Shrewsbury is booked out a year in advance.” About 70% of people come in “incredibly creative” fancy dress: “We’ve had giant pickles, sausages …”
As well as the usual oompah music, there are skiffle groups and local party bands. “It’s a wedding disco vibe,” says Heath. Other entertainment includes carpool karaoke, a giant silent disco and a big comedy tent. “It’s not just about coming and getting drunk,” she says. Of course, lots of people are there for the beer, which is sourced from Shropshire breweries. “We’re trying to be authentic but put a Shropshire spin on it.”
Heath thinks celebrating Oktoberfest is a way to beat the post-summer blues and add some excitement to a quiet time of year, before the countdown to Christmas starts. “It’s the last hurrah of the season. We have two 130-metre marquees, so there are no weather worries. Wellies and lederhosen – that’s a look!” Ultimately, she says, “It’s about bringing people together and making memories. It’s about the beer, the food and the vibe.”
No wonder more and more Oktoberfests are springing up. New ones this year range from a down-to-earth beer and bratwurst knees-up in Darlington Market Square, County Durham, to an upmarket event at Horsley Towers, a country house in Surrey, with craft beer, wine and gin.
What do the Munich organisers of a 200-year-old tradition make of these British upstarts? “The city of Munich is very proud that many events around the world, including in the UK, are inspired by Oktoberfest,” says a spokesperson. “We are delighted that our festival has such international appeal and helps to share Bavarian culture and hospitality with a global audience.”
You sense there’s a “but” coming. “At the same time, the Oktoberfest in Munich remains the one and only official Oktoberfest. It is a protected name and a unique tradition that has been celebrated on the Theresienwiese since 1810. While many ‘Oktoberfest-style’ events capture the spirit of beer, food and music, they cannot replicate the history, scale and local roots of the original festival in Munich.”
True. But not everyone can make it to Munich. For many British beer-lovers, it’s much more convenient to raise a stein in your nearest town square or park. Or, as in Folkestone, to combine it with a fun day out at the seaside. All together now: “Prost!”

The American dream remains elusive in the valley that inspired East of Eden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:00:54 UTC
18:00:54 KST

Nestled between two mountain ranges at the crook of central California’s coastline sits a valley known as the “salad bowl of the world”.
Farm workers stoop over neatly lined rows of crops off Highway 101 to harvest more than half of the nation’s supply of lettuce and nearly a third of its strawberries. The soil here is so rich that author John Steinbeck made the Salinas valley the promised land in his literary depictions of people chasing the American dream: immigrants, farm workers, westward-moving hopefuls, hungering for a better life.
It’s a story that continues to capture the American imagination: Netflix has adapted Steinbeck’s 1952 blockbuster novel, East of Eden, into a limited series starring Florence Pugh, released 1 October.
“This will be a valley of great richness one day,” Steinbeck wrote of the farmland in East of Eden. “And happy people will live here, thousands and thousands.”
But Steinbeck also understood just how difficult it can be to achieve that elusive American dream. Even after some his characters found their way to Salinas and other parts of California’s agricultural valley, many remained stuck in low-paying jobs, making barely enough to scrape by, let alone own their own land.
That reality persists in the Salinas of today – an area at the sharp edge of a national affordability crisis that is reshaping politics across the US, and much of the rest of the world.
A recent Brookings Institution analysis found that Salinas is the least affordable city in the US for the middle class, defined as the middle 60% of income earners. Nearly 60% of the middle class in the Salinas area – which spans households making $38,000 to $193,000 – can’t afford basic necessities, double the national average, according to the analysis. And for Salinas’s Latino middle class, which make up 40% of all middle-class households, three-quarters struggle to afford everyday life.
Residents specifically say that homeownership, the modern symbol of the American dream, is out of reach. It’s an issue that is playing out across the country: half of all renter households and about a quarter of homeowner households spend more than 30% of their income on housing, according to the latest data from the US census.
“It really calls in question: what is the middle class?” said Andre Perry, a senior fellow at Brookings who oversaw the study. Many towns like Salinas that served as havens for the middle class are now out of reach. “People go to Salinas as a reprieve from San Francisco and some of these high-priced cities, but in actuality, they’re finding it more difficult to live,” he said.
Solutions are not easy to come by. The rising cost of living has torn Salinas apart. New housing has grown at a snail’s pace, and a rent-stabilization policy has bitterly divided residents.
If life in places like Salinas becomes too expensive for American families, where do they go next?
‘Everything’s changed’
Steinbeck had a conflicted relationship with his home town, said Gavin Jones, chair of the English department at Stanford University and a Steinbeck scholar, one that he often reflected in his writing. For many of Steinbeck’s characters, California and its farmland ultimately prove to be gutting disappointments after everything they sacrificed to get there.
“It’s kind of the promised land. It’s this realm of richness,” said Jones of the role Salinas played in Steinbeck’s magnum opus. “But then of course, it’s also a fallen paradise … it’s not quite Eden, it’s east of Eden.”
Steinbeck was born to a solidly middle-class family and was raised in a turreted, Victorian-style house that still stands just a few blocks away from Salinas’s downtown. He was long critical of the hypocrisy and “underbelly” he saw in his social demographic, Jones said, and worked alongside immigrant workers on nearby farms while dropping in and out of Stanford University.
Steinbeck was also “very American” in his idealized vision of social mobility, ascendancy and agency, Jones added, and would have likely been outraged at the affordability struggles many still face in the US, accentuated by the increasingly “K-shaped economy” with the rich getting richer as the poor slide down the other side.
“One wonders if the conditions are that much different today in the central valley, especially for agricultural workers … from the conditions that Steinbeck represented in the 1930s,” Jones said.
Gaye Freedman, 75, and her husband had been searching for somewhere affordable to live for years before they moved to Salinas in 2017, where their son was raising a baby as a single dad. Though they passed up more affordable cities in northern California, the beautiful, year-round weather – cool, foggy mornings that give way to balmy afternoons – as well as proximate medical care for older adults made their decision easier.
But Freedman, who earned a doctorate degree in educational psychology from the University of Southern California, was unable to find much work in Salinas that paid much beyond minimum wage. She currently works part-time at a school.
Between part-time jobs and social security, Freedman and her husband make about $75,000 total and pay $1,850 for their one-bedroom apartment, which became a rent-stabilized unit in 2024. After rent and Medicare payments, they don’t have much left to spare on groceries, gas and unexpected maintenance on their 14-year-old car. The balance on their credit card, she said, keeps climbing.
“This is the first time in my life I’ve actually had to think about what I’m cooking, because I can’t afford to cook what I usually would,” she said. “We’re eating a lot more stews and spaghetti and chicken. I’m definitely thinking of what lasts more than one day.”
Freedman and her husband have considered moving, but many of the affordable cities nearby lack medical care facilities or infrastructure that will be crucial for the couple as they get older.
Other residents cited similar concerns of getting pushed out by the cost of living. Salvador Herrera, 52, a former construction worker who grew up in Salinas, said gone are the days of his childhood where a family could raise their children in their own apartment unit or home. In Salinas, it is now common for multiple families to live together: garages are partitioned with curtains; single bedrooms are crammed with young children and parents; and bathrooms are shared among dozens.
Herrera supports his family using disability payments after an injury on the job left him unable to work. Rising rent has sometimes meant weeks where he has just $50 to spend on groceries for himself and his two children.
“Everything’s changed. Especially the housing, it’s way too expensive. And the pay is cheap nowadays,” he said.
Salinas’s close proximity to Silicon valley leaves it vulnerable to the same housing woes faced by the rest of the Bay Area, housing experts say.
Its surrounding farmland also makes it difficult to expand and build there, all of which has led to a persistent lack of housing supply that has pushed up prices for years. Meanwhile, the median household income in Salinas is just shy of $90,000, compared with a median of roughly $150,000 in San Jose or San Francisco.
“We got caught up early on Bay Area economics,” Salinas mayor Dennis Donohue said at a Starbucks across from the Salinas Sports Complex, where he was attending an agricultural biotechnology conference. “You have all the economic challenges of the Bay Area impacting Salinas and this area without corresponding economic opportunities.”
All of this pressure comes even as California is home to some of the most progressive housing policies in the US, with rent caps on most households statewide and further protections at the local level. Still, residents face the highest median monthly housing costs in the country, according to the latest census data.
Critics on both sides of the political aisle have in part criticized the state’s governor, Gavin Newsom, for the state’s cost-of-living crisis, including sky-high housing costs. Newsom, who is considering a presidential run, has blamed Trump but may well find voters – and his opponents – put the blame closer to home.
Meanwhile, housing is one of the most potent issues at the voting polls: a recent survey from CNBC found that the high cost of housing was the most pressing concern for voters aged 18 to 34 years old.
Trouble in paradise
The Salinas city council sent Freedman and many more struggling households a lifeline in 2024, when it passed a rent-stabilization ordinance that capped annual rent increases on certain multifamily rental properties to either 2.75% or three-quarters of the annual inflation rate, whichever is less. Freedman says she’s saved thousands of dollars already because of the caps her landlord now places on her rent increases each year.
But the town has been heavily divided on the policy. When a new city council board took over the next year, it repealed the policy, arguing the ordinance unfairly penalized apartment property owners and would discourage much-needed housing construction.
A referendum vote was announced for this November after advocacy groups gathered enough signatures. Rent stabilization will remain until then, but it’s unclear where voters will land.
It’s a deeply emotional issue for Salinas, said Tony Barrera, a longtime resident and a city council representative who was among the minority who voted to keep rent stabilization in 2025. His district is overwhelmingly supportive of keeping the measures in place: 70% are renters and 80% are field workers, he said. About a third are undocumented, which means they won’t be able to vote in the fall.
But he also raised concerns that landlords in his district would not be able to afford their mortgage or property maintenance with the ordinance. If they sell their homes, he added, that could end up driving rents up further for his constituents.
“I’m caught in the middle,” he said.
Matt Huerta, an affordable housing expert based in Salinas and an advocate for rent stabilization, said that landlords can apply for exemptions if they need to raise rents higher than the ordinance allows.
“We recognize that sometimes costs are higher than inflation. Sometimes tariffs come in, and all of a sudden you can’t get that refrigerator or water heater,” he said. “There’s an application process for that.”
Amy Salmina, a property manager in Salinas, said many of the middle-class homeowners she works with have been selling their properties due to rising costs. Most are in their 60s and bought rental properties as investments, but rising property taxes and insurance have ultimately handed them greater losses.
Housing specifically for the middle class is severely lacking in Salinas, she added, and economic opportunities aren’t keeping up with growth.
“We have so much help [for] the low-income, which is great,” she said. “But we’re forgetting about the middle class,” she added, referring to families who make “too much money to get any assistance or to get lower-income housing”.
Salmina’s family has lived in Salinas for four generations, but she is doubtful that her children will be able to afford to stay.
“My son’s a firefighter. I don’t even know how they’re going to be able to buy a house,” she said. “I told all my kids: ‘Look, unless you have two incomes, you guys won’t be able to stay here.’”
Those fighting against rent stabilization say that the law would exacerbate the town’s housing crisis, because it could disincentivize investors or developers looking to build in the area. But advocates argue that the city’s rent-stabilization ordinance only applies to buildings built before 1995, so newly built units can still be listed at market price.
For years, the city has struggled with a housing supply that hasn’t kept pace with its population. Even though the Salinas city council approved a plan in 2008 to build 11,500 new residential units, the Great Recession made it nearly impossible to finance any new construction, said Donohue, who had been in the middle of his first mayoral term at the time.
New construction was also stopped by Covid and has been slow to pick up even six years later. Now, with mortgage rates surpassing 7%, a 20-month high, and the US Federal Reserve poised to raise interest rates further, borrowing costs are exacerbating the crisis.
But Donohue has optimism for the future of the town, which he says exports “vegetables and too many of our kids”. He and other local officials are trying to bring more job opportunities to the area, while the city council recently approved a down payment assistance plan for first-time homebuyers.
“I’m the mayor of the hometown of John Steinbeck,” Donohue said. “If any city should know how to tell a story, it should be this one. I’m confident the city, the book, will have a happy ending.”
He just can’t tell you how long it will take.
