How local can a global restaurant really be?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:13:35 UTC
17:13:35 KST

In hospitality, standardisation creates a sense of trust; in gastronomy, it can sometimes disconnect a restaurant from the place it inhabits. While speaking with Mark Vaessen, Global Culinary Chef of OKU Hotels, in Bodrum, we found ourselves returning to one question: What truly makes a restaurant local — the ingredients it uses, or how deeply it understands the place to which those ingredients belong?
Consistency is one of the fundamental principles of hospitality. When you stay with the same brand in Istanbul, Paris or Tokyo, you expect certain standards, from the room to the service. In gastronomy, however, that same logic can work in reverse. What is an advantage in a hotel room can easily become a disadvantage in the kitchen. If the dish you eat in Ibiza is replicated in Bodrum and the one in Bodrum appears again in Kos, eventually the destination becomes little more than the view outside the restaurant window.
This was precisely what Vaessen and I discussed in Bodrum. OKU’s hotels in Ibiza, Kos, Andalusia and Bodrum share certain codes: The sea, olive oil, vegetables, fire and a culture of sharing. But for Vaessen, that is where the similarities between their kitchens should end. Consistency, in his view, should lie not in serving the same dishes but in a shared philosophy: Good ingredients, clean flavours, simplicity and generosity. Everything else should respond to the place. One sentence captures his entire approach: “Bodrum should taste like Bodrum.”
“Local” has become one of the restaurant world’s favourite words. Menus are filled with terms such as local, seasonal and farm-to-table. Buying vegetables from a nearby grower and serving locally caught fish are, of course, valuable choices. But as Vaessen points out, buying a local tomato does not automatically make a restaurant local.
First, you have to understand where you are. That means visiting markets, eating in local restaurants, talking to fishermen, farmers and producers; listening to chefs who grew up there and learning what people eat at home — and why. Buying an ingredient and understanding the culture to which it belongs are two very different things. Locality is not simply a matter of distance; it is also about how well you can read the knowledge accumulated around an ingredient.
That is exactly what Vaessen did after arriving in Bodrum, eating his way through local restaurants and discovering the region’s food. What struck him most was not a new ingredient or technique, but how much flavour could be achieved with so little intervention. Vegetables, wild herbs, olive oil, fish… When the ingredient is good enough, there is often very little you need to do to it.
He was also struck by a way of eating that we ourselves may barely notice: Small plates arriving one after another, dishes placed in the middle of the table to be shared, food and conversation flowing into one another. This social rhythm of eating also resonates with the culture of sharing that OKU seeks to create. But Bodrum reminded him of something more fundamental: Travelling as a chef does not always mean adding a new technique to your repertoire. Sometimes it teaches you to do less.
Perhaps this is one of the significant shifts taking place in contemporary gastronomy. There was a time when we measured a chef’s skill by how much technique could be brought to a plate; transformation, surprise and the creation of new textures were highly prized. Today, another form of mastery is coming to the fore: Rather than demonstrating everything you are capable of doing, knowing when to stop.
Vaessen takes a similar view when it comes to intervening in traditional dishes. He believes that a chef’s desire to leave a signature on every plate can sometimes have more to do with ego than with making the food better. Before reinterpreting a dish, he argues, you first need to understand why it exists, how people remember it and what makes it special.
Techniques can then change and an element can be reinterpreted. But if everything is altered simply to make the chef’s signature visible, the memory of the dish can disappear with it. Vaessen’s position is disarmingly simple: Sometimes the smartest thing a chef can do is taste something and say, “This is already good. Don’t touch it.”
This idea becomes even more interesting at Teyo, OKU Bodrum’s restaurant centred around Japanese influences and techniques. The kitchen in Bodrum is led by Executive Chef Muhammed Karaaslan. Ultimately, it is in the hands of Karaaslan and his team that the relationship between a global culinary philosophy and local ingredients is tested every day.
At first glance, Japan and Bodrum may seem like two distant culinary cultures. Vaessen, however, sees their common ground not in recipes but in their attitude towards ingredients. He draws a parallel between the Japanese respect for seasonality and produce and the Aegean instinct for simplicity when faced with excellent fish, olive oil and wild herbs. In both, the point is not to obscure the ingredient but to preserve its character.
Fire is another language they share. Cooking over fire may look simple, but it demands an understanding of when to intervene and when to leave the ingredient alone. This is where Vaessen sees Teyo’s potential in Bodrum: Not in allowing Japanese technique to overpower Bodrum’s ingredients, but in letting the two speak to one another. The distinction matters. In restaurants that bring different cuisines together, local produce can easily become little more than a stage on which to showcase a foreign technique. The real challenge is to create an encounter in which neither side loses its identity. Vaessen also believes the menu should continue to evolve as the team eats in local restaurants, meets producers, listens to those around them and gains a deeper understanding of the ingredients.
Seen from this perspective, OKU’s kitchens in Bodrum, Kos, Ibiza and Andalusia offer an interesting case study. All four share the sea, olive oil, vegetables, fire, seasonality and a culture of sharing, yet each expresses them differently. Vaessen’s aim is not to turn them into versions of the same restaurant, but to allow knowledge to circulate between them.
An ingredient or technique discovered in Bodrum might inspire the team in Ibiza, but it should not simply be reproduced there; it needs to be reinterpreted through Ibiza’s own ingredients and culinary culture. The wild herbs, local olive oil and clean, saline character of the Aegean that Vaessen would like to take from Bodrum are therefore not recipes to be exported, but starting points for new culinary ideas.
Perhaps this is the most interesting possibility globalisation offers gastronomy: Not replicating the same plates in different parts of the world, but allowing places to learn from one another. The global restaurant of the future may not be defined by how perfectly it can reproduce itself around the world. The real skill may lie in understanding how much it needs to change each time it arrives somewhere new.
And the starting point is remarkably simple: Sit down at the table, taste the food of that place and truly listen.

Choosing life, building hope: Former hostage turns to disability advocacy to honor wife, daughters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:13:30 UTC
17:13:30 KST

"I cannot change what was taken from me, but I can choose what I build,” says Eli Sharabi, a former resident of Kibbutz Be’eri who was taken hostage by Hamas terrorists on Oct. 7, 2023, and freed after enduring 491 days of brutal imprisonment in the tunnels of Gaza.
The image of an emaciated Sharabi freed from Hamas captivity, walking slowly through a jeering throng of Gazans into the hands of the International Red Cross on February 8, 2025, is permanently imprinted on the Israeli psyche. Sharabi, who lost 30 kilos during his imprisonment, weighed just 44 kilos upon his release. It was only after he returned to Israel that he learned that his wife Lianne, 48, and daughters Noiya, 16, and Yahel, 13, were murdered by Hamas terrorists in their Kibbutz Be’eri home on Oct. 7.
After his release, Sharabi became a prominent voice for the remaining hostages, met with world leaders, addressed the United Nations Security Council, and recounted his ordeal in interviews and his memoir, Hostage, which became an international bestseller.
Outwardly, at least, Sharabi, now 54, looks much as he did before his captivity, returning to a healthy weight. We sit at Shalva, the Israel Association for the Care and Inclusion of Persons with Disabilities, at the organization’s Jerusalem headquarters, with Kalman Samuels, Shalva’s founder and president, and his son Nachman, the group’s CEO.
Shalva provides therapy, education, rehabilitation, and family support for people with disabilities, from infancy through adulthood. Founded by Samuels and his wife Malki in 1990, it promotes inclusion while helping families navigate the challenges of caring for a loved one with disabilities.
What is Sharabi’s connection to Shalva?
“When my wife was younger and lived in England, she volunteered with children who had special needs,” he explains. Sharabi’s oldest daughter Noiya followed in her mother’s footsteps.
Noiya and Yahel often played with a girl with special needs who lived on the kibbutz, and they valued their relationship with her.
When Sharabi was working as the business manager for Kibbutz Be’eri, he came to the Shalva campus for a convention in 2017. “I was fascinated with the place, and after I came home to Be’eri, I told my wife and daughters, ‘I have to take you there.’ Sharabi never had the chance to bring them, but he says he always knew the work being done there would resonate with them.
Then came the horrors of Oct. 7. Sharabi, along with hundreds of other hostages, was held captive by the terrorists in Hamas’s underground tunnels in Gaza, under inhuman conditions. At that time, he did not know that his wife and daughters had been murdered.
“I remember sitting 50 meters underground, thinking about all the possible scenarios that could have happened to my family. I told my fellow hostages that if my wife and my daughters hadn’t survived, I would have no doubt where I would memorialize them – it would be through Shalva.”
After Sharabi was freed, he spent 10 days in the hospital, and then traveled throughout the world, met with world leaders, and lobbied for the remaining hostages’ freedom. Several months later, he visited Shalva, to ask the organization to name a room in memory of his wife and daughters.
Samuels recalls that Sharabi had told him, “I speak around the world, but there’s only one place that I want to actually be part of and create something and work together with. This is at Shalva.”
He explains the genesis of Sharabi’s interest in Shalva. “Eli called my wife Malki two weeks after he got out of Gaza. He told her he had visited Shalva once as the CFO of a company at a conference, and he went back and told his wife and children how amazing this magical place is.
“They were all involved in special education, and they begged him to take them to show them this magical place. That never happened.
“Two weeks after he came out [of Hamas captivity], he said, ‘Malki, Shalva is the only place I want a memorial for my wife and two daughters who were murdered.’
“Malki cried and said, ‘Eli, please come down in person, and we’ll do it together.’” Several months later, Sharabi came to Shalva, and Malki shared the idea she had. She went up one flight of stairs in the lobby and pointed out the area she wanted to dedicate to Sharabi’s wife and children.
“Malki asked him for a picture of him with his wife and daughters, and he sent a photograph. From that photo, the artist painted the image, and Eli provided the wording on the wall. That was his wording, and the butterflies, of course, we added. The wall was completed several months ago.”
Honoring the departed: Diagnostic services, family support, and trauma treatment
Samuels and the Shalva team wanted to do more with Sharabi to help him fulfill his mission of memorializing his wife and daughters. Before their meeting, the government had turned to Shalva and asked them to create a center in Ashkelon to help residents of the South. The proposed center would provide diagnostic services, family support, and trauma treatment.
Samuels’s son Yochanan, along with the Shalva team, began investigating possible sites for the new Shalva center, and decided to build a new facility. They asked Sharabi for permission to call the center the Shalva Sharabi Family Center. “Eli said ‘yes,’ and that’s how we began,” he says.
Since then, Sharabi has traveled worldwide, raising funds for the new center, which is still under construction. The facility will serve 28 Gaza border communities as well as the southern region, operating from a permanent facility in the Marina View complex opposite the Ashkelon marina.
The Shalva Sharabi Center will address two pressing needs in southern Israel: accessible services for people with disabilities, and support for those affected by trauma. Families across the South often contend with long journeys, lengthy waiting lists, and fragmented care when seeking specialist assessments and treatment.
Building on Shalva’s existing model, the Family Center will bring diagnosis, therapy, rehabilitation, and family support together under one roof. Multidisciplinary teams will provide assessments and individualized care for infants, children, and adults. Services will include occupational therapy, physiotherapy, speech therapy, and Shalva’s “Me and My Mommy” early intervention program, alongside parental guidance and peer support.
The Horizons Pavilion will focus on trauma recovery and resilience for children and adults, soldiers, first responders, civilians, and families affected by the Oct. 7 Hamas-led massacres and the war. The initiative draws on Shalva’s experience providing therapeutic care, respite, and emotional support to evacuees, particularly people with disabilities and their families.
The center’s location near the Ashkelon Marina makes it an ideal site to combine individual and group therapies with outdoor and sea-based activities, designed to support recovery. Its programs will seek to strengthen coping skills, restore independence, and help individuals and families rebuild their connections to community life.
For Sharabi, the Shalva Sharabi Center in Ashkelon will remind him of his wife Lianne’s smile, Noiya’s passion for working with children with special needs, and how Yahel used to play with the child with special needs, in Kibbutz Be’eri. “This project gives me a great deal of strength, and is a meaningful way to honor the memory of Lianne, Noiya, and Yahel,” he says.
Having his name associated with the Shalva Center in Ashkelon epitomizes Sharabi’s philosophy of refusing to give up hope. “It just shows that life goes on. We cannot stop time. We can shape our future,” he adds.
“I can choose to stay in bed and cry all day. I chose differently from the moment I decided to act. Initially, it was for the remaining hostages who were held in Gaza; after that, for Jewish communities all around the world fighting antisemitism. For me, doing things means choosing life and helping to change the lives of others for good.
“The community of Be’eri lost more than 100 people in one day. So for me, it’s a big victory – after spending 491 days in captivity, most of them spent in Hamas tunnels – to believe that one day, I could come back to life and have a second chance to do things and impact others and influence Israeli society. It’s more than a dream.”
Sharabi says it will be deeply moving to walk into the Shalva Sharabi Center one day and see children and families receiving care. “It will be amazing. I can’t think of anything else that will provide the same amount of emotional happiness.”
Samuels and Sharabi: Different but intersecting worlds
Both Sharabi and Samuels say that although they come from different worlds, they have learned a great deal from each other. Sharabi says the partnership has introduced him to a world he barely knew. “I learned that, first of all, I know nothing about this world of kids with special needs and education. I always had my businesses and my career.
“The philanthropic world wasn’t part of my world, and it’s become very meaningful to me. It’s much more satisfying than another business. I learned a lot from Kalman about his passion. He is relentless about caring for all these kids, getting them and their families the services they need. It’s amazing to be with the Samuels family and to understand and learn.”
Samuels shares that he has learned how to rise above despair from Sharabi. “There’s every reason in the world that Eli should not have been able to get back on his feet. Yet he made a decision, early on, to ensure that his wife and daughter’s names would be in the public sphere and always remembered. Thank God, it is happening.
“But the idea that a person can get out of that and be a source of inspiration and hope for generations of people… Eli is spreading hope, which is probably the most important, most powerful element of mankind. When a person loses hope, he’s finished. And if a person has hope, it doesn’t matter what his situation is; life still has power. Eli has become this symbol of hope for the world.”
Like Sharabi, Shalva is also associated with that word. Its motto, “Inspiring Hope. Changing Lives,” suggests that the partnership between Sharabi and Shalva will bring hope and provide much-needed services for Israelis living in the South.
The Family Center, the first phase of the Shalva Sharabi Family Center in Ashkelon, is scheduled to open in January 2027, and the trauma center is planned to open in spring 2027. Samuels says they have raised $5 million toward the $10.5 million budget to complete the project. With nearly half the funding secured, the support of additional partners will help turn Sharabi’s vision of a living memorial into a place of healing for families across the South.
The drawing on the inside wall of the Shalva lobby features Eli, his wife, and his two daughters, with the words “Memory and hope light the way” in English and Hebrew, accompanied by three-dimensional images of three butterflies, to symbolize his family.
Samuels relates that when the artist began to paint the butterflies, a large butterfly flew inside the building and perched on the ledge. The artist, who was standing on a ladder some six meters above the building’s entrance, was a bit unnerved by the incident, he says.
On the second day, a different butterfly flew in, and on the third day, when she painted the third image, yet another butterfly arrived. “We have been in that building for over 10 years, and I have never seen a butterfly inside the lobby,” Samuels says. “The artist saw three large butterflies that sat and perched themselves near her.”
Samuels, who considers himself a realistic person with his feet on the ground, found the butterflies’ appearance inexplicable.
“For me, I feel very clearly that it’s just a good sign of the acceptance of his prayer – that his wife and daughters wanted to be there,” he says. “They didn’t get there in life, and somehow [Eli] wanted to give them a sense of peace.”■

Side by Side: Helping people with disabilities connect socially
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:13:06 UTC
17:13:06 KST

"The goal is not inclusion. What I’m looking for is belonging. There’s a huge difference between being included and belonging,” said Jacki Edry. A Netanya-based author, educator, and advocate for those with special needs, she is now creating a new program – Side by Side: Building Community, Together – to help fulfill the social needs of young adults with disabilities.
“Belonging means that you’re part of the community. Everybody looks after you, and you look out for everybody else, because communities take care of each other,” she added.
Edry is a mother of five, one of whom, a 29-year-old son, is on the autism spectrum. Through her son’s experiences, she realized that there was a desperate need in Israel for a program to help those with disabilities find a true sense of belonging.
People are generally familiar with autistic savants who serve in the army’s elite 8200 unit, as well as those on the other extreme of the spectrum, who can barely communicate and require 24/7 supervision. However, many of those with autism generally do not fall into these extremes, she said, something that is true of people with all kinds of disabilities.
“There are lots of people in the middle. Most people are not at one end or the other. Most people are somewhere in between,” she said.
Edry's son has few opportunities to interact with his peers
While the Welfare and Social Affairs Ministry does not release detailed statistics on the functioning levels of people with disabilities, Edry said there are clearly thousands who are not served by any existing programs or frameworks.
After years in an educational system that provides them with a daily schedule, activities, social contact, and professional support, disabled people “age out” of the school system at age 21. They can suddenly find themselves with far fewer opportunities to meet people, participate in their communities, and build meaningful adult lives.
Edry has seen this happen with her son, who works part-time at a local branch of the Aroma café chain, thanks to Edry’s persistence and a kind manager who was willing to invest time showing her son the ropes. But outside of his working hours, her son spends most of his time at home and has few opportunities to interact with his peers. She searched hard, but didn’t find any programs that could help him.
She noted that Temple Grandin, a well-known autistic professor and activist in the US, wrote that she made friends when she was younger because she had opportunities to do interesting things with others.
“You build relationships by doing interesting things together – through a common interest. So, this program developed along those lines. One goal is to have people with disabilities become much more integrated into the community. But I didn’t want it to be a traditional ‘mentoring’ situation,” she noted.
“I therefore created a model where all participants would have the opportunity to do something meaningful together, through volunteering in the community and doing good for others.”
'They have fun together...they do wonderful things'
SHE IS DEVELOPING the Side by Side program in partnership with Et La’asot (A time to Act), an Israeli nonprofit organization that works with children and young people with disabilities and their families. Founded in 2006, Et La’asot runs programs across the country, including recreational activities, camps and vacations, weekend getaways, play centers, mentoring, family assistance, and volunteer training.
“Et La’asot’s existing model works with high school students,” said Edry. “High school students have volunteer requirements, and they work with children with disabilities. They have fun together. They travel around the country; they have play centers, one-on-one activities, and all kinds of programs. They do wonderful things.
“When I approached Et La’asot and proposed creating a similar model for older people, they were happy to partner with me to bring this project to fruition.”
Plans include volunteering with elderly people, assisting with food distribution, working in agriculture and animal care, and taking part in other community projects. The groups will also participate in trips, social activities, and special events.
But there was a problem. “People in their 20s and 30s often don’t have time simply to volunteer. The people I’m looking for are students who need to work to support themselves and pay tuition. So, I thought we could combine those things.
“The students will receive a grant for participating, and we can bring disabled and non-disabled young adults together to do enjoyable and meaningful things. If they go out and volunteer together in the community, they will be helping somebody else. They will be doing something useful together, something meaningful.”
Side by Side does not receive government funding. “A few very generous people have given us grants to get started. One donor has given $10,000 and is willing to match another $10,000, so donations made now, up to that amount, will be matched.”
The pilot program would start in Netanya, but Edry emphasized that it should become national.
Edry devoted herself to finding treatment and education after son's autism diagnosis
THE MORE you know about Edry, the more inspiring it is that she has taken on this ambitious project with the potential to help so many. Born and raised in a secular family in Great Neck, Long Island, she moved to Israel in her 20s, married a man from a more religiously observant background, and became interested in Judaism, gradually becoming observant herself. After one of her sons was diagnosed with autism, she devoted herself to finding treatment and education that would be most helpful to him, and he flourished.
About 13 years ago, when her son was a teen, she was diagnosed with a large tumor on her brainstem. Fortunately, it was benign, but she required complicated surgery that left her with numerous disabilities, including difficulties with sensory processing, similar to the types of neurodivergence typical of autistic individuals. These disabilities present her with many daily challenges. But her commitment to helping her son realize his potential has never wavered, and she is focused on reaching others in his situation.
In addition to taking the program national, she envisions Side by Side eventually adding a professional component.
“If my son had an apprenticeship – if professionals were willing to teach him one-on-one – he could learn many different types of jobs very well. I think most people with skills similar to his, if given that opportunity, could learn.
“There is a school in Colorado called TACT, which prepares people for apprenticeships and properly paying jobs – electricians, auto mechanics, plumbers, all different kinds of trades. The program has a waiting list for graduates. If we had something like that in Israel, it would be incredible.”
But in its initial phase, Side by Side will concentrate on creating social bonds.
“It is an opportunity for students to meet somebody different from themselves and realize that somebody who may need support can contribute to the community as well.”
The most important part of the program, she said, is that “by doing something meaningful together, hopefully real friendships will develop.”■
For more information, visit the Et La’asot website at www.etlaasot.org.il/BuildingCommunity

Morocco's first female head of government: Symbol or real reform?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:10:00 UTC
17:10:00 KST

Morocco's first female leader: Symbol or real reform?
October 3, 2026
After the announcement that Morocco would appoint its first female head of government – Marrakech mayor Fatima Zahra Mansouri – citizens interviewed by local television reporters were mostly enthusiastic.
"It would be great if we had a female prime minister for a change. She'd lift our spirits a bit," one woman said.
"Why don't we give women a chance? We've never had one [a female head of government] before," said another. "May God bless her and help her stay on a straight path."
"Regardless of who takes on the role, it should be a change for the better in Morocco," a man added.
But there were also naysayers. Some locals questioned how she would take part in official events where tradition and protocol dictate that only men attend.
"People are saying that a nation cannot succeed if a woman is in charge, even if she's only half in charge," one man told a television reporter, referring to the fact that Morocco's King Mohammed VI has the final say in national politics.
Morocco is a constitutional monarchy, so elections are held but the king has ultimate executive power. The head of the country's government, or prime minister, leads the cabinet and administration and executes public policy.
The king chose Fatima Zahra Mansouri, minister of planning and mayor of Marrakesh, over Fouzi Lekjaa, head of Morocco's football federation and budget minister. The pair are senior members of the Authenticity and Modernity Party, or PAM, which won the most seats in the country's parliamentary elections in September.
"If you talk to Moroccans, there are some who are really proud of having a woman at the top and they see a chance for her to have impact on women's representation in society," confirms Anja Freudenreich, who heads the Morocco office of Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation (FES) in Rabat. "But others see her appointment as bare symbolism."
Mansouri will lead what is colloquially being called the "World Cup government" as Morocco prepares to invest billions before it hosts the 2030 football World Cup along with Spain and Portugal. Mansouri is seen to have shown leadership after the devastating 2023 Morocco earthquake.
Her appointment makes her the third woman to lead a government in the Arab world.
Will Mansouri improve the lot of Moroccan women?
There is no doubt that Mansouri's appointment has important symbolic value, observers say.
Two Tunisian women, Najla Bouden and current prime minister Sara Zaafarani, became heads of an Arab government before Mansouri's appointment. A 2022 surveyby polling organization Arab Barometer found Tunisian attitudes towards women in power had changed as a result.
Researchers from Arab Barometer believed the change — with only 40% agreeing that "in general, men are better at political leadership than women" in 2022 compared to 56% four years earlier — was the result of a "role-model effect." Before the appointment of Bouden and Zaafarani, there had been no major changes, they pointed out.
According to a 2025 survey by the organization, attitudes toward women's roles have also been changing in Morocco. Mansouri could accelerate that.
"We've already noticed how impactful this [appointment] is in terms of social and cultural norms," said Stephanie Willman Bordat, co-founder of Rabat-based advocacy organization, Mobilizing for Rights Associates (MRA).
"People in public spaces, in cafes, on trains on their commute and just regular folks are having conversations about women's leadership and the taboo that says women can't be heads of government or women can't be bosses of men. There's good public debate and dialogue on this."
"And on a global level, in terms of women's participation, this is really something to encouraging," Bordat, who has lived in Morocco for two decades, told DW. "Especially when you look at the global climate of backlash and regression in women's rights."
Mansouri's prime ministership "is certainly notable as female leadership in the region is rare," Freudenreich of FES agreed. "It does have a highly symbolic character and I'm sure she does, or she will have, a role model function for women and girls in Morocco as well as in the region."
No major changes from past
However, Mansouri is unlikely to initiate a major change from past politics, Freudenreich suggested.
She's more of a pragmatist than a rebel — a quality that's likely to see her navigate the much-discussed issues of protocol — and her party's electoral manifesto doesn't go into any major detail on women's issues, she pointed out.
Before the September elections, MRA looked at which parties had women's issues in their electoral manifestos. Mansouri's party, PAM, appeared to offer only three such policies.
Other parties were more vocal on women's issues than PAM, with some saying they would push for updates to the Moroccan family code, or "moudawana." This sets rules on all-important aspects of Moroccan women's lives like custody of children, divorce, property rights, marriage, polygamy and domestic violence. It has not been updated since 2004.
Did the king pick a symbol or is he genuine?
In 2023, King Mohammed VI asked the then-prime minister to look into further updates to the family code. Discussions around that are ongoing and reforms are still pending, MRA's Bordat said.
"But what's really interesting is that now we can say, well, women can be heads of government so women can also be heads or co-heads of family," she argued.
The Moroccan king, who took the throne in 1999, has been broadly supportive of women's rights, Ahmed Benchemsi, advocacy and communications director for Human Rights Watch's Middle East and North Africa division, confirmed. Still, his organization would like to see things improve further.
"With regard to women's rights, a symbol won't serve women's rights as much as legal reform," Benchemsi told DW.
"Activism around women's rights remains relatively permitted — an exception to the heightened governmental scrutiny and judicial proceedings against other areas of activism in Morocco," the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace wrote in a July 2025 commentary. "The king's leadership on gender reforms creates space for this activity, as advocates are often working in conjunction with parts of the government rather than against it."
Given popular discontent with the economy and high youth unemployment and protests, "improving women's status is a promise the government can deliver on in a challenging period," the organization noted.
But right now, Bordat argued that Mansouri's appointment shouldn't be seen as "something to be either celebrated or criticized."
The country is still waiting to see how Mansouri will form a governing coalition, she argued. How many female ministers the new government appoints, and what powers they are granted, will also be closely observed.
After that, "the real question is what civil society organizations, NGOs and citizens will do with this opportunity?" Bordat concluded. "That is, how do we hold all of the political parties and all of the newly elected representatives accountable and engaged … so we can continue to advance women's rights in Morocco?"

Prime Minister's XIIIs thrash PNG in 11- and 12-try victories in Port Moresby

The Australians scored 11 tries and exposed the PNG side's defensive frailties almost at will in what was the 20th men's Prime Minister's XIII match.
It was hardly a conventional game at the National Football Stadium on Saturday, with Australia switching on and off as players became accustomed to their makeshift position.
Ezra Mam spent time at fullback. Jock Madden appeared to be playing on an edge. Jamal Fogarty stood in the centres, and Josh Curran kicked a goal.
At one stage they had three regular hookers on the field.
In one piece of consistency, captain David Fifita started and finished the match as a devastating left centre.
Commentator Cooper Cronk mused it was coach Ben Teo's way of keeping the Aussies engaged after a long, hard season.
It was at times chaotic and they dropped the ball a lot, but it was fun. Less so for the PNG side, who were not just outclassed but also ill-disciplined, missing 47 tackles — 28 in the first half alone.
With the PNG Chiefs' arrival in the NRL fast approaching, it is clear the next level of local players are still a long way from that standard.
On a positive note, earlier on Saturday the Junior Kumuls scored a historic first win over the Australian Schoolboys, 18-10.
If Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters hasn't settled on his squad for this month's Rugby League World Cup, several players put their hands up.

For former NRL and current London Broncos coach Jason Demetriou, who will guide the PNG Kumuls at the World Cup, there was not a lot to love.
Sylvester Namo should be there, while uncapped centre Stanford Talita and fullback Sanny Wabo were dangerous at times and could find their way into Demetriou's squad.
In the women's game, Australia was also successful, dishing out a 66-6 thumping of their hosts.
PNG might have scored for the first time in three years, but Australia was a class above, crossing for 12 tries to one to rack up the biggest winning margin in the fixture's history.
While the standard of PNG's second-tier players has improved alongside the growth of the national women's competition, the Santos Cup, so too has that of the Australians.
Several showed they would not be out of place if called up to coach Jess Skinner's Jillaroos for this month's 2026 Rugby League World Cup.
Jada Taylor scored three tries and was almost impossible to handle at times, showing her versatility by playing on the wing, despite playing her club football at fullback.
Half Kasey Reh, centre Tahlia O'Brien, hooker Taneka Todhunter and back-rower Tayla Preston were others who impressed in what was effectively an audition in front of Skinner for a grander stage.
PNG Orchids coach Craig Sandercock, who this year guided Wests Tigers to their first NRLW finals series, would also have enjoyed the opportunity to see the next generation of PNG players.
There was no doubt they were outclassed, and they struggled for time with the ball, having just 37 per cent possession.
However, they had an 85 per cent completion rate and tried hard in defence, before tiring late in each half.

Tour companies are exploiting premature hype over an unconfirmed Noah’s Ark location in the foothills of Mount Ağrı in eastern Türkiye, marketing luxury expedition packages that reach $3,600 despite the lack of solid scientific proof from recent surveys.
Professor Cenker Atila , from Sivas Cumhuriyet University Faculty of Letters Archaeology Department, led the Noah’s Ark Research Project, bringing 20 scientists from five countries to the boat-shaped structure between Telçeker and Üzengili villages in Doğubayazıt district. Teams modeled the terrain with drones, scanned the subsurface with radar and extracted 1,000 soil samples for laboratory analysis while conducting core drilling.
Project Vice President Andrew Jones said the most significant finding is the structure is not a monolithic rock block. The core machine continuously extracted soil samples despite large boulders. “Some people claimed this was a natural formation, a monolithic rock taking the shape of a ship through erosion over millions of years,” he said.
Jones said current data does not point to a definitive conclusion, emphasizing that researchers are using scientific methods. Tests will determine if organic, pitch-black soil found deep underground is rotted wood or evidence of human activity. “This could be a natural formation or a man-made structure,” he said.
Atila recently addressed social media claims asserting the ark’s existence was 100 percent proven. “Although we have not reached a 100 percent result yet, we obtained astonishing data,” he said. The findings will be published in scientific articles shortly.
Despite lacking conclusive evidence, global agencies offer 12-day tours covering the formation and alleged Biblical sites, including İshak Paşa Palace, Van Castle and its museum, Urfa and Göbeklitepe, though many locations lack biblical connections. The tour website presents a university letterhead document authored by Atila as an authorization letter, asserting that the study is conducted in partnership with the firm and supported by Turkish institutions.
The Durupınar formation, discovered in 1959 by Turkish mapmaker İlhan Durupınar, has long drawn international attention due to its striking resemblance to a massive vessel. While geologists maintain the structure is a natural limestone formation created by landslides, creationist groups continuously fund expeditions hoping to find biblical artifacts on the mountain.

Relocated olive trees yield fruit in Antalya 10 years later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:06:30 UTC
17:06:30 KST

Two monumental olive trees rescued from a road project in the western province of Manisa a decade ago are producing record yields in the southern province of Antalya, proving the long-term viability of botanical preservation efforts.
The trees, aged 1,200 and 800 years, were uprooted from an expropriated area in Manisa’s Zeytinliova town in the Akhisar district on Feb. 22, 2016. Crews used special extraction methods before transporting them by truck.
Antalya Commodity Exchange President Ali Çandır spearheaded the initiative to move the trees to Zeytinpark, an urban green space housing 12,000 olive trees. The site contains varieties including Tavşan Yüreği, Memecik, Manzanilla and Ayvalık.
Under the careful oversight of agricultural engineers, the relocated trees eventually took root in the Mediterranean soil. What began as a modest first harvest grew into an abundant output, turning the grove into a key highlight for guests.
“Their root systems are fully settled. We keep them alive with special care,” Çandır said, noting the 1,200-year-old tree will produce 80 to 90 kilograms of olives this year. “The tree took hold, and we are harvesting more fruit now,” he said.
Antalya expects to harvest 70,000 tons of olives overall this season. Zeytinpark anticipates generating 7 tons of olive oil and 3 tons of table olives from its groves, where workers meticulously collect the crop for sale.
Olive cultivation plays a critical role in climate change adaptation, efficient agricultural water use and sustainable production, Çandır said. The exchange leads ongoing projects to increase the number of olive trees across the province.
Türkiye ranks among the top global producers of olive oil, with the Aegean and Mediterranean regions serving as primary cultivation hubs. Authorities relocate ancient trees threatened by infrastructure to preserve the botanical heritage.

China launches anti-dumping probe into EU p-Nitrotoluene imports
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:04:46 CST
17:04:46 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China has launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports of p-Nitrotoluene from the European Union (EU), the Ministry of Commerce said Saturday.
According to the ministry's statement, it received a formal application on Sept. 14, 2026, from two domestic producers representing China's p-Nitrotoluene industry, requesting an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU.
In response to a media query, a ministry spokesperson said preliminary evidence submitted by the applicants showed that the volume of p-Nitrotoluene imports from the EU remained at a high level from 2022 to 2025, with prices falling by nearly 60 percent cumulatively over the period. The dumped imports from the EU caused damage to the production and operations of China's domestic industry, the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson pointed out that the application met the requirements for initiating an anti-dumping investigation under Chinese law and World Trade Organization rules, adding that China will conduct the investigation in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, fully protect the rights of all interested parties, and render an objective and impartial ruling.
Noting that China has consistently taken a prudent and restrained approach to trade remedy measures, the spokesperson said the EU has launched 28 trade remedy investigations against China since 2025, about half of them involving chemical products, including three recent consecutive investigations into Chinese chemical products such as polyvinyl chloride.
China has repeatedly called on the EU to face up to its own economic and trade issues and address each other's concerns through dialogue and consultation, the spokesperson said.
According to the statement, the investigation began on Saturday and is expected to conclude before Oct. 3, 2027. It may be extended by six months under special circumstances.
P-Nitrotoluene, also known as 4-Nitrotoluene, is mainly used to produce chemicals that are widely applied in dyes, pigments, pesticides, and pharmaceuticals, according to the ministry. ■

Latvia holds parliamentary election amid multi-party contest
China

Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics prepares to cast his ballot at a polling station in Riga, Latvia, Oct. 3, 2026. Voting in the Latvian parliamentary election began on Saturday morning, with 1,428 candidates vying for 100 seats in the 15th Saeima, Latvia's parliament. (Photo by Edijs Palens/Xinhua)
RIGA, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Voting in the Latvian parliamentary election began on Saturday morning, with 1,428 candidates vying for 100 seats in the 15th Saeima, Latvia's parliament.
Polling stations across Latvia opened at 8 a.m. local time (0500 GMT), and voting will continue until 8 p.m. A total of 14 political parties and party coalitions participated in the election. According to the Central Election Commission of Latvia, a total of 933 polling stations were set up across the country and 88 overseas for this election.
The main political forces participating in this election include the current government's ruling coalition, namely the United List, the New Unity, the National Alliance, as well as the Union of Greens and Farmers. In addition, political parties and alliances such as The Progressives, the Latvia First, the For Stability!, the Harmony Centre, and the New Conservative Party are also competing.
Under Latvia's electoral system, 100 seats in the parliament are produced through proportional representation. Besides, each political party or political alliance must obtain at least 5 percent of the vote to enter the parliament.
According to the country's constitution, after the new parliament is formed, the president will hold consultations with the political forces entering the parliament and invite the candidate for prime minister to form a new government. The new government must be approved by a vote of confidence in the parliament before it can assume its duties. ■

====================================================================================================

UK urged to act as Polymarket takes bets on whether HSBC and Lloyds will fail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:00:53 UTC
17:00:53 KST

UK authorities are being urged to intervene after it emerged that the online prediction market Polymarket has been taking thousands of dollars worth of bets over whether HSBC and Lloyds will fail.
Polymarket – the US-owned company which holds bets on anything from football matches, to the existence of aliens, to when a bomb drops on a city – has allowed users to take $77,507 (£58,530) worth of positions on whether the world’s biggest banks will go under by the end of this year.
That includes lenders ranging from JP Morgan to BNP Paribas, as well as two of the largest on UK high streets: HSBC and Lloyds Banking Group.
While residents from UK, US, Canada and EU are banned from betting on Polymarket’s offshore platform, it leaves punters from across roughly 150 countries in a position to monetarily benefit from events that would create huge financial instability and threaten the health of entire economies.
In a sign that authorities are taking the issue seriously, the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) told the Guardian it had been speaking to international regulators about prediction markets, as part of efforts to protect “market integrity”.
There are growing concerns over insider trading and market manipulation on Polymarket by bad actors hoping to win big on online bets.
That raises the stakes for the banking industry, which has already been told to prepare for the risk of social media-fuelled bank runs, where customers withdraw cash at speed. Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse collapsed in 2023 after big stock sell-offs and bank runs, both of which were accelerated by a frenzy of speculation on platforms such as X and WhatsApp.
The Treasury committee member and Liberal Democrat MP Bobby Dean said UK authorities should intervene. “Polymarket has a poor reputation for stopping insider trading or bad actors placing bets on their platform, so it’s easy to see how it could be exploited to try to aggravate real shifts in market sentiment,” he said.
“If the bank-related activity grows on the platform and then a particular market was to escalate rapidly, it could even trigger bank runs,” Dean added.
“I would urge our regulators to get in contact with their counterparts in the US to raise concerns. We should not turn a blind eye to the risks because they are relatively small today, we’ve all seen how quickly things can move in this sector.”
Polymarket bosses said they did not see a problem with the bets themselves, arguing they were democratising markets that were previously restricted to elite traders and institutions.
The company’s chief legal officer, Neal Kumar, said: “The information in these markets is already public. Banks, hedge funds and credit professionals have had access to credit default swap markets for years. You shouldn’t need to work at an institution like that to have access to information on a topic of this importance like bank failures.
“Polymarket simplifies the question, providing a much larger audience with information, and markets serve as a powerful source of information and combating disinformation.”
However, academics have warned these platforms are creating a serious moral hazard, giving market participants “an incentive to engage in corrupt, illegal, or dangerous actions in order to rig the outcome of the contract”.
Meanwhile, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) used its twice-yearly risk report last month to warn that “a growing number of incidents illustrates that prediction markets are rife with inside trading”.
“Market manipulation and insider trading risks reach new levels in the context of prediction markets, particularly on DLT-based [distributed ledger technology] platforms such as Polymarket, which operate with limited identity verification and where the platform itself may not know who is behind a given wager.”
Polymarket’s offshore platform is built on a blockchain. Accounts are linked to crypto wallets that can be publicly traced but are difficult to link back to an individual.
While Polymarket is headquartered in the US, its markets are international and its users are anonymous. Some users from restricted countries can find workarounds via virtual private networks (VPNs), despite this violating Polymarket’s terms of use.
ESMA’s report pointed to cases such as the US-Israel strike on Iran in February, when several newly created wallets reportedly generated $1.2m profits shortly before the military operation became public. That followed the US capture of Venezuela’s leader, Nicolás Maduro, in January, where a US soldier was criminally charged for allegedly using classified information to place profitable bets on Polymarket ahead of the operation.
And, in April this year, police were notified over suspected tampering of weather sensors at the Charles de Gaulle airport that were used to settle Polymarket weather contracts.
The Bank of England said its supervisors engage regularly with companies on a wide range of market developments and emerging risks. Lloyds and HSBC declined to comment.
The Treasury did not respond to requests for comment.

Ethiopia's Tigray rebels abandon regional capital Mekelle as government forces enter city
Ethiopian federal forces have entered the capital of the northern Tigray region and seized its airport, witnesses said Saturday, reversing a takeover by rebels from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) that prompted the suspension of commercial flights last month. The TPLF has been fighting against pro-government forces since September 23, raising fears of an all-out civil war similar to that of 2020-2022.
Ethiopian federal forces entered the Tigray state capital on Saturday, a humanitarian source told AFP, after residents reported that the region's rebels had abandoned the city.
Fighting erupted on September 23 in northern Ethiopia as the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched attacks into neighbouring states, raising fears of a return to the devastating 2020-2022 civil war.
But federal forces and pro-government militias have pushed them back in recent days and were heading north towards the regional capital, Mekelle.

The TPLF has long been the dominant force in Tigray, ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year.

Their insurgent campaign ultimately led to the TPLF retaking the city in mid-2021.
"We operate under a strategy to strike the enemy wherever we choose," Debretsion said.
Neighbourhood tensions
The conflict has triggered a breakdown in Ethiopia's relations with Eritrea and Egypt, which Ethiopia accuses of supporting the rebels.

Counter-offensive
The rebels initially made advances in neighbouring Afar and Amhara states, working alongside local militias.
But they were pushed back this week, and the government launched a counter-offensive into Tigrayan territory along three axes towards Mekelle, according to the Critical Threats Project, part of the American Enterprise Institute think tank.

But social media accounts are difficult to verify, media access is heavily restricted and there have been significant communications blackouts.

The TPLF ruled all of Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, when it was marginalised with the rise of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who hails from the Oromia region.
The tensions led to a civil war from 2020 to 2022 – one of the deadliest in the world in recent times – that left more than 600,000 dead, according to the African Union.
The Pretoria peace agreement of 2022, brokered by African institutions and Washington, maintained an uneasy calm until last year, but was never fully implemented.

Taiwan high-end probe card industry sees new growth opportunities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:57:19 UTC
16:57:19 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s high-end probe card industry is seeing growing opportunities as rapid advances in AI chips increase the complexity of wafer testing, CTEE reported Friday.
As advanced packaging stacks multiple semiconductor chips, known as dies, into a single package, a defect in any one of them can render an expensive AI chip unusable if it is not detected before packaging. This has increased the importance of probe cards in the semiconductor supply chain, according to Business Next.
Taiwan has developed a comprehensive probe card supply chain, spanning materials and manufacturing equipment upstream to complete probe card systems downstream. Major suppliers Mpi Corp., Chunghwa Precision Test Tech Co., and WinWay Technology Co. have been expanding their high-end testing businesses in recent years.
Mpi, which holds the largest global market share in both cantilever and vertical probe cards, is operating at full capacity as AI and high-performance computing applications drive stronger orders. Industry sources said its orders are booked through 2027, with further capacity expansions expected next year.
Probe cards accounted for 72.2% of Mpi’s total revenue in 2025, when it posted consolidated revenue of NT$13.38 billion (US$420.5 million). The company has also developed probe cards with finer pitches, more pins, and higher-speed capabilities to test advanced chips, ranging from driver and logic chips to those used in silicon photonics, according to Pocket Securities.
Chunghwa Precision is expanding its testing business for AI processors, including graphics processing units and application-specific chips, or ASICs. Its customers include MediaTek, Qualcomm, AMD, Nvidia, and Apple.
The company said its production capacity had doubled from the end of last year to August and is expected to increase another 50% from its August level by the first half of 2027. For ASIC testing, Chunghwa Precision has been in talks with major cloud service providers, with some products already entering mass production, according to Pocket Securities.
WinWay has recorded rapid growth in its AI-related business this year, driven by higher shipments of high-end sockets and advanced probe cards used to test AI chips. Test sockets remain its main source of revenue, while probe cards account for a smaller share of its product mix but are expanding steadily, according to Pocket Securities.
Probe cards are used during wafer testing, which takes place after front-end processing is completed but before chips are packaged. They make contact with individual dies on a wafer to identify defective chips before packaging.
This helps manufacturers avoid wasting packaging costs on faulty chips while providing test data that can be fed back into the manufacturing process to improve yields. The probes repeatedly make contact with wafers during testing and gradually wear or deform, typically lasting about one million contacts before they need to be calibrated or replaced.
According to Mordor Intelligence, the global probe card market was valued at about NT$65.2 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach NT$119 billion by 2029, representing a compound annual growth rate of 10.6%. Asia-Pacific is currently the largest and fastest-growing regional market, the report said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The National Science and Technology Council said Saturday it achieved a historic breakthrough by concluding a Science, Innovation and Technology Arrangement with the UK.
The agreement covers cooperation in satellite communications, silicon photonics exchanges, and internships in Taiwan for semiconductor researchers from the UK, the council said in a statement. Taiwan envoy to the UK Vincent Yao and UK representative in Taipei Ruth Bradley-Jones signed the arrangement in London Friday.
The groundwork for the agreement originated with talks between Council Minister Wu Cheng-wen (吳誠文) and UK Minister for Space, Cyber and Regulatory Reform Baroness Lloyd of Effra in London earlier this year. After Friday’s signing, both sides discussed the first wave of cooperation projects under the new agreement, the council said.
The UK Space Agency proposed joint research and development in advanced satellite communications technology with the Taiwan Space Agency. Separately, the UK will provide seed funding for a Silicon Photonics Academic Alliance, a platform for talent exchanges and cooperation between industry and academics. An initiative to have UK master’s students in semiconductor studies undertake internships in Taiwan will continue.
The arrangement opens a new win-win chapter in technology cooperation between Taiwan and the UK, according to the council.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — More than 600,000 people in Taiwan received publicly funded flu vaccines in the first two days of this year’s campaign, as influenza activity remains high.
The country’s publicly funded flu and COVID-19 vaccination programs are being rolled out in two stages this year. The first stage began Thursday, covering 11 groups, including people aged 65 and older, medical personnel, preschool children, and other high-risk individuals, according to the Ministry of Health and Welfare.
A total of 601,000 people had received flu vaccines as of Friday, while 209,000 had received COVID-19 vaccines. Flu vaccinations reached 335,000 on Thursday alone, setting a record for the highest single-day total since Taiwan introduced the two-stage vaccination program in 2021.
The government purchased more than 7.05 million doses of publicly funded flu vaccines for the year, along with 2.4 million COVID-19 vaccine doses. The second stage will begin Nov. 2, when adults aged 50-64 who do not have high-risk chronic conditions will be eligible for both vaccines.
The high vaccination rate comes as influenza activity enters its peak period. The number of outpatient and emergency visits for flu-like illnesses remained above the epidemic threshold last week, reaching 138,654, the Centers for Disease Control said.
The center expects flu activity to remain elevated through mid-October before gradually declining. Weekly visits could reach between 150,000 and 160,000.
Since the current flu season began, Taiwan has recorded 1,673 severe cases and 334 deaths. People aged 65 and older accounted for 65.9% of severe cases, while 83.4% of patients had chronic illnesses. In addition, 67.7% had not received this season’s flu vaccine, according to Ettoday Health.

16:53:00 KST

Bulgaria Plans Central Registry to Track Food Prices
The government is developing a central electronic registry for food prices to give regulators real-time data for monitoring prices and detecting unfair commercial practices, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said in response to a question from GERB-SDS MP Aleksandar Ivanov about food prices and the “Basket Care” initiative.
Radev said work on the registry was actively progressing, although the process was complicated. He noted that Bulgaria had not previously had such a system, while similar registries operate in several European countries.
The prime minister said the registry would form part of a broader monitoring framework that would also include legislative changes and the working methodologies of the Commission for Consumer Protection (CPCo) and the Commission for Protection of Competition (CPC).
"Once we have the laws and the toolkit in place, and once we have this registry, which is quite complex, these regulators will possess the actual data, mechanisms, and information needed to determine whether unfair commercial practices or unjustified price hikes are occurring," Radev said.
While the registry is being developed, the government has held talks with major supermarket chains that have made voluntary commitments, Radev said. He described the approach as an attempt to balance the principles of a free-market economy with the need to oversee potential violations throughout the pricing chain.
"This 'Care Basket' approach needs to be supplemented by these more substantial measures, and we will begin implementing them," the prime minister said.
Radev also cited food price data covering the year, saying prices rose from January through April before food price deflation began in May.
"We have seen the onset of food price deflation since May: minus 0.5 percent, minus 2 percent in June, minus 1 point in July, minus 0.2 percent in August, and a 0.5 percent increase in September. So yes, food prices are trending upwards again," Radev said.
He said talks with major supermarket chains had produced results but were “not enough.” Radev also said price discussions had to take into account all factors affecting costs, including fuel and transportation expenses.
Ivanov argued that the “Basket of Care” initiative was failing to produce the desired effect, pointing to inflation figures and saying households continued to experience the impact of rising prices.
"Is it enough? More can be done, and we will try and continue in this direction," Radev said.

To reclaim its sovereignty, Senegal must approach debt differently
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:51:04 UTC
16:51:04 KST

To reclaim its sovereignty, Senegal must approach debt differently
The country must break the cycle of flawed structural adjustment that only feeds its debt crisis.
Earlier this month, the International Monetary Fund and Senegal announced a new loan programme worth $2.2bn. This came after a previous deal was suspended following the discovery in July 2024 of concealed debt equivalent to approximately 25 percent of the country’s GDP, which brought public debt to over 130 percent of GDP, one of the highest ratios in Africa.
This is what might be called a democratic betrayal of debt: The Senegalese people, who had been assured that their country was a model of macroeconomic stability, were presented with a bill that had been accumulating in secret for years.
The discovery caused outrage and much public debate about how Senegal has been managing its debt. The idea of economic independence gained momentum and helped the governing Pastef party secure 80 percent of seats in the parliamentary elections in November that year.
Today, almost two years later, the sovereignty agenda that animated the Senegalese voters is in jeopardy, not through formal renunciation, but through a gradual shift of framework, vocabulary and objective. The government is treating the international financial institutions as the only viable recourse for managing foreign debt instead of seeking a less painful alternative approach.
The criticism
Senegal has been one of the IMF’s most continuous programme countries. It has repeatedly sought its assistance since 1979.
The structural adjustment introduced by the fund and the World Bank produced stagnation, rising poverty and no economic transformation. It systematically dismantled the institutional infrastructure through which economic change could have been achieved.
In 2004, the country was approved for debt relief under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries Initiative (HIPC) and got $488m of its debt cancelled, but had to accept adjustment conditionalities, including privatisation of state companies and deregulation, which impacted access to essential services, decent employment, small businesses, and the poor. The relief was real; the structural transformation it was supposed to enable remained elusive.
The question today is who failed whom first. Recalculations put Senegal’s real public debt at the end of 2023 at 99 percent of GDP, compared to the 74 percent initially reported. A divergence of 25 percentage points of GDP, maintained over several consecutive years, is not an accidental omission. The IMF attributed the error to the Senegalese government
This was, at minimum, a systemic failure in the exercise of a conventional responsibility. The institution’s aim, on this reading, is not the development of debtor countries, but their maintenance in a disciplined poverty.
The continental record confirms Senegal is no exception. African countries in IMF programmes have struggled with debt management. Zambia started borrowing from the IMF in the 1980s. The conditions the fund imposed – trade liberalisation, public spending cuts and privatisation – caused its economy to shrink.
Zambia was then forced to seek HIPC relief as well. It was approved but implementation was repeatedly delayed over the painful adjustment policies requested.
Ethiopia also faced delays of several years after it requested debt treatment in February 2021 under the G20 Common Framework. It was not until March 2025 that terms were agreed with creditors – more than a year after it defaulted on debt. Meanwhile, austerity measures imposed as part of a $3.4bn agreement with the IMF led to rising poverty and inequality.
The solutions
The position advanced here is not a wholesale rejection of external financing, but a call for a different sequence: debt treatment rather than restructuring; audit and accountability before new conditionality; fiscal space for productive investment rather than catch-up taxation; ownership and control over natural resources, rather than ceding them to foreign powers; sustaining social protection rather than curtailing essential services; and the grounding of any borrowing negotiation in a regional and continental balance of power rather than in a structurally unequal bilateral exchange.
Concretely, the Senegalese parliament, jointly with civil society, must without delay create the institutional conditions for a citizens’ debt audit, structured around three democratic minimums: was the debt legal, was it legitimate, did it serve the people?
This should lead to an independent examination of all debt contracted between 2019 and 2024, including the responsibility of arrangers, creditors and the IMF’s own surveillance failure, as a prerequisite for any new debt conditionality, alongside a suspension clause on the service of disputed debt for the duration of the audit.
On fiscal policy, the country needs a differentiated approach. When seeking to expand its tax-to-GDP ratio, it should not raise taxes across the board and cut social spending. Instead, it should focus on taxing extractive industries and wealthy individuals.
A minimum share of state investment in infrastructure, agro-industrial transformation and energy should be protected. The terms of derivative instruments linked to domestic debt, notably the Total Return Swaps, should be capped and made public.
When seeking debt restructuring under the G20 Common Framework, it should aim for a binding timetable and a less asymmetric arbitration mechanism. Any new conditionality accepted should carry a reversibility clause, triggered by pre-defined thresholds, in the event of a major economic shock, to avoid self-defeating austerity.
Hydrocarbon revenue should have its own safeguards, resting on four pillars: a transparent stabilisation fund that accumulates revenue surpluses during boom periods; a dedicated investment envelope for productive and social sectors, including energy transition, agricultural transformation, education, health, water, sanitation and digital infrastructure; an active liability management strategy prioritising the reduction of the costliest components of the external debt; and robust citizen participation and parliamentary oversight over hydrocarbon revenue allocation.
Finally, Senegal should enshrine in national legislation the requirement of prior parliamentary authorisation and full disclosure of any public borrowing.
A South-South coalition
Senegal cannot do all of this alone. It needs to build a South-South coalition with other African countries struggling with debt to collectively weigh on debt restructuring terms. This is precisely the argument Burkinabe President Thomas Sankara made to the Organisation of African Unity in July 1987: creditors coordinate, borrowers should too.
The Borrowers’ Platform, established in April, is the first institutional answer to that call. It must fulfil three functions: close the information and capacity asymmetry between creditors and debtors; develop common positions on conditionality provisions incompatible with developmental sovereignty; and give collective expression to the principle affirmed in UN General Assembly Resolution 1803 of 1962, that peoples retain inalienable authority over their natural wealth.
In coordination with the African Union, Senegal can help set up a framework enabling African governments to demand a binding 20-to-30-year moratorium on debt service, resting on four provisions: the immediate suspension of all payments without accumulation of arrears; the mandatory allocation of freed resources to sovereign development expenditures, according to priorities set by national parliaments rather than creditors; a multilateral legal framework under UN auspices, shielding the mechanism from the regressive conditionalities of the Paris Club and the IMF; and a mid-term review clause based on human development indicators.
Senegal should also champion a regional mutualisation of liquidity risk on sovereign issues within the West Africa Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU). The country should also set up a strategic and sovereign process to establish its own currency in collaboration with other countries that currently use the West African CFA franc. The government needs to understand that borrowing in foreign currencies is skyrocketing its debt payments.
In all of these efforts, Senegal’s parliament should play a key role. As the institution which was given a broad mandate in the 2024 elections, it needs to lead the way on establishing a new approach to foreign debt anchored in transparency, legality and sovereignty.
The alternative – accepting the restructuring on current terms and deferring the sovereignty agenda to a later phase – would not be pragmatism. It would be replication of a model that has failed Africa for 40 years.
The Senegalese people deserve better than a better-managed version of structural adjustment. They voted for a rupture. Parliament must hold to that mandate.

Türkiye revises phone loan and credit card rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:50:26 UTC
16:50:26 KST

Türkiye’s banking regulator has revised loan terms for mobile phone purchases and doubled the credit limit threshold used to determine minimum credit card payments.
Consumer loans for phones costing up to 40,000 Turkish Liras can run for a maximum of 12 months, while loans for more expensive devices are limited to three months, the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BDDK) announced on Oct. 2.
For refurbished phones purchased from refurbishment centers or authorized sellers, the price ceiling for 12-month loans is 50,000 liras. Loans for devices above that price are capped at three months.
Credit card installments remain prohibited for phones other than refurbished models. Refurbished phones can be purchased in up to 12 monthly installments, regardless of price.
The regulator also raised the card limit threshold used to calculate minimum payments from 50,000 to 100,000 liras.
For cards with limits of up to 100,000 liras, the minimum payment is set at 20 percent of the monthly statement balance. The rate is 40 percent for cards with higher limits.

Drones Strike Russian Tsymbulovo Jet-UAV Base in Oryol

16:49:00 KST

Ukrainian strike drones targeted the Tsymbulovo droneport in Russia’s western Oryol region early Saturday morning, Oct. 3, sparking multiple fires across facilities used to prepare, store, and launch high-speed jet-powered strike drones against Ukraine, according to open-source monitoring groups and satellite thermal data.
Fires were detected by NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) beginning around 1:33 a.m. local time across the perimeter of the military facility near the village of Tsymbulovo, monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The thermal signatures clustered directly across operational sectors identified as primary storage hangars, pre-flight preparation workshops, and launching pads.
The Tsymbulovo installation functions as one of the Russian armed forces’ largest dedicated unmanned aviation hubs, constructed and modified to field next-generation turbojet loitering munitions.
According to an investigation by The Telegraph in August, the droneport accommodated 16 specialized launch ramps, more than 100 strike drones prepped for immediate deployment toward Ukrainian airspace, and independent solar power arrays ensuring uninterrupted operations during electrical grid disruptions.
Satellite imagery analyzed earlier this year indicated that Moscow established the complex primarily to facilitate launches of jet-powered Geran-4 and heavier Geran-5 drones alongside older, piston-driven Geran-2 and Geran-3 platforms, with dedicated launching pads configured for rapid salvo firing.
Stubb: Every Russian Threat Should Bring More Support for Ukraine
Rapid expansion
The strike follows weeks of expansion at the Oryol base. Satellite reconnaissance documented continuous construction throughout September, including eight reinforced domed shelters, new paved launch pads, and 14 newly erected hangars flanking access roads, according to Ukrainian military monitoring group Strategic Aviation.
Russian engineers had also begun converting several surface-level storage shelters into hardened underground bunkers to shield munitions from preemptive Ukrainian strikes, while erecting tall utility towers to mount anti-drone netting arrays and communications repeaters.
The rapid build-out in Oryol directly influenced the composition of Russian aerial barrages targeting the Ukrainian capital.
Military monitoring data showed that by late September, the share of advanced Geran-5 turbojet drones among unmanned systems fired at Kyiv had surged to roughly 75 percent, up from just 10 percent a month earlier.
The operational shift prompted Russian forces to disperse munitions into hardened facilities, reducing the number of drones left exposed on open aprons from nearly 100 down to approximately 10.

News
Surva tradition comes to life on the walls of a six-story building in Pernik
Saturday 3 October 2026 10:05
Saturday, 3 October 2026, 10:05
PHOTO finegraffart.com
Font size
Masks, horns and heavy bells — a new mural inspired by the kukeri tradition and the International Festival of Masquerade Games Surva in Pernik transforms the façade of a six-story building into a kind of stage for one of Bulgaria’s most recognizable folk traditions.
The impressive “GHOSTBUSTERS” project covers two walls measuring 18 by 15 meters in total. It was created by the visual artists of Fine Graff Art Studio, whose mission is to promote contemporary art in Bulgaria by making it part of the urban environment and a place for encounters with important cultural themes and local stories.
PHOTO finegraffart.com
In their latest work, the title also carries a symbolic meaning, making a direct reference to the kukeri as ones who drive away evil. They are central figures in the ancient winter ritual of “Surva”, in which masks, bells, and ritual actions have a symbolic protective function. This tradition also forms the basis of the International Festival of Masquerade Games Surva which every January brings together masquerade groups from Bulgaria and abroad.
PHOTO finegraffart.com
The first composition conveys the raw and imposing presence of the kukeri figure. The second features this ancient guardian alongside the face of a young person from Pernik, who not only observes the tradition but takes part in it and embraces it as part of his identity.
The artwork, now part of the everyday urban environment, was created in less than two weeks. It can now be freely viewed and photographed in the center of Pernik.

New KAAN prototype nears first flight
Unknown

07:47:48 UTC
16:47:48 KST

Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAŞ) aims to fly a new prototype of its KAAN fighter jet before year-end, General Manager Mehmet Demiroğlu has said.
Speaking to Anadolu at the Teknofest aerospace and technology festival in Şanlıurfa, Demiroğlu said the P1 prototype had completed system checks and low-speed taxi tests. High-speed taxi trials will follow further ground testing before its first flight.
He said P1 could fly in October or November if testing proceeds without setbacks, while work on the P2 prototype continues.
An earlier aircraft, designated P0, made KAAN’s first flight in 2024.
Demiroğlu also outlined progress on TUSAŞ’s trainer aircraft and production plans.
Series production of the Hürjet jet trainer has begun, with deliveries scheduled to start for the Turkish Air Force in late 2027 and Spain in late 2028. Two prototypes have logged more than 600 flight hours, while a third made its first flight in September.
TUSAŞ signed a contract in September to supply Azerbaijan with 14 Hürkuş-II turboprop trainers. Demiroğlu said deliveries would draw on aircraft being produced for the Turkish Air Force to meet Azerbaijan’s request for faster supply.
He said the company expected further export agreements for both training and light-attack versions of the Hürkuş.
To meet delivery schedules and control costs, TUSAŞ plans to outsource about 70 percent of production while retaining final assembly. Domestic subcontractors will take on more work on components including wings, tails and fuselages, Demiroğlu said.
Flight qualification tests are also underway for two Hava SOJ electronic warfare aircraft. TUSAŞ aims to deliver both in 2027, with testing being carried out alongside Aselsan and the Defense Industries Presidency.
