Arab media outlets reported Saturday morning that the IDF attempted to kill Ali al-Amoudi, considered one of Hamas’ most senior officials in the Gaza Strip and widely seen as the Gaza “successor” to Yahya Sinwar, the architect of the October 7 massacre who was killed during the war. Al-Amoudi does not formally hold the title of Hamas leader in Gaza but is running for the position in the group’s internal elections.
Palestinians reported earlier Saturday morning that five people, including four women, were killed when the Israeli Air Force struck a building in western Gaza City before dawn. According to the reports, rescue crews evacuated the dead and additional wounded people to hospitals and continued searching for more casualties trapped beneath the rubble.
If the reports are accurate, the strike would mark a continuation of the IDF’s campaign targeting senior Hamas officials in recent weeks. The most recent senior figure killed was Hamas’ commander in northern Gaza, Izz al-Din Bik, who was killed in a strike on an apartment in Gaza City on Tuesday. On Wednesday of the previous week, Mohammed Abu Alwan, the head of Hamas’ finance department, was also killed. During the war, he managed to transfer more than 1 billion shekels to finance the terrorist organization’s activities in Gaza. A week and a half earlier, Hamas’ Rafah Brigade commander, Nael Abu Obeid, was killed in a drone strike.
Al-Amoudi is a member of Hamas’ political bureau and a former prisoner who headed the organization’s information and media department before the war. Over the past year, he has become one of the central figures managing Hamas affairs in the Gaza Strip. He is now running against Nizar Awadallah for the leadership of the movement’s political bureau in Gaza.
Al-Amoudi was born in the Gaza Strip and lives in Khan Younis. He was arrested by Israel in 2004 and sentenced to life imprisonment. He was released in 2011 as part of the Gilad Shalit prisoner exchange, along with Yahya Sinwar and more than 1,000 other terrorists. His ties to Sinwar are considered one of the defining features of his activity within the terrorist organization. The two met during their years in Israeli prisons and remained close after their release. During Sinwar’s first term as head of Hamas’ political bureau in Gaza, from 2017 to 2021, al-Amoudi served as the director of his office.
In 2021, al-Amoudi was elected to Hamas’ political bureau and was appointed that same year to head the movement’s information department. In that role, he was involved in shaping Hamas’ communications and messaging strategy and coordinating between the organization’s political leadership and its operational apparatuses.
Following Sinwar’s killing in October 2024 and the deaths of a series of other senior Hamas leaders in Gaza during the war, al-Amoudi’s standing grew. According to reports, he assumed responsibility for managing the affairs of Hamas’ political bureau in Gaza and became a central figure in running the organization on the ground. During this period, his name was linked to a series of organizational changes and appointments within Hamas’ Gaza apparatus. Some of those moves reportedly sparked disagreements among senior members of the organization, with questions also raised within Hamas over how he had acquired his authority.
Al-Amoudi is now competing with Nizar Awadallah for Hamas’ top position in the Gaza Strip. The first round produced no decisive result and the final round was suspended after Awadallah filed an appeal over aspects of the process.
According to sources cited by Al Arabiya and Al Hadath, Khaled Mashaal and Zaher Jabarin support Awadallah, while al-Amoudi has the backing of Khalil al-Hayya, head of Hamas’ political bureau. However, Asharq Al-Awsat reported that it was not known with certainty whether al-Hayya supports either candidate.
Despite his longstanding ties to Sinwar and his involvement in managing Hamas in Gaza, al-Amoudi is not identified as a commander of Hamas’ military wing. He is a senior political and organizational official whose influence has grown significantly following the killing of much of the organization’s senior leadership during the war.

Leonardo tests land version of its 40mm naval gun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:46:09 UTC
16:46:09 KST

- The first photo of Leonardo's Hystrix 40 ADS shows the land-based counter-drone gun, built on the Marlin 40 naval turret, undergoing testing.
- Leonardo unveiled the system in February and said a prototype was expected before the end of 2026.
The first photo of Leonardo’s Hystrix 40 ADS, a land-based counter-drone gun built around the Italian company’s Marlin 40 naval turret, has appeared online, showing the system during testing.
The image was posted on X by the account A-129 Mangusta, which said it was sent by a follower and showed the system recently undergoing tests.
The turret is the Marlin 40 in its Independent Line of Sight configuration, a mount originally designed for warships. The post did not say where or when the photo was taken, and Leonardo has not commented on it.
Leonardo unveiled the Hystrix family on Feb. 2 as part of Michelangelo Dome, its integrated air defense architecture linking sensors, command systems and weapons. At the time, the company showed the Hystrix 40 ADS only in renderings and said a prototype was expected before the end of 2026. The photo suggests that prototype is now in testing.
Hystrix takes Leonardo’s naval guns and moves them onto land to shoot down drones, loitering munitions and other low-flying threats. The family is planned in three calibers: the Hystrix 76 ADS, based on the 76/62 naval gun, as the long-range layer; the Hystrix 40 ADS as the mid layer; and the Hystrix 30 ADS, based on the Lionfish 30 turret. Leonardo has said the guns are meant to complement air defense missiles, offering sustained fire at lower cost per shot.
The Marlin 40 fires standard 40 mm L70 ammunition, the same family of rounds used by Bofors-type guns, including shells with programmable fuzes. On ships, it can fire single shots or bursts at 100 or 300 rounds per minute, carries up to 80 ready rounds, and has an effective range of about 4.5 km (2.8 miles). The turret turns a full 360 degrees and elevates from minus 20 to plus 85 degrees, so it can track targets almost directly overhead. The mount is in service with about 30 navies.
In the Independent Line of Sight version, the gun carries its own electro-optical director with a daylight camera, infrared camera and laser rangefinder. The director can rotate separately from the barrel, letting the system search for, track and engage targets on its own without an external radar. For the land version, Leonardo plans programmable airburst and proximity-fuzed rounds that detonate near small drones.
Leonardo is also working with MBDA Italy on adding the Fulgur very short-range air defense missile, still in development, to extend the Hystrix 40 ADS’s reach, EDR Magazine reported in February. Of the three calibers, the 40 mm version is the one most likely to fit on wheeled or tracked vehicles without major changes, according to the magazine.
The concept has an export track record. Leonardo has already sold trailer-mounted Marlin 40 ILOS turrets to an unnamed country in the Far East for its air force’s air defense, with local industry assembling them, and is bidding for a similar order from the same country’s army.

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and his Saudi and Pakistani counterparts met in New York on Sept. 24 to review preparations for the alliance’s institutions to begin work. They condemned attacks on Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed its right to defend itself under the U.N. Charter.
The three countries’ military chiefs met in Riyadh the following day.

existing elements, custom furniture, and reused pieces renovate the space through a light-touch approach.
Wood and Glass Rework Kolonaki Apartment into Workspace
Greek practice Local Local converts a ground-floor apartment in Athens’ Kolonaki neighborhood into its first permanent studio, using light-touch interventions that retain the apartment’s existing architectural character.
The leased space required non-structural changes, so the practice repaired and lightened the original wooden floors, painted the walls white, restored the rippled-glass doors in a darker tone, and retained the arched entrance. The L-shaped plan is organized around a main workspace and a meeting room, which occupies a former bedroom.
Furniture combines existing pieces with custom designs. A solid-cypress table by architect Sofia Xanthakou’s cousin became the starting point for a large co-working table and two window-facing workstations, combining solid wood with Formica. Existing office chairs remain alongside the new pieces.
Books, Lighting, and Marble Define Local Local’s Workspace
Books form another central element of the studio. A Vitsoe shelving system displays Xanthakou’s library, accumulated through her architecture studies and work in Boston and London. Michael Anastassiades ceiling lights illuminate the workspace, while a custom perforated metal frame spanning one wall serves as a pistachio-colored pinboard for collaborative work away from screens.
At the entrance, two site-specific marble sculptures by artist Theodore Psychoyos form a console and seating area. The meeting room retains its original wardrobe, with its doors removed and replaced by roll-up blinds to create open storage for material samples and paperwork. A freestanding Michael Anastassiades light completes the room.
Studio Local Local uses existing architectural elements, reused furniture, custom pieces, and restrained material interventions to create a workplace shaped by the character of the original apartment.

Russia has intensified strikes on military-related logistics and defense industrial base in recent weeks in response to Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s 40-day PR ‘pressure campaign’, which included long-range strikes targeting oil refineries and civilian infrastructure deep inside Russia.

Estonian men have lived shorter lives than women for 150 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:45:00 UTC
16:45:00 KST

Estonian men have lived shorter lives than women for 150 years
The difference between the life expectancy of Estonian men and women has been studied and described since the 1970s. A new study by an Estonian population researcher now shows that men's lives here have, for various reasons, been markedly shorter than women's for a century and a half.
"We have solid evidence that part of the gender gap in life expectancy is biological. Men are more vulnerable to certain diseases than women, and some gap is inevitable. But when this gap is three times larger here than in Sweden, questions arise," says Tallinn University and Estonian Demography Centre researcher Mark Gortfelder.
The social organization of the two countries and men's life choices must differ significantly for such a gap to exist.
In his recent study, Gortfelder analyzed the reasons for the life‑expectancy gap between men and women in Estonia both in the near and distant past. To do so, he examined nationwide sex‑ and age‑specific distributions from the late 19th century to today. For the mid‑19th century, he had to generalize based on local data, such as from Mulgimaa, Tartu, and the Governorate of Estonia. "The innovative part of my article was that I added as much of the older period as possible," the researcher notes.
Land scarcity, poverty, and tuberculosis
For the past 150 years, Estonian men's life expectancy has been shorter than women's. In the mid and late 19th century, the gap was roughly ten percent; in the interwar period, it was already two percentage points larger. It widened dramatically after World War II, reaching 20 percent in 1948. "After that, it fell slightly until the 1960s, then began rising again, and in the last 10–20 years it has fallen once more," Gortfelder says.
Behind the percentage are both personal choices — such as individual behavior — and societal factors that shaped men's and women's living conditions. For example, the gap was widest in recent history in 1995, when it reached 17 percent. "This shows that in that year, men's health behavior — and more broadly, their situation in society — was worse. Their expected life span was nearly one‑fifth shorter," the researcher explains.
In his study, he tried to identify across eras the reasons and circumstances that shaped Estonia's life‑expectancy gap. For example, Gortfelder sees excessive alcohol consumption as one possible factor in the 19th century, though this remains only an assumption because no data on alcohol use from that time exist.
However, land hunger was a real factor in the 19th century. It affected men especially, who in traditional society were responsible for providing for the household. "Land scarcity meant that a very large share of the population had no land at all. It was very difficult for them to fulfill their role, and this caused frustration. Perhaps they therefore tended more toward alcoholism," he suggests.
Between the two world wars, Estonia carried out a land reform. Although it alleviated land hunger, the farms created were, according to Gortfelder, far below what agronomists considered a self‑sufficient economic unit. "Land reform helped solve some social problems, but it was not a complete cure. Feelings of deprivation and poor living conditions persisted," he says. This may explain why the gender gap remained relatively large in interwar Estonia.
Poor living conditions also contributed to the spread of tuberculosis at the turn of the 20th century. In industrialized Western countries, the disease affected women more than men. "In Estonia we see the opposite — we had an agrarian society, and through that tuberculosis had a greater negative impact on men," Gortfelder notes.
Path dependence in recent history
There are no good data on Estonia's population during World War II. However, Gortfelder was able to include data from the difficult postwar period. "We had a large number of people who were suspicious to the occupying authorities and were fought against. Many people, especially men of military age, hid out of fear," he says.
Data show that in 1948 the gender gap in life expectancy was nearly 19 percent. Compared with Sweden, it was more than twice as large. Moreover, the data reflect only the legal population — forest brothers hiding from Soviet authorities were not counted. "We can assume that their living conditions in the forest were not rosy. We are likely underestimating the real gap with that 19 percent, because the 'non‑legal' population is not included," the researcher argues.
Especially after Stalin's death, when the atmosphere became somewhat more liberal, the Soviet Union was very successful at preventing the spread of infectious diseases. By around 1960, their prevalence had fallen to nearly zero compared with historical norms.
However, socialist countries failed to keep pace with the cardiovascular revolution in the West. "From around 1965, Western countries managed to significantly reduce mortality from cardiovascular diseases through new treatments and by emphasizing individual responsibility. Estonia and the broader Eastern Bloc clearly lagged behind," Gortfelder explains. The gender gap widened in the latter half of the Soviet era partly because men are biologically more vulnerable to heart disease.
With the collapse of socialism, many heavy‑industry enterprises went bankrupt and disappeared. Again, economic change may have affected men more, as they were often the breadwinners working in factories. "Estonia stands out here from the broader post‑Soviet region, because conditions east of us were even worse," Gortfelder notes.
After the low point of the 1990s, Estonia has been very successful in reducing the gender gap in life expectancy. "We are in a somewhat better position than Latvia and Lithuania. I won't even start talking about Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine," he says. The change can be attributed partly to Estonia's healthcare system, which is accessible to almost everyone, and partly to a greater emphasis on personal responsibility for health.
"Today the gap is still around ten percent, which is quite large compared with Western Europe. Compared with Sweden, it is almost three times larger," he points out. The gap is difficult to close because it is tied to path dependence — cultural and behavioral norms pass from one generation to the next and change only partially. The healthcare system also does not address the gap sufficiently, Gortfelder says. "To reach Sweden's level, we need somewhat greater cultural transformation, which we have not yet seen," he says.
Mark Gortfelder publishes his research findings in the journal Historical Life Course Studies.

EU Pours €130 Million Into Border Surveillance Drones
The European Commission is adding €130 million ($146 million) to an EU scheme that helps member states buy drones and counter-drone systems, as part of a broader push to strengthen border oversight.
The announcement brings total European Union investments in border surveillance tech past €500 million ($563 million), as reported by Euronews.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The funding allocation was introduced during a meeting of justice and home affairs ministers in Luxembourg, marking their first face-to-face talks on border management and migration since the crisis in Ceuta earlier this summer.
EU Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner emphasized that deploying emerging technologies like drones is vital for both securing external boundaries and safeguarding critical infrastructure.
Back in February, the Commission rolled out an action plan addressing drone-related security and counter-drone mechanisms, offering national governments €250 million ($281 million) in funding for monitoring land and sea borders, according to Euronews.
That initiative covers up to 90% of costs for projects including drone purchases, anti-drone installations, system integration into national networks, and tools designed to mitigate hybrid threats.
Brussels separately directed €170 million ($191 million) to the EU border agency Frontex and national agencies through the Border Management and Visa Instrument to buy unmanned monitoring gear.
At the same time, Greece suggested temporary suspensions on the right to apply for asylum during emergencies caused by mass irregular migrant arrivals. The proposal holds backing from member states including Poland, Germany, Austria, and Denmark.
Brussels is also expected to widen the scope of Frontex, particularly in handling crisis responses and monitoring digital hybrid threats, with a mandate review planned for later this year. European leaders will further address migration policy and border governance during the European Council summit set for October 15–16, Euronews reported.
Germany had recently partnered with Kyiv to tap into Ukrainian expertise on Russian hybrid warfare.
Under a new security agreement, Ukrainian specialists will share operational experience in counter-drone defense, counterespionage, and cybercrime, with German police set to train at specialized counter-drone facilities inside Ukraine.

After Chandrayaan-3, ICMR asks scientists to attempt the ‘impossible’ in healthcare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:40:59 UTC
16:40:59 KST

Rs 8 crore on offer for health innovations that have never been tried anywhere in the world (Representativ e imaeg
NEW DELHI: After Chandrayaan-3 made India the first country to successfully land near the Moon’s south polar region, the government is now asking scientists to attempt something equally audacious in healthcare: develop something the world has never tried before.The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has launched its “First in the World Challenge”, inviting researchers to develop breakthrough vaccines, drugs, therapeutics, diagnostics and other health technologies that have never been thought of, tested or tried anywhere in the world.The initiative will offer up to Rs 8 crore for a single project, depending on how advanced the proposed innovation is. ICMR describes it as a high-risk, high-reward programme, acknowledging that some projects may fail but saying successful ones could bring about a major change in healthcare.The grants will be released in stages: up to Rs 1 crore for proof-of-concept, Rs 4 crore for prototypes and Rs 8 crore for final products or implementation models. Funding will be linked to deliverables, with ICMR reviewing each stage before approving the next.The opportunity is open beyond ICMR scientists. Researchers from government medical colleges, Institutes of National Importance, universities, recognised research laboratories and eligible NGOs can apply.
Indian startups, micro, small and medium enterprises and industry are also eligible.The scheme targets genuinely new health technologies, not incremental improvements. ICMR will first check whether a proposal is truly “first in the world”, followed by assessment of its relevance and potential impact by a panel of experts, innovators, policymakers and scientists.
The programme aims to take innovations from the lab to deployment, requiring researchers to detail regulatory, validation, commercialisation and technology-transfer plans, as well as demonstrate the technology’s clinical need, advantages over existing options and readiness for deployment.Applications will open on October 7 and close on November 30, with results due on December 31. Each proposal must include at least one co-principal investigator from the principal investigator’s institution. ICMR says the initiative is willing to back high-risk ideas with uncertain outcomes but potentially transformative gains, in pursuit of breakthroughs no one has achieved before.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. TEHRAN – Iran said on Oct 3 that it had executed a man convicted of a raft of charges, including firing a military-grade weapon at police officers during anti-government protests earlier in 2026.
Siavash Jamshidi was accused of targeting security personnel during mass demonstrations that peaked in January, in which thousands of people were killed.
Since that time, the Iranian authorities have stepped up executions of convicts linked to the unrest.
“Jamshidi was sentenced to death on charges of moharebeh through brandishing and firing a firearm, as well as conspiracy and collusion against national security,” Iran’s judiciary said, using the legal term moharebeh to mean “waging war against God”.
The judiciary’s Mizan Online website said he was also found guilty of offences not related to the protests, including “fraud, making threats, theft, possession and carrying of an illegal military-grade weapon”.
Other charges included “complicity in kidnapping, brandishing a weapon to intimidate and intentional infliction of bodily harm”.
Mizan said Jamshidi was “active” during the demonstrations, which were sparked in December 2025 by grievances over living costs in Iran, but peaked on Jan 8 and 9 with huge rallies.
The Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths in the unrest, attributing the violence to “terrorist acts” orchestrated by the United States and Israel.
Foreign-based non-governmental organisations, however, maintain that Iranian security forces fired on protesters.
US President Donald Trump threatened at the time to intervene militarily in Iran. Weeks later, in late February, the US and Israel launched a joint attack on the Islamic republic, triggering the Middle East war.
Since then, arrests and executions have multiplied in Iran, linked both to the war and the protests.
In 2025, Iran executed at least 1,639 people, the largest number in any year since 1989, according to the NGOs Iran Human Rights and Together Against the Death Penalty.
Amnesty International says Iran carries out more executions than any country except China. AFP

Nearly half of India’s medical colleges fail to comply with NMC disability-unit directive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:37:34 UTC
16:37:34 KST

NEW DELHI: Nearly half of India’s medical colleges (44.5%) have failed to set up Enabling Units mandated by the National Medical Commission for students with benchmark disabilities. Of 798 colleges, 355 remain non-compliant, with several naming sanitation inspectors, residents, tutors and head clerks as single points of contact, according to an affidavit filed by the Commission in the Supreme Court on Tuesday.At Maharashtra Government Medical College, Nandurbar, a sanitation inspector, has been designated as the coordinator of the Enabling Unit. Other colleges have named residents, tutors and head clerks as points of contact.Dr Satendra Singh, disability-rights activist and doctor associated with Doctors with Disabilities: Agents of Change, questioned the choice of personnel for the role. “It’s unheard of for a sanitation inspector or head clerk to be made in-charge of such a committee in a medical college. They have neither the designated administrative or academic responsibility for undergraduate or postgraduate training nor the training or authority to deal with disability accommodation, clinical training, patient safety or assessment.
”He added, “They cannot take or escalate decisions on postings, duty hours, assistive devices, accessible infrastructure, examination accommodations or clinical-rotation modifications. Tutors and residents are also a floating population, often at an institution for only a limited period. How would a postgraduate student in pharmacology, who may not even be an alumnus of that institution, know what assistance a wheelchair-using medical student needs in an operation theatre or have the authority to direct the theatre staff?”The NMC circular does not prescribe a doctor or clinical faculty member as the single point of contact. It does, however, assign the Enabling Unit responsibility for reasonable accommodation, academic and clinical support, barrier-free access, coordination, record-keeping and information dissemination.The compliance exercise was undertaken following the Supreme Court’s August 4, 2026 order in Anmol vs Union of India, which directed the NMC to seek college-wise compliance with its July 27 circular through Deans and Principals.
The court warned that if colleges failed to respond or follow the directions, “a serious view will be taken against the individual colleges.”The NMC’s affidavit said 515 of 798 colleges had responded by September 28: 443 reported full compliance, 26 partial or ongoing compliance, and 46 submitted only the committee-constitution order. As many as 283 colleges did not respond. Majority of NMC-designated medical assessment boards and appellate boards themselves fail to comply, despite NMC warning that “serious view” would be takenThe commission had set September 10 as the deadline and issued reminders on September 23 and 24, the latter warning that late submissions would not be accepted and show-cause notices would follow. Colleges were required to provide details of the unit, its members and POC, functionality, accessibility, communication to students, records and compliance status.

Microwave drone killer joins U.S. Army’s Jailbreak drill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:37:13 UTC
16:37:13 KST

- Epirus said it connected its Leonidas high-power microwave weapon to a wider command network during the U.S. Army's Operation Jailbreak Falcon Fury.
- The company will show Leonidas GV, a mobile version built with General Dynamics Land Systems, at the AUSA meeting on Oct. 12-14.
Epirus has plugged its Leonidas high-power microwave drone killer into a wider U.S. Army command-and-control network during Operation Jailbreak Falcon Fury, an Army effort to make counter-drone sensors, weapons and software from different makers work together.
The California company said on X that it joined the event to show how Leonidas can link sensors and its microwave weapon into a broader command network, so operators can pick the right weapon for each drone threat. Epirus did not say when or where the demonstration took place, which command system Leonidas was connected to, or how many drones it engaged.
Epirus also said it will bring a new mobile version, Leonidas GV, built with General Dynamics Land Systems, to the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 12-14. The company described it as mobile high-power microwave defense that can hit many drones at once. It did not release specifications.
Operation Jailbreak is the U.S. Army’s push to open up its own systems so new and old equipment can share data, instead of running on closed, single-vendor software. More than 50 companies took part in its first sprint at Fort Carson, Colorado, this spring, with counter-drone and air defense as the first focus, DefenseScoop reported. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has framed the effort as a way to plug in the tens of thousands of drone interceptors the service rushed to the field during Operation Epic Fury against Iran.
Leonidas works differently from guns, missiles or lasers. It fires bursts of microwave energy that overload the electronics inside drones, knocking out navigation, communications or motors. Because the beam covers an area, one shot can disable several drones flying close together, which is why the U.S. Army sees it as a last line of defense against swarms.
The U.S. Army has been testing Leonidas for more than three years. In January 2023, the Rapid Capabilities and Critical Technologies Office awarded Epirus a $66.1 million deal for four prototypes under the Indirect Fire Protection Capability-High-Power Microwave program, known as IFPC-HPM. Epirus delivered all four by March 2024. Testing showed the weapon worked, but the U.S. Army found it needed better integration with the rest of the air defense kill chain, and in October 2024 it paid Epirus nearly $17 million for an upgraded sensor suite and closed-loop fire control.
In July 2025, the U.S. Army ordered two second-generation systems for $43.5 million. A month later, Epirus said Leonidas disabled all 61 drones flown across five scenarios at a demonstration at Camp Atterbury, Indiana, including a 49-drone swarm taken down with a single burst.
Epirus and General Dynamics Land Systems have worked together since 2021. The pair first put Leonidas on a Stryker armored vehicle, then on General Dynamics’ TRX tracked robot in October 2025. In March, they unveiled the Leonidas Autonomous Ground Vehicle, a self-driving Ford F-600 truck built with Kodiak AI.

The eviction of an 87-year-old woman has turned anger over rents that have nearly doubled in ten years into a threat to Pedro Sánchez's minority government.
Demonstrators are set to march in more than 50 Spanish cities on Saturday, a day after parliament voted down two government decrees meant to give tenants stronger protection.
The Tenants' Union, which has been coordinating the protests, called the demonstrations. "There is an irreparable disconnect between what the people want and what the parties vote for," it said in a statement.
In Madrid, marchers are due to leave from several points around the city at noon and converge on Plaza de Cibeles in the centre. Activists have already been camped for about a week in Puerta del Sol, one of the capital's main tourist squares.
The anger was triggered by the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who was carried out on a stretcher from the Madrid flat where she had lived for around seven decades. Housing campaigners say an investment company had bought the property and sought to raise her rent by 275 percent. After the backlash, the new owners agreed to let her return at a low rent.
Calls for a general election
The government drew up its measures in response to the nationwide protests that followed. The package rejected on Friday would have renewed rental contracts automatically when they expired and restricted evictions of vulnerable tenants. It also took aim at so-called vulture funds, investment firms that buy properties cheaply in pursuit of higher returns.
The decrees needed the votes of the Catalan separatist party Junts, which opposed them on the grounds that they lacked rigour.
The defeat is a further setback for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. It has revived doubts over whether his minority government can last until the next scheduled general election in 2027.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the conservative Popular Party (PP), the main opposition, urged Sánchez after the vote to "call elections as soon as possible". After eight years in power, he said, the prime minister had the backing of "neither the streets nor parliament". Recent opinion polls have generally put the PP ahead of the Socialists.
Housing has been a leading concern for Spaniards for years, with supply falling short of demand and costs soaring, as they have elsewhere in the European Union. Average rents have almost doubled over the past decade and asking prices for homes are up about 90 percent, according to the real estate website Idealista.

Fires on the grounds of the Russian Tsymbulova drone launch site in the Oryol region were detected by NASA’s FIRMS satellites on the night of October 3.
This was reported by the Telegram channel 𝔽𝕒𝕝𝕔𝕠𝕟 𝕚𝕟𝕤𝕚𝕘𝕙𝕥 ᵐᵃᵖ.
Most likely, this is the result of strikes by the Ukrainian Defense Forces, as Russian monitoring channels reported drone activity in the area that night.
Preliminary reports indicate that several fire outbreaks were detected near a site used for the storage, preparation, and launch of Russian drones.
The Tsymbulova drone port is a large Russian military complex near the village of the same name, used to launch drones—including the Geran-4 and Geran-5—into Ukrainian territory.
The distance from the facility to the Ukrainian border is approximately 175–180 km.
Russia continues to actively expand and fortify the Tsymbulova drone port. Satellite imagery as of September 29 shows a new area with eight dome-shaped shelters for jet drones and an additional launch pad southeast of the launch sites. Nearby, paved areas have been prepared for the installation of eight more shelters and two launch systems.
The Russians have fully completed six hangars for strike UAVs, construction of which began in early September. Along the access road to the drone port, construction of 14 more new hangars has been observed.
Ground-based shelters for equipment were converted into underground facilities, which significantly increased their protection against direct hits from Ukrainian UAVs. Near the launch sites for the Geran-5, areas were prepared for six additional launchers, and towers are being erected to support anti-drone nets and communications.
In addition, the Russians are preparing to expand the drone port further—in the northeastern part of the facility, construction equipment is preparing a site for new warehouses.
Despite the construction, the Ukrainian Defense Forces regularly strike this facility. Ukrainian drones hit, in particular, bunkers and hangars. Some of them penetrated the shelters, causing explosions and damage to the structures, and debris from destroyed UAVs was found at the launch preparation site.

U.S. Navy Triton spy drone gets stuck at runway’s end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:32:38 UTC
16:32:38 KST

- A photo released by open-source account TheIntelFrog shows a U.S. Navy MQ-4C Triton stuck at the end of Runway 5 at Naval Station Mayport.
- The U.S. Navy has not said when the incident happened, what caused it, or how badly the unmanned aircraft was damaged.
A U.S. Navy MQ-4C Triton surveillance drone ended up stuck at the end of a runway beside the St. Johns River at Naval Station Mayport, Florida, a photo released by open-source account TheIntelFrog shows.
The image, posted on X, shows the large unmanned aircraft off the end of Runway 5, the strip that runs toward the river near where it meets the Atlantic Ocean. The account joked that the drone “got stuck trying to take a drink” from the river.
The U.S. Navy had not publicly commented on the incident. It is not clear when it happened, whether the drone was landing or taking off, what caused it to leave the runway, or how badly it was damaged. Because the Triton flies without a crew aboard, no one was in the aircraft.
The MQ-4C Triton is a high-altitude, long-endurance drone built by Northrop Grumman for maritime surveillance. It is a naval version of the U.S. Air Force’s RQ-4 Global Hawk, strengthened and fitted with de-icing and lightning protection so it can drop down through clouds to get a closer look at ships. The Triton carries maritime radar, electro-optical and infrared cameras, and electronic sensors, and it works alongside the Navy’s P-8A Poseidon patrol aircraft.
Naval Station Mayport, at the mouth of the St. Johns River near Jacksonville, is the East Coast home of the Triton fleet. The U.S. Navy chose the base in 2017 as the operating site for the aircraft and their maintenance crews, while the pilots and sensor operators fly the missions remotely from nearby Naval Air Station Jacksonville. The first Triton arrived at Mayport in December 2021 after a deployment to Guam.
The drones belong to Unmanned Patrol Squadron 19, known as “Big Red,” the Navy’s first all-unmanned aviation squadron. The squadron also flies Tritons from forward bases, including Guam and Naval Air Station Sigonella in Italy.
Mayport-based Tritons have been busy closer to home. In January, a Triton flew a nine-hour surveillance mission over the Caribbean north of Venezuela after taking off from Mayport, The Defence Blog reported, based on public flight-tracking data.
This is not the first mishap for the squadron. In 2020, VUP-19 temporarily stood down operations to investigate a Triton crash-landing, USNI News reported.

Spain's Sánchez faces snap election speculation after key parliament defeat
Unknown

Spain's housing crisis is worsening, with local media reporting Saturday morning that amid widespread protests, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez could call an early election in about two months rather than next summer. On Friday, parliament in Madrid rejected a package of emergency measures introduced by the government that it said were intended to help residents cope with soaring housing costs.
The parliamentary debate lasted about five hours as protesters gathered outside demanding assistance for renters. The government's proposal was defeated after the Catalan separatist party Junts — whose support Sánchez needed after the 2023 election to form a minority government — followed through on an earlier announcement that it would oppose the two decrees put to a vote.
The defeat fueled speculation that Sánchez could dissolve parliament, though he has yet to address the possibility. In a speech to lawmakers, he said the measures proposed by his government were essential: "Behind these decrees is the desire to bring order and a sense of humanity to a market that, if we do not rein it in, will destroy our society. Do the right thing, or history will judge you, sooner than you think."
Average rent in Spain has nearly doubled over the past decade. The average price per square meter rose from 8.20 euros ($9.31) in 2016 to 15.10 euros ($17.15) this year. The measures proposed by the government and rejected by parliament included a ban on evictions of "vulnerable" people, tax incentives to encourage property owners to rent out homes, measures aimed at curbing real estate speculation and provisions making rental contracts automatically renewable at the tenant's discretion.
Sánchez is currently grappling with a series of scandals and crises, including the mass arrival of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta as well as legal proceedings involving his Socialist Party and members of his family.
Oriol Bartomeus, a political science professor at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, told The Associated Press that holding an early election in about two months could also benefit the prime minister: "It is clear that the issue of housing is more favorable than corruption. But if he calls elections now, he has to wait 54 days to hold them, and in that time absolutely anything can happen."
Carla Cremonte, a 34-year-old Madrid resident who took part in the protest outside parliament on Friday, said: "I don’t know what might happen, whether elections will be called, but in the streets we will continue fighting and the atmosphere is one of a general strike."
The mass protests in Spain erupted in recent days over the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, 87, from the Madrid home where she had lived for more than 70 years after she was unable to keep up with the sharp rise in rent in recent years.
"I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs," she said in a video recorded from her hospital bed, where she has remained since the eviction.
Abascal's father first rented the apartment in 1956, and she remained there as a rent-controlled tenant after her parents died. The building changed ownership beginning in 2018, and an investment fund that acquired her apartment raised her monthly rent from 500 euros ($570) to 2,650 euros ($3,021). Although the rent was later reduced to 1,650 euros ($1,881), it still represented a 230% increase and remained beyond what Abascal could afford on her pension.
Footage of Abascal's eviction from her apartment on Wednesday sparked outrage and criticism of the authorities and real estate investment firms, which are accused of pushing residents out of their homes as prices rise.
Protesters set up camp in Madrid's central Puerta del Sol square, pitching tents and declaring that they would not leave until the government seriously addressed the housing crisis. Demonstrations were also held in other cities, with protesters demanding stronger protections for renters, measures to combat fraud and a ban on evicting tenants when no alternative housing is available.

U.S. sends unmanned systems to Guantanamo for new command
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:26:36 UTC
16:26:36 KST

- U.S. Southern Command has deployed unmanned systems to Naval Station Guantanamo Bay to support Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere missions.
- The deployment is the first step toward a training and mission-support site there for SOUTHCOM's Autonomous Warfare Command, created in April.
U.S. Southern Command has deployed unmanned systems to Naval Station Guantanamo Bay in Cuba, the first step toward a training and mission-support site there for its new Autonomous Warfare Command.
Marine Gen. Francis L. Donovan, the SOUTHCOM commander, saw the systems during a visit to the base, the command said in a post on X. The systems are supporting missions of Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere, SOUTHCOM’s operational headquarters for counter-cartel and other regional operations.
The command said the Guantanamo site will be a place where teams can train with autonomous systems and integrate them into operations, support current mission needs, and feed lessons from real operations back into training and the development of new capabilities.
Donovan directed the creation of the SOUTHCOM Autonomous Warfare Command, known as SAWC, on April 21. The command said that once fully established, SAWC will employ autonomous, semi-autonomous and unmanned platforms across all domains against threats in Latin America and the Caribbean. It describes SAWC as bringing together people, unmanned systems, data and communications to give commanders a decision and operational advantage.
SOUTHCOM said at the time that it would work with the military services and the Department of War’s Defense Autonomous Warfare Group to find the expertise and equipment the new command needs. A SOUTHCOM spokesperson told DefenseScoop the command would take a deliberate and phased approach to standing it up. SAWC is among the first organizations of its kind at a U.S. geographic combatant command.
The command has since tied SAWC to ongoing operations. In September, SOUTHCOM published images of a U.S. Marine with Combat Logistics Battalion 8 preparing to launch a HANX drone on Sept. 16, saying SAWC was leading efforts to use low-cost autonomous and unmanned systems for surveillance during operations against drug traffickers.
Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere, which the unmanned systems at Guantanamo now support, was activated on Aug. 4. It replaced Joint Task Force Southern Spear, the headquarters behind the U.S. military’s strikes on suspected drug boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. The new task force links U.S. forces with the 18 partner nations of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition.
Naval Station Guantanamo Bay sits on Cuba’s southeastern coast and is the oldest U.S. overseas military base. Its location gives U.S. forces a foothold between the Atlantic, the Caribbean and the approaches to Central and South America, where SOUTHCOM runs most of its maritime surveillance and interdiction missions.

Russian Drill Simulates Incursion and ‘Security Zone’ in Tsentr-2026 Games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:22:00 UTC
16:22:00 KST

Russian armed forces practiced transitioning from defensive operations to a counter-offensive and carving out a “security zone” inside the territory of a neighboring state during the large-scale strategic military exercise Tsentr-2026, according to official Kremlin dispatches and Russian defense ministry briefings.
The maneuvers, conducted between Sept. 28 and Oct. 3, were formally designated to practice repelling conventional aggression on the Central Asian strategic vector and ensuring military security across the Caspian Sea basin.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, operational details presented to Russian President Vladimir Putin revealed that the drills incorporated cross-border offensive actions.
Reporting to Putin on the progress of the maneuvers, Russian Deputy Defense Minister Yunus-Bek Yevkurov stated that after repelling an adversary’s opening assault, coalition forces launched a large-scale counter-offensive.
Yevkurov detailed that starting Oct. 2, troops rehearsed operations to “liberate seized territory” and establish a “security zone on adjacent territory” belonging to the opposing state.
Putin traveled in person to the Chebarkul military training ground in the Chelyabinsk region on Friday, Oct. 2, to observe the concluding phase of the exercises, stating that Russian formations were directly integrating operational tactics and doctrine developed during the full-scale war in Ukraine.
Russia Plans Record $200B Defense Budget as Healthcare, Education, Face Cuts
Central Asian vector
While Russian defense officials did not formally name the hypothetical neighboring adversary, defense analysts at Ukrainian military portal Militarnyi noted that Kazakhstan most closely matches the operational geography of the scenario.
Kazakhstan shares an extensive land border with Russia’s Chelyabinsk region where the Chebarkul training facility is situated, represents a central political entity in Central Asia, and possesses an extensive coastline along the Caspian Sea.
Analysts emphasized that while the operational design closely mirrors regional geography, the identification of Kazakhstan remains an analytical assessment rather than an officially confirmed element of Moscow’s war games.
The strategic maneuvers involved significant firepower across multiple domains. Four Russian long-range strategic bombers conducted simulated strikes against designated “critical infrastructure” of the adversary, supported by tactical aviation, artillery units, strike drones, mechanized armored columns, and surface combatants of the Caspian Flotilla.
According to Russian defense ministry figures, the Tsentr-2026 exercise mobilized more than 47,000 military personnel, over 2,000 pieces of heavy weaponry and military hardware, 90 combat and transport aircraft, and 77 naval ships and support vessels.
Operations were executed across 11 designated military ranges and the maritime zone of the Caspian Sea. Moscow additionally hosted foreign military contingents from Belarus, China, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Tajikistan.
European pre-war legislation
The offensive maneuvers in Central Asia coincide with heightened defense vigilance across NATO’s eastern flank, where frontline European governments are preparing for prospective cross-border escalation.
In Poland, the Ministry of National Defense confirmed on Friday that it is drafting comprehensive legislation to introduce a formal “pre-war” phase of defense readiness, enabling early troop deployments and institutional mobilization before martial law is legally declared.
The draft statute is designed to bridge the regulatory gap between peacetime governance and wartime mobilization, linking national operational plans directly to NATO’s Response System.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has repeatedly warned that Europe has entered a “pre-war era,” cautioning that allied intelligence dispatches indicate Moscow is evaluating hybrid drone and missile strikes against nations supporting Kyiv, which the Kremlin could portray as accidents to test the resolve of NATO’s Article 5 collective defense guarantee.
The legislative drive also follows escalatory rhetoric from senior Russian officials directed at frontline European states. Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev threatened Lithuania in September with destruction if it rescinded restrictions on nuclear weapons, asserting NATO would not risk global war to defend Vilnius.
Days later, Kremlin security aide Nikolai Patrushev threatened that Moscow could deploy its “entire arsenal” against Poland, claiming Warsaw could be destroyed within days following Polish warnings that the alliance would decisively defeat any conventional Russian attack.

Drone fragments found in Moldova after explosions
Kyiv • UNN
Explosions were heard in four districts of Moldova; drone fragments were found and fires were recorded. There were no casualties.
Explosions were heard in Moldova on the morning of October 3, and drone fragments were found. This was reported by the country's police, writes UNN.
Details
"This morning, several residents of the Căușeni, Ștefan Vodă, Anenii Noi, and Hîncești districts reported explosions outside some populated areas," the statement said.
At 7:50 a.m. local time, as reported, police were notified of an explosion outside the city of Căușeni, where thick smoke was observed. "Drone fragments were found at the scene," the statement said.
"Drone fragments were also found near the settlements of Dubovca and Hîncești," Moldova's police reported.
It was also reported that "at the same time, near the settlement of Crocmaz, in the Ștefan Vodă district, an explosion occurred in a vineyard, near an agricultural brigade. No casualties have been reported. The incident resulted in a vegetation fire, and the brigade's windows were damaged."
Moldova's police also showed drone fragments found in the Anenii Noi district, between the villages of Delacău and Puhăceni; drone fragments found near the village of Crocmaz, Ștefan Vodă district, in the area of an agricultural brigade; drone fragments found in the Hîncești district, on the outskirts of the village of Dubovca; drone fragments found in the Anenii Noi district, between the villages of Delacău and Puhăceni; and drone fragments found near the village of Constantinovca, Căușeni district, where a vegetation fire broke out after the explosion.
Police are working at the scene and documenting the incidents; the circumstances of the incidents have yet to be established. Citizens are urged to remain calm, avoid areas where explosions have been reported, and not touch or approach suspicious objects or fragments.

Russian tank shoots down attacking drones in war games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:15:10 UTC
16:15:10 KST

- A Russian T-90M used its Arena-M active protection system to shoot down FPV and fixed-wing drones in a staged column attack at Tsentr-2026.
- Ukrainian troops have reported Arena-M intercepting drones in combat, but its known configuration carries only 12 interceptor munitions.
A Russian T-90M tank used its Arena-M active protection system to shoot down attacking drones during the Tsentr-2026 strategic exercise, in a staged attack on a tank column at the Chebarkul training range in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region.
In the demonstration, several types of drones, including fixed-wing models and standard first-person-view (FPV) quadcopter drones, simulated a strike on a column of tanks. The T-90M’s onboard system detected and destroyed the incoming drones. The test took place under controlled exercise conditions, and Russia did not say how many drones were launched, how many were intercepted, or whether any got through.
Arena-M is a hard-kill system, meaning it physically destroys threats instead of jamming them. A radar on the tank watches for incoming projectiles, calculates their path and fires a small defensive munition that breaks up the threat with a spray of fragments before it hits the armor. The system was built by the KBM design bureau in Kolomna to stop anti-tank rockets and guided missiles, which fly much faster than drones. The baseline version can intercept projectiles traveling up to 1,000 meters per second.
Small drones are harder for that kind of radar to track. They move slowly, reflect little radar energy and often dive onto the tank from above, where older systems did not look. KBM has worked to close that gap. In 2025, Russia said Arena-M received a software update with a dedicated mode for intercepting drones, and in early 2026 a new variant designed to counter one-way attack drones and loitering munitions completed development.
The system has already been used in combat in Ukraine, where T-72B3A and T-90M tanks fitted with Arena-M have been seen on the front line, Meta-Defense reported. Ukrainian troops have acknowledged that it works. One Ukrainian unit reported that Arena-M on a single Russian T-72B3A tank destroyed seven FPV drones, and that it took 15 to 20 drones to knock out a tank fitted with the system along with cage armor.
That points to the system’s main weakness. Arena-M’s known configuration carries 12 interceptor munitions. Once they are used up, the tank has to rely on its armor, anti-drone cages and electronic warfare, and FPV drones are cheap enough for Ukrainian units to launch in large numbers against a single target.
Arena-M has been fitted to some T-90M, T-72B3 and T-80BVM tanks. Uralvagonzavod first showed a T-90M with the system in February 2025, and photos of production T-90Ms with Arena-M being transported on public roads appeared in July 2026. But a batch of new T-90M and T-72B3M tanks shown leaving the factory in September did not carry the system, suggesting it is not yet standard on every new tank.
Tsentr-2026 ran from Sept. 28 to Oct. 3 and involved more than 47,000 troops, according to the Russian Defense Ministry. President Vladimir Putin visited the Chebarkul range on Oct. 1.

Ethiopia government forces retake airport in Tigray's capital, sources say
Oct 3 - Ethiopia's federal military has recaptured the main airport in the capital of the northern Tigray region, three sources said on Saturday, dealing a major setback to an opposition alliance in its stronghold.
Clashes pitting a rebel alliance led by Tigray's ruling party against the government and its allied forces broke out in northern Ethiopia last week, in the most serious escalation of violence since a 2020-2022 civil war.
The fighting has stoked fears that it could escalate into a wider regional conflict, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries in the Horn of Africa and the Gulf.
In Washington, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said the United States strongly urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to "exercise maximum restraint and return to dialogue and cooperation as agreed in their 2018 peace framework."
"The Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis," Pigott said. "A conflict jeopardizes ongoing U.S. collaboration on shared interests with both countries."
The federal government in Addis Ababa severed diplomatic ties with Eritrea this week, accusing it of supporting the rebel alliance alongside Sudan and Egypt. The three countries deny this.
Troops from the Ethiopian National Defence Forces had regained control of Alula Aba Nega Airport in Tigray's capital Mekelle, one source with knowledge of events in the city and a humanitarian source told Reuters.
A third source, a Mekelle resident who asked not to be named for security reasons, confirmed the taking of the airport by government forces and added they could hear gunfire outside the city centre.
This source said they had seen some Tigrayan Defence Force fighters abandoning their posts and heading home, and that there was looting of government facilities taking place in the city.
Reuters could not immediately verify the assertions and the region's ruling party, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), could not be immediately reached for comment. A source close to the TPLF however told Reuters the city was encircled by government troops and allied militias.
Mekelle's airport, which is around 10 km (6 miles) from the centre of the city, was one of three airports in the region that were seized by the opposition forces at the start of the fighting on September 23.
The taking of Mekelle by government forces would be a major setback for the opposition alliance, although analysts say it would be unlikely to end the conflict.
In 2020, federal forces captured Mekelle within the first month of the two year war before the TPLF reclaimed it seven months later. REUTERS

Resilience key to Iran’s tourism survival under difficult conditions: HEGTA chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:13:36 UTC
16:13:36 KST

Resilience key to Iran’s tourism survival under difficult conditions: HEGTA chief
TEHRAN - Resilience and a fundamental rethink of planning are essential for Iran’s tourism sector as rising travel costs, transport and investment constraints, sanctions and regional conditions put pressure on the industry, the head of the Tourism Group of Iran’s Social Security Organization (HEGTA) said on Friday.
Alireza Tabesh said the main challenge was no longer simply increasing demand, but turning Iran’s extensive tourism resources into marketable products that create economic and social value.
He made the remarks at a ceremony marking the end of Tourism Week and the celebration of Mehregan at Tehran’s Homa Hotel, attended by tourism industry professionals, hoteliers, tour operators, guides and journalists.
“The question is why there is still such a gap between these extensive capacities and their actual share of the tourism economy,” he said, describing tourism as an interconnected chain in which destinations, transport, accommodation, services, storytelling, local communities, sales and the travel experience must work together.
Tabesh said declining household purchasing power did not mean the end of travel demand, but was changing travel patterns. Shorter, closer and more affordable trips could provide part of the sector’s response to current economic conditions, he added.
He also stressed the importance of Iran’s living cultural heritage as a tourism resource. Nowruz, Yalda and Mehregan, he said, are not merely calendar events but expressions of a living cultural memory that can be transformed into meaningful travel experiences.
“Mehregan, with its links to nature, the harvest season, family, community, music, food and collective rituals, can become more than a cultural occasion; it can become a travel experience,” he said.
He then called for locally rooted tourism products that connect cultural traditions with accommodation, transport, food, handicrafts, heritage, nature and local businesses, while protecting cultural authenticity and ensuring that local communities share in the economic benefits.
Tabesh said HEGTA could connect its capacities in hotel management, transport and organized travel to develop marketable tourism products. He also urged greater cooperation among government bodies, municipalities, private companies, cultural institutions and transport operators.
Technology, data and artificial intelligence, he added, should move beyond slogans and be used to understand markets, improve decision-making and design products suited to travelers’ needs.
“Hope in tourism emerges when we recognize realities, prepare for different scenarios and use existing capacities to create value and social vitality,” Tabesh said.

Asian Games | Wong secures first tennis gold for Hong Kong, China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
15:11:57 CST
16:11:57 KST

Wong Coleman of Hong Kong, China hits a return during the Men's Singles Gold Medal Match of Tennis between Wu Yibing of China and Wong Coleman of Hong Kong, China at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Zeguo)
NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Coleman Wong won the first Asian Games tennis gold medal for Hong Kong, China after defeating China's Wu Yibing 6-2, 6-4 in the men's singles final at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Saturday.
The victory also secured Wong a qualification berth for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games, while Wu claimed his second silver medal at the Asian Games after Jakarta 2018.
Wong took early control of the match, breaking Wu's serve in the fifth and seventh games to win the opening set 6-2. The second set remained deadlocked at 4-4 before Wong broke in the ninth game and then served out the match.
"Winning an Asian Games gold medal was my dream, and although I didn't achieve it today, it's alright. I gave it my absolute all and lost to a deeply respectable opponent," Wu said after the match. "A loss is a loss, no excuses. I hope I'll have the chance to compete in the next Asian Games."
The two players have played tight matches in recent years. At the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023, Wu squandered five match points in a final-set tiebreak before falling to Wong in a two-hour, 48-minute round-of-16 thriller. Wu won their duel at China's 15th National Games in 2025, completing a comeback victory in the semifinals after two hours and 47 minutes.
Reflecting on his rivalry with Wong, Wu noted that their first encounter at the Hangzhou Asian Games left a lasting impression.
"Although he is younger than me, he is a very mature athlete and has made tremendous progress over the past few years. Every match against him gets harder. He executed better than I did today. I'm really glad players from Hong Kong and the Chinese mainland can share the stage in an Asian Games final. Chinese tennis, as a whole, is moving forward step by step," said the 26-year-old Wu.
Wong also reflected fondly on their rivalry. "I still remember that National Games match. It was a match we both deeply enjoyed. I'm thrilled we met in the final this time rather than the semifinals, and that we could enjoy competing on Asia's biggest stage. I hope we'll have many more exciting battles ahead," he said. ■

High school students in Paris’ deprived suburbs spark national protest movement

High school students in Paris’ deprived suburbs spark national protest movement
- High school students in poor Paris suburbs protest against dilapidated schools, overcrowded classrooms, and teacher shortages, highlighting severe inequalities in education resources.
- Protests spread nationwide with over 1,200 schools involved; police used tear gas and rubber bullets, leading to injuries and arrests amid government budget cuts.
- Experts link unrest to long-term underfunding, government cuts of 3,256 teacher positions, and rising demands on schools, making inequality reduction difficult.
AI generated
AUBERVILLIERS, France – Maisa, a 17-year-old in a poor Paris suburb who aspires to be an English teacher, joined tens of thousands of other students and their supporters this week in protests that spread across France over dilapidated schools, classroom overcrowding and teacher shortages.
At Lycee Le Corbusier school in Aubervilliers, a suburb north of Paris in the Seine-Saint-Denis department, protesters said schools in poor neighbourhoods like theirs faced the worst conditions.
“Last year I took the high school French exam without a French teacher, and teachers have a huge impact,” Maisa said. “These are not conditions to study in.”
As protests raged at more than 1,200 French high schools this week, police responded with tear gas and rubber bullets in some cases. More than 5,000 people were arrested, and some protesters were seriously hurt with eye injuries, broken teeth and blows to the head. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called it a “climate of unacceptable violence” and called for order.
Amelia, 15, joined Maisa in the crowd outside the school gates and held a sign reading: “Our address should not decide our future.” She said she was demonstrating to demand the same rights as students elsewhere in the country.
“The education authority is not investing enough in the suburbs. It’s classist and racist,” she said.
Ulysse Rabate, a political scientist at Paris 8 University, said the protests show the way that France’s marginalised urban neighbourhoods are increasingly influencing national politics.
“When there is a collapse of the public service, of public education, those who feel it the most, and the most violently, are those at the bottom,” he said.
Political flashpoint
The nationwide demonstrations and blockades, which began last week, have become a political flashpoint at a sensitive moment for the government, which announced a series of deeply unpopular spending cuts in its 2027 budget on Oct 1.
The education budget is set to increase by a below-inflation 1.7% to €65.53 billion (S$94.34 billion), excluding teacher pensions.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that education remained a priority and the below-inflation budget increase was due to population decline.
The Education Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The protests started in the Parisian suburbs, where poverty levels are high, then spread to Paris itself and other French towns, including Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours and Lille.
At Lycee Le Corbusier, classes including maths, humanities, English and sport have been cancelled since the start of the academic year due to a teacher shortage, according to Karima Kara Ali, an elected parent representative.
In Seine-Saint-Denis, two-thirds of high schools took part in protests on Oct 1, the CGT labour union said. Youth, teachers and parents in four towns complained of unsanitary school conditions and chronic staff shortages, including of nurses and social workers.
Louise Paternoster, a representative for the Seine-Saint-Denis branch of the CGT’s education union, said the area does not get adequate resources for its student population and their educational needs. Two-thirds of schools in the department have unfilled teacher positions, according to a union survey.
Not enough teachers
“Our students are losing out on study time. Some schools don’t have drinking water. We are not equal to other departments,” she said, blaming shortages on government cuts of 3,256 teacher positions nationwide in 2026.
In Pantin, a town on the north-eastern edge of Paris, teacher Dilan Roche joined her students as they protested outside their school this week to support their demands and protect them from the police.
“What they wrote on banners, we wrote in a letter to the local education authority: overcrowded classes, no nurses, no social workers – which is problematic for students with learning difficulties, many living in precarity,” she said.
While France ranks in the middle of Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries for spending on education, the average expenditure per secondary school student has remained little changed over the last decade, standing at €11,660 in 2024 and €11,910 in 2010, according to Education Ministry data.
The last nationwide high school protest movement on this scale demanding more funding came in the 1990s. That followed the government sharply expanding access to the baccalaureate, the school-leaving exam that typically paves the way to university, without providing schools with sufficient additional resources, said Clemence Cardon-Quint, a professor at Paul Valery University who researches education funding.
The movement won an increase in funding, but spending per student later stagnated despite growing demands on schools.
Cardon-Quint said students and teachers have taken on additional responsibilities over the years, including navigating Parcoursup, the university admissions system introduced in 2018 and criticised by some students and teachers as opaque and discriminatory.
“In a period of budgetary restraint, it is more difficult to reduce inequalities,” said Cardon-Quint. REUTERS

Russia shows Shturm robotic tank system in big exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:02:41 UTC
16:02:41 KST

- Russia used uncrewed T-72B3M-based tanks from its Shturm robotic assault system to support assault troops during the Tsentr-2026 exercise.
- The tanks are remotely controlled from a separate crewed vehicle on a tank chassis, with a reported control range of about 3 km.
Russia has used uncrewed tanks from its Shturm heavy robotic assault system in combat drills for the first time, sending remotely controlled T-72-based vehicles to support assault troops during its Tsentr-2026 strategic exercise.
Russian President Vladimir Putin was shown the vehicles at the Chebarkul training range in the Chelyabinsk region, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 2. The ministry said the machines are built on the T-72B3M tank chassis and have uncrewed fighting compartments, in two versions: one with a tank-type turret and one armed like a BMPT tank support vehicle. During the main stage of the drills, they provided fire support to assault units.
The Shturm system pairs remotely controlled combat vehicles with a crewed control vehicle, all built on T-72 or T-90 tank chassis. The combat vehicles can still be driven by a crew on board if needed. The most visible feature of the main version is a shortened 125 mm gun, designed so the turret can swing freely between buildings in urban fighting. It also carries a bulldozer blade, all-around armor against shoulder-fired anti-tank weapons, and launchers for rocket flamethrowers or other weapons on the turret. A version with a 152 mm gun is reported to be in development.
During the drills, operators controlled the armored group from a safe distance using joysticks, FPV headsets and tablets over a multichannel, jam-resistant link, the Rostec weapons project “Russian Weapons” told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. Russian outlet ANNA News reported that each vehicle was driven by three operators working as commander, gunner and driver, seated in the separate control vehicle.
That control setup is one of the system’s main limitations. The robotic tanks cannot operate on their own. They depend on a dedicated crewed control vehicle, essentially a second tank chassis without a turret, which has to stay close enough to keep the radio link. Earlier Russian reports put the control radius at about 3 km (1.9 miles), meaning the crew still has to work near the fight in an armored vehicle of its own.
The Defense Ministry has not published any data on how the link performs under heavy electronic warfare, the main threat to remote-controlled systems on the battlefield in Ukraine, where both sides jam drones and ground robots daily.
Uralvagonzavod began work on Shturm under a Russian Defense Ministry order around 2018. The first images of a test vehicle appeared in July 2025 at the company’s plant in Nizhny Tagil, with a crew on board. At the time, The National Interest questioned whether the remote control and autonomy features were ready.
The Tsentr-2026 exercise, which ran from Sept. 28 to Oct. 3 and involved more than 47,000 troops, also featured T-14 Armata tanks, the Zarya laser air defense system and other robotic vehicles, according to the Defense Ministry.

Flydubai co-pilot used crash axe to attack captain, says UAE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:01:17 UTC
16:01:17 KST

The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 used an axe to attempt to carry out a “terrorist attack” during the Israel-bound flight, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.
Disaster was narrowly averted on Wednesday when passengers and crew intervened to stop the co-pilot’s attempt to take control of the plane, which had 182 people onboard and plunged 16,625ft in just over 30 seconds. The descent was so extreme that part of the rudder was ripped off.
Investigators have been trying to establish how the alleged attacker, who was seen by witnesses repeatedly stabbing the pilot in the cockpit, managed to smuggle a weapon onboard.
But on Saturday, Gen Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, a UAE prosecutor, said the co-pilot had used a crash axe to mount the attack, an implement typically kept inside the cockpit to use in emergencies, such as crashes or fires, and which would not have needed to be brought onboard covertly.
“Investigations into the incident involving flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack,” Al Shamsi was quoted as saying by the state news agency WAM.
Media outlets have named the co-pilot as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national. Speaking to the Associated Press, a Gulf diplomat said investigations were under way to establish whether he acted as a “lone wolf or had any connection with any extremist groups”.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. He was then moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, according to the official, before being hired by the UAE-based budget airline flydubai.
It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired.
A British university, Buckinghamshire New University, said a student named Hamam al-Hammami had “previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management” at the institution. It added: “He did not undertake any pilot training at the university.”
A flydubai spokesperson on Saturday said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still under investigation and the airline was not in a position to comment further.
The airline’s flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv have been suspended until further notice following the attack.
A former flydubai crew member told the Wall Street Journal that all its pilots were subject to security screening before flights, as well as medical checks at least once a year.
How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is a central question for investigators. It also raises serious concerns about background checks in aviation recruitment. Israel says it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots out of its airspace who come from nations with which it does not maintain diplomatic relations. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.
Security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the US and other western governments, an official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss details of the investigation.
On Friday, Anwar Gargash, a senior adviser to the UAE president, called the attack a “dangerous terrorist act”. The incident is a test for the UAE government, which has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has also bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.
Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said on Friday that the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalisation” but provided no evidence. He added that Israel was looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone’s direction and warned that anyone involved would pay a “heavy price”.
Most of the passengers onboard were Israeli nationals.
The Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who had multiple stab wounds, has been praised for his bravery. He said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed loud noises to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilise the plane.
In a video call with the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, Machchhar said: “I was lying on the floor injured but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside.
“Others came in and also played a role [in controlling the situation]. I was of course fighting for my own life, but at the same time I knew I was not going to let others die.
After passengers restrained the attacker, two reserve pilots, who were onboard, safely landed the plane at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia at 06.58 local time. The captain and co-pilot were taken to the UAE, as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.
Netanyahu on Saturday said he wanted to invite Machchhar and Modi to light a flame at a national ceremony for Israel’s Independence Day next May, saying the role was usually reserved for Israeli citizens.
In a video his office released of his telephone conversation with the hospitalised captain, he said: “You are a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel and you are a hero of the entire world.”
